# Functional analysis {#sec-hilbert-spaces-operators}

Functional analysis studies vector spaces of functions and sequences together with a notion of size, and the linear
maps between them. It is the language of quantum mechanics, of partial differential equations and of the
renormalisation of field theories, and it supplies the Fredholm index that counts the zero modes of the Dirac
operator in the reductions of the later parts. This chapter develops the subject from normed spaces to operator
algebras, on explicit examples. Normed and Banach spaces defines norms and completeness, with the sequence spaces
$\ell^p$, the function spaces $L^p$ and $C(K)$, bounded linear maps and dual spaces. The four principles proves the
Hahn-Banach, uniform-boundedness, open-mapping and closed-graph theorems and shows by counterexamples why each
hypothesis is needed. Weak topologies and reflexivity treats weak and weak-* convergence and the Banach-Alaoglu
theorem. Inner product and Hilbert spaces, Bounded operators and Spectral theory specialise to the inner-product case,
where geometry and the spectral theorem are available. Compact and Fredholm operators proves the Fredholm alternative
and defines the index. Unbounded operators and the Laplacian, Sobolev spaces and Traces, determinants and heat kernels
treat the differential operators of physics and their spectra. Banach and C*-algebras ends with the spectrum of an
element of an algebra and the continuous functional calculus. Every statement is followed by at least three examples
of increasing complexity and at least three exercises of increasing difficulty with hidden solutions. The sequence
spaces, the Pauli matrices, the exponentials $e^{inx}$ on the circle, the spherical harmonics and the Gaussian are the
running examples.

## Normed and Banach spaces {#sec-banach-spaces}

A norm measures the size of a vector and turns a vector space into a metric space in which limits, series and
continuity make sense. This part defines norms and complete normed spaces, introduces the three families of spaces
that the rest of the chapter works in, the sequence spaces $\ell^p$, the function spaces $L^p$ and the continuous
functions $C(K)$, and then studies the linear maps between normed spaces and the dual space of continuous linear
functionals. The line of argument follows the lecture notes of @arcozzi2025 [Ch. 1 and 3], with the Hilbert-space
special cases of @picard2020primer [App. B] as examples.

### Norms and normed spaces

On $\mathbb{R}^n$ the Euclidean length is one way among many to measure a vector: the largest coordinate or the sum
of the absolute values of the coordinates serve as well. The figure draws the unit balls of several such measures
in the plane, and the definition below names the three properties that all of them share.

![Unit balls $\{x \in \mathbb{R}^2 : \|x\|_p \leq 1\}$ of the norms $\|x\|_p = (|x_1|^p + |x_2|^p)^{1/p}$ for $p =
1, \tfrac32, 2, 4$ and $\|x\|_\infty = \max(|x_1|, |x_2|)$. Each ball is convex and symmetric under $x \mapsto -x$;
the balls grow with $p$, and only the disc $p = 2$ comes from an inner product. Generated by
`figures/fa2-unit-balls.sage`.](figures/fa2-unit-balls.svg){#fig-fa2-unit-balls width=60%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-norm}
#### Norm

A **norm** on a real or complex vector space $X$ (@def-vector-space) is a map $\|\cdot\| : X \to [0, \infty)$ that
is **definite**, $\|x\| = 0$ only for $x = 0$, **homogeneous**, $\|\lambda x\| = |\lambda|\,\|x\|$ for scalars
$\lambda$, and satisfies the **triangle inequality** $\|x + y\| \leq \|x\| + \|y\|$. The pair $(X, \|\cdot\|)$ is a
**normed space**; it is a metric space with the distance $d(x, y) = \|x - y\|$, so that a sequence **converges** to
$x$ when $\|x_n - x\| \to 0$. Two norms $\|\cdot\|_a$, $\|\cdot\|_b$ on $X$ are **equivalent** if $c\|x\|_a \leq
\|x\|_b \leq C\|x\|_a$ for constants $0 < c \leq C$ and all $x$; equivalent norms have the same convergent sequences.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first examples live in $\mathbb{R}^n$, where every coordinate gives a way of measuring. The three norms below are
the ones drawn in the figure for $n = 2$, and the example compares them with explicit constants.

::: {#exm-fan-rn-norms}
#### Three norms on $\mathbb{R}^n$

$\|x\|_1 = \sum_k|x_k|$, $\|x\|_2 = (\sum_k|x_k|^2)^{1/2}$ and $\|x\|_\infty = \max_k|x_k|$ are norms on
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\mathbb{C}^n$. For $x = (3, -4)$ they give $7$, $5$ and $4$. They are equivalent: $\|x\|_\infty
\leq \|x\|_2 \leq \|x\|_1 \leq n\|x\|_\infty$, and the constants are attained, the first two by $x = (1, 0, \dots,
0)$ and the last by $x = (1, 1, \dots, 1)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

On a space of functions the same three ideas give the supremum norm and the integral norms. The second example
shows that on the continuous functions they are no longer equivalent, because a function can be large on a small
set.

::: {#exm-fan-function-norms}
#### Supremum and integral norms

On the continuous functions on $[0, 1]$, $\|f\|_\infty = \max_x|f(x)|$ and $\|f\|_1 = \int_0^1|f(x)|\,dx$ are norms
@arcozzi2025 [Sec. 1.1.1]. For $f_n(x) = x^n$ one finds $\|f_n\|_\infty = 1$ and $\|f_n\|_1 = 1/(n + 1) \to 0$, so
$f_n \to 0$ in $\|\cdot\|_1$ but not in $\|\cdot\|_\infty$, and no inequality $\|f\|_\infty \leq C\|f\|_1$ can hold.
The inequality $\|f\|_1 \leq \|f\|_\infty$ does hold, so the supremum norm is the stronger of the two.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Inner products are the source of the most important norms, and the parallelogram law tells which norms come from
one. The third example states the criterion and applies it to the norms of the figure.

::: {#exm-fan-inner-product-norm}
#### Norms from inner products

An inner product (@def-inner-product) gives the norm $\|u\| = \langle u, u\rangle^{1/2}$; the triangle inequality
follows from Cauchy-Schwarz, which @picard2020primer [Lemma B.1.5] derives from the non-negativity of the Gram
determinant $\langle u, u\rangle\langle v, v\rangle - |\langle u, v\rangle|^2$. Such a norm satisfies the
parallelogram law $\|u + v\|^2 + \|u - v\|^2 = 2\|u\|^2 + 2\|v\|^2$, and conversely a norm satisfying it comes from
an inner product @picard2020primer [Lemma B.1.7 and the remark after it]. For $u = (1, 0)$, $v = (0, 1)$ the law
reads $2\cdot 2^{2/p} = 4$ in $\|\cdot\|_p$, true only for $p = 2$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The checks that a proposed norm is one are short, but the triangle inequality is the delicate part, as the first
exercise shows by an example where it fails. The exercise also shows why the exponents $p < 1$ are excluded from the
family drawn in the figure.

::: {#exr-fan-norm-axioms}
#### When the triangle inequality fails

Show that $\|\cdot\|_1$ and $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ are norms on $\mathbb{C}^n$. Then show that $N(x) = (\sqrt{|x_1|} +
\sqrt{|x_2|})^2$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ is definite and homogeneous but violates the triangle inequality, by evaluating it
on $(1, 0)$, $(0, 1)$ and their sum.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Definiteness and homogeneity are clear, and $|x_k + y_k| \leq |x_k| + |y_k|$ summed (or maximised) over $k$ gives the
triangle inequality for $\|\cdot\|_1$ (or $\|\cdot\|_\infty$). For $N$: $N(\lambda x) = (\sqrt{|\lambda|}
(\sqrt{|x_1|} + \sqrt{|x_2|}))^2 = |\lambda|N(x)$, and $N(x) = 0$ forces $x = 0$. But $N(1, 0) = N(0, 1) = 1$ while
$N(1, 1) = 4 > 2$. The unit "ball" $\{N \leq 1\}$ is the region inside the astroid-like curve $\sqrt{|x_1|} +
\sqrt{|x_2|} = 1$, which is not convex; a norm always has a convex unit ball.

A check of the three norms with Sage, including the triangle inequality of the two genuine norms on random complex vectors:

{{< sage exr-fan-norm-axioms >}}
:::

The parallelogram law is a computable test, and the second exercise applies it numerically to the whole family
$\|\cdot\|_p$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$. Its result is that the Euclidean norm is the only member of the family with an inner
product behind it.

::: {#exr-fan-parallelogram}
#### The parallelogram law for $\|\cdot\|_p$

Compute $D(p) = \|u + v\|_p^2 + \|u - v\|_p^2 - 2\|u\|_p^2 - 2\|v\|_p^2$ for $u = (1, 0)$, $v = (0, 1)$
and for $u = (1, 1)$, $v = (1, -1)$, as a function of $p \geq 1$, and find where it vanishes. What is $D$ for
$\|\cdot\|_\infty$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For the first pair $D(p) = 2\cdot 4^{1/p} - 4$, which vanishes only at $p = 2$ and is positive for $p < 2$; for the
second pair the roles are exchanged, $D(p) = 8 - 4\cdot 4^{1/p}$, negative for $p < 2$. For $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ the
first pair gives $D = -2$. So no $\|\cdot\|_p$ with $p \neq 2$ satisfies the law, and by the converse of
@exm-fan-inner-product-norm none of them comes from an inner product.

Sage computes $D(p)$ symbolically for both pairs and finds the zeros:

A norm gives a translation-invariant, homogeneous distance, and the third exercise shows the converse, following an
exercise of @arcozzi2025. It explains why normed spaces are exactly the metric vector spaces whose metric respects
the linear structure.

::: {#exr-fan-metric-from-norm}
#### Metrics that come from norms

Let $d$ be a metric on a vector space $X$ with $d(x + a, y + a) = d(x, y)$ and $d(\lambda x, \lambda y) =
|\lambda|d(x, y)$. Show that $\|x\| = d(x, 0)$ is a norm and that $d(x, y) = \|x - y\|$ @arcozzi2025 [Exercise 1.1].
Give a translation-invariant metric on $\mathbb{R}$ that does not come from a norm.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Translation invariance gives $d(x, y) = d(x - y, 0) = \|x - y\|$. Definiteness is that of $d$; homogeneity is
$d(\lambda x, 0) = d(\lambda x, \lambda 0) = |\lambda|d(x, 0)$; and $\|x + y\| = d(x + y, 0) \leq d(x + y, y) + d(y,
0) = d(x, 0) + d(y, 0)$. The metric $d(x, y) = \min(|x - y|, 1)$ is translation invariant but not homogeneous: $d(2,
0) = 1 \neq 2d(1, 0) = 2$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In finite dimensions all norms measure convergence in the same way, which is why $\mathbb{R}^n$ has one topology. The
theorem below states this; its proof uses the compactness of the unit sphere of $\|\cdot\|_1$, and it fails in every
infinite-dimensional space, as @exm-fan-function-norms already showed on $C[0, 1]$.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-norm-equivalence}
#### Equivalence of norms in finite dimension

On a finite-dimensional vector space any two norms are equivalent. Consequently every finite-dimensional normed space
is complete, every linear subspace of finite dimension of a normed space is closed, and a set in a finite-dimensional
normed space is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded. On every infinite-dimensional normed space there
are norms that are not equivalent to the given one.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The best constants between the norms of $\mathbb{R}^n$ grow with the dimension, which is the first sign of the
infinite-dimensional failure. The first example records the constants between $\|\cdot\|_1$ and $\|\cdot\|_2$.

::: {#exm-fan-rn-constants}
#### Constants that grow with the dimension

On $\mathbb{R}^n$, $\|x\|_2 \leq \|x\|_1 \leq \sqrt n\,\|x\|_2$: the second inequality is Cauchy-Schwarz applied to
$(|x_1|, \dots, |x_n|)$ and $(1, \dots, 1)$, with equality at $x = (1, \dots, 1)$. The constant $\sqrt n$ is finite
for each $n$, as the theorem says, but unbounded in $n$; on the finitely supported sequences, the union of all the
$\mathbb{R}^n$, the two norms are therefore not equivalent.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Polynomials of a fixed degree form a finite-dimensional space of functions, so the supremum and integral norms of
@exm-fan-function-norms become equivalent on it. The second example finds how the constant depends on the degree.

::: {#exm-fan-polynomial-norms}
#### Polynomials of bounded degree

On the polynomials of degree at most $n$ on $[0, 1]$, the theorem gives $\|p\|_\infty \leq C_n\|p\|_1$. The
polynomial $p(x) = (1 - x)^n$ has $\|p\|_\infty = 1$ and $\|p\|_1 = 1/(n + 1)$, so $C_n \geq n + 1$: the norms are
equivalent in each degree, but no single constant works for all polynomials, in agreement with the failure on $C[0,
1]$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

An infinite-dimensional space has a norm inequivalent to any given one, and on the sequences the construction is
explicit. The third example gives it for the finitely supported sequences.

::: {#exm-fan-inequivalent-sequences}
#### Inequivalent norms on sequences

On the space $c_{00}$ of finitely supported sequences, $\|a\|_\infty$ and $\|a\|_w = \sum_n|a_n|$ are norms with
$\|a\|_\infty \leq \|a\|_w$, but $a^{(N)} = (1, \dots, 1, 0, \dots)$ ($N$ ones) has $\|a^{(N)}\|_w = N\|a^{(N)}\|_
\infty$. The sequence $a^{(N)}/N$ tends to $0$ in $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ and has norm $1$ in $\|\cdot\|_w$ for every $N$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise asks for the proof of the theorem. The argument is the standard one and shows exactly where
finite dimension enters, namely in the compactness of a sphere.

::: {#exr-fan-norm-equivalence-proof}
#### Proof of the equivalence theorem

Let $\|\cdot\|$ be any norm on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Show that $\|x\| \leq M\|x\|_1$ with $M = \max_k\|e_k\|$, deduce that
$\|\cdot\|$ is continuous for $\|\cdot\|_1$, and use the compactness of $\{\|x\|_1 = 1\}$ to find $m > 0$ with
$\|x\| \geq m\|x\|_1$. Conclude that any two norms on $\mathbb{R}^n$ are equivalent.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\|x\| = \|\sum_kx_ke_k\| \leq \sum_k|x_k|\,\|e_k\| \leq M\|x\|_1$, and $|\|x\| - \|y\|| \leq \|x - y\| \leq M\|x -
y\|_1$ makes $\|\cdot\|$ continuous. On the compact set $S = \{\|x\|_1 = 1\}$ (closed and bounded in $\mathbb{R}^n$)
it attains a minimum $m$, and $m > 0$ because $0 \notin S$. By homogeneity $\|x\| \geq m\|x\|_1$ for all $x$. Two
norms are each equivalent to $\|\cdot\|_1$, hence to each other.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The constants between the $p$-norms can be computed exactly, and the extremal vectors are the simplest ones. The
second exercise finds the best constants between $\|\cdot\|_p$ and $\|\cdot\|_q$.

::: {#exr-fan-p-norm-constants}
#### Best constants between $p$-norms

For $1 \leq p < q \leq \infty$ show $\|x\|_q \leq \|x\|_p \leq n^{1/p - 1/q}\|x\|_q$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, with both
constants attained. Evaluate the constant $n^{1/p - 1/q}$ for $n = 3$ with $p = 1$, $q = 2$ and with $p = 2$, $q =
\infty$, and check it on $(1, 1, 1)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $\|x\|_p = 1$ then $|x_k| \leq 1$, so $|x_k|^q \leq |x_k|^p$ and $\|x\|_q \leq 1$; homogeneity gives the first
inequality, with equality at $e_1$. The second is Hölder's inequality (@thm-holder-inequality) with exponents $q/p$
and its conjugate applied to $\sum_k|x_k|^p\cdot 1$, with equality at $(1, \dots, 1)$. For $n = 3$ both constants are
$3^{1/2}$: $\|(1, 1, 1)\|_1 = 3 = \sqrt3\cdot\sqrt3 = \sqrt3\,\|(1, 1, 1)\|_2$ and $\|(1, 1, 1)\|_2 = \sqrt3 =
\sqrt3\,\|(1, 1, 1)\|_\infty$.

Sage evaluates the constants and tests both inequalities on random vectors:

:::

Since a finite-dimensional subspace is complete, it is closed, and this fact has a quick but instructive proof. The
third exercise asks for it and for a counterexample when the dimension is infinite.

::: {#exr-fan-finite-subspace-closed}
#### Finite-dimensional subspaces are closed

Use the theorem to show that a finite-dimensional subspace $F$ of a normed space $X$ is complete, hence closed in
$X$. Then show that the polynomials are a subspace of $(C[0, 1], \|\cdot\|_\infty)$ that is not closed.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Choose a basis of $F$; the norm of $X$ restricted to $F$ is equivalent to the coordinate norm $\|\cdot\|_1$, in which
a Cauchy sequence has Cauchy coordinates, which converge in $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. So $F$ is complete, and a
complete subset of a metric space is closed. The Taylor polynomials of $e^x$ converge uniformly on $[0, 1]$ to $e^x$,
which is not a polynomial (all its derivatives are $e^x \neq 0$), so the polynomials are not closed; by
@thm-stone-weierstrass their closure is all of $C[0, 1]$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### Completeness and Banach spaces

A normed space can have Cauchy sequences without limits, just as the rationals do. The figure shows such a sequence
among the continuous functions with the integral norm: the ramps converge in the norm towards a jump, which is not a
continuous function, and the definition below names the spaces in which this cannot happen.

![Left: the continuous ramps $f_n$, equal to $0$ on $[0, \tfrac12 - \tfrac1n]$, to $1$ on $[\tfrac12, 1]$ and linear
in between, for $n = 2, 4, 8, 16$. They form a Cauchy sequence in $\|f\|_1 = \int_0^1|f|$ since $\|f_m - f_n\|_1 \leq
\tfrac1{2\min(m, n)}$, and converge in this norm to the step function, which is not continuous. Right: the distances
$\|f_n - f_{2n}\|_1$ and $\|f_n - f_{2n}\|_\infty$; the second stays at $\tfrac12$, so in the supremum norm the
sequence is not Cauchy. Generated by `figures/fa2-incomplete-ramps.sage`.](figures/fa2-incomplete-ramps.svg){#fig-fa2-incomplete-ramps width=95%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-banach-space}
#### Banach space

A sequence $(x_n)$ in a normed space is a **Cauchy sequence** if $\|x_n - x_m\| \to 0$ as $m, n \to \infty$
(@def-cauchy-sequence). A normed space is **complete**, or a **Banach space**, if every Cauchy sequence in it
converges to an element of the space. Every normed space $X$ has a **completion**: a Banach space $\tilde X$ with a
linear isometry $i : X \to \tilde X$ whose range is dense, unique up to a unique linear isometry, built from the
classes of Cauchy sequences of $X$ that are at distance zero from each other @arcozzi2025 [Thm. 1.1 and Prop. 1.1].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Every finite-dimensional normed space is a Banach space, and the argument is the coordinate argument of
@cini2023quantum [Sec. 2.8]. The first example records it.

::: {#exm-fan-finite-dim-complete}
#### Finite dimensions

In $\mathbb{C}^n$ with $\|\cdot\|_2$, a Cauchy sequence $x^{(m)}$ has $|x^{(m)}_k - x^{(l)}_k| \leq \|x^{(m)} -
x^{(l)}\|_2$, so each coordinate is a Cauchy sequence of complex numbers with a limit $x_k$, and $\|x^{(m)} - x\|_2^2
= \sum_k|x^{(m)}_k - x_k|^2 \to 0$ as a finite sum of null sequences @cini2023quantum [Sec. 2.8]. By
@thm-norm-equivalence the same holds for any norm on a finite-dimensional space.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The bounded sequences with the supremum norm are a Banach space by a uniform version of the same argument. The second
example gives it, together with the closed subspaces of convergent and null sequences that recur in the duality
theory.

::: {#exm-fan-ell-infinity}
#### Bounded and null sequences

$\ell^\infty = \{a : \sup_n|a_n| < \infty\}$ with $\|a\|_\infty = \sup_n|a_n|$ is a Banach space: a Cauchy sequence
$a^{(m)}$ converges coordinatewise to some $a$, and letting $l \to \infty$ in $|a^{(m)}_n - a^{(l)}_n| \leq
\varepsilon$ gives $\|a^{(m)} - a\|_\infty \leq \varepsilon$ for large $m$. The convergent sequences $c$ and the null
sequences $c_0 = \{a : a_n \to 0\}$ are closed subspaces, hence Banach spaces too.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The continuous functions with the integral norm are the standard incomplete space, and the third example works out
the sequence of the figure. Its completion is the space $L^1$ of the next section.

::: {#exm-fan-ramps-incomplete}
#### The ramps of the figure

For the ramps $f_n$ of the figure and $m > n$, $f_m - f_n$ vanishes outside $[\tfrac12 - \tfrac1n, \tfrac12]$ and has
modulus at most $1$ there, so $\|f_m - f_n\|_1 \leq \tfrac1n$: the sequence is Cauchy in $\|\cdot\|_1$. If it had a
continuous limit $f$, then $f = 0$ on $[0, \tfrac12)$ and $f = 1$ on $[\tfrac12, 1]$, which is impossible. So
$(C[0, 1], \|\cdot\|_1)$ is not a Banach space.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The two meanings of the word "complete" in quantum mechanics are easily confused, and the first exercise separates
them. A complete set of vectors spans the space, while a complete space contains the limits of its Cauchy sequences.

::: {#exr-fan-two-completes}
#### Two meanings of "complete"

@cini2023quantum [Sec. 2.2.3] calls a set of vectors complete if every vector is a linear combination of them, and a
space complete if Cauchy sequences converge [Sec. 2.8]. Show that the vectors $\delta^{(n)}$ (a one in place $n$)
span $c_{00}$, which is not complete in $\|\cdot\|_2$, and that they do not span the complete space $\ell^2$ in the
algebraic sense, although every $a \in \ell^2$ is the norm limit of $\sum_{n \leq N}a_n\delta^{(n)}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Every finitely supported sequence is a finite combination of the $\delta^{(n)}$. In $c_{00}$ the sequence $a^{(N)} =
(1, \tfrac12, \dots, \tfrac1N, 0, \dots)$ is Cauchy in $\|\cdot\|_2$, since $\|a^{(M)} - a^{(N)}\|_2^2 =
\sum_{N < n \leq M}n^{-2}$, but its limit $(1/n)$ is not finitely supported, so $c_{00}$ is not complete. The element
$(1/n)$ of $\ell^2$ is not a finite combination of the $\delta^{(n)}$, yet $\|(1/n) - a^{(N)}\|_2^2 = \sum_{n > N}
n^{-2} \to 0$. In a Hilbert space "complete orthonormal set" therefore means that the closed span is everything
(@def-orthonormal-basis), not the algebraic span.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A Banach space has no countable algebraic basis, a consequence of completeness that @arcozzi2025 [Sec. 3.1] proves
for Hilbert spaces by an explicit vector. The second exercise carries the argument out in $\ell^2$.

::: {#exr-fan-no-countable-basis}
#### No countable Hamel basis

Let $v_1, v_2, \dots$ be linearly independent in $\ell^2$, and let $e_1, e_2, \dots$ be the orthonormal vectors that
Gram-Schmidt makes from them. Show that $x = \sum_mm^{-1}e_m$ exists in $\ell^2$ and is not a finite linear
combination of the $v_n$ @arcozzi2025 [Prop. 3.1].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The partial sums $\sum_{m \leq M}m^{-1}e_m$ are Cauchy, since $\|\sum_{M < m \leq K}m^{-1}e_m\|^2 = \sum_{M < m \leq
K}m^{-2}$, so $x$ exists by completeness. A finite combination of $v_1, \dots, v_N$ lies in the span of $e_1, \dots,
e_N$, which is orthogonal to $e_{N + 1}$, whereas $\langle e_{N + 1}, x\rangle = 1/(N + 1) \neq 0$. So $x$ is not
in the span of the $v_n$, which therefore cannot be an algebraic basis.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The completion of a normed space can be identified concretely in the standard cases. The third exercise asks for
the completions of the three incomplete spaces met so far.

::: {#exr-fan-completions}
#### Three completions

Identify the completions of $(c_{00}, \|\cdot\|_\infty)$, $(c_{00}, \|\cdot\|_2)$ and $(\mathbb{Q}, |\cdot|)$ (a
normed space over $\mathbb{Q}$), using that each space sits densely and isometrically in a Banach space.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The completion is the closure of the space in any Banach space containing it isometrically, by the uniqueness in
@def-banach-space. $c_{00}$ is dense in $c_0$ for $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ (truncate a null sequence) and $c_0$ is closed
in $\ell^\infty$, so the completion is $c_0$, not $\ell^\infty$: the constant sequence $(1, 1, \dots)$ is at distance
$1$ from $c_{00}$. For $\|\cdot\|_2$ the completion is $\ell^2$, and for $\mathbb{Q}$ it is $\mathbb{R}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

In a complete space a series whose norms are summable converges, and this property characterises completeness. The
theorem below states it; it is the tool behind the completeness of $L^p$ in the next section.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-absolute-series}
#### Absolutely convergent series

A normed space $X$ is a Banach space if and only if every series $\sum_nx_n$ with $\sum_n\|x_n\| < \infty$
converges in $X$, and then $\|\sum_nx_n\| \leq \sum_n\|x_n\|$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The series criterion makes several completeness proofs one line long. The first example applies it to the bounded
sequences with the norm of @exm-fan-ell-infinity.

::: {#exm-fan-series-ell-infinity}
#### A series in $\ell^\infty$

The sequences $x_n = 2^{-n}\delta^{(n)}$ in $\ell^\infty$ have $\sum\|x_n\|_\infty = 1$, and $\sum_nx_n = (2^{-1},
2^{-2}, \dots)$ converges in $\ell^\infty$; in fact its tail has norm $\|\sum_{n > N}x_n\|_\infty = 2^{-N-1}$. The
series $\sum_n\delta^{(n)}$ has terms of norm $1$ and its partial sums $(1, \dots, 1, 0, \dots)$ do not converge in
$\ell^\infty$, as consecutive partial sums stay at distance $1$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The exponential of a matrix is the most familiar absolutely convergent series in a Banach space of linear maps. The
second example writes it in this language; the same argument works for any bounded operator once
@def-bounded-linear-map is available.

::: {#exm-fan-matrix-exponential-series}
#### The exponential series

For a matrix $A$ with the operator norm, $\|A^k/k!\| \leq \|A\|^k/k!$ and $\sum_k\|A\|^k/k! = e^{\|A\|}$, so
$e^A = \sum_kA^k/k!$ converges, with $\|e^A\| \leq e^{\|A\|}$ (@def-matrix-exp). For $A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0
& 0\end{pmatrix}$ the series stops, $e^A = 1 + A$, and $\|e^A\| = \tfrac{1 + \sqrt5}{2} < e$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In an incomplete space an absolutely convergent series may diverge, and the third example builds one from the ramps
of the figure. The series of differences telescopes to the ramps themselves.

::: {#exm-fan-series-incomplete}
#### A divergent absolutely convergent series

In $(C[0, 1], \|\cdot\|_1)$ put $x_1 = f_2$ and $x_k = f_{2^k} - f_{2^{k - 1}}$ with the ramps of the figure. Then
$\|x_k\|_1 \leq 2^{-k}$, so $\sum\|x_k\|_1 < \infty$, but the partial sums $\sum_{k \leq K}x_k = f_{2^K}$ have no
continuous limit (@exm-fan-ramps-incomplete). The theorem identifies this as the failure of completeness.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise asks for the proof of the theorem. Both directions are short, and the converse uses a fast Cauchy
subsequence.

::: {#exr-fan-absolute-series-proof}
#### Proof of the series criterion

Prove @thm-absolute-series. For the converse, given a Cauchy sequence $(y_n)$ choose $n_1 < n_2 < \dots$ with
$\|y_{n_{k + 1}} - y_{n_k}\| < 2^{-k}$, sum the differences, and show that a Cauchy sequence with a convergent
subsequence converges.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $X$ is complete and $\sum\|x_n\| < \infty$, the partial sums satisfy $\|s_M - s_N\| \leq \sum_{N < n \leq M}
\|x_n\|$, which is small, so they converge; the norm bound passes to the limit. Conversely, with the subsequence
chosen as stated, $y_{n_1} + \sum_k(y_{n_{k + 1}} - y_{n_k})$ converges by hypothesis, that is, $y_{n_k} \to y$.
Then $\|y_n - y\| \leq \|y_n - y_{n_k}\| + \|y_{n_k} - y\|$ is small for large $n$ and $k$, so $y_n \to y$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Neumann series of @sec-banach-algebras is the absolutely convergent series used most often in this chapter. The
second exercise sums it for a matrix and estimates the tail.

::: {#exr-fan-neumann-matrix}
#### A geometric series of matrices

For $A = \tfrac12\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$ show that $\sum_kA^k$ converges and equals $(1 -
A)^{-1}$, and bound $\|(1 - A)^{-1} - \sum_{k < N}A^k\|$ by $2^{-N}\cdot 2$. Compute $A^2$ and use it to write the partial sums in
closed form.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\|A\| = \tfrac12$ (its eigenvalues are $\pm\tfrac12$ and it is symmetric), so $\sum\|A^k\| = 2$ and the series
converges by @thm-absolute-series. $(1 - A)\sum_{k < N}A^k = 1 - A^N \to 1$, so the sum is $(1 - A)^{-1} =
\tfrac43\begin{pmatrix} 1 & \tfrac12 \\ \tfrac12 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, and the tail is bounded by $\sum_{k \geq N}
2^{-k} = 2^{1 - N}$. Since $A^2 = \tfrac14$, the even partial sums are $\sum_{k < 2M}A^k = (1 + A)\sum_{j < M}4^{-j} =
\tfrac43(1 - 4^{-M})(1 + A)$, which visibly tend to $\tfrac43(1 + A) = (1 - A)^{-1}$, with error $4^{-M}\cdot\tfrac43
\|1 + A\| = 2\cdot 4^{-M}$, attaining the bound.

Sage computes the sum and compares the error of the partial sums with the bound $2^{1 - N}$, which is attained for even $N$:

{{< sage exr-fan-neumann-matrix >}}
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

Completeness is a property of the norm and not only of the topology, and the third exercise shows it with two
equivalent norms. It also shows that completeness is preserved by equivalent norms.

::: {#exr-fan-completeness-equivalent}
#### Completeness and equivalent norms

Show that if $\|\cdot\|_a$ and $\|\cdot\|_b$ are equivalent norms on $X$, then $(X, \|\cdot\|_a)$ is complete if and
only if $(X, \|\cdot\|_b)$ is. Then show that $\|f\|_{C^1} = \|f\|_\infty + \|f'\|_\infty$ makes $C^1[0, 1]$ a Banach
space, while $\|f\|_\infty$ alone does not.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Equivalent norms have the same Cauchy sequences and the same convergent sequences. For $C^1$: if $(f_n)$ is Cauchy
in $\|\cdot\|_{C^1}$, then $f_n \to f$ and $f_n' \to g$ uniformly, both continuous (@exr-fan-ck-complete), and
$f_n(x) = f_n(0) + \int_0^xf_n'$ gives $f(x) = f(0) + \int_0^xg$, so $f \in C^1$ with $f' = g$ and $f_n \to f$ in
$\|\cdot\|_{C^1}$. In the supremum norm, $\sqrt{(x - \tfrac12)^2 + 1/n}$ is a Cauchy sequence of $C^1$ functions
whose uniform limit $|x - \tfrac12|$ is not differentiable.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

### The spaces $\ell^p$ and $L^p$

The norms $\|\cdot\|_p$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ have infinite-dimensional versions on sequences and on functions, and
these are the basic Banach spaces of analysis. The figure compares the two directions in which the norms $\|\cdot\|
_p$ are ordered: on sequences they decrease with $p$, on functions on an interval of length one they increase.

![Left: $p \mapsto \|a\|_p$ for the sequences $a_n = 1/n$ (finite exactly for $p > 1$) and $a_n = 2^{-n}$,
decreasing in $p$, so $\ell^p \subset \ell^q$ for $p < q$. Right: $p \mapsto \|f\|_{L^p(0, 1)}$ for $f(x) =
x^{-1/4}$ (finite exactly for $p < 4$) and $f(x) = x$, increasing in $p$, so $L^q(0, 1) \subset L^p(0, 1)$ for $p <
q$. Generated by `figures/fa2-lp-norms.sage`.](figures/fa2-lp-norms.svg){#fig-fa2-lp-norms width=95%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-lp-space}
#### $L^p$ space

Let $1 \leq p < \infty$ and let $(X, \mu)$ be a measure space, such as an interval or $\mathbb{R}^n$ with Lebesgue
measure, or $\{1, 2, 3, \dots\}$ with the counting measure. The space $L^p(X, \mu)$ consists of the measurable
functions with $\|f\|_p = (\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu)^{1/p} < \infty$, two functions being identified when they agree
almost everywhere; $L^\infty$ consists of the essentially bounded functions with $\|f\|_\infty$ the essential
supremum. For the counting measure these are the **sequence spaces** $\ell^p = \{a : \sum_n|a_n|^p < \infty\}$ and
$\ell^\infty$. For $1 \leq p \leq \infty$, $L^p$ and $\ell^p$ are Banach spaces; $L^2$ is the Hilbert space of
@def-l2-space.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The sequences $1/n^\alpha$ are the test cases of the sequence spaces: whether they belong to $\ell^p$ is decided by
the $p$-series. The first example records the result.

::: {#exm-fan-power-sequences}
#### Power sequences

$a_n = n^{-\alpha}$ with $\alpha > 0$ lies in $\ell^p$ exactly when $\alpha p > 1$ (@sec-series), and always in
$\ell^\infty$. So $1/n$ lies in every $\ell^p$ with $p > 1$ but not in $\ell^1$, and $1/\sqrt n$ lies in $\ell^p$
for $p > 2$ only. The left panel of the figure shows $\|1/n\|_p$ decreasing in $p$ and blowing up as $p \to 1$.
:::

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

Power functions play the same role for $L^p$, but the condition depends on whether the singularity is at zero or the
decay is at infinity. The second example compares the two ends of $(0, \infty)$.

::: {#exm-fan-power-functions}
#### Power functions

On $(0, 1)$, $x^{-\alpha}$ lies in $L^p$ exactly when $\alpha p < 1$; on $(1, \infty)$ exactly when $\alpha p > 1$.
So $x^{-1/4}$ lies in $L^p(0, 1)$ for $p < 4$ (right panel of the figure), and $1/x$ is in $L^2(1, \infty)$ but not
in $L^1(1, \infty)$. On $(0, \infty)$ no power lies in any $L^p$, and neither of $L^1(\mathbb{R})$, $L^2(\mathbb{R})$
contains the other: $x^{-1/2}\mathbf{1}_{(0, 1)}$ is in $L^1$ only, and $(1 + |x|)^{-1}$ in $L^2$ only.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Gaussian lies in every $L^p(\mathbb{R})$, and its norms can be computed in closed form. The third example does
so; the result reappears in the Sobolev part through the Fourier transform.

::: {#exm-fan-gaussian-lp}
#### The Gaussian in $L^p$

For $g(x) = e^{-x^2/2}$, $\|g\|_p^p = \int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{-px^2/2}dx = \sqrt{2\pi/p}$, so $\|g\|_p = (2\pi/p)^{1/(2p)}$
for $1 \leq p < \infty$ and $\|g\|_\infty = 1$. In particular $\|g\|_1 = \sqrt{2\pi}$ and $\|g\|_2 = \pi^{1/4}$, and
$\|g\|_p \to 1$ as $p \to \infty$, as it must for a continuous function with maximum $1$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The inclusions between the sequence spaces follow from the monotonicity shown in the figure. The first exercise proves
it and gives the opposite inclusion for functions on a set of finite measure.

::: {#exr-fan-lp-inclusions}
#### Inclusions

Show that $\|a\|_q \leq \|a\|_p$ for sequences and $1 \leq p < q \leq \infty$, so that $\ell^p \subset \ell^q$. On
$(0, 1)$ show $\|f\|_p \leq \|f\|_q$, so that $L^q(0, 1) \subset L^p(0, 1)$. Find a sequence in $\ell^4$ that is not
in $\ell^2$ and a function in $L^2(0, 1)$ that is not in $L^4(0, 1)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $\|a\|_p = 1$ then $|a_n| \leq 1$ and $\sum|a_n|^q \leq \sum|a_n|^p = 1$; homogeneity gives the general case. On
$(0, 1)$, Hölder's inequality (@thm-holder-inequality) with exponents $q/p$ and $q/(q - p)$ gives $\int|f|^p\cdot 1
\leq (\int|f|^q)^{p/q}$. Examples: $a_n = n^{-1/3}$ has $\sum n^{-4/3} < \infty$ and $\sum n^{-2/3} = \infty$;
$f(x) = x^{-1/3}$ has $\int x^{-2/3} = 3$ and $\int x^{-4/3} = \infty$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Completeness of $\ell^p$ is the uniform version of the coordinate argument, and the second exercise asks for it. The
same proof with integrals in place of sums, and Fatou's lemma in place of the limit of finite sums, gives the
completeness of $L^p$.

::: {#exr-fan-ellp-complete}
#### Completeness of $\ell^p$

Let $(a^{(m)})$ be Cauchy in $\ell^p$, $1 \leq p < \infty$. Show that it converges coordinatewise to a sequence $a$,
that $\sum_{n \leq N}|a^{(m)}_n - a_n|^p \leq \varepsilon^p$ for every $N$ once $m$ is large, and conclude that $a
\in \ell^p$ and $a^{(m)} \to a$ in $\ell^p$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|a^{(m)}_n - a^{(l)}_n| \leq \|a^{(m)} - a^{(l)}\|_p$, so each coordinate is Cauchy with a limit $a_n$. Given
$\varepsilon$, choose $M$ with $\|a^{(m)} - a^{(l)}\|_p \leq \varepsilon$ for $m, l \geq M$; then $\sum_{n \leq N}
|a^{(m)}_n - a^{(l)}_n|^p \leq \varepsilon^p$, and $l \to \infty$ in this finite sum gives the stated bound. Letting
$N \to \infty$, $a^{(m)} - a \in \ell^p$ with norm $\leq \varepsilon$, so $a = a^{(m)} - (a^{(m)} - a) \in \ell^p$ and
$a^{(m)} \to a$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The integrals and series of the examples can be evaluated in closed form, which makes the membership criteria
quantitative. The third exercise treats a few borderline cases.

::: {#exr-fan-lp-borderline}
#### Borderline memberships

Compute $\|n^{-1}\|_p^p = \zeta(p)$ for $p = 2, 3, 4$, the integral $\int_0^1x^{-p/4}dx$ as a function of
$p < 4$, and the Gaussian norms $\|e^{-x^2/2}\|_p$ for $p = 1, 2, 3$. For which $p$ is $\log(1/x)$ in $L^p(0, 1)$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\zeta(2) = \pi^2/6$, $\zeta(4) = \pi^4/90$, $\int_0^1x^{-p/4} = 4/(4 - p)$, and the Gaussian norms follow
@exm-fan-gaussian-lp. With $x = e^{-t}$, $\int_0^1\log(1/x)^pdx = \int_0^\infty t^pe^{-t}dt = \Gamma(p + 1) <
\infty$, so $\log(1/x)$ lies in every $L^p(0, 1)$ with $p < \infty$, though it is unbounded. For the Gaussian, $\|e^{-x^2/2}\|_1 = \sqrt{2\pi}$, $\|e^{-x^2/2}\|_2 = \pi^{1/4}$
and $\|e^{-x^2/2}\|_3 = (2\pi/3)^{1/6}$; $\zeta(3)$ has no known closed form, but $1 < \zeta(3) < 1 + \int_1^\infty
x^{-3}dx = \tfrac32$.

Sage evaluates the zeta values, the integrals and the Gaussian norms, and the moments of $\log(1/x)$ numerically:

:::

The triangle inequality for $\|\cdot\|_p$ is not obvious, and it rests on an inequality between products and norms.
The theorem below states it; it is also the tool that identifies the dual spaces of $\ell^p$ and $L^p$ in the last
section of this part.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-holder-inequality}
#### Hölder's inequality

Let $1 \leq p, q \leq \infty$ be **conjugate exponents**, $\tfrac1p + \tfrac1q = 1$ (with $\tfrac1\infty = 0$). For
$f \in L^p$ and $g \in L^q$ the product lies in $L^1$ and $\int|fg|\,d\mu \leq \|f\|_p\|g\|_q$ (**Hölder**); for $1
< p < \infty$ equality holds exactly when $|f|^p$ and $|g|^q$ are proportional. For $f, g \in L^p$, $\|f + g\|_p \leq
\|f\|_p + \|g\|_p$ (**Minkowski**), so $\|\cdot\|_p$ is a norm. The case $p = q = 2$ is the Cauchy-Schwarz
inequality.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The proof of Hölder's inequality reduces it to an inequality between two numbers. The first example is that
inequality, Young's inequality, with its geometric meaning.

::: {#exm-fan-young}
#### Young's inequality

For $s, t \geq 0$ and conjugate $p, q$, $st \leq s^p/p + t^q/q$, by concavity of the logarithm: $\log(\tfrac1p s^p +
\tfrac1q t^q) \geq \tfrac1p\log s^p + \tfrac1q\log t^q = \log st$. Applied to $s = |f(x)|/\|f\|_p$ and $t =
|g(x)|/\|g\|_q$ and integrated, it gives $\int|fg|/(\|f\|_p\|g\|_q) \leq \tfrac1p + \tfrac1q = 1$, which is
Hölder's inequality.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Hölder's inequality gives the best constant in comparisons between norms, as already used in
@exr-fan-p-norm-constants. The second example checks it on explicit vectors of $\mathbb{R}^3$, where both sides can
be computed by hand.

::: {#exm-fan-holder-r3}
#### A numerical instance

For $p = 3$, $q = \tfrac32$, $x = (1, 2, 3)$, $y = (3, 2, 1)$: $\sum x_ky_k = 10$, $\|x\|_3 = 36^{1/3} \approx 3.302$
and $\|y\|_{3/2} = (3^{3/2} + 2^{3/2} + 1)^{2/3} \approx 4.335$, with product $\approx 14.31 \geq 10$. Equality would
require $|x_k|^3 \propto |y_k|^{3/2}$, that is $y_k \propto x_k^2$, as for $y = (1, 4, 9)$, where $\sum x_ky_k = 36 =
\|x\|_3\|y\|_{3/2}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Minkowski's inequality is the triangle inequality that makes $\|\cdot\|_p$ a norm, and it fails for $p < 1$. The third
example shows the failure on the same vectors as @exr-fan-norm-axioms.

::: {#exm-fan-minkowski}
#### Minkowski's inequality and its failure

For $p = 3$ and $f = (1, 0)$, $g = (0, 1)$, $\|f + g\|_3 = 2^{1/3} \leq 2 = \|f\|_3 + \|g\|_3$. For $p = \tfrac12$ the
same vectors give $\|f + g\|_{1/2} = (1 + 1)^2 = 4 > 2$: the expression $(\sum|a_k|^p)^{1/p}$ is not a norm for $p <
1$, which is why the family stops at $p = 1$ and why its unit "balls" are not convex for $p < 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise asks for the proof of Minkowski's inequality from Hölder's. The trick is to split $|f + g|^p$ into
two products, each of which Hölder controls.

::: {#exr-fan-minkowski-proof}
#### Minkowski from Hölder

For $1 < p < \infty$ write $|f + g|^p \leq |f|\,|f + g|^{p - 1} + |g|\,|f + g|^{p - 1}$, apply Hölder's inequality to
each term with exponents $p$ and $q = p/(p - 1)$, and deduce $\|f + g\|_p \leq \|f\|_p + \|g\|_p$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|f + g|^{p - 1} \in L^q$ with $\||f + g|^{p - 1}\|_q = \|f + g\|_p^{p - 1}$, since $(p - 1)q = p$. Hölder gives
$\int|f|\,|f + g|^{p - 1} \leq \|f\|_p\|f + g\|_p^{p - 1}$, and similarly for $g$. Adding, $\|f + g\|_p^p \leq
(\|f\|_p + \|g\|_p)\|f + g\|_p^{p - 1}$; dividing by $\|f + g\|_p^{p - 1}$ (if non-zero) gives the claim. That
$f + g \in L^p$ in the first place follows from $|f + g|^p \leq 2^p\max(|f|, |g|)^p \leq 2^p(|f|^p + |g|^p)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Hölder's inequality for three functions follows by applying it twice, and it is used for products of fields in the
Sobolev part. The second exercise derives it.

::: {#exr-fan-holder-three}
#### Hölder for three factors

Show that $\int|fgh| \leq \|f\|_p\|g\|_q\|h\|_r$ when $\tfrac1p + \tfrac1q + \tfrac1r = 1$. Deduce that the product of
three functions in $L^3$ is integrable, and that $\|fg\|_1 \leq \|f\|_2\|g\|_2$ is the case $r = \infty$, $h = 1$ on a
probability space.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Let $\tfrac1s = \tfrac1q + \tfrac1r$, so $\tfrac1p + \tfrac1s = 1$. Hölder gives $\int|f|\,|gh| \leq \|f\|_p\|gh\|_s$,
and Hölder with exponents $q/s$, $r/s$ applied to $|g|^s|h|^s$ gives $\|gh\|_s \leq \|g\|_q\|h\|_r$. With $p = q = r =
3$ the right side is finite. With $r = \infty$ and $h = 1$, $\|h\|_\infty = 1$ and the exponents are $p = q = 2$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The equality case of Hölder's inequality is what makes the duality theorem work: for each $f$ there is a $g$ that
attains the bound. The third exercise constructs it and checks it numerically.

::: {#exr-fan-holder-equality}
#### The extremal function

For $f \in L^p$, $1 < p < \infty$, $f \neq 0$, set $g = \overline{\operatorname{sgn}f}\,|f|^{p - 1}/\|f\|_p^{p - 1}$,
where $\operatorname{sgn}f = f/|f|$ (and $0$ where $f = 0$). Show $\|g\|_q = 1$ and $\int fg = \|f\|_p$. Work it out
for $f = (1, -2, 3)$ and $p = 3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|g|^q = |f|^{(p - 1)q}/\|f\|_p^{(p - 1)q} = |f|^p/\|f\|_p^p$, which integrates to $1$, and $fg = |f|^p/\|f\|_p^{p -
1}$ integrates to $\|f\|_p^p/\|f\|_p^{p - 1} = \|f\|_p$. For $f = (1, -2, 3)$, $p = 3$: $\|f\|_3 = 36^{1/3}$ and $\overline{\operatorname{sgn}f}\,|f|^2 = (1, -4, 9)$, so $g =
(1, -4, 9)/36^{2/3}$ and $\sum f_kg_k = (1 + 8 + 27)/36^{2/3} = 36^{1/3}$, while
$\|g\|_{3/2}^{3/2} = (1 + 8 + 27)/36 = 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### The space $C(K)$

Continuous functions on a compact set, measured by their largest value, form the Banach space in which uniform
approximation takes place. The figure shows the Bernstein polynomials of a function with a corner converging to it
uniformly, which is the content of the Weierstrass theorem stated after the definition.

![Left: the Bernstein polynomials $B_nf(x) = \sum_{k = 0}^n f(k/n)\binom nk x^k(1 - x)^{n - k}$ of $f(x) = |x -
\tfrac12|$ for $n = 4, 16, 64$, converging uniformly to $f$ on $[0, 1]$. Right: the uniform error $\|B_nf - f\|_\infty$
against $n$ on logarithmic axes, decaying like $n^{-1/2}$; the error is largest at the corner $x = \tfrac12$.
Generated by `figures/fa2-bernstein.sage`.](figures/fa2-bernstein.svg){#fig-fa2-bernstein width=95%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-continuous-function-space}
#### Space of continuous functions

For a compact Hausdorff space $K$ (@def-compact, @def-hausdorff), such as a closed interval, a closed ball or a
sphere, $C(K)$ is the space of continuous functions $f : K \to \mathbb{C}$ with the **supremum norm** $\|f\|_\infty =
\max_{x \in K}|f(x)|$. Convergence in this norm is uniform convergence (@def-uniform-convergence), and $C(K)$ is a
Banach space. For a locally compact space $X$, the continuous functions **vanishing at infinity**, $C_0(X)$ (for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, $|f| < \varepsilon$ outside a compact set), form a Banach space with the same norm
@arcozzi2025 [Sec. 1.2.1].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The interval is the basic compact space, and the first example measures some functions on it. It also shows that the
supremum of a continuous function on a compact set is attained.

::: {#exm-fan-ck-interval}
#### Functions on an interval

On $K = [0, 1]$, $\|x - x^2\|_\infty = \tfrac14$ (at $x = \tfrac12$) and $\|\sin 2\pi x\|_\infty = 1$. The functions
$f_n(x) = x^n$ converge pointwise to a function that is $0$ on $[0, 1)$ and $1$ at $x = 1$, which is not continuous,
so $(x^n)$ has no limit in $C[0, 1]$, consistent with $\|f_n - f_{2n}\|_\infty = \tfrac14$ (at $x^n = \tfrac12$).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

On the circle, continuous functions are the continuous periodic functions, and the uniform norm controls the Fourier
coefficients. The second example records the inequality, which links $C(S^1)$ with the sequence spaces.

::: {#exm-fan-ck-circle}
#### The circle and Fourier coefficients

$C(S^1)$ is the space of continuous $2\pi$-periodic functions. The Fourier coefficients (@def-fourier-coefficient)
satisfy $|\hat f(n)| \leq \|f\|_\infty$, so $f \mapsto \hat f$ maps $C(S^1)$ into $\ell^\infty(\mathbb{Z})$, in fact
into $c_0$ by the Riemann-Lebesgue lemma. If $\sum_n|\hat f(n)| < \infty$, the Fourier series converges uniformly,
and $\|f\|_\infty \leq \sum_n|\hat f(n)|$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

On $\mathbb{R}$ the bounded continuous functions do not form a separable space, and the functions vanishing at
infinity are the right replacement. The third example gives the standard members of $C_0(\mathbb{R})$ and a
bounded function outside it.

::: {#exm-fan-c0-line}
#### Functions vanishing at infinity

$e^{-x^2}$, $1/(1 + x^2)$ and $\sin(x)/x$ lie in $C_0(\mathbb{R})$; $\sin x$ and the constant $1$ are bounded and
continuous but do not vanish at infinity. The Fourier transform of a function in $L^1(\mathbb{R})$ lies in
$C_0(\mathbb{R})$ (the Riemann-Lebesgue lemma), for instance $\int_{-1}^1e^{-ikx}dx = 2\sin(k)/k$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise proves that $C(K)$ is complete, which is the theorem that a uniform limit of continuous functions
is continuous. The same argument gives the completeness of $C^k[0, 1]$ used in @exr-fan-completeness-equivalent.

::: {#exr-fan-ck-complete}
#### Completeness of $C(K)$

Let $(f_n)$ be Cauchy in $C(K)$. Show that $f_n(x)$ converges for every $x$, that the convergence is uniform, and
that the limit $f$ is continuous by an $\varepsilon/3$ argument. Conclude that $C(K)$ is a Banach space.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|f_n(x) - f_m(x)| \leq \|f_n - f_m\|_\infty$, so $f_n(x) \to f(x)$; letting $m \to \infty$ in $|f_n(x) - f_m(x)|
\leq \varepsilon$ for $n, m \geq N$ gives $\|f_n - f\|_\infty \leq \varepsilon$. For continuity at $x_0$, fix such an
$n$ and choose a neighbourhood where $|f_n(x) - f_n(x_0)| < \varepsilon$; then $|f(x) - f(x_0)| \leq |f(x) - f_n(x)| +
|f_n(x) - f_n(x_0)| + |f_n(x_0) - f(x_0)| < 3\varepsilon$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Pointwise convergence is not enough for convergence in $C(K)$, and the moving bump shows it. The second exercise
computes its norms, and the bump returns in the weak-convergence part.

::: {#exr-fan-moving-bump}
#### A pointwise but not uniform limit

Let $f_n(x) = nx\,e^{1 - nx}$ on $[0, 1]$. Show that $f_n(x) \to 0$ for every $x$ but $\|f_n\|_\infty = 1$, so that
$f_n \not\to 0$ in $C[0, 1]$, while $\|f_n\|_1 \to 0$. Find where the maximum is attained.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$f_n(0) = 0$, and for $x > 0$, $nx\,e^{-nx} \to 0$. The derivative $n e^{1 - nx}(1 - nx)$ vanishes at $x = 1/n$, where
$f_n = 1$, so $\|f_n\|_\infty = 1$. With $t = nx$, $\|f_n\|_1 = \tfrac en\int_0^nte^{-t}dt \leq e/n \to 0$. The bump
moves to $0$ and becomes thinner but keeps its height.

Sage locates the maximum and computes the $L^1$ norms:

{{< sage exr-fan-moving-bump >}}
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

The error of the Bernstein approximation of a function with a corner can be computed at the corner, where it is
largest. The third exercise relates it to the central limit theorem and explains the rate seen in the figure.

::: {#exr-fan-bernstein-corner}
#### The Bernstein error at a corner

For $f(x) = |x - \tfrac12|$, write $B_nf(\tfrac12) - f(\tfrac12)$ as an expectation over a binomial distribution, show
that it behaves like $1/\sqrt{2\pi n}$, and compute it exactly for $n = 2$. Why is the error largest at the corner?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$B_nf(\tfrac12) - f(\tfrac12) = \mathbb{E}|S_n/n - \tfrac12|$ for a binomial $S_n$ with parameter $\tfrac12$, and by
the central limit theorem (@thm-central-limit-theorem) this is $\approx\tfrac{1}{2\sqrt n}\mathbb{E}|Z| = \tfrac{1}
{2\sqrt n}\sqrt{2/\pi} = 1/\sqrt{2\pi n}$. Away from the corner $f$ is linear, and $B_n$ reproduces linear functions
exactly, so the error comes from the kink. For $n = 2$, $B_2f(\tfrac12) =
\tfrac14\cdot\tfrac12 + \tfrac12\cdot 0 + \tfrac14\cdot\tfrac12 = \tfrac14$, against $1/\sqrt{4\pi} \approx 0.28$.

Sage evaluates the binomial expectation exactly and compares it with $1/\sqrt{2\pi n}$:

{{< sage exr-fan-bernstein-corner >}}
:::

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

Polynomials are dense in $C[a, b]$, which makes $C[a, b]$ separable and lets identities be proved on polynomials
first. The theorem below states this and its generalisation to compact spaces.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-stone-weierstrass}
#### Weierstrass approximation theorem

Every continuous function on $[a, b]$ is a uniform limit of polynomials; explicitly, for $f \in C[0, 1]$ the Bernstein
polynomials $B_nf$ converge to $f$ uniformly. More generally (**Stone-Weierstrass**), if $K$ is a compact Hausdorff
space and $\mathcal{A} \subset C(K)$ is a subalgebra that contains the constants, separates the points of $K$ and is
closed under complex conjugation, then $\mathcal{A}$ is dense in $C(K)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The trigonometric polynomials are an algebra on the circle that contains the constants, separates points and is closed
under conjugation. The first example applies the theorem to them.

::: {#exm-fan-trig-dense}
#### Trigonometric polynomials

On $S^1$ the trigonometric polynomials $\sum_{|n| \leq N}c_ne^{inx}$ form an algebra ($e^{inx}e^{imx} = e^{i(n +
m)x}$), closed under conjugation ($\overline{e^{inx}} = e^{-inx}$), containing $1$, and separating points ($e^{ix}$
is injective on the circle). By Stone-Weierstrass they are dense in $C(S^1)$. This is the uniform version of the
completeness of the Fourier basis (@exm-onb-fourier-parseval).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Spherical harmonics are the polynomials of the sphere, and the same theorem makes them dense. The second example
applies it on $S^2$.

::: {#exm-fan-polynomials-sphere}
#### Polynomials on the sphere

On $S^2 \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ the restrictions of polynomials in $x, y, z$ form an algebra containing the constants,
closed under conjugation, and separating points (the coordinates do). They are dense in $C(S^2)$, and since every
polynomial restricted to $S^2$ is a finite sum of spherical harmonics (@def-spherical-harmonic), finite sums of
spherical harmonics are dense in $C(S^2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The hypotheses of Stone-Weierstrass are all needed, and the third example drops two of them. Each failure is a
closed proper subalgebra.

::: {#exm-fan-stone-weierstrass-fails}
#### When the hypotheses fail

On $[-1, 1]$ the even polynomials form an algebra with $1$, closed under conjugation, but they do not separate $x$ and
$-x$; their closure is the even continuous functions, so $x$ is not approximated. On the closed unit disc, the
polynomials in $z$ separate points but are not closed under conjugation; their uniform limits are holomorphic inside,
so $\bar z$ is not approximated: $\|\bar z - p(z)\|_\infty \geq 1$ for every polynomial $p$ @arcozzi2025 [Sec. 1.4].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The Bernstein proof of the Weierstrass theorem is probabilistic, and the first exercise asks for its key computation.
It reduces uniform convergence to the variance of a binomial distribution.

::: {#exr-fan-bernstein-proof}
#### Bernstein's proof

Show $B_n1 = 1$, $B_nx = x$, $B_nx^2 = x^2 + x(1 - x)/n$. For $f \in C[0, 1]$ with modulus of continuity
$\omega(\delta) = \sup_{|x - y| \leq \delta}|f(x) - f(y)|$, show $|B_nf(x) - f(x)| \leq \omega(\delta) + 2\|f\|_\infty
x(1 - x)/(n\delta^2)$ and conclude that $B_nf \to f$ uniformly.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$B_nf(x) = \mathbb{E}f(S_n/n)$ with $S_n$ binomial$(n, x)$; the three identities are $\mathbb{E}1 = 1$,
$\mathbb{E}S_n/n = x$, $\mathbb{E}(S_n/n)^2 = x^2 + x(1 - x)/n$. Split $|B_nf - f| \leq \mathbb{E}|f(S_n/n) - f(x)|$
into $|S_n/n - x| \leq \delta$, contributing at most $\omega(\delta)$, and the rest, contributing at most
$2\|f\|_\infty P(|S_n/n - x| > \delta) \leq 2\|f\|_\infty x(1 - x)/(n\delta^2)$ by Chebyshev. Choose $\delta$ with
$\omega(\delta) < \varepsilon$, then $n$ large; $x(1 - x) \leq \tfrac14$ makes the bound uniform.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Density of polynomials makes $C[0, 1]$ separable, while the bounded sequences are not. The second exercise proves both
statements @arcozzi2025 [Exercise 3.10].

::: {#exr-fan-separability}
#### Separable and non-separable

Show that the polynomials with rational coefficients are a countable dense subset of $C[0, 1]$. Show that the
sequences of zeros and ones form an uncountable subset of $\ell^\infty$ in which any two points are at distance $1$,
and conclude that $\ell^\infty$ is not separable, while $\ell^p$ is for $p < \infty$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Approximate $f$ by a polynomial within $\varepsilon/2$ and its coefficients by rationals within $\varepsilon/(2(n +
1))$; the set of rational polynomials is countable. The $0$-$1$ sequences are in bijection with the subsets of
$\mathbb{N}$, hence uncountable, and two different ones differ by $1$ in some place. Balls of radius $\tfrac12$ around
them are disjoint, so a dense set must meet each, and cannot be countable. In $\ell^p$, $p < \infty$, the finitely
supported rational sequences are dense.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Weierstrass theorem implies that a continuous function is determined by its moments. The third exercise proves
this uniqueness, which is the starting point of the moment problem in probability.

::: {#exr-fan-moments}
#### Functions determined by their moments

Let $f \in C[0, 1]$ with $\int_0^1f(x)x^ndx = 0$ for all $n \geq 0$. Show that $\int_0^1|f|^2 = 0$, hence $f = 0$, by
approximating $\bar f$ uniformly by polynomials.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By hypothesis $\int fp = 0$ for every polynomial $p$. Choose $p_n \to \bar f$ uniformly. Then $|\int f\bar f - \int
fp_n| \leq \|f\|_\infty\|\bar f - p_n\|_\infty \to 0$, so $\int|f|^2 = 0$ and the continuous function $|f|^2$
vanishes identically.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### Bounded linear maps

A linear map between normed spaces is continuous exactly when it stretches vectors by a bounded factor. The figure
shows the factor for one matrix and three norms on the plane: the image of each unit ball and the smallest ball of the
same norm that contains it.

![The image of the unit ball of $\|\cdot\|_1$ (left), $\|\cdot\|_2$ (centre) and $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ (right) under $A =
\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, inside the ball of radius $\|A\|$ of the same norm: $\|A\|_{1 \to 1} = 3$
(largest column sum), $\|A\|_{2 \to 2} = 1 + \sqrt2$ (largest singular value) and $\|A\|_{\infty \to \infty} = 3$
(largest row sum). The marked points are vectors where the norm is attained. Generated by
`figures/fa2-operator-norms.sage`.](figures/fa2-operator-norms.svg){#fig-fa2-operator-norms width=95%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-bounded-linear-map}
#### Bounded linear map

A linear map $T : X \to Y$ between normed spaces (@def-linear-map) is **bounded** if $\|Tx\| \leq C\|x\|$ for some
constant $C$ and all $x$; the smallest such constant is the **operator norm** $\|T\| = \sup_{\|x\| \leq 1}\|Tx\|$.
A linear map is bounded if and only if it is continuous, if and only if it is continuous at $0$. The bounded linear
maps form a normed space $\mathcal{B}(X, Y)$, which is a Banach space when $Y$ is, and $\|ST\| \leq \|S\|\,\|T\|$
@arcozzi2025 [Thm. 3.6, Exercise 3.4]; @picard2020primer [Lemma B.4.3] gives the Hilbert-space case. On a Hilbert
space this is the bounded operator of @def-bounded-operator.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
On $\mathbb{C}^n$ with the norms $\|\cdot\|_1$ and $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ the operator norm of a matrix has a closed
form, unlike the Euclidean case. The first example derives the two formulas drawn in the figure.

::: {#exm-fan-matrix-norms}
#### Column and row sums

For a matrix $A$ on $(\mathbb{C}^n, \|\cdot\|_1)$, $\|Ax\|_1 \leq \sum_j|x_j|\sum_i|A_{ij}| \leq (\max_j\sum_i|A_{ij}|)
\|x\|_1$, with equality at the basis vector of the largest column: $\|A\|_{1 \to 1}$ is the largest column sum. On
$(\mathbb{C}^n, \|\cdot\|_\infty)$ the same argument gives the largest row sum, attained at $x_j =
\overline{\operatorname{sgn}A_{ij}}$ for the largest row $i$. For the matrix of the figure both are $3$.
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Multiplication by a fixed function is the simplest operator on a function space, and its norm is the size of the
multiplier. The second example computes it on $L^p$ @arcozzi2025 [Exercise 3.11].

::: {#exm-fan-multiplication-lp}
#### Multiplication operators on $L^p$

For $g \in L^\infty$, $M_gf = gf$ satisfies $\|gf\|_p \leq \|g\|_\infty\|f\|_p$, and the bound is sharp: if $|g| > \lambda$
on a set $E$ of positive finite measure, $f = \mathbf{1}_E$ gives $\|gf\|_p \geq \lambda\|f\|_p$. So $\|M_g\| =
\|g\|_\infty$ on every $L^p$, $1 \leq p \leq \infty$, as for the Hilbert case $p = 2$ in @exm-bo-multiplication.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

An integral operator with a continuous kernel is bounded on $C[0, 1]$, and its norm is the largest integral of the
kernel's modulus. The third example computes it for the Volterra operator, which reappears in the Fredholm part.

::: {#exm-fan-volterra-norm}
#### The Volterra operator on $C[0, 1\rbrack$

$(Vf)(x) = \int_0^xf(t)\,dt$ satisfies $|Vf(x)| \leq x\|f\|_\infty$, so $\|V\| \leq 1$, with equality at $f = 1$,
$Vf(x) = x$. More generally $(Kf)(x) = \int_0^1k(x, t)f(t)\,dt$ with continuous $k$ has $\|K\|_{C \to C} = \max_x
\int_0^1|k(x, t)|\,dt$; for $V$, $k(x, t) = \mathbf{1}_{t \leq x}$ is not continuous, but the formula still gives
$\max_xx = 1$.
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The equivalence of continuity and boundedness is the first theorem about linear maps, and the first exercise asks for
its proof. It uses only homogeneity and the triangle inequality.

::: {#exr-fan-bounded-continuous}
#### Bounded means continuous

Show that for a linear map $T$ between normed spaces the following are equivalent: $T$ is continuous; $T$ is
continuous at $0$; $T$ is bounded @waterstraat2016 [Sec. 1.1]. Show that a bounded $T$ is Lipschitz with constant
$\|T\|$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Continuity implies continuity at $0$. If $T$ is continuous at $0$, there is $\delta > 0$ with $\|Tx\| \leq 1$ for
$\|x\| \leq \delta$; for $x \neq 0$, $\|Tx\| = \tfrac{\|x\|}{\delta}\|T(\delta x/\|x\|)\| \leq \|x\|/\delta$, so $T$
is bounded with $\|T\| \leq 1/\delta$. If $T$ is bounded, $\|Tx - Ty\| = \|T(x - y)\| \leq \|T\|\,\|x - y\|$, which is
Lipschitz continuity.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The completeness of the space of bounded maps is used constantly, for instance to sum operator series. The second
exercise asks for the proof @arcozzi2025 [Thm. 3.6].

::: {#exr-fan-bounded-maps-complete}
#### $\mathcal{B}(X, Y)$ is a Banach space

Let $Y$ be a Banach space and $(T_n)$ Cauchy in $\mathcal{B}(X, Y)$. Show that $Tx = \lim T_nx$ exists and is linear,
that $\|T\|$ is finite, and that $\|T_n - T\| \to 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\|T_nx - T_mx\| \leq \|T_n - T_m\|\,\|x\|$, so $(T_nx)$ is Cauchy in $Y$ and converges; the limit is linear because
each $T_n$ is. Given $\varepsilon$, for $n, m \geq N$ and $\|x\| \leq 1$, $\|T_nx - T_mx\| \leq \varepsilon$; letting
$m \to \infty$, $\|T_nx - Tx\| \leq \varepsilon$. So $T - T_N$ is bounded, hence $T$ is, and $\|T_n - T\| \leq
\varepsilon$ for $n \geq N$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

The Euclidean operator norm of a matrix is the largest singular value, and for small matrices it can be computed
exactly. The third exercise does so for the matrix of the figure and compares the three norms.

::: {#exr-fan-operator-norms-matrix}
#### Three norms of one matrix

For $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, show that $\|A\|_{2 \to 2} = 1 + \sqrt2$ from the eigenvalues of
$A^{\mathsf T}A$, compute the other two norms of the figure and $\|A^{-1}\|_{2 \to 2}$. Show that
$\|A\|_{2 \to 2}^2 \leq \|A\|_{1 \to 1}\|A\|_{\infty \to \infty}$ here.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$A^{\mathsf T}A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 5\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $3 \pm 2\sqrt2 = (1 \pm \sqrt2)^2$, so
$\|A\|_{2 \to 2} = 1 + \sqrt2 \approx 2.414$ and, $A^{-1}$ having the same singular values inverted and swapped,
$\|A^{-1}\|_{2 \to 2} = 1/(\sqrt2 - 1) = 1 + \sqrt2$. The largest column and row sums of $A$ are $1 + 0 = 1$, $2 + 1 = 3$ and $1 + 2 = 3$, $0 + 1 = 1$, so the other two
norms are $3$. Then $(1 + \sqrt2)^2 = 3 + 2\sqrt2 \approx 5.83 \leq 9$.

Sage computes the three norms and the norm of the inverse:

### Dual spaces

The continuous linear functionals on a normed space form its dual, which is the space of all bounded ways of
measuring a vector by a number. The figure shows, for the norms $\|\cdot\|_3$ and $\|\cdot\|_{3/2}$ of the plane, the
supporting line that realises the norm of a vector as the value of a dual vector of norm one.

![The unit ball of $\|\cdot\|_3$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ (blue) and of the dual norm $\|\cdot\|_{3/2}$ (orange). For $x =
(1, 2)/\|(1, 2)\|_3$ on the unit sphere, the functional $\varphi(z) = \langle y, z\rangle$ with $y = (1, 4)/\|(1,
4)\|_{3/2}$ has $\|y\|_{3/2} = 1$ and $\varphi(x) = 1$: the line $\varphi = 1$ (dashed) touches the ball at $x$, so
$\|\varphi\| = 1 = \|y\|_{3/2}$. Generated by `figures/fa2-dual-norms.sage`.](figures/fa2-dual-norms.svg){#fig-fa2-dual-norms width=60%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-continuous-dual}
#### Continuous dual space

The **dual space** of a normed space $X$ over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ is $X^* =
\mathcal{B}(X, \mathbb{K})$, the space of continuous linear functionals (@def-linear-functional) with the norm
$\|\varphi\| = \sup_{\|x\| \leq 1}|\varphi(x)|$. It is a Banach space even when $X$ is not. The dual of $X^*$ is the
**bidual** $X^{**}$, and each $x \in X$ defines $\hat x \in X^{**}$ by $\hat x(\varphi) = \varphi(x)$. In finite
dimensions $X^*$ is the algebraic dual of @def-dual-space; in infinite dimensions it is a proper subspace of it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The dual of $\mathbb{C}^n$ with a $p$-norm is $\mathbb{C}^n$ with the conjugate norm, as the figure shows for $p = 3$.
The first example derives it from Hölder's inequality.

::: {#exm-fan-dual-cn}
#### Duals of $(\mathbb{C}^n, \|\cdot\|_p)$

Every functional on $\mathbb{C}^n$ is $\varphi_y(x) = \sum_ky_kx_k$. By Hölder, $|\varphi_y(x)| \leq \|y\|_q\|x\|_p$,
and the extremal vector of @exr-fan-holder-equality gives equality, so $\|\varphi_y\| = \|y\|_q$ with $\tfrac1p +
\tfrac1q = 1$. The dual of $\|\cdot\|_1$ is $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ and conversely, and $\|\cdot\|_2$ is its own dual.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Evaluating a continuous function at a point is a functional on $C(K)$, and integrating against a measure is the
general one. The second example computes the norms of these functionals.

::: {#exm-fan-dual-ck}
#### Point evaluations and integrals

On $C[0, 1]$, $\delta_a(f) = f(a)$ has $|\delta_a(f)| \leq \|f\|_\infty$ with equality at $f = 1$, so $\|\delta_a\| = 1$,
and $\|\delta_a - \delta_b\| = 2$ for $a \neq b$ (take $f$ with $f(a) = 1$, $f(b) = -1$). The functional
$\varphi_g(f) = \int_0^1gf$ with $g \in L^1$ has norm $\|g\|_1$. By the Riesz-Markov theorem every functional on
$C(K)$ is integration against a complex measure, with norm its total variation @arcozzi2025 [Sec. 1.2].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

On $L^2$ evaluation at a point is not bounded, and on any infinite-dimensional space some linear functionals are
not continuous. The third example constructs one @arcozzi2025 [Prop. 3.2].

::: {#exm-fan-unbounded-functional}
#### A discontinuous linear functional

On $c_{00}$ with $\|\cdot\|_\infty$, $\varphi(a) = \sum_nna_n$ is linear and finite, but $\varphi(\delta^{(n)}) = n$
with $\|\delta^{(n)}\|_\infty = 1$, so $\varphi$ is unbounded. On a Banach space such functionals exist only by the
axiom of choice: extending $\delta^{(n)} \mapsto n$ through a Hamel basis gives an everywhere-defined, unbounded
functional on $\ell^2$ @arcozzi2025 [Prop. 3.2]. Its kernel is a dense hyperplane @waterstraat2016 [Lemma 1.1.10].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The norm of a functional on $\ell^1$ is the supremum of its values on the unit vectors. The first exercise proves
$(\ell^1)^* = \ell^\infty$ by this observation @arcozzi2025 [Exercise 3.7].

::: {#exr-fan-dual-ell1}
#### The dual of $\ell^1$

For $\varphi \in (\ell^1)^*$ set $y_n = \varphi(\delta^{(n)})$. Show $|y_n| \leq \|\varphi\|$, that $\varphi(a) =
\sum_ny_na_n$ for every $a \in \ell^1$, and that $\|\varphi\| = \|y\|_\infty$. Conclude that $(\ell^1)^*$ is
isometric to $\ell^\infty$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|y_n| = |\varphi(\delta^{(n)})| \leq \|\varphi\|$. For $a \in \ell^1$ the partial sums $\sum_{n \leq N}a_n
\delta^{(n)}$ converge to $a$ in $\ell^1$, so by continuity $\varphi(a) = \lim\sum_{n \leq N}a_ny_n$. Then $|\varphi(a)|
\leq \|y\|_\infty\|a\|_1$, so $\|\varphi\| \leq \|y\|_\infty \leq \|\varphi\|$. Conversely each $y \in \ell^\infty$
defines such a functional, so $y \mapsto \varphi$ is an isometric isomorphism.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The limit of a convergent sequence is a functional on $c$ that no element of $\ell^1$ represents. The second exercise
shows this, which is the first sign that $\ell^1$ is not reflexive @arcozzi2025 [Exercise 3.7].

::: {#exr-fan-limit-functional}
#### The limit functional

On the space $c$ of convergent sequences with $\|\cdot\|_\infty$, show that $L(a) = \lim_na_n$ is a functional of norm
$1$. Show that there is no $y \in \ell^1$ with $L(a) = \sum_ny_na_n$ for all $a \in c$ (test on the $\delta^{(n)}$).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|\lim a_n| \leq \sup|a_n|$, with equality at $a = (1, 1, \dots)$, so $\|L\| = 1$. If $L(a) = \sum y_na_n$, then $y_n
= L(\delta^{(n)}) = 0$ for every $n$, so $L = 0$, contradicting $L(1, 1, \dots) = 1$. On $c_0$ the same reasoning
shows every functional is $\sum y_na_n$ with $y \in \ell^1$, so $c_0^* = \ell^1$, while $c^*$ needs the extra
functional $L$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The norm of a functional on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with a $p$-norm can be found by maximising over the unit sphere with a
Lagrange multiplier. The third exercise compares the result with the dual-norm formula.

::: {#exr-fan-dual-norm-lagrange}
#### Dual norms by Lagrange multipliers

Maximise $\varphi(x) = x_1 + 4x_2$ over the unit sphere $x_1^3 + x_2^3 = 1$, $x_k \geq 0$, of $\|\cdot\|_3$ on
$\mathbb{R}^2$ with a Lagrange multiplier, and compare with $\|(1, 4)\|_{3/2}$. Find the maximiser and compare with the extremal vector of @exr-fan-holder-equality.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\|(1, 4)\|_{3/2} = (1 + 8)^{2/3} = 9^{2/3} \approx 4.327$. The maximiser is $x = (1, 2)/9^{1/3}$, since by the
equality case $|x_k|^3 \propto |y_k|^{3/2}$ gives $x \propto (1, 2)$; this is the point of contact in the figure. Indeed the
Lagrange condition $(1, 4) = 3\mu(x_1^2, x_2^2)$ gives $x_2/x_1 = 2$, so $x = (1, 2)/9^{1/3}$ and $\varphi(x) =
9/9^{1/3} = 9^{2/3}$.

Sage solves the Lagrange system and compares the maximum with $9^{2/3}$:

{{< sage exr-fan-dual-norm-lagrange >}}
:::

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

For $1 \leq p < \infty$ the dual of $L^p$ is $L^q$, which is the infinite-dimensional version of
@exm-fan-dual-cn. The theorem below states it; for $p = 2$ it is the Riesz representation theorem
(@thm-riesz-representation).

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-lp-duality}
#### Duality of $L^p$ spaces

Let $1 \leq p < \infty$ and $\tfrac1p + \tfrac1q = 1$, and let $\mu$ be $\sigma$-finite (for example Lebesgue measure
or counting measure). Every $\varphi \in (L^p)^*$ is $\varphi(f) = \int gf\,d\mu$ for a unique $g \in L^q$, and
$\|\varphi\| = \|g\|_q$; so $(L^p)^* \cong L^q$ isometrically, and in particular $(\ell^p)^* \cong \ell^q$. Moreover
$c_0^* \cong \ell^1$. For $p = \infty$ the map $L^1 \to (L^\infty)^*$ is isometric but not onto: $(\ell^\infty)^*$
is strictly larger than $\ell^1$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The duality pairs the spaces of the figure of the $\ell^p$ section in a fixed way. The first example lists the
pairs that recur in this chapter.

::: {#exm-fan-dual-pairs}
#### Dual pairs

$(\ell^2)^* = \ell^2$, $(\ell^{3/2})^* = \ell^3$, $(\ell^1)^* = \ell^\infty$ and $c_0^* = \ell^1$; on $(0, 1)$,
$(L^4)^* = L^{4/3}$. Since $x^{-1/4} \in L^p(0, 1)$ exactly for $p < 4$, the functional $\varphi(g) =
\int_0^1x^{-1/4}g$ is bounded on $L^q(0, 1)$ exactly for $q > \tfrac43$, with norm $\|x^{-1/4}\|_p$, $p = q/(q - 1)$.
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The bidual of $c_0$ is $\ell^\infty$, which is larger than $c_0$, so $c_0$ is not its own bidual. The second example
computes this by applying the theorem twice.

::: {#exm-fan-bidual-c0}
#### The bidual of $c_0$

$c_0^* = \ell^1$ and $(\ell^1)^* = \ell^\infty$, so $c_0^{**} = \ell^\infty$, and the canonical map $a \mapsto \hat a$
of @def-continuous-dual is the inclusion $c_0 \subset \ell^\infty$. The constant sequence $(1, 1, \dots)$ is an element
of the bidual that does not come from $c_0$. For $1 < p < \infty$, by contrast, $(\ell^p)^{**} = (\ell^q)^* = \ell^p$,
and these spaces are the model of the reflexive spaces of @sec-weak-topologies.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The dual of $\ell^\infty$ contains functionals that are not given by sequences, such as generalised limits. The third
example describes one, constructed with the Hahn-Banach theorem of the next part.

::: {#exm-fan-banach-limit}
#### A functional on $\ell^\infty$ not in $\ell^1$

The limit functional $L$ on $c$ has norm $1$; by the Hahn-Banach theorem (@thm-hahn-banach) it extends to some
$\Lambda \in (\ell^\infty)^*$ of norm $1$. Such a $\Lambda$ vanishes on $c_0$ but $\Lambda(1, 1, \dots) = 1$, so it is
not $a \mapsto \sum y_na_n$ for any $y \in \ell^1$ (which would give $y_n = \Lambda(\delta^{(n)}) = 0$). Hence
$(\ell^\infty)^* \supsetneq \ell^1$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
