:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The proof of the duality theorem for sequences is a direct extension of @exr-fan-dual-ell1, and the first exercise
asks for it. The extremal vector of Hölder's inequality supplies the lower bound on the norm.

::: {#exr-fan-ellp-dual-proof}
#### The dual of $\ell^p$

For $1 < p < \infty$ and $\varphi \in (\ell^p)^*$, put $y_n = \varphi(\delta^{(n)})$. Apply $\varphi$ to the truncation
of the extremal vector of $(y_1, \dots, y_N)$ to show $(\sum_{n \leq N}|y_n|^q)^{1/q} \leq \|\varphi\|$, and conclude
$y \in \ell^q$, $\varphi(a) = \sum y_na_n$ and $\|\varphi\| = \|y\|_q$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Let $a_n = \overline{\operatorname{sgn}y_n}|y_n|^{q - 1}$ for $n \leq N$ and $0$ beyond. Then $\varphi(a) = \sum_{n \leq
N}|y_n|^q$ and $\|a\|_p = (\sum_{n \leq N}|y_n|^{(q - 1)p})^{1/p} = (\sum_{n \leq N}|y_n|^q)^{1/p}$, since $(q - 1)p
= q$. From $\varphi(a) \leq \|\varphi\|\,\|a\|_p$ we get $(\sum_{n \leq N}|y_n|^q)^{1 - 1/p} \leq \|\varphi\|$, that
is, the claim. Letting $N \to \infty$, $\|y\|_q \leq \|\varphi\|$; density of $c_{00}$ in $\ell^p$ gives $\varphi(a) =
\sum y_na_n$, and Hölder gives the reverse inequality.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The norm of the functional $\varphi(f) = \int_0^1x^{-1/4}f$ on $L^q(0, 1)$ can be computed exactly. The second
exercise does so and tests the bound on two functions.

::: {#exr-fan-lp-functional-norm}
#### The norm of an integral functional

For $q = 2$, compute the norm of $\varphi(f) = \int_0^1x^{-1/4}f(x)\,dx$ on $L^2(0, 1)$ and a function at which it is
attained. Check the bound $|\varphi(f)| \leq \|\varphi\|\,\|f\|_2$ on $f = 1$ and $f = x$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By the theorem $\|\varphi\| = \|x^{-1/4}\|_2 = (\int_0^1x^{-1/2})^{1/2} = \sqrt2$, attained at $f = x^{-1/4}/\sqrt2$.
For $f = 1$, $\varphi(1) = \tfrac43 \leq \sqrt2$; for $f = x$, $\varphi(x) = \tfrac47$ and $\|x\|_2 = 1/\sqrt3$, with
$\tfrac47 \approx 0.571 \leq \sqrt2/\sqrt3 \approx 0.816$.

Sage computes the norm, the maximiser and the two test values:

{{< sage exr-fan-lp-functional-norm >}}
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The duality theorem fails for $p = \infty$, and the failure is detected by the separability of the dual. The third
exercise uses the fact that a space with a separable dual is itself separable @arcozzi2025 [Thm. 3.8].

::: {#exr-fan-ell1-not-dual-of-ellinfty}
#### Why $(\ell^\infty)^* \neq \ell^1$, again

Using @arcozzi2025 [Thm. 3.8] (if $X^*$ is separable, so is $X$) and @exr-fan-separability, show that
$(\ell^\infty)^*$ is not isometric to $\ell^1$, and deduce that $\ell^1$ is not reflexive.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $(\ell^\infty)^*$ were (isometric to) $\ell^1$, which is separable, then by the theorem $\ell^\infty$ would be
separable, contradicting @exr-fan-separability. The same argument shows that $\ell^1$ is not reflexive: if $\ell^1 =
(\ell^1)^{**} = (\ell^\infty)^*$, then $(\ell^\infty)^*$ would be separable.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### Exercises

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The exercises of this part combine norms, completeness, the standard spaces, bounded maps and duals. They prepare the
four principles of the next part, each of which uses completeness in an essential way.

Completeness of the bounded maps and the series criterion together give a quick proof that operators close to the
identity are invertible. The first integrative exercise carries it out on $\ell^p$.

::: {#exr-fan-banach-identity-perturbation}
#### Operators near the identity

Let $X$ be a Banach space and $T \in \mathcal{B}(X)$ with $\|T\| < 1$. Show that $\sum_kT^k$ converges in
$\mathcal{B}(X)$ to $(1 - T)^{-1}$, with $\|(1 - T)^{-1}\| \leq 1/(1 - \|T\|)$. Apply this on $\ell^p$ to $T =
\tfrac12S$, with $S$ the right shift, and compute $(1 - T)^{-1}\delta^{(1)}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\sum\|T^k\| \leq \sum\|T\|^k = 1/(1 - \|T\|)$, so the series converges by @thm-absolute-series in the Banach space
$\mathcal{B}(X)$ (@def-bounded-linear-map), and $(1 - T)\sum_{k \leq N}T^k = 1 - T^{N + 1} \to 1$, similarly on the
other side. For $T = \tfrac12S$, $\|T\| = \tfrac12$ on every $\ell^p$, and $(1 - T)^{-1}\delta^{(1)} = \sum_k2^{-k}
S^k\delta^{(1)} = (1, \tfrac12, \tfrac14, \dots)$, of $\ell^p$ norm $(1 - 2^{-p})^{-1/p} \leq 2$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The dual of a space depends on its norm, and different norms on the same functions give different duals. The second
integrative exercise compares the duals of the continuous functions with two norms.

::: {#exr-fan-dual-depends-on-norm}
#### Duals depend on the norm

Show that the point evaluation $\delta_{1/2}$ is a bounded functional on $(C[0, 1], \|\cdot\|_\infty)$ but not on $(C[0,
1], \|\cdot\|_1)$, using the ramps or the bumps of this part. Identify the dual of $(C[0, 1], \|\cdot\|_1)$ using its
completion.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|f(\tfrac12)| \leq \|f\|_\infty$. In $\|\cdot\|_1$, the tent $h_n$ of height $1$ supported on $[\tfrac12 - \tfrac1n,
\tfrac12 + \tfrac1n]$ has $\|h_n\|_1 = \tfrac1n$ and $\delta_{1/2}(h_n) = 1$, so $\delta_{1/2}$ is unbounded. A bounded
functional on a dense subspace extends uniquely to the completion with the same norm @arcozzi2025 [Exercise 3.5], so
the dual of $(C[0, 1], \|\cdot\|_1)$ is the dual of its completion $L^1(0, 1)$, which is $L^\infty(0, 1)$ by
@thm-lp-duality.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The space $\ell^p$ with $1 < p < \infty$ sits between $\ell^1$ and $\ell^\infty$, and the shift acts on all of them
with the same norm. The third integrative exercise computes norms of the shift and of a diagonal operator on all the
$\ell^p$ and compares them with their finite truncations.

::: {#exr-fan-ellp-operators}
#### Operators on all the $\ell^p$

Show that the right shift $S$ and the diagonal operator $D = \operatorname{diag}(1, \tfrac12, \tfrac13, \dots)$ have
$\|S\| = 1$ and $\|D\| = 1$ on every $\ell^p$, and that $\|D^k\| = 1$, while $\|(D - \tfrac12)\| = \tfrac12$. Compute
the $1 \to 1$ and $\infty \to \infty$ norms of the $6 \times 6$ truncations of $S$, $D$ and
$S + D$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$S$ preserves every $\ell^p$ norm, so $\|S\| = 1$. For a diagonal operator $\|D\| = \sup_n|d_n|$ on every $\ell^p$ (as
in @exm-fan-multiplication-lp), giving $1$ for $D$ and $D^k$ and $\sup_n|1/n - \tfrac12| = \tfrac12$ for $D -
\tfrac12$. For the truncation of $S + D$ the largest column sum is $1 + 1 = 2$ (first column) and the largest row sum is
$1 + \tfrac12 = \tfrac32$ (second row), so the $1 \to 1$ and $\infty \to \infty$ norms are $2$ and $\tfrac32$, and
the Euclidean norm, bounded by $\sqrt{2\cdot\tfrac32} = \sqrt3$ (@exr-fan-operator-norms-matrix), lies between.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

## The four principles {#sec-four-principles}

Four theorems carry most of the weight of functional analysis on Banach spaces. The Hahn-Banach theorem supplies
enough continuous functionals to separate points; the Baire category theorem turns completeness into a statement
about the size of sets; the uniform boundedness principle and the open mapping theorem, both consequences of Baire's,
turn pointwise information into uniform estimates. This part states each theorem, proves the shorter ones in the
exercises, and shows by counterexamples why each hypothesis, completeness above all, is needed. The proofs follow
@arcozzi2025 [Sec. 3.2, 3.5 and 3.6]; closed operators follow @picard2020primer [Sec. B.4] and @waterstraat2016 [Sec.
1.2].

### The Hahn-Banach theorem

A functional defined on a subspace can be extended to the whole space without increasing its norm. In a Hilbert space
this is an orthogonal projection followed by the Riesz representation, but in a general normed space there is no
projection, and the extension needs an argument by induction on dimensions closed off by Zorn's lemma.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-hahn-banach}
#### Hahn-Banach theorem

Let $X$ be a real vector space, $p : X \to \mathbb{R}$ **sublinear** ($p(x + y) \leq p(x) + p(y)$ and $p(tx) = tp(x)$
for $t \geq 0$), $Y \subset X$ a subspace and $\ell : Y \to \mathbb{R}$ linear with $\ell \leq p$ on $Y$. Then $\ell$
has a linear extension $L$ to $X$ with $L \leq p$ on $X$; over $\mathbb{C}$ the same holds with $|\ell| \leq p$
@arcozzi2025 [Thms. 3.4 and 3.5]. Consequences for a normed space $X$: every $\lambda \in Y^*$ extends to some $L \in
X^*$ with $\|L\| = \|\lambda\|$; for every $x \in X$ there is $\varphi \in X^*$ with $\|\varphi\| = 1$ and $\varphi(x)
= \|x\|$; the canonical map $x \mapsto \hat x$ of $X$ into $X^{**}$ is an isometry; and for a subspace $Z$ and $y$ at
distance $d(y, Z) > 0$ there is $\varphi \in X^*$ with $\|\varphi\| = 1$, $\varphi|_Z = 0$ and $\varphi(y) = d(y, Z)$
@arcozzi2025 [Cors. 3.1-3.3, Thm. 3.7]. In geometric form, two disjoint convex sets, one of them open, are separated
by a closed real hyperplane @ramesh2020weak [Thm. 2.15].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
In a Hilbert space the extension is explicit and unique, which is the case to compare with. The first example
writes it down @arcozzi2025 [Exercise 3.1].

::: {#exm-fan-hb-hilbert}
#### Extension in a Hilbert space

Let $M$ be a closed subspace of a Hilbert space $H$ and $\lambda \in M^*$. By the Riesz representation theorem
(@thm-riesz-representation) on $M$, $\lambda(m) = \langle y, m\rangle$ for some $y \in M$ with $\|y\| = \|\lambda\|$.
Then $L(x) = \langle y, x\rangle$ extends $\lambda$ with $\|L\| = \|y\|$. It is the only norm-preserving extension:
any other is $\langle y + z, x\rangle$ with $z \perp M$, of norm $(\|y\|^2 + \|z\|^2)^{1/2}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Outside Hilbert spaces the norm-preserving extension is usually not unique, and the plane with the norm $\|\cdot\|_1$
already shows it. The second example finds all the extensions.

::: {#exm-fan-hb-nonunique}
#### Many extensions in $(\mathbb{R}^2, \|\cdot\|_1)$

On $Y = \mathbb{R}e_1$ let $\ell(te_1) = t$, of norm $1$. Every extension is $L_c(x) = x_1 + cx_2$, and its norm for
$\|\cdot\|_1$ is the dual norm $\|(1, c)\|_\infty = \max(1, |c|)$ (@exm-fan-dual-cn). So every $c \in [-1, 1]$ gives a
norm-preserving extension: the unit ball of $\|\cdot\|_1$ has a corner at $e_1$, and every line through the corner
that does not cut the ball supports it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The norming functionals of the theorem can be written down in the standard spaces. The third example lists them; in
each case the functional touches the unit ball at $x/\|x\|$.

::: {#exm-fan-norming-functionals}
#### Norming functionals

In $\ell^p$, $1 < p < \infty$, the norming functional of $x$ is the extremal vector of @exr-fan-holder-equality. In
$C[0, 1]$, if $|f|$ attains its maximum at $x_0$, then $\varphi = \overline{\operatorname{sgn}f(x_0)}\,\delta_{x_0}$
has $\|\varphi\| = 1$ and $\varphi(f) = \|f\|_\infty$; for $f(x) = x - x^2$ this is $\delta_{1/2}$. In $\ell^1$ the
functional $y = (\overline{\operatorname{sgn}x_n}) \in \ell^\infty$ norms $x$, and it is not unique when some $x_n =
0$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The uniqueness in Hilbert spaces is a consequence of the strict convexity of the unit ball, and the first exercise
proves it directly @arcozzi2025 [Exercise 3.6]. The argument uses only the parallelogram law.

::: {#exr-fan-hb-hilbert-proof}
#### Uniqueness in Hilbert spaces

Let $L, L'$ be two extensions of $\lambda \in M^*$ to $H$ with $\|L\| = \|L'\| = \|\lambda\|$. Represent them by
vectors $y, y'$ and use the parallelogram law on $\tfrac12(y + y')$ to show $y = y'$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Both $y$ and $y'$ have norm $\|\lambda\|$, and $\tfrac12(L + L')$ also extends $\lambda$, so $\|\tfrac12(y + y')\| \geq
\|\lambda\|$. The parallelogram law gives $\|\tfrac12(y - y')\|^2 = \tfrac12\|y\|^2 + \tfrac12\|y'\|^2 - \|\tfrac12(y +
y')\|^2 \leq \|\lambda\|^2 - \|\lambda\|^2 = 0$, so $y = y'$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In $\ell^1$ the norm-preserving extensions of a functional on a line form a large set, which the second exercise
describes @arcozzi2025 [Exercise 3.9]. The answer is a whole face of the dual unit ball.

::: {#exr-fan-hb-ell1}
#### All extensions in $\ell^1$

On the line $\mathbb{C}\delta^{(1)} \subset \ell^1$ let $\ell(t\delta^{(1)}) = t$. Using $(\ell^1)^* = \ell^\infty$
(@exr-fan-dual-ell1), find all $L \in (\ell^1)^*$ extending $\ell$ with $\|L\| = 1$. How does this differ from
@exm-fan-hb-hilbert?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$L$ is given by $y \in \ell^\infty$ with $L(\delta^{(1)}) = y_1 = 1$ and $\|L\| = \|y\|_\infty = 1$. So the extensions
are exactly the sequences $(1, y_2, y_3, \dots)$ with $|y_n| \leq 1$: an infinite-dimensional family, compared with the
single extension in a Hilbert space.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The distance functional of the theorem can be computed in the plane, where the dual norm is explicit. The third
exercise does so and compares the functional with the dual norm.

::: {#exr-fan-hb-distance}
#### The distance functional

In $(\mathbb{R}^2, \|\cdot\|_\infty)$ let $Z = \mathbb{R}(1, 1)$ and $y = (1, 0)$. Compute $d(y, Z)$ and find the
functional $\varphi$ of the theorem with $\|\varphi\| = 1$, $\varphi(1, 1) = 0$ and $\varphi(y) = d(y, Z)$, by
minimising $\|y - t(1, 1)\|_\infty$ over $t$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\|y - t(1, 1)\|_\infty = \max(|1 - t|, |t|)$ is minimal at $t = \tfrac12$, so $d(y, Z) = \tfrac12$. A functional
vanishing on $(1, 1)$ is $\varphi(x) = c(x_1 - x_2)$, of norm $\|(c, -c)\|_1 = 2|c|$; so $c = \tfrac12$, and
$\varphi(y) = \tfrac12 = d(y, Z)$.

A grid search in Sage confirms the minimum and the functional:

{{< sage exr-fan-hb-distance >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The isometry of the canonical embedding is the reason every normed space sits in a Banach space of the same norm. The
fourth exercise asks for the proof @arcozzi2025 [Thm. 3.7].

::: {#exr-fan-hb-bidual}
#### The canonical embedding is isometric

Show $\|\hat x\|_{X^{**}} \leq \|x\|$ from $|\varphi(x)| \leq \|\varphi\|\,\|x\|$, and the reverse inequality from the
norming functional of $x$. Deduce that the closure of $\{\hat x\}$ in $X^{**}$ is a completion of $X$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|\hat x(\varphi)| = |\varphi(x)| \leq \|\varphi\|\,\|x\|$ gives $\|\hat x\| \leq \|x\|$; the norming functional
$\varphi$ has $\|\varphi\| = 1$ and $\hat x(\varphi) = \|x\|$, giving equality. $X^{**}$ is a Banach space
(@def-continuous-dual), so the closure of the isometric image of $X$ is complete and contains $X$ densely, which is the
completion of @def-banach-space.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### The Baire category theorem

In a complete metric space a set that is "thin" in a precise sense cannot fill the space, even after a countable union.
The figure shows a function that the theorem produces in abundance, a continuous function with no derivative at any
point, and the definition below makes "thin" precise.

![Left: partial sums $W_N(x) = \sum_{n = 0}^N2^{-n}\cos(3^n\pi x)$ of the Weierstrass function for $N = 1, 3, 8$ on
$[-1, 1]$; they converge uniformly, since the terms are bounded by $2^{-n}$, to a continuous function that is
differentiable nowhere. Right: the difference quotients $|W(h) - W(0)|/h$ at $h = 3^{-m}$, growing like
$4(\tfrac32)^m$. Generated by `figures/fa2-weierstrass-function.sage`.](figures/fa2-weierstrass-function.svg){#fig-fa2-weierstrass-function width=95%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-meagre-set}
#### Meagre set

A subset $A$ of a metric space $M$ is **nowhere dense** if its closure contains no open ball, and **meagre** (or of the
**first category**) if it is a countable union of nowhere dense sets. A set whose complement is meagre is
**comeagre** (or **residual**); a property that holds on a comeagre set holds for a **generic** point. A closed set is
nowhere dense if and only if its complement is open and dense.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A single point of $\mathbb{R}$ is nowhere dense, so every countable set is meagre. The first example draws the
conclusion for the rationals, which are dense and meagre at the same time.

::: {#exm-fan-rationals-meagre}
#### The rationals

$\mathbb{Q} = \bigcup_{q}\{q\}$ is a countable union of closed sets with empty interior, hence meagre in $\mathbb{R}$,
although it is dense. Its complement, the irrationals, is comeagre. "Meagre" and "of measure zero" are different
notions: the irrationals in $[0, 1]$ have measure one, and there are comeagre sets of measure zero.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Cantor set is uncountable but nowhere dense, so size in the sense of cardinality and in the sense of category
also differ. The second example records its construction.

::: {#exm-fan-cantor}
#### The Cantor set

Remove the open middle third of $[0, 1]$, then of each remaining interval, and so on; after $n$ steps $2^n$ intervals
of total length $(\tfrac23)^n$ remain, and the Cantor set $C$ is their intersection. It is closed, and it contains no
interval, since it lies in intervals of length $3^{-n}$; so it is nowhere dense, though it is uncountable (points of $C$
are the numbers with ternary digits $0$ and $2$).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In a normed space every proper closed subspace is nowhere dense, which is the fact that the Baire argument against
countable bases uses. The third example states it with the finitely supported sequences in $\ell^2$.

::: {#exm-fan-subspaces-nowhere-dense}
#### Proper subspaces

A proper closed subspace $F$ of a normed space contains no ball: if $B(x, r) \subset F$ then $B(0, r) \subset F - x =
F$, and then $F$ contains every vector, by scaling. So the finite-dimensional subspaces $F_N = \operatorname{span}\{
\delta^{(1)}, \dots, \delta^{(N)}\}$ of $\ell^2$ are nowhere dense (closed by @thm-norm-equivalence), and $c_{00} =
\bigcup_NF_N$ is meagre in $\ell^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise characterises nowhere dense closed sets by their complements. It is the form in which Baire's
theorem is usually applied.

::: {#exr-fan-nowhere-dense-complement}
#### Nowhere dense and open dense

Show that a closed set $F$ is nowhere dense if and only if $M \setminus F$ is open and dense, and that $A$ is nowhere
dense if and only if its closure is. Deduce that a countable intersection of open dense sets is comeagre.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$M \setminus F$ is open since $F$ is closed. It is dense if and only if every ball meets it, if and only if no ball lies
inside $F$. Nowhere density of $A$ is defined through $\bar A$, which is closed and has closure $\bar A$. If $U_n$ are
open and dense, $F_n = M \setminus U_n$ are closed nowhere dense, and $\bigcap U_n = M \setminus\bigcup F_n$ is the
complement of a meagre set.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The total length of the Cantor construction tends to zero, while the number of intervals doubles at each step. The
second exercise computes both and shows that $\tfrac14$ is a point of the Cantor set.

::: {#exr-fan-cantor-stages}
#### Stages of the Cantor set

Describe the $2^n$ intervals of the $n$-th stage for $n \leq 6$, compute their total length $(\tfrac23)^n$,
and check that $\tfrac14 = 0.0202\ldots_3$ lies in every stage. Is $\tfrac14$ an endpoint of some interval?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The $n$-th stage consists of the intervals $[0.d_1\dots d_n{}_3, 0.d_1\dots d_n{}_3 + 3^{-n}]$ with ternary digits
$d_k \in \{0, 2\}$, so there are $2^n$ of them, each of length $3^{-n}$. The lengths are $1, \tfrac23, \tfrac49, \dots, (\tfrac23)^6 = \tfrac{64}{729}$. $\tfrac14$ has ternary expansion
$0.\overline{02}_3$, using only the digits $0$ and $2$, so it lies in every stage, but it is not an endpoint, since
endpoints have finite expansions (ending in repeated $0$s or $2$s from some digit on, like $\tfrac13 = 0.1_3 =
0.0\overline{2}_3$).

Sage generates the stages exactly and the ternary digits of $\tfrac14$:

{{< sage exr-fan-cantor-stages >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The rationals are dense and meagre, and the third exercise shows that they cannot be written as a countable
intersection of open sets. The proof uses @thm-baire, applied in the complete space $\mathbb{R}$.

::: {#exr-fan-rationals-not-gdelta}
#### $\mathbb{Q}$ is not a countable intersection of open sets

Suppose $\mathbb{Q} = \bigcap_nU_n$ with $U_n$ open. Show that each $U_n$ is dense, and that $\mathbb{R} = \bigcup_n(
\mathbb{R} \setminus U_n) \cup \bigcup_q\{q\}$ writes $\mathbb{R}$ as a countable union of nowhere dense sets.
Conclude with Baire's theorem.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$U_n \supset \mathbb{Q}$ is dense, so $\mathbb{R} \setminus U_n$ is closed nowhere dense. Every real number is either
rational or outside some $U_n$, which gives the countable union. Each piece is nowhere dense, so $\mathbb{R}$ would be
meagre, contradicting the Baire theorem for the complete metric space $\mathbb{R}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

Completeness rules out a countable union of thin sets filling the space. The theorem below states this; the proof is
a nested sequence of balls whose centres form a Cauchy sequence.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-baire}
#### Baire category theorem

A complete metric space is not meagre in itself: if $M = \bigcup_nA_n$, some $\bar A_n$ contains a ball. Equivalently,
a countable intersection of open dense subsets of a complete metric space is dense @arcozzi2025 [Thm. 3.12]. In the
Banach space $C[0, 1]$ the functions that are differentiable at some point form a meagre set, so a generic continuous
function is differentiable nowhere.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first consequence is that a Banach space cannot be too small in dimension. The first example combines the theorem
with @exm-fan-subspaces-nowhere-dense.

::: {#exm-fan-baire-no-countable-basis}
#### No countable basis, by category

If an infinite-dimensional Banach space $X$ had a countable algebraic basis $v_1, v_2, \dots$, then $X = \bigcup_N
\operatorname{span}\{v_1, \dots, v_N\}$ would be a countable union of proper closed subspaces, each nowhere dense, which
the theorem forbids. This is a second proof of @exr-fan-no-countable-basis, and it shows in particular that $c_{00}$
admits no complete norm.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The theorem shows that the reals are uncountable without decimal expansions. The second example gives the argument,
which is the simplest application of the theorem.

::: {#exm-fan-reals-uncountable}
#### $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable

If $\mathbb{R} = \{r_1, r_2, \dots\}$, then $\mathbb{R} = \bigcup_n\{r_n\}$ would be a countable union of nowhere dense
closed sets, contradicting the theorem for the complete metric space $\mathbb{R}$. The same argument shows that a
complete metric space without isolated points, such as the Cantor set, is uncountable.
:::

:::

The Weierstrass function of the figure is an explicit continuous nowhere-differentiable function, while the theorem
says that such functions are the rule. The third example describes it.

::: {#exm-fan-weierstrass-function}
#### The Weierstrass function

$W(x) = \sum_{n \geq 0}a^n\cos(b^n\pi x)$ with $0 < a < 1$ and an odd integer $b$ with $ab \geq 1$ converges
uniformly by the Weierstrass test, so $W \in C(\mathbb{R})$, and it is differentiable nowhere (Weierstrass for $ab > 1 +
\tfrac32\pi$, Hardy for $ab \geq 1$). The figure uses $a = \tfrac12$, $b = 3$: at $x = 0$ the difference quotients at $h
= 3^{-m}$ are about $-4(\tfrac32)^m$ (@exr-fan-weierstrass-quotients).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The proof of the theorem is a nested-balls argument. The first exercise asks for it in full @arcozzi2025 [Thm. 3.12].

::: {#exr-fan-baire-proof}
#### Proof of Baire's theorem

Let $A_n$ be nowhere dense in a complete metric space $M$. Construct closed balls $\bar B(x_n, r_n)$ with $r_n <
2^{-n}$, $\bar B(x_{n + 1}, r_{n + 1}) \subset B(x_n, r_n)$ and $\bar B(x_n, r_n) \cap \bar A_n = \emptyset$. Show that
$(x_n)$ is Cauchy and its limit lies outside every $A_n$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Since $\bar A_1$ contains no ball, $M \setminus\bar A_1$ is a non-empty open set, containing some ball $\bar B(x_1,
r_1)$ with $r_1 < \tfrac12$. Inductively, $B(x_n, r_n) \setminus\bar A_{n + 1}$ is open and non-empty and contains a
closed ball of radius $< 2^{-n - 1}$. For $m > n$, $x_m \in B(x_n, r_n)$, so $d(x_m, x_n) < 2^{-n}$ and $(x_n)$ is
Cauchy, with limit $x$ in each closed ball $\bar B(x_n, r_n)$, hence in no $\bar A_n$. So $\bigcup A_n \neq M$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The growth of the difference quotients of the Weierstrass function can be computed exactly at $x = 0$. The second
exercise does this by splitting the series at $n = m$.

::: {#exr-fan-weierstrass-quotients}
#### Difference quotients at the origin

For $W(x) = \sum_n2^{-n}\cos(3^n\pi x)$ and $h = 3^{-m}$, show that the terms with $n \geq m$ contribute exactly
$-4\cdot 2^{-m}$ to $W(h) - W(0)$, and bound the terms with $n < m$ by $\tfrac{\pi^2}{2}\sum_{n < m}2^{-n}9^{n - m}$.
Conclude that $|W(h) - W(0)|/h \geq (4 - \tfrac{\pi^2}7)(\tfrac32)^m$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For $n \geq m$, $3^nh = 3^{n - m}$ is odd, so $\cos(3^{n - m}\pi) - 1 = -2$, and $\sum_{n \geq m}2^{-n}(-2) = -4\cdot
2^{-m}$. For $n < m$, $|\cos t - 1| \leq t^2/2$ with $t = 3^{n - m}\pi$ gives the bound, and
$\tfrac{\pi^2}{2}9^{-m}\sum_{n < m}(\tfrac92)^n = \tfrac{\pi^2}{2}9^{-m}\tfrac{(9/2)^m - 1}{7/2} \leq
\tfrac{\pi^2}{7}2^{-m}$. So $|W(h) - W(0)| \geq (4 - \tfrac{\pi^2}7)2^{-m}$, and dividing by $h = 3^{-m}$ gives the
claim; since $4 - \pi^2/7 \approx 2.59 > 0$, the quotients tend to infinity and $W$ is not differentiable at $0$.

Sage evaluates the quotients with sixty terms of the series in high precision; the terms with $n \geq m$ add up to $-4\cdot2^{-m}$ up to the truncation:

{{< sage exr-fan-weierstrass-quotients >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The theorem needs completeness, and the space of polynomials shows what goes wrong without it. The third exercise
makes this precise.

::: {#exr-fan-baire-needs-completeness}
#### Completeness is needed

Show that the polynomials with the supremum norm on $[0, 1]$ form a normed space that is a countable union of nowhere
dense sets. Which step of the proof of the theorem fails?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The polynomials of degree $\leq N$ form a finite-dimensional, hence closed, proper subspace $P_N$, which is nowhere
dense (@exm-fan-subspaces-nowhere-dense), and the polynomial space is $\bigcup_NP_N$. In the proof the centres of the
nested balls form a Cauchy sequence whose limit, a continuous function, need not be a polynomial: the last step uses
completeness.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

### Uniform boundedness

A family of bounded operators that is bounded at each point of a Banach space is bounded uniformly. The figure shows
the most famous consequence: the norms of the Fourier partial-sum functionals grow without bound, so some continuous
function has a divergent Fourier series.

![Left: the Dirichlet kernels $D_N(x) = \sin((N + \tfrac12)x)/\sin(x/2)$ for $N = 4, 8$, whose peak height $2N + 1$
grows while their integral stays $2\pi$. Right: the Lebesgue constants $L_N = \tfrac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^\pi|D_N|$, the
norms of $f \mapsto S_Nf(0)$ on $C(S^1)$, against $\tfrac4{\pi^2}\log N$; they grow like the logarithm.
Generated by `figures/fa2-lebesgue-constants.sage`.](figures/fa2-lebesgue-constants.svg){#fig-fa2-lebesgue-constants width=95%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-uniform-boundedness}
#### Uniform boundedness principle

Let $X$ be a Banach space, $Y$ a normed space and $\mathcal{F} \subset \mathcal{B}(X, Y)$ a family with $\sup_{T \in
\mathcal{F}}\|Tx\| < \infty$ for every $x \in X$. Then $\sup_{T \in \mathcal{F}}\|T\| < \infty$ (**Banach-Steinhaus**)
@arcozzi2025 [Thm. 3.13]. Consequently, if $T_n \in \mathcal{B}(X, Y)$ and $Tx = \lim T_nx$ exists for every $x$, then
$T$ is bounded with $\|T\| \leq \liminf\|T_n\|$ @arcozzi2025 [Cor. 3.4]; @ramesh2020weak [Thm. 2.16]. Equivalently, if
$\sup_{T \in \mathcal{F}}\|T\| = \infty$, the points $x$ with $\sup_T\|Tx\| = \infty$ form a comeagre set.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The Fourier partial sums at a point are functionals on $C(S^1)$, and their norms are the Lebesgue constants of the
figure. The first example applies the principle to them.

::: {#exm-fan-divergent-fourier}
#### A continuous function with divergent Fourier series

$\Lambda_Nf = S_Nf(0) = \tfrac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^\pi D_N(x)f(x)\,dx$ (@def-fourier-partial-sum) has norm $\|\Lambda_N\| =
L_N = \tfrac1{2\pi}\int|D_N|$ on $C(S^1)$ (@exm-fan-dual-ck), and $L_N \geq \tfrac4{\pi^2}\log N \to \infty$. By the
principle there is $f \in C(S^1)$ with $\sup_N|S_Nf(0)| = \infty$, and such $f$ are generic. Uniform convergence of
Fourier series needs more than continuity, for instance $\sum|\hat f(n)| < \infty$ (@exm-fan-ck-circle).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A pointwise limit of bounded operators is bounded, which in Hilbert space is a familiar fact about projections. The
second example shows the limit of the truncations and the limit of the shifts.

::: {#exm-fan-pointwise-limits}
#### Pointwise limits

The truncations $P_N a = (a_1, \dots, a_N, 0, \dots)$ on $\ell^p$, $p < \infty$, have $\|P_N\| = 1$ and $P_Na \to a$, so
the limit $1$ is bounded with norm $\leq 1$. The powers of the backward shift satisfy $(S^*)^na \to 0$ for every $a \in
\ell^2$, although $\|(S^*)^n\| = 1$: the bound $\|T\| \leq\liminf\|T_n\|$ can be strict, and pointwise convergence does
not imply norm convergence.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Without completeness the principle fails, and the finitely supported sequences give the counterexample. The third
example constructs a pointwise bounded but unbounded family on them.

::: {#exm-fan-ubp-incomplete}
#### Completeness is needed

On $c_{00}$ with $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ let $\varphi_n(a) = na_n$. For each $a \in c_{00}$ the sequence $\varphi_n(a)$ is
eventually $0$, so $\sup_n|\varphi_n(a)| < \infty$; but $\|\varphi_n\| = n$. The principle fails because $c_{00}$ is not
complete; on its completion $c_0$, the sequence $a_n = n^{-1/2}$ gives $\varphi_n(a) = \sqrt n \to \infty$.
:::

**Lean.** Pending.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The proof is a direct application of Baire's theorem to the sets where the family is bounded by $m$. The first exercise
asks for it @arcozzi2025 [Thm. 3.13].

::: {#exr-fan-ubp-proof}
#### Proof of the principle

Let $A_m = \{x : \sup_T\|Tx\| \leq m\}$. Show that the $A_m$ are closed and cover $X$, that some $A_m$ contains a ball
$\bar B(z, r)$, and that then $\|T\| \leq 2m/r$ for all $T \in \mathcal{F}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$A_m = \bigcap_T\{x : \|Tx\| \leq m\}$ is an intersection of closed sets, and by hypothesis every $x$ lies in some
$A_m$. By @thm-baire some $A_m$ contains $\bar B(z, r)$. For $\|x\| \leq 1$, $z + rx$ and $z$ lie in $A_m$, so
$\|T(rx)\| \leq \|T(z + rx)\| + \|Tz\| \leq 2m$, that is $\|Tx\| \leq 2m/r$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Lebesgue constants grow like a logarithm, and a lower bound of this form follows from an elementary estimate.
The second exercise computes the first two exactly and proves the growth.

::: {#exr-fan-lebesgue-constants}
#### Growth of the Lebesgue constants

Show $L_0 = 1$ and $L_1 = \tfrac13 + \tfrac{2\sqrt3}{\pi}$. Then use $|\sin(x/2)| \leq |x|/2$ to show $L_N \geq
\tfrac1\pi\int_0^\pi|\sin((N + \tfrac12)x)|\,\tfrac{2}{x}\,dx$, and bound this below by $\tfrac{4}{\pi^2}\sum_{k = 1}^N
\tfrac1k$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$D_0 = 1$ gives $L_0 = 1$. $D_1 = 1 + 2\cos x$ changes sign at $x = \pm\tfrac{2\pi}3$, and integrating $|1 + 2\cos x|$
gives $2\pi L_1 = (\tfrac{4\pi}3 + 2\sqrt3) + (2\sqrt3 - \tfrac{2\pi}3) = \tfrac{2\pi}3 + 4\sqrt3$. For the lower
bound, $D_N$ is even and $|\sin(x/2)| \leq x/2$, so $L_N \geq \tfrac1\pi\int_0^\pi|\sin((N + \tfrac12)x)|\tfrac2x
dx$. With $t = (N + \tfrac12)x$ this is $\tfrac2\pi\int_0^{(N + 1/2)\pi}|\sin t|\tfrac{dt}t \geq \tfrac2\pi\sum_{k =
1}^N\tfrac1{k\pi}\int_{(k - 1)\pi}^{k\pi}|\sin t|\,dt = \tfrac4{\pi^2}\sum_{k = 1}^N\tfrac1k \geq \tfrac4{\pi^2}
\log(N + 1)$.

Sage integrates $|D_N|$ between its zeros and compares with the lower bound and with the asymptotic $\tfrac4{\pi^2}\log N$:

{{< sage exr-fan-lebesgue-constants >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A set that every functional sees as bounded is bounded in norm, which the third exercise derives from the principle
@ramesh2020weak [Def. 2.22, Rem. 2.23 and the text after it]. The bidual embedding of @thm-hahn-banach turns vectors
into functionals on $X^*$.

::: {#exr-fan-weakly-bounded}
#### Weakly bounded sets are bounded

Let $A \subset X$ with $\sup_{a \in A}|\varphi(a)| < \infty$ for every $\varphi \in X^*$. Apply the principle to the
family $\{\hat a : a \in A\} \subset \mathcal{B}(X^*, \mathbb{K})$, using that $X^*$ is complete, and conclude that
$\sup_{a \in A}\|a\| < \infty$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$X^*$ is a Banach space (@def-continuous-dual), and $\hat a(\varphi) = \varphi(a)$ is bounded in $a$ for each fixed
$\varphi$ by hypothesis. The principle gives $\sup_a\|\hat a\| < \infty$, and $\|\hat a\| = \|a\|$ by
@thm-hahn-banach.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### Open mapping and closed graph

A bounded bijection between Banach spaces has a bounded inverse, and a linear map whose graph is closed is bounded.
Both statements fail for the differentiation operator, which is closed but unbounded because it is not defined on the
whole space; the figure shows why it is unbounded, and the definition below names the operators with closed graphs.

![Left: $f_n(x) = \sin(n^2x)/n$ on $[0, \pi]$ for $n = 1, 2, 4$; they tend to $0$ uniformly. Right: $\|f_n\|_\infty =
1/n$ and $\|f_n'\|_\infty = n$ on logarithmic axes: differentiation is unbounded on $C^1[0, \pi] \subset C[0, \pi]$, yet
its graph is closed. Generated by `figures/fa2-unbounded-derivative.sage`.](figures/fa2-unbounded-derivative.svg){#fig-fa2-unbounded-derivative width=95%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-closed-operator}
#### Closed operator

A linear operator $T : D(T) \subset X \to Y$ between Banach spaces, defined on a subspace $D(T)$, is **closed** if its
graph $\{(x, Tx) : x \in D(T)\}$ is closed in $X \times Y$, that is, if $x_n \to x$ and $Tx_n \to y$ with $x_n \in D(T)$
imply $x \in D(T)$ and $Tx = y$ @picard2020primer [Def. B.4.1]. It is **closable** if the closure of its graph is the
graph of an operator. On $D(T)$ the **graph norm** $\|x\|_T = \|x\| + \|Tx\|$ (or $(\|x\|^2 + \|Tx\|^2)^{1/2}$ in
Hilbert spaces) makes $D(T)$ a Banach space exactly when $T$ is closed @picard2020primer [Lemma B.4.2]. The unbounded
operators of @def-unbounded-operator are closed in the cases met in this chapter.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Differentiation is the model closed operator, and it is the operator the figure shows to be unbounded. The first
example proves that its graph is closed @waterstraat2016 [Ex. 1.2.16].

::: {#exm-fan-derivative-closed}
#### Differentiation on $C[0, 1\rbrack$

$T = d/dx$ with $D(T) = C^1[0, 1] \subset C[0, 1]$ is closed: if $f_n \to f$ and $f_n' \to g$ uniformly, then $f_n(x) =
f_n(0) + \int_0^xf_n'$ gives $f(x) = f(0) + \int_0^xg$, so $f \in C^1$ and $f' = g$. Its graph norm is the $C^1$ norm of
@exr-fan-completeness-equivalent, and $T$ is unbounded, as the functions $\sin(n^2x)/n$ of the figure show.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Every bounded operator defined on the whole space is closed, but a densely defined operator can also fail to be
closable. The second example gives the standard non-closable functional.

::: {#exm-fan-not-closable}
#### A non-closable operator

Let $T : C[0, 1] \subset L^2(0, 1) \to \mathbb{C}$, $Tf = f(0)$. The functions $f_n(x) = \max(0, 1 - nx)$ have $\|f_n\|_2 =
(3n)^{-1/2} \to 0$ and $Tf_n = 1$, so $(0, 1)$ lies in the closure of the graph together with $(0, 0)$: the closure is not
a graph, and $T$ is not closable @picard2020primer [Lemma B.4.2(2)].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The time derivative of @picard2020primer is closed with a bounded inverse once the right weighted space is chosen. The
third example describes it; it is the model of the evolution equations that the book solves by operator methods.

::: {#exm-fan-time-derivative}
#### The weighted time derivative

For $\rho > 0$ let $H_{\rho} = \{f : e^{-\rho t}f \in L^2(\mathbb{R})\}$ with $\|f\|_\rho^2 = \int|f|^2e^{-2\rho t}dt$
@picard2020primer [Def. 1.1.1]. The closure $\partial_{0, \rho}$ of $d/dt$ on compactly supported $C^1$ functions is a closed
operator that is invertible, with $(\partial_{0, \rho}^{-1}f)(t) = \int_{-\infty}^tf(s)\,ds$ and $\|\partial_{0, \rho}^{-1}
\| \leq 1/\rho$ @picard2020primer [Thm. 1.1.4]. On $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ ($\rho = 0$) the derivative is not invertible.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The graph norm turns a closed operator into a bounded one on a Banach space, and the first exercise proves this
@picard2020primer [Lemma B.4.2(1)]. It is the reason closed operators can be treated with the theorems of this part.

::: {#exr-fan-graph-norm}
#### The graph norm

Show that $(D(T), \|\cdot\|_T)$ is complete if and only if $T$ is closed, and that $T : (D(T), \|\cdot\|_T) \to Y$ is
bounded with norm at most $1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$x \mapsto (x, Tx)$ is an isometry from $(D(T), \|\cdot\|_T)$ onto the graph with the norm $\|x\| + \|y\|$ of $X \times Y$,
which is complete. So $D(T)$ is complete if and only if the graph is complete, if and only if it is closed in $X \times
Y$. Boundedness: $\|Tx\| \leq \|x\| + \|Tx\| = \|x\|_T$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A closable operator has a smallest closed extension, and the criterion of @picard2020primer [Lemma B.4.2(2)] decides
closability. The second exercise applies it to differentiation on $L^2$.

::: {#exr-fan-closable-criterion}
#### Closability

Show that $T$ is closable if and only if $x_n \to 0$ and $Tx_n \to y$ imply $y = 0$. Apply this to $T = d/dx$ on
$C^1_c(0, 1) \subset L^2(0, 1)$ by integrating against a test function $\psi$, and conclude that it is closable.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The closure of the graph is a graph if and only if it contains no $(0, y)$ with $y \neq 0$, which is the stated
condition. For $d/dx$: if $f_n \to 0$ and $f_n' \to g$ in $L^2$, then for $\psi \in C^\infty_c(0, 1)$, $\int g\psi =
\lim\int f_n'\psi = -\lim\int f_n\psi' = 0$, so $g = 0$ by density of the test functions. The closure is the weak
derivative on the Sobolev space of @sec-sobolev-spaces with zero boundary values.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The weighted inverse of the time derivative can be tested on explicit functions, and the bound $1/\rho$ follows
from an integration by parts. The third exercise proves it and computes an example.

::: {#exr-fan-time-derivative-bound}
#### The bound $\|\partial_{0, \rho}^{-1}\| \leq 1/\rho$

For compactly supported $C^1$ functions $u$, show $\operatorname{Re}\int\bar uu'\,e^{-2\rho t}dt = \rho\|u\|_\rho^2$ by
integrating by parts, and deduce $\rho\|u\|_\rho \leq \|u'\|_\rho$. For $\rho = 1$ and $f = \mathbf{1}_{[0, a]}$,
compute $u(t) = \int_{-\infty}^tf$ and the limit of $\|u\|_\rho/\|f\|_\rho$ as $a \to \infty$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\tfrac{d}{dt}|u|^2 = 2\operatorname{Re}\bar uu'$, so $2\operatorname{Re}\int\bar uu'e^{-2\rho t} = -\int|u|^2
\tfrac{d}{dt}e^{-2\rho t} = 2\rho\|u\|_\rho^2$, and Cauchy-Schwarz gives $\rho\|u\|_\rho^2 \leq \|u\|_\rho\|u'\|_\rho$.
For $f = \mathbf{1}_{[0, a]}$ and $\rho = 1$: $\|f\|_1^2 = \int_0^ae^{-2t}dt = \tfrac12(1 - e^{-2a})$, and $u = t$ on
$[0, a]$, $u = a$ after, so $\|u\|_1^2 = \int_0^at^2e^{-2t}dt + \tfrac{a^2}2e^{-2a} = \tfrac14 - e^{-2a}(\tfrac a2 +
\tfrac14)$. The ratio tends to $(\tfrac14/\tfrac12)^{1/2} = 1/\sqrt2 < 1$, within the bound.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

Surjective bounded maps between Banach spaces are open, and the two other statements follow from this one. The
theorem below collects the three; each fails without completeness, as the examples show.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-open-mapping}
#### Open mapping theorem

Let $X$, $Y$ be Banach spaces and $T \in \mathcal{B}(X, Y)$ surjective. Then $T$ maps open sets to open sets; in
particular $T(B_X(0, 1)) \supset B_Y(0, \eta)$ for some $\eta > 0$ @arcozzi2025 [Thm. 3.15]; @waterstraat2016 [Thm.
1.1.3]. **Inverse mapping theorem**: a bounded bijection between Banach spaces has a bounded inverse @arcozzi2025 [Thm.
3.16]. **Closed graph theorem**: a closed operator $T : X \to Y$ defined on all of $X$ is bounded @arcozzi2025 [Thm.
3.17].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Two complete norms that are comparable are equivalent, which is the inverse mapping theorem applied to the identity.
The first example gives it @arcozzi2025 [Exercise 3.17].

::: {#exm-fan-comparable-norms}
#### Comparable complete norms

If $\|x\|_2 \leq \|x\|_1$ on $X$ and $X$ is complete for both, the identity $(X, \|\cdot\|_1) \to (X, \|\cdot\|_2)$ is a
bounded bijection, so its inverse is bounded: $\|x\|_1 \leq C\|x\|_2$. On $C[0, 1]$, $\|\cdot\|_1 \leq\|\cdot\|_\infty$
but the norms are not equivalent (@exm-fan-function-norms), which shows again that $\|\cdot\|_1$ is not complete there.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Without completeness of the domain, a bounded bijection may have an unbounded inverse. The second example gives one on
the finitely supported sequences.

::: {#exm-fan-inverse-unbounded}
#### An unbounded inverse

The identity $(c_{00}, \|\cdot\|_1) \to (c_{00}, \|\cdot\|_\infty)$ is bounded with norm $1$, since $\|a\|_\infty \leq
\|a\|_1$, and bijective; its inverse is unbounded by @exm-fan-inequivalent-sequences. Similarly $D = \operatorname{diag}
(1, \tfrac12, \tfrac13, \dots)$ is a bounded injection of $\ell^2$ with dense range and unbounded inverse
$\operatorname{diag}(1, 2, 3, \dots)$; its range is not closed, so it is not onto.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A symmetric operator defined on the whole Hilbert space is automatically bounded, a result physicists meet as the
reason why the position and momentum operators cannot be everywhere defined. The third example derives it from the
closed graph theorem.

::: {#exm-fan-hellinger-toeplitz}
#### The Hellinger-Toeplitz theorem

Let $A : H \to H$ be linear with $\langle Ax, y\rangle = \langle x, Ay\rangle$ for all $x, y$. If $x_n \to x$ and
$Ax_n \to z$, then $\langle z, y\rangle = \lim\langle x_n, Ay\rangle = \langle x, Ay\rangle = \langle Ax, y\rangle$, so
$z = Ax$: $A$ is closed and, by the theorem, bounded. Since $x$ (@exm-ub-multiplication-domain) is unbounded, it cannot be defined on
all of $L^2(\mathbb{R})$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The open mapping theorem is not quantitative, as the first exercise shows in the plane @arcozzi2025 [Exercise 3.16].
The constant $\eta$ depends on the operator and can be arbitrarily small.

::: {#exr-fan-open-mapping-not-quantitative}
#### No uniform constant

For $\varepsilon > 0$ find a linear bijection $T$ of $(\mathbb{R}^2, \|\cdot\|_2)$ with $\|T\| = 1$ whose image of the
unit ball contains no ball $B(0, \varepsilon')$ with $\varepsilon' > \varepsilon$, and compute $\|T\|$ and
$\|T^{-1}\|$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$T = \operatorname{diag}(1, \varepsilon)$ maps the unit disc onto the ellipse with semi-axes $1$ and $\varepsilon$, which
contains $B(0, \varepsilon)$ but no larger centred ball; $\|T\| = 1$ and $\|T^{-1}\| = 1/\varepsilon$. In the theorem
$\eta = 1/\|T^{-1}\|$ for a bijection.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The closed graph theorem follows from the inverse mapping theorem applied to the projection from the graph. The
second exercise asks for this deduction @arcozzi2025 [proof of Thm. 3.17].

::: {#exr-fan-closed-graph-proof}
#### From inverse mapping to closed graph

Let $T : X \to Y$ be closed and everywhere defined. Show that $\pi_X : (x, Tx) \mapsto x$ is a bounded bijection from the
graph (a Banach space) to $X$, and conclude that $T = \pi_Y\circ\pi_X^{-1}$ is bounded.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The graph is closed in the Banach space $X \times Y$, hence complete. $\pi_X$ is linear, bounded ($\|x\| \leq \|x\| +
\|Tx\|$) and bijective since $T$ is defined everywhere. By the inverse mapping theorem $\pi_X^{-1}$ is bounded, and
$\pi_Y : (x, Tx) \mapsto Tx$ is bounded, so $T$ is a composition of bounded maps.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The inverse of a closed bijective operator is bounded even though the operator itself is not. The third exercise
proves this and applies it to the derivative with an initial condition.

::: {#exr-fan-closed-inverse}
#### Inverses of closed operators

Let $T : D(T) \subset X \to Y$ be closed and bijective onto $Y$. Show that $T^{-1} : Y \to X$ is closed and everywhere
defined, hence bounded. Apply this to $T = d/dx$ on $\{f \in C^1[0, 1] : f(0) = 0\}$, find $T^{-1}$ and its norm.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The graph of $T^{-1}$ is the graph of $T$ with the factors exchanged, hence closed, and $T^{-1}$ is defined on all of
$Y$; the closed graph theorem makes it bounded. For the derivative with $f(0) = 0$, $T$ is closed (as in
@exm-fan-derivative-closed, the condition $f(0) = 0$ passes to limits) and bijective onto $C[0, 1]$, with $T^{-1} = V$
the Volterra operator of @exm-fan-volterra-norm, of norm $1$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

### Exercises

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
These exercises combine the four principles. Each uses completeness at an essential point, and each shows a
different way in which pointwise information becomes uniform.

Weak Lipschitz bounds imply strong ones, by the uniform boundedness principle applied to difference quotients. The first
integrative exercise proves it @arcozzi2025 [Exercise 3.12].

::: {#exr-fan-weak-lipschitz}
#### Weakly Lipschitz curves

Let $f : [a, b] \to X$ with $|\varphi(f(t + h)) - \varphi(f(t))| \leq C(\varphi)|h|$ for every $\varphi \in X^*$.
Show that $f$ is Lipschitz in norm, applying @exr-fan-weakly-bounded to the set of difference quotients $(f(t + h) -
f(t))/h$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The set $A = \{(f(t + h) - f(t))/h\}$ satisfies $\sup_{a \in A}|\varphi(a)| \leq C(\varphi)$ for each $\varphi$, so by
@exr-fan-weakly-bounded (the principle applied in the complete space $X^*$) $\sup_{a \in A}\|a\| = C < \infty$, which is
$\|f(t + h) - f(t)\| \leq C|h|$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The closed graph theorem shows that the norm of a Banach space in which the coordinate functionals are continuous is
essentially unique. The second integrative exercise proves it for sequence spaces.

::: {#exr-fan-sequence-norms-unique}
#### Inclusions of sequence spaces are bounded

Let $E$, $F$ be Banach spaces of sequences on which each coordinate $a \mapsto a_n$ is continuous, with $E \subset F$.
Show that the inclusion $E \to F$ has a closed graph and is therefore bounded. Deduce $\|a\|_q \leq C\|a\|_p$ for $p <
q$ without computing $C$, and compare with @exr-fan-lp-inclusions.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $a^{(k)} \to a$ in $E$ and $a^{(k)} \to b$ in $F$, then coordinatewise $a^{(k)}_n \to a_n$ and $\to b_n$, so $a = b$:
the graph is closed. The closed graph theorem gives boundedness. For $\ell^p \subset \ell^q$ this gives some $C$; the
direct computation shows $C = 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The partial sums of the Fourier series at $0$ can be made large by a continuous function close to the sign of the
Dirichlet kernel. The third integrative exercise constructs such functions and shows that the Lebesgue constant is
the exact norm.

::: {#exr-fan-large-partial-sums}
#### Large Fourier partial sums

For $N = 8$, let $g = \operatorname{sgn}D_N$, and let $g_\varepsilon$ be a continuous function with $\|g_\varepsilon
\|_\infty = 1$ that agrees with $g$ except within $\varepsilon$ of the zeros of $D_N$. Estimate $|S_Ng_\varepsilon(0) - L_N|$
in terms of $\varepsilon$. Explain why this shows $\|\Lambda_N\| = L_N$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$S_Ng(0) = \tfrac1{2\pi}\int D_Ng = \tfrac1{2\pi}\int|D_N| = L_N$, and $|S_Ng_\varepsilon(0) - L_N| \leq
\tfrac1{2\pi}(2N + 1)\cdot 2\cdot 2\varepsilon\cdot 2N$, which tends to $0$ with $\varepsilon$. Since $|\Lambda_Nf| \leq
L_N\|f\|_\infty$ for all $f$, the norm is exactly $L_N$; the principle then yields the divergent Fourier series of
@exm-fan-divergent-fourier.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

## Weak topologies and reflexivity {#sec-weak-topologies}

In infinite dimensions the closed unit ball is never compact in norm, so bounded sequences need not have convergent
subsequences. Weakening the notion of convergence restores compactness: a sequence converges weakly when every
continuous functional converges along it. This part defines weak and weak-* convergence on the examples of
oscillating, travelling and concentrating bumps, proves that the dual unit ball is weak-* compact (the Banach-Alaoglu
theorem), and characterises the reflexive spaces, in which bounded sequences always have weakly convergent
subsequences. The exposition follows @ramesh2020weak and @arcozzi2025 [Sec. 3.4].

### Weak and weak-* convergence

A sequence of functions can lose its norm to oscillation, escape to infinity or concentrate at a point, and in each
case it converges to zero in a weaker sense. The figure shows the three mechanisms, and the definitions below make
"weaker" precise.

![Three ways to converge weakly but not in norm. Left: $\sin(nx)$ on $[0, 2\pi]$ for $n = 2, 8$, with $\int_0^{2\pi}x
\sin(nx)\,dx = -2\pi/n \to 0$ while $\|\sin nx\|_2 = \sqrt\pi$. Centre: the travelling bump $e^{-(x - n)^2}$ for $n = 0, 3,
6$, tending to $0$ weakly in $L^2(\mathbb{R})$. Right: the concentrating bumps $n\mathbf{1}_{[0, 1/n]}$ for $n = 2, 4, 8$,
which have integral $1$ and converge weak-* to $\delta_0$ as functionals on $C[0, 1]$. Generated by
`figures/fa2-weak-convergence.sage`.](figures/fa2-weak-convergence.svg){#fig-fa2-weak-convergence width=95%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-weak-convergence}
#### Weak convergence

A sequence $(x_n)$ in a normed space $X$ **converges weakly** to $x$, written $x_n \rightharpoonup x$, if $\varphi(x_n)
\to \varphi(x)$ for every $\varphi \in X^*$. The **weak topology** $\sigma(X, X^*)$ is the coarsest topology in which every
$\varphi \in X^*$ is continuous; it is Hausdorff by @thm-hahn-banach, and its convergent sequences are the weakly
convergent ones @ramesh2020weak [Def. 2.7, Prop. 2.8, Thm. 2.9]. Norm convergence implies weak convergence; a weakly
convergent sequence in a Banach space is bounded, and $\|x\| \leq \liminf\|x_n\|$ @arcozzi2025 [Prop. 3.4];
@ramesh2020weak [Prop. 2.17]. In a Hilbert space, $x_n \rightharpoonup x$ means $\langle y, x_n\rangle \to \langle y,
x\rangle$ for every $y$.
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Every orthonormal sequence in a Hilbert space converges weakly to zero, which is Bessel's inequality in disguise. The
first example records it @arcozzi2025 [eq. 3.4.2].

::: {#exm-fan-orthonormal-weak}
#### Orthonormal sequences

If $(e_n)$ is orthonormal in a Hilbert space and $y \in H$, Bessel's inequality (@def-orthonormal-system) gives
$\sum_n|\langle y, e_n\rangle|^2 \leq \|y\|^2$, so $\langle y, e_n\rangle \to 0$: $e_n \rightharpoonup 0$. Since
$\|e_n\| = 1$, the inequality $\|0\| \leq \liminf\|e_n\|$ is strict, and no subsequence converges in norm, as $\|e_m -
e_n\| = \sqrt2$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Oscillating functions are the physical instance of the previous example, and the figure shows them. The second example
computes their weak limit.

::: {#exm-fan-oscillation-weak}
#### Oscillations

In $L^2(0, 2\pi)$, $\sin(nx) = \sqrt\pi\,\cdot$ (an orthonormal vector), so $\sin(nx) \rightharpoonup 0$, and for $g(x) =
x$ the pairing is $\int_0^{2\pi}x\sin(nx)\,dx = -2\pi/n$ (integrate by parts). In contrast $\sin^2(nx) = \tfrac12 -
\tfrac12\cos(2nx) \rightharpoonup \tfrac12$, not $0^2$: weak limits do not commute with non-linear functions.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Weak convergence in $\ell^p$ depends on $p$, and at $p = 1$ it coincides with norm convergence for sequences. The
third example compares the unit vectors in the different $\ell^p$.

::: {#exm-fan-unit-vectors-ellp}
#### Unit vectors in $\ell^p$

For $1 < p < \infty$, $(\ell^p)^* = \ell^q$ (@thm-lp-duality) and $y(\delta^{(n)}) = y_n \to 0$ for $y \in \ell^q$, so
$\delta^{(n)} \rightharpoonup 0$. In $\ell^1$ the functional $y = (1, 1, \dots) \in \ell^\infty$ gives $y(\delta^{(n)})
= 1$, so $\delta^{(n)} \not\rightharpoonup 0$; by **Schur's lemma** weakly convergent sequences in $\ell^1$ converge in
norm @ramesh2020weak [Thm. 2.31]. In $c_0$, $\delta^{(n)} \rightharpoonup 0$ again, since $c_0^* = \ell^1$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A bump that slides off to infinity keeps its shape and norm but disappears weakly. The fourth example treats the
travelling bump of the figure.

::: {#exm-fan-travelling-bump}
#### The travelling bump

Let $f \in L^2(\mathbb{R})$ and $f_n(x) = f(x - n)$. For $g$ with compact support, $\int gf_n = 0$ once the supports are
disjoint; for general $g \in L^2$, approximate it by such $g$ and use $\|f_n\|_2 = \|f\|_2$. Hence $f_n \rightharpoonup 0$
in $L^2(\mathbb{R})$. In $L^1(\mathbb{R})$ the same sequence does not converge weakly: the pairing with $g = 1 \in
L^\infty$ is $\int f$ for every $n$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
When the norms converge as well, weak convergence becomes norm convergence in a Hilbert space. The first exercise
proves it @ramesh2020weak [Exercise 2.18].

::: {#exr-fan-weak-plus-norm}
#### Weak convergence with norms

In a Hilbert space let $x_n \rightharpoonup x$ and $\|x_n\| \to \|x\|$. Expand $\|x_n - x\|^2$ and show $x_n \to x$. Find
a sequence in $\ell^2$ with $x_n \rightharpoonup x$ and $\|x_n\| \to c > \|x\|$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\|x_n - x\|^2 = \|x_n\|^2 - 2\operatorname{Re}\langle x, x_n\rangle + \|x\|^2 \to \|x\|^2 - 2\|x\|^2 + \|x\|^2 = 0$. The
sequence $x_n = \delta^{(1)} + \delta^{(n)}$ converges weakly to $\delta^{(1)}$ with $\|x_n\| = \sqrt2 > 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In the sequence spaces with $1 < p < \infty$ weak convergence is easy to test. The second exercise proves the criterion
@ramesh2020weak [Exercise 15].

::: {#exr-fan-weak-ellp-criterion}
#### Weak convergence in $\ell^p$

Let $1 < p < \infty$. Show that $a^{(k)} \rightharpoonup a$ in $\ell^p$ if and only if $(a^{(k)})$ is bounded and
$a^{(k)}_n \to a_n$ for every $n$. Show that the condition fails in $\ell^1$ with $a^{(k)} = \delta^{(k)}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Weak convergence implies boundedness (@def-weak-convergence) and, testing on $\delta^{(n)} \in \ell^q$, coordinatewise
convergence. Conversely, with $\|a^{(k)} - a\|_p \leq C$, for $y \in \ell^q$ split $\sum y_n(a^{(k)}_n - a_n)$ at $N$: the
tail is at most $C(\sum_{n > N}|y_n|^q)^{1/q}$, small for large $N$ since $q < \infty$, and the head tends to $0$. In
$\ell^1$ the tail argument fails because $q = \infty$: $\delta^{(k)}$ is bounded and tends to $0$ coordinatewise, but not
weakly (@exm-fan-unit-vectors-ellp).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A weakly convergent sequence has convex combinations that converge in norm, by the Hahn-Banach separation theorem.
The third exercise checks this for the unit vectors @ramesh2020weak [Cor. 2.25].

::: {#exr-fan-mazur}
#### Averages of unit vectors

In $\ell^p$, $1 < p < \infty$, compute $\|\tfrac1N\sum_{n \leq N}\delta^{(n)}\|_p$ and show that the averages converge to
$0$ in norm although $\delta^{(n)}$ does not. What happens in $\ell^1$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\|\tfrac1N\sum_{n \leq N}\delta^{(n)}\|_p = \tfrac1N N^{1/p} = N^{1/p - 1} \to 0$ for $p > 1$. In $\ell^1$ the norm is
$1$ for every $N$, consistent with $\delta^{(n)} \not\rightharpoonup 0$ there: by Mazur's lemma, a sequence whose convex
combinations stay away from $0$ cannot converge weakly to $0$.

The norms of the averages, computed in Sage:

{{< sage exr-fan-mazur >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The dual of a space carries a second, still weaker, notion of convergence, in which functionals converge at every
point of the original space. The definition below introduces it; the Banach-Alaoglu theorem shows that it has the
compactness that norm convergence lacks.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-weak-star-convergence}
#### Weak-* convergence

A sequence $(\varphi_n)$ in the dual $X^*$ **converges weak-*** to $\varphi$, written $\varphi_n
\xrightarrow{w^*}\varphi$, if $\varphi_n(x) \to \varphi(x)$ for every $x \in X$ @ramesh2020weak [Def. 3.1, Prop. 3.3].
The **weak-* topology** $\sigma(X^*, X)$ is the coarsest topology on $X^*$ making every evaluation $\varphi \mapsto
\varphi(x)$ continuous; it is Hausdorff and coarser than the weak topology of $X^*$, with which it coincides when $X$ is
reflexive @ramesh2020weak [Rem. 3.2]. If $X$ is a Banach space, a weak-* convergent sequence is bounded and $\|\varphi\| \leq
\liminf\|\varphi_n\|$ @arcozzi2025 [Prop. 3.5].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Point evaluations on $C[0, 1]$ converge weak-* when the points converge, but never in norm. The first example shows this
and explains why weak-* convergence is the natural notion for measures.

::: {#exm-fan-delta-weak-star}
#### Moving point masses

In $C[0, 1]^*$, $\delta_{1/n}(f) = f(1/n) \to f(0)$ for every continuous $f$, so $\delta_{1/n} \xrightarrow{w^*}\delta_0$.
But $\|\delta_{1/n} - \delta_0\| = 2$ (@exm-fan-dual-ck), so there is no norm convergence. Measures that converge
"physically" converge weak-*.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The concentrating bumps of the figure are functions, but as functionals on $C[0, 1]$ they converge to the Dirac
functional. The second example proves it.

::: {#exm-fan-concentrating-bumps}
#### Approximate identities

$\varphi_n(f) = n\int_0^{1/n}f(x)\,dx$ has $\|\varphi_n\| = \|n\mathbf{1}_{[0, 1/n]}\|_1 = 1$, and $|\varphi_n(f) - f(0)|
\leq \max_{[0, 1/n]}|f - f(0)| \to 0$ by continuity: $\varphi_n \xrightarrow{w^*}\delta_0$. The limit is not given by an
$L^1$ function, so the sequence has no weak limit in $L^1$ itself; this is the origin of the Dirac delta as a limit of
functions (@def-dirac-delta).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

On $\ell^1 = c_0^*$ the two notions of convergence differ, as the unit vectors show. The third example compares them
@ramesh2020weak [Exercise 5].

::: {#exm-fan-weak-star-not-weak}
#### Weak-* but not weak

Regard $\ell^1$ as $c_0^*$. For $a \in c_0$, $\delta^{(n)}(a) = a_n \to 0$, so $\delta^{(n)} \xrightarrow{w^*}0$. Regard
$\ell^1$ as a Banach space with dual $\ell^\infty$: then $y = (1, 1, \dots)$ gives $y(\delta^{(n)}) = 1$, so $\delta^{(n)}$
does not converge weakly. The difference is exactly the element $(1, 1, \dots) \in \ell^\infty \setminus c_0$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Weak-* convergence can be tested on a dense set if the sequence is bounded. The first exercise proves this, and it is
the criterion used in practice @ramesh2020weak [Exercise 16].

::: {#exr-fan-weak-star-dense}
#### Testing on a dense set

Let $X$ be a Banach space and $(\varphi_n)$ in $X^*$. Show that $\varphi_n \xrightarrow{w^*}\varphi$ if and only if
$(\varphi_n)$ is bounded and $\varphi_n(x) \to \varphi(x)$ for $x$ in a dense subset $D$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Necessity: boundedness by the uniform boundedness principle (@thm-uniform-boundedness). Sufficiency: let $\|\varphi_n\|,
\|\varphi\| \leq C$, $x \in X$, and $d \in D$ with $\|x - d\| < \varepsilon$. Then $|\varphi_n(x) - \varphi(x)| \leq
|\varphi_n(x - d)| + |\varphi_n(d) - \varphi(d)| + |\varphi(d - x)| \leq 2C\varepsilon + |\varphi_n(d) - \varphi(d)|$, which
is less than $3C\varepsilon$ for large $n$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Riemann sums are functionals on $C[0, 1]$, and they converge weak-* to the integral. The second exercise proves this with
the criterion of the first and computes the rate for a polynomial.

::: {#exr-fan-riemann-sums}
#### Riemann sums converge weak-*

Let $\mu_n(f) = \tfrac1n\sum_{k = 1}^nf(k/n)$. Show $\|\mu_n\| = 1$ and $\mu_n \xrightarrow{w^*}\mu$ with $\mu(f) = \int_0^1
f$, testing on polynomials. Compute $\mu_n(x^2) - \tfrac13$ exactly.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|\mu_n(f)| \leq \|f\|_\infty$ with equality at $f = 1$. For $f = x^m$, $\mu_n(f)$ is a Riemann sum of $x^m$, which
converges to $\tfrac1{m + 1}$; polynomials are dense (@thm-stone-weierstrass), so @exr-fan-weak-star-dense applies. For
$x^2$: $\tfrac1{n^3}\sum_kk^2 = \tfrac{(n + 1)(2n + 1)}{6n^2} = \tfrac13 + \tfrac1{2n} + \tfrac1{6n^2}$.

Sage computes the errors of the Riemann sums exactly for several monomials and numerically for $e^x$:

{{< sage exr-fan-riemann-sums >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Weak-* convergence and norm convergence combine to give convergence of the pairing. The third exercise proves this
@ramesh2020weak [Prop. 3.5(3) and Exercise 8].

::: {#exr-fan-weak-star-pairing}
#### Pairings of convergent sequences

Let $X$ be a Banach space, $\varphi_n \xrightarrow{w^*}\varphi$ in $X^*$ and $x_n \to x$ in $X$. Show that $\varphi_n(x_n)
\to \varphi(x)$. Show by an example in $\ell^2$ that the conclusion fails if $x_n$ only converges weakly.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|\varphi_n(x_n) - \varphi(x)| \leq \|\varphi_n\|\,\|x_n - x\| + |\varphi_n(x) - \varphi(x)|$; the first term tends to $0$
because $\|\varphi_n\|$ is bounded, the second by hypothesis. In $\ell^2 = (\ell^2)^*$ take $\varphi_n = x_n =
\delta^{(n)}$: both tend to $0$ weakly, but $\varphi_n(x_n) = 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### The Banach-Alaoglu theorem

The closed unit ball of an infinite-dimensional space is not compact in norm, but the unit ball of a dual space is
compact in the weak-* topology. The theorem below states this; its separable, sequential form is proved by the diagonal
argument of the Arzelà-Ascoli theorem and is the version used in analysis.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-banach-alaoglu}
#### Banach-Alaoglu theorem

For every normed space $X$, the closed unit ball $B_{X^*} = \{\varphi \in X^* : \|\varphi\| \leq 1\}$ is compact in the
weak-* topology @arcozzi2025 [Thm. 3.10]; @ramesh2020weak [Thm. 4.1]. If $X$ is separable, every bounded sequence in
$X^*$ has a weak-* convergent subsequence @arcozzi2025 [Thm. 3.11]. Consequently every Banach space is isometric to a
closed subspace of $C(K)$ for the compact space $K = (B_{X^*}, \sigma(X^*, X))$ @ramesh2020weak [Thm. 4.2].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Bounded sequences in $\ell^\infty = (\ell^1)^*$ have weak-* convergent subsequences, since $\ell^1$ is separable. The
first example finds the limit of a bounded sequence that has no norm limit.

::: {#exm-fan-alaoglu-ellinfty}
#### Truncated constants in $\ell^\infty$

$s^{(N)} = (1, \dots, 1, 0, \dots)$ ($N$ ones) has $\|s^{(N)}\|_\infty = 1$ and $s^{(N)}(a) = \sum_{n \leq N}a_n \to
\sum_na_n$ for every $a \in \ell^1$, so $s^{(N)} \xrightarrow{w^*}(1, 1, \dots)$. It has no norm limit, since
$\|s^{(N)} - s^{(M)}\|_\infty = 1$, and no limit in $c_0$ at all.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Probability measures on a compact interval form a weak-* compact set, by the theorem. The second example applies this to
the empirical measures of a sequence of points.

::: {#exm-fan-empirical-measures}
#### Limits of empirical measures

For points $x_1, x_2, \dots \in [0, 1]$, the empirical measures $\mu_n = \tfrac1n\sum_{k \leq n}\delta_{x_k}$ have norm $1$
in $C[0, 1]^*$, so a subsequence converges weak-* to a positive functional of norm $1$, a probability measure. For $x_k
= \{k\sqrt2\}$ (fractional part), Weyl's equidistribution theorem identifies the limit as Lebesgue measure for the whole
sequence; for $x_k = k/n$ in the $n$-th block one obtains the Riemann sums of @exr-fan-riemann-sums.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Weak-* compactness of $B_{X^*}$ does not make the unit ball of $X$ weakly compact, and $\ell^1$ with its two
dualities shows the difference. The third example explains it @ramesh2020weak [Rem. 2.32].

::: {#exm-fan-ell1-ball}
#### The unit ball of $\ell^1$

As the dual of $c_0$, $B_{\ell^1}$ is weak-* compact, and $\delta^{(n)} \xrightarrow{w^*}0$. As a space in its own right,
$B_{\ell^1}$ is not weakly compact: by Schur's lemma a weakly convergent subsequence of $\delta^{(n)}$ would converge in
norm, but $\|\delta^{(m)} - \delta^{(n)}\|_1 = 2$. The ball is weakly compact exactly in reflexive spaces
(@def-reflexive-space).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The sequential form of the theorem is proved by a diagonal argument on a countable dense set. The first exercise asks
for the steps @arcozzi2025 [Thm. 3.11].

::: {#exr-fan-alaoglu-proof}
#### The diagonal argument

Let $X$ be separable with dense sequence $(z_j)$ and $\|\varphi_n\| \leq 1$. Choose nested subsequences along which
$\varphi_n(z_j)$ converges for $j = 1, 2, \dots$, take the diagonal subsequence, and show that it converges at every $z_j$,
then at every $x$ by @exr-fan-weak-star-dense, to a functional of norm $\leq 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|\varphi_n(z_1)| \leq \|z_1\|$, so a subsequence makes $\varphi_n(z_1)$ converge (Bolzano-Weierstrass); refine it for
$z_2$, and so on. The $k$-th element of the $k$-th subsequence defines a diagonal subsequence that is eventually a
subsequence of each, so it converges at every $z_j$. By @exr-fan-weak-star-dense it converges at every $x$, and the
limit $\varphi(x) = \lim\varphi_{n_k}(x)$ is linear with $|\varphi(x)| \leq \|x\|$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The ball of $c_0$ is not weakly compact, which the second exercise shows with the same truncated constants as in the
first example. The weak limit they would need lies outside $c_0$.

::: {#exr-fan-c0-ball}
#### The unit ball of $c_0$

Show that $s^{(N)} = (1, \dots, 1, 0, \dots)$ has no weakly convergent subsequence in $c_0$: a weak limit $s$ would have
$s_n = \lim_N s^{(N)}_n = 1$ for all $n$. Conclude that $B_{c_0}$ is not weakly compact.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The coordinate functionals $\delta^{(n)} \in \ell^1 = c_0^*$ give $s_n = \lim_Ns^{(N)}_n = 1$ for any weak limit $s$ of a
subsequence, so $s = (1, 1, \dots) \notin c_0$. Weak compactness of $B_{c_0}$ would give a weakly convergent subsequence
by the Eberlein-Šmulian theorem; even without it, a weakly compact set would contain a weak cluster point of
$(s^{(N)})$, which, by the same coordinate argument, would have to be $(1, 1, \dots)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Weak compactness and weak lower semicontinuity of the norm give minimisers. The third exercise finds the vector of
smallest norm in a closed hyperplane of $\ell^2$ by this route and then explicitly.

::: {#exr-fan-minimiser}
#### A minimiser in $\ell^2$

Let $A = \{x \in \ell^2 : \sum_nx_n/n = 1\}$. Show that a minimising sequence for $\|x\|_2$ on $A$ has a weakly convergent
subsequence whose limit lies in $A$ and minimises the norm. Find the minimiser and the minimum using Cauchy-Schwarz.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A minimising sequence is bounded; by @thm-banach-alaoglu (for $\ell^2 = (\ell^2)^*$, separable) a subsequence converges
weakly to some $x$. The functional $y = (1/n) \in \ell^2$ keeps $\langle y, x\rangle = 1$, so $x \in A$, and $\|x\| \leq
\liminf\|x_n\|$, so $x$ is a minimiser. Cauchy-Schwarz gives $1 = \langle y, x\rangle \leq \|y\|\,\|x\|$, so $\|x\| \geq
1/\|y\| = \sqrt6/\pi$, with equality for $x = y/\|y\|^2$, that is $x_n = \tfrac6{\pi^2n}$.

Truncating to $N$ coordinates, Sage shows the minimum and the first coordinate of the minimiser converging to the limits:

{{< sage exr-fan-minimiser >}}
:::

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
