### Reflexive spaces

A Banach space is reflexive when it is its own bidual through the canonical embedding. The figure shows what can go wrong
in a non-reflexive space: a functional whose norm is approached but never attained on the unit ball.

![Left: for $\varphi(a) = \sum_n2^{-n}a_n$ on $c_0$, which has $\|\varphi\| = \|(2^{-n})\|_1 = 1$, the values
$\varphi(s^{(N)}) = 1 - 2^{-N}$ on the unit vectors $s^{(N)} = (1, \dots, 1, 0, \dots)$ approach $1$ but no $a \in
B_{c_0}$ attains it. Right: the same functional on $\ell^2$, $\varphi(a) = \langle y, a\rangle$ with $y = (2^{-n})$, attains
its norm $\|y\|_2 = 1/\sqrt3$ at $a = y/\|y\|_2$, as in every reflexive space. Generated by
`figures/fa2-norm-attaining.sage`.](figures/fa2-norm-attaining.svg){#fig-fa2-norm-attaining width=95%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-reflexive-space}
#### Reflexive space

A Banach space $X$ is **reflexive** if the canonical isometry $x \mapsto \hat x$ of $X$ into $X^{**}$ (@thm-hahn-banach) is
onto @arcozzi2025 [Sec. 3.3]; @ramesh2020weak [Sec. 3]. Equivalently: the closed unit ball of $X$ is weakly compact
@ramesh2020weak [Thm. 5.2]; or every $\varphi \in X^*$ attains its norm on the unit sphere (**James's theorem**)
@ramesh2020weak [Thm. 5.7]. Closed subspaces of reflexive spaces are reflexive, and $X$ is reflexive if and only if $X^*$ is
@ramesh2020weak [Cor. 5.3, Thm. 5.4]. In a reflexive space every bounded sequence has a weakly convergent subsequence.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Finite-dimensional spaces and Hilbert spaces are reflexive, the second by applying the Riesz representation twice. The
first example records both.

::: {#exm-fan-hilbert-reflexive}
#### Hilbert spaces

If $\dim X < \infty$ then $\dim X^{**} = \dim X$ and the injective map $x \mapsto \hat x$ is onto. For a Hilbert space,
every $\Phi \in H^{**}$ is, by @thm-riesz-representation applied in the Hilbert space $H^*$, of the form $\Phi(\varphi) =
\langle\varphi_z, \varphi\rangle_{H^*}$ for some $\varphi_z = \langle z, \cdot\rangle$; unwinding the inner product of $H^*$
gives $\Phi(\varphi) = \varphi(z) = \hat z(\varphi)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The sequence spaces $\ell^p$ with $1 < p < \infty$ are reflexive by the duality theorem applied twice. The second example
gives the computation and its analogue for $L^p$.

::: {#exm-fan-ellp-reflexive}
#### $\ell^p$ and $L^p$ for $1 < p < \infty$

$(\ell^p)^* = \ell^q$ and $(\ell^q)^* = \ell^p$ (@thm-lp-duality), and the composite identification $\ell^p \to (\ell^p)^{**}$
sends $a$ to the functional $y \mapsto \sum_ny_na_n$, which is $\hat a$. So $\ell^p$ is reflexive, and similarly
$L^p(X, \mu)$ for $1 < p < \infty$. Bounded sequences in these spaces have weakly convergent subsequences, as in
@exr-fan-minimiser.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The spaces $c_0$, $\ell^1$, $\ell^\infty$, $C[0, 1]$ and $L^1$ are not reflexive, and the figure shows the failure of
James's criterion on $c_0$. The third example lists the reasons.

::: {#exm-fan-non-reflexive}
#### Non-reflexive spaces

$c_0^{**} = \ell^\infty \neq c_0$ (@exm-fan-bidual-c0). $\ell^1$ is separable but its dual $\ell^\infty$ is not, so
$(\ell^1)^{**} = (\ell^\infty)^*$ is not separable (@exr-fan-ell1-not-dual-of-ellinfty) and cannot be $\ell^1$; then
$\ell^\infty = (\ell^1)^*$ is not reflexive either. $C[0, 1]$ and $L^1(0, 1)$ contain closed subspaces isometric to $c_0$
and $\ell^1$, and closed subspaces of reflexive spaces are reflexive.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The functional of the figure shows James's theorem at work. The fourth example proves that it does not attain its norm.

::: {#exm-fan-c0-not-attained}
#### A functional on $c_0$ that does not attain its norm

$\varphi(a) = \sum_n2^{-n}a_n$ has $|\varphi(a)| \leq \|a\|_\infty\sum_n2^{-n} = \|a\|_\infty$ and $\varphi(s^{(N)}) =
1 - 2^{-N}$, so $\|\varphi\| = 1$. If $\|a\|_\infty \leq 1$ and $\varphi(a) = 1$, then $\sum 2^{-n}(1 - \operatorname{Re}
a_n) = 0$ with non-negative terms, so $a_n = 1$ for all $n$, and $a \notin c_0$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise is the continuous analogue of the last example: a functional on $C[0, 1]$ whose norm is approached by
continuous functions but attained only by a discontinuous one. James's theorem then shows that $C[0, 1]$ is not reflexive.

::: {#exr-fan-ck-not-attained}
#### A functional on $C[0, 1\rbrack$

Show that $\varphi(f) = \int_0^{1/2}f - \int_{1/2}^1f$ has norm $1$ on $C[0, 1]$ and that $|\varphi(f)| < 1$ for every $f$
with $\|f\|_\infty \leq 1$. Conclude that $C[0, 1]$ is not reflexive.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|\varphi(f)| \leq \|f\|_\infty$, and continuous $f$ equal to $1$ on $[0, \tfrac12 - \tfrac1n]$, to $-1$ on $[\tfrac12 +
\tfrac1n, 1]$ and linear between give $\varphi(f) = 1 - \tfrac1{2n}$, so $\|\varphi\| = 1$. If $\|f\|_\infty \leq 1$ and
$|\varphi(f)| = 1$, then (after a phase) $\int_0^{1/2}(1 - \operatorname{Re}f) + \int_{1/2}^1(1 + \operatorname{Re}f) = 0$,
forcing $f = 1$ on $[0, \tfrac12)$ and $f = -1$ on $(\tfrac12, 1]$, which is not continuous. By James's theorem $C[0, 1]$
is not reflexive.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In a reflexive space the distance to a closed convex set is attained, and in $c_0$ it need not be. The second exercise
compares the two @ramesh2020weak [Cor. 5.5].

::: {#exr-fan-nearest-point}
#### Nearest points

Let $A = \{a : \varphi(a) = 1\}$ with $\varphi$ as in @exm-fan-c0-not-attained. Show that $\inf_{a \in A}\|a\|_\infty = 1$ in
$c_0$ but that no $a \in A$ has norm $1$. Show that in a reflexive space every non-empty closed convex set has an element
of minimal norm.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$1 = |\varphi(a)| \leq \|a\|_\infty$ on $A$, and $s^{(N)}/(1 - 2^{-N}) \in A$ has norm $1/(1 - 2^{-N}) \to 1$. A minimiser
of norm $1$ would attain $\|\varphi\|$, which is impossible. In a reflexive space a minimising sequence is bounded, a
subsequence converges weakly; a closed convex set is weakly closed @ramesh2020weak [Prop. 2.24], so the limit lies in the
set, and the norm is weakly lower semicontinuous.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Reflexivity passes to closed subspaces and to duals, which the third exercise proves from the definition and the weak
compactness criterion @ramesh2020weak [Cor. 5.3, Thm. 5.4].

::: {#exr-fan-reflexive-dual}
#### Reflexivity of duals

Show that if $X$ is reflexive then $X^*$ is reflexive, by identifying $(X^*)^{**} = (X^{**})^*$ with $X^*$. Deduce that
$\ell^1$ is not reflexive from the fact that $c_0$ is not, using $c_0^* = \ell^1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $J : X \to X^{**}$ is onto, every $\Psi \in X^{***}$ defines $\psi = \Psi\circ J \in X^*$, and for $\Phi = Jx \in
X^{**}$, $\hat\psi(\Phi) = \Phi(\psi) = \psi(x) = \Psi(Jx) = \Psi(\Phi)$, so $\Psi = \hat\psi$ and $X^*$ is reflexive.
Conversely, if $X^*$ is reflexive then so is $X^{**}$, and $X$, a closed subspace of $X^{**}$, is reflexive. If $\ell^1 =
c_0^*$ were reflexive, $c_0$ would be, contradicting @exm-fan-non-reflexive.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### Exercises

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
These exercises combine weak convergence, the Banach-Alaoglu theorem and reflexivity with the operators and duals of the
earlier parts. They prepare the compact operators of @sec-fredholm-operators, which are characterised by what they do
to weakly convergent sequences.

A compact operator turns weak convergence into norm convergence, which is the mechanism behind the discreteness of
spectra. The first integrative exercise proves it for a diagonal operator and in general @arcozzi2025 [Thm. 4.1].

::: {#exr-fan-compact-weak-to-norm}
#### Compact operators improve convergence

Show that $D = \operatorname{diag}(1, \tfrac12, \tfrac13, \dots)$ on $\ell^2$ maps every weakly convergent sequence to a norm
convergent one, by splitting $D$ into a finite-rank part and a part of norm $\leq 1/N$. Show that the identity does not
have this property.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Let $x_k \rightharpoonup x$, with $\|x_k - x\| \leq C$. Write $D = D_N + R_N$, with $D_N$ the first $N$ diagonal entries and
$\|R_N\| \leq \tfrac1{N + 1}$. $D_N(x_k - x)$ involves finitely many coordinates, each tending to $0$, so it tends to $0$
in norm, while $\|R_N(x_k - x)\| \leq C/(N + 1)$. Hence $\limsup\|D(x_k - x)\| \leq C/(N + 1)$ for every $N$. The identity
maps $\delta^{(k)} \rightharpoonup 0$ to itself, which does not converge in norm.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Weak limits of products are not products of weak limits, and this is the source of effective coefficients in
homogenisation. The second integrative exercise computes the weak limits of $\sin^2(nx)$ and of $\sin(nx)\cos(nx)$.

::: {#exr-fan-weak-products}
#### Weak limits of products

In $L^2(0, 2\pi)$ find the weak limits of $\sin(nx)$, $\sin^2(nx)$ and $\sin(nx)\cos(nx)$, and of $\sin^2(nx)$ paired
with $g(x) = x$ exactly. Show that $f_n \rightharpoonup f$ and $g_n \rightharpoonup g$ do not imply $f_ng_n \rightharpoonup
fg$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\sin(nx) \rightharpoonup 0$; $\sin^2(nx) = \tfrac12 - \tfrac12\cos(2nx) \rightharpoonup \tfrac12$; $\sin(nx)\cos(nx) =
\tfrac12\sin(2nx) \rightharpoonup 0$. Exactly, $\int_0^{2\pi}x\sin^2(nx)\,dx = \pi^2 - \tfrac12\int_0^{2\pi}x\cos(2nx)\,dx =
\pi^2$, since the last integral vanishes. With $f_n = g_n = \sin(nx) \rightharpoonup 0$, $f_ng_n \rightharpoonup \tfrac12
\neq 0$.

Sage evaluates the pairings with several test functions for $n = 1, 10, 100$:

{{< sage exr-fan-weak-products >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Every Banach space is a space of continuous functions in disguise, by the Banach-Alaoglu theorem. The third integrative
exercise proves this embedding @ramesh2020weak [Thm. 4.2].

::: {#exr-fan-embedding-ck}
#### Every Banach space sits in a $C(K)$

Let $K = B_{X^*}$ with the weak-* topology. Show that $K$ is compact Hausdorff, that $e_x(\varphi) = \varphi(x)$ is continuous
on $K$, and that $x \mapsto e_x$ is a linear isometry of $X$ into $C(K)$. What is $K$ for $X = \mathbb{R}^2$ with
$\|\cdot\|_\infty$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$K$ is compact by @thm-banach-alaoglu and Hausdorff (@def-weak-star-convergence). $e_x$ is continuous for $\sigma(X^*,
X)$ by definition of that topology. Linearity is clear, and $\|e_x\|_\infty = \sup_{\|\varphi\| \leq 1}|\varphi(x)| = \|x\|$
by the norming functional of @thm-hahn-banach. For $(\mathbb{R}^2, \|\cdot\|_\infty)$, $K$ is the unit ball of the dual
norm $\|\cdot\|_1$, the square with vertices $(\pm1, 0)$, $(0, \pm1)$, and $e_x(y) = x_1y_1 + x_2y_2$ attains its
maximum modulus $\|x\|_\infty$ at a vertex.
:::

## Inner product and Hilbert spaces {#sec-hilbert-spaces}

An inner product assigns a complex number to two vectors and gives a vector space lengths, angles and orthogonality.
This section defines inner products and orthonormal systems, introduces completeness and the two model Hilbert
spaces $\ell^2$ and $L^2$, defines orthonormal bases with Parseval's identity, and quotes the Riesz representation
theorem; the Gram-Schmidt process and the orthogonal projection are then carried out on explicit vectors and
functions.

### Inner products

A bilinear form (@def-bilinear-form) assigns a number to two vectors, and on a real space a positive definite
symmetric one gives lengths and angles. On a complex space the form must be adjusted so that $\langle u, u\rangle$
stays real and positive, and the definition below fixes the convention used throughout: the inner product is
antilinear in its first slot and linear in its second, which is the convention of quantum mechanics.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-inner-product}
#### Inner product

An **inner product** on a complex vector space $V$ (@def-vector-space) is a map $\langle\cdot, \cdot\rangle : V
\times V \to \mathbb{C}$ that is **linear in the second slot**, $\langle u, \alpha v + \beta w\rangle =
\alpha\langle u, v\rangle + \beta\langle u, w\rangle$, **conjugate symmetric**, $\langle v, u\rangle =
\overline{\langle u, v\rangle}$, and **positive definite**, $\langle u, u\rangle > 0$ for $u \neq 0$. The two
rules together make it **antilinear in the first slot**, $\langle \alpha u, v\rangle = \bar\alpha\langle u,
v\rangle$. The **norm** is $\|u\| = \sqrt{\langle u, u\rangle}$; it satisfies the **Cauchy-Schwarz inequality**
$|\langle u, v\rangle| \leq \|u\|\,\|v\|$ and the **triangle inequality** $\|u + v\| \leq \|u\| + \|v\|$. A vector
space with an inner product is an **inner product space**, and on a real vector space the same definition with
real scalars recovers a positive definite symmetric bilinear form.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first instance is the complex version of the dot product, in which the conjugation on the first vector is
exactly what makes $\langle u, u\rangle$ a sum of squared moduli. It also shows why the conjugate is needed at all:
without it the "length" of $(1, i)$ would be zero.

::: {#exm-ip-cn}
#### $\mathbb{C}^n$

$\langle u, v\rangle = \sum_k \bar u_k v_k$ is an inner product on $\mathbb{C}^n$, with $\|u\|^2 = \sum |u_k|^2$.
For $u = (1, i)$ this gives $\|u\|^2 = 1 + 1 = 2$, whereas the unconjugated sum $\sum u_k u_k = 1 + i^2 = 0$ would
not be a norm; $\langle (1, i), (i, 1)\rangle = \bar 1\cdot i + \bar i\cdot 1 = i - i = 0$, so the two vectors are
orthogonal.
:::

Matrices form a vector space, and the trace supplies an inner product on it that will reappear as the
Hilbert-Schmidt inner product of operators. The example computes it on the Pauli matrices, which turn out to be
orthogonal to each other and to the identity.

::: {#exm-ip-matrices}
#### Matrices with the trace form

$\langle A, B\rangle = \operatorname{tr}(A^\dagger B)$, with $A^\dagger = \bar A^{\mathsf{T}}$ the conjugate
transpose, is an inner product on the $n \times n$ complex matrices: $\langle A, A\rangle = \sum_{jk}|A_{jk}|^2$.
The identity and the three Pauli matrices $\sigma_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$, $\sigma_2 =
\begin{pmatrix} 0 & -i \\ i & 0\end{pmatrix}$, $\sigma_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{pmatrix}$ satisfy
$\langle\sigma_a, \sigma_b\rangle = 2\delta_{ab}$ and $\langle 1, \sigma_a\rangle = \operatorname{tr}\sigma_a = 0$
(@exr-ip-sage-matrices): they are an orthogonal basis of the $2 \times 2$ matrices.
:::

Functions on an interval form an infinite-dimensional vector space, and the integral replaces the sum of the
previous examples. The third example is the inner product that the rest of the chapter uses, and it shows a
first orthogonality relation between exponentials.

::: {#exm-ip-functions}
#### Continuous functions on an interval

On the continuous complex functions on $[0, 2\pi]$, $\langle f, g\rangle = \int_0^{2\pi}\overline{f(x)}g(x)\,dx$
is an inner product (the Riemann integral of @sec-riemann-integral), and positive definiteness holds because a
continuous $|f|^2$ with zero integral vanishes identically. For $e_n(x) = e^{inx}$ one finds $\langle e_m,
e_n\rangle = \int_0^{2\pi}e^{i(n - m)x}dx = 2\pi\delta_{mn}$, the orthogonality of modes of @sec-fourier-series.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality is quoted in the definition, and its proof is the one computation every reader
should do once: minimise $\|u - tv\|^2$ over $t$. The first exercise asks for this proof and for the triangle
inequality that follows from it.

::: {#exr-ip-cauchy-schwarz}
#### Cauchy-Schwarz from positivity

Prove $|\langle u, v\rangle| \leq \|u\|\,\|v\|$ by expanding $0 \leq \|u - tv\|^2$ for a suitable complex $t$, and
deduce the triangle inequality.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $v = 0$ there is nothing to prove; otherwise set $t = \langle v, u\rangle/\|v\|^2$. Then $0 \leq \|u - tv\|^2 =
\|u\|^2 - \bar t\langle v, u\rangle - t\langle u, v\rangle + |t|^2\|v\|^2 = \|u\|^2 - |\langle u, v\rangle|^2/
\|v\|^2$, using $\langle u, v\rangle = \overline{\langle v, u\rangle}$, which is the inequality. For the triangle
inequality, $\|u + v\|^2 = \|u\|^2 + 2\operatorname{Re}\langle u, v\rangle + \|v\|^2 \leq \|u\|^2 + 2\|u\|\|v\| +
\|v\|^2 = (\|u\| + \|v\|)^2$.
:::

The norm determines the inner product: the polarisation identity recovers $\langle u, v\rangle$ from the lengths
of four vectors. The second exercise asks for this identity and for the parallelogram law, which is the property
that distinguishes norms coming from inner products from all others.

::: {#exr-ip-polarisation}
#### Polarisation and the parallelogram law

Show that $\|u + v\|^2 + \|u - v\|^2 = 2\|u\|^2 + 2\|v\|^2$ (parallelogram law), and that $\langle u, v\rangle =
\tfrac14\sum_{k=0}^3 i^{-k}\,\|u + i^k v\|^2$ with the antilinear-first-slot convention.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Expanding, $\|u \pm v\|^2 = \|u\|^2 \pm 2\operatorname{Re}\langle u, v\rangle + \|v\|^2$, and adding gives the
parallelogram law. For polarisation, $\|u + i^kv\|^2 = \|u\|^2 + \|v\|^2 + 2\operatorname{Re}(i^k\langle u,
v\rangle)$; the constant terms cancel in $\sum_k i^{-k}$ since $\sum_k i^{-k} = 0$, and $\sum_k i^{-k}\cdot
2\operatorname{Re}(i^k z) = \sum_k i^{-k}(i^kz + i^{-k}\bar z) = 4z + \bar z\sum_k i^{-2k} = 4z$ because $\sum_k
(-1)^k = 0$. Dividing by $4$ gives $\langle u, v\rangle$.
:::

Sage computes traces and conjugate transposes exactly, so the orthogonality of the Pauli matrices and the
Cauchy-Schwarz inequality on random vectors can be checked without rounding. The last exercise does both, and
finds the coefficients of a matrix in the Pauli basis by taking inner products.

::: {#exr-ip-sage-matrices}
#### The Pauli basis in Sage

With Sage, check $\operatorname{tr}(\sigma_a^\dagger\sigma_b) = 2\delta_{ab}$, expand $M = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 -
i \\ 2 + i & 3\end{pmatrix}$ as $c_0 1 + \sum_a c_a\sigma_a$ with $c = \tfrac12\langle\sigma, M\rangle$, and verify
Cauchy-Schwarz for two explicit complex vectors.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The coefficients are $c_0 = 2$, $c_1 = 2$, $c_2 = 1$, $c_3 = -1$, as $M$ is Hermitian with real coefficients in the
Pauli basis:

{{< sage exr-ip-sage-matrices >}}
:::
::::

### Orthonormal systems

Two vectors are orthogonal when their inner product vanishes, and a family of mutually orthogonal unit vectors is
the right-angled coordinate frame of an inner product space. The figure shows the Gram-Schmidt process turning two
vectors of the plane into such a frame, and the orthogonal projection onto a line; the definition below names the
frame, the process and the projection.

![Left: Gram-Schmidt in the plane turns $v_1 = (2, 1)$, $v_2 = (1, 2)$ into the orthonormal pair $e_1, e_2$; the
dashed segment is the component of $v_2$ along $e_1$, and $v_2 - \langle e_1, v_2\rangle e_1$ is orthogonal to
$e_1$. Right: the best approximation of $e^x$ on $[-1, 1]$ by polynomials of degree at most $2$ in the $L^2$ norm,
the orthogonal projection onto the span of the first three Legendre polynomials, compared with the Taylor
polynomial of the same degree; the projection has the smaller $L^2$ error. Generated by
`figures/gram_schmidt_projection.sage`.](figures/gram_schmidt_projection.svg){#fig-gram-schmidt-projection
width=95%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-orthonormal-system}
#### Orthonormal system

Vectors $u, v$ are **orthogonal**, $u \perp v$, if $\langle u, v\rangle = 0$. A family $(e_k)$ is an
**orthonormal system** if $\langle e_j, e_k\rangle = \delta_{jk}$. The **Gram-Schmidt process** turns linearly
independent vectors $v_1, v_2, \dots$ into an orthonormal system spanning the same subspaces: $e_1 = v_1/\|v_1\|$,
and $e_k = w_k/\|w_k\|$ with $w_k = v_k - \sum_{j < k}\langle e_j, v_k\rangle e_j$. For a finite orthonormal
system $e_1, \dots, e_n$ the **orthogonal projection** onto their span is $Pu = \sum_k \langle e_k, u\rangle
e_k$; $u - Pu$ is orthogonal to the span, $Pu$ is the point of the span closest to $u$, and $\|Pu\|^2 = \sum_k
|\langle e_k, u\rangle|^2 \leq \|u\|^2$ (**Bessel's inequality**).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
In the plane an orthonormal system is a pair of perpendicular unit vectors, and any rotation of the standard
basis gives one. The first example writes down such a pair in $\mathbb{C}^2$ with complex entries, and expands a
vector in it by taking inner products.

::: {#exm-on-rotated-basis}
#### An orthonormal pair in $\mathbb{C}^2$

$e_1 = (1, i)/\sqrt2$, $e_2 = (1, -i)/\sqrt2$ satisfy $\langle e_1, e_1\rangle = (1 + 1)/2 = 1$ and $\langle e_1,
e_2\rangle = (1 + \bar i(-i))/2 = (1 - 1)/2 = 0$, an orthonormal system; they are the eigenvectors of
$\sigma_2$ (@sec-spectral-theory). A vector $u = (a, b)$ has components $\langle e_1, u\rangle = (a - ib)/\sqrt2$
and $\langle e_2, u\rangle = (a + ib)/\sqrt2$, and $|\langle e_1, u\rangle|^2 + |\langle e_2, u\rangle|^2 = |a|^2 +
|b|^2 = \|u\|^2$.
:::

Applied to the monomials $1, x, x^2, \dots$ in the inner product of $L^2(-1, 1)$, Gram-Schmidt produces the Legendre
polynomials up to normalisation. The example carries out the first three steps, each of which needs only the
integrals of even powers of $x$ over $[-1, 1]$.

::: {#exm-on-legendre}
#### Gram-Schmidt on $1, x, x^2$

With $\langle f, g\rangle = \int_{-1}^1 \bar f g\,dx$: $w_1 = 1$; $w_2 = x - \langle 1, x\rangle/\langle 1,
1\rangle = x$ since $\int_{-1}^1 x\,dx = 0$; $w_3 = x^2 - \tfrac{\langle 1, x^2\rangle}{\langle 1, 1\rangle} -
\tfrac{\langle x, x^2\rangle}{\langle x, x\rangle}x = x^2 - \tfrac13$. These are $P_0$, $P_1$ and $\tfrac23P_2$,
the Legendre polynomials of @sec-sturm-liouville, and normalising gives $e_k = \sqrt{(2k + 1)/2}\,P_k$
(@prp-hilbert-space-computations, @exr-on-legendre-p3).
:::

The exponentials of @exm-ip-functions become an orthonormal system after dividing by $\sqrt{2\pi}$, and the
orthogonal projection onto finitely many of them is a truncated Fourier series. The third example makes this
identification, which is the bridge between this chapter and @sec-fourier-series.

::: {#exm-on-exponentials}
#### The exponentials $e^{inx}/\sqrt{2\pi}$

$e_n(x) = e^{inx}/\sqrt{2\pi}$, $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, is an orthonormal system in the functions on $[0, 2\pi]$ by
@exm-ip-functions. The projection onto $\operatorname{span}\{e_{-N}, \dots, e_N\}$ is $P_Nf = \sum_{|n| \leq N}
\langle e_n, f\rangle e_n = \sum_{|n| \leq N} c_n e^{inx}$ with $c_n = \tfrac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}e^{-inx}f(x)dx$,
the $N$-th partial Fourier sum, and Bessel's inequality reads $2\pi\sum_{|n| \leq N}|c_n|^2 \leq \int_0^{2\pi} |
f|^2dx$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Carrying out Gram-Schmidt by hand on three vectors of $\mathbb{R}^3$ and then letting Sage repeat it is the
quickest way to internalise the process. The first exercise does this and checks the resulting frame.

::: {#exr-on-gram-schmidt-r3}
#### Gram-Schmidt in $\mathbb{R}^3$

Orthonormalise $v_1 = (1, 1, 0)$, $v_2 = (1, 0, 1)$, $v_3 = (0, 1, 1)$ by hand, and check with Sage that the result
is orthonormal and spans the same space.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$e_1 = (1, 1, 0)/\sqrt2$; $w_2 = v_2 - \tfrac12(1, 1, 0) = (\tfrac12, -\tfrac12, 1)$, $e_2 = (1, -1, 2)/\sqrt6$;
$w_3 = v_3 - \tfrac12(1, 1, 0) - \tfrac16(1, -1, 2) = (-\tfrac23, \tfrac23, \tfrac23)$, $e_3 = (-1, 1, 1)/\sqrt3$.
Sage's `gram_schmidt` returns the orthogonal vectors $w_k$ before normalisation:

{{< sage exr-on-gram-schmidt-r3 >}}
:::

Bessel's inequality and the best-approximation property of the projection are both consequences of one identity,
the Pythagorean decomposition $\|u\|^2 = \|Pu\|^2 + \|u - Pu\|^2$. The second exercise asks for the identity and
for both consequences.

::: {#exr-on-bessel-inequality}
#### Bessel's inequality and best approximation

For an orthonormal system $e_1, \dots, e_n$ and $Pu = \sum_k\langle e_k, u\rangle e_k$, show that $u - Pu \perp
e_j$ for every $j$, that $\|u\|^2 = \|Pu\|^2 + \|u - Pu\|^2$, and that $\|u - Pu\| \leq \|u - w\|$ for every $w$ in
the span of the $e_k$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\langle e_j, u - Pu\rangle = \langle e_j, u\rangle - \sum_k\langle e_k, u\rangle\delta_{jk} = 0$. Since $Pu$ is in
the span, $\langle Pu, u - Pu\rangle = 0$, and $\|u\|^2 = \|Pu + (u - Pu)\|^2 = \|Pu\|^2 + \|u - Pu\|^2$ with the
cross terms vanishing; as $\|Pu\|^2 = \sum|\langle e_k, u\rangle|^2$ this is Bessel's inequality. For $w$ in the
span, $u - w = (u - Pu) + (Pu - w)$ with $Pu - w$ in the span and so orthogonal to $u - Pu$; hence $\|u - w\|^2 =
\|u - Pu\|^2 + \|Pu - w\|^2 \geq \|u - Pu\|^2$, with equality only for $w = Pu$.
:::

The Gram-Schmidt process on monomials can be continued indefinitely, and the fourth step already requires several
integrals. The last exercise lets Sage do the integrals and compares with the Legendre polynomial $P_3$ and with
Rodrigues' formula.

::: {#exr-on-legendre-p3}
#### The fourth Legendre polynomial

Continue @exm-on-legendre in Sage to $x^3$, normalise the four orthogonal polynomials in $L^2(-1, 1)$, and check
that they are $\sqrt{(2k + 1)/2}\,P_k(x)$ for $k = 0, 1, 2, 3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$w_4 = x^3 - \tfrac35x = \tfrac25P_3$, and all four normalised polynomials agree with $\sqrt{(2k + 1)/2}P_k$:

{{< sage exr-on-legendre-p3 >}}
:::
::::

### Hilbert spaces

An inner product space in which Cauchy sequences (@def-cauchy-sequence) need not converge is like the rationals
inside the reals: limits that "should" exist are missing. The definition below adds completeness, and the result is
the class of spaces in which infinite expansions in orthonormal systems make sense.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-hilbert-space}
#### Hilbert space

A **Hilbert space** is an inner product space $H$ that is **complete**: every Cauchy sequence, $\|u_m - u_n\| \to
0$ as $m, n \to \infty$, converges to some $u \in H$ in the norm, $\|u_n - u\| \to 0$. A subspace that is closed in
the norm is again a Hilbert space. Every inner product space has a **completion**, a Hilbert space containing it as
a dense subspace, obtained as for $\mathbb{R}$ from $\mathbb{Q}$ by adjoining limits of Cauchy sequences.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Finite-dimensional inner product spaces are automatically complete, because convergence in norm is convergence of
each coordinate. The first example records this, so that the real content of completeness lies in infinite
dimensions.

::: {#exm-hs-finite}
#### $\mathbb{C}^n$ is complete

In $\mathbb{C}^n$ with the standard inner product, $|u_k - v_k| \leq \|u - v\|$ for each coordinate, so a Cauchy
sequence of vectors has Cauchy, hence convergent, coordinates, and converges to the vector of the limits. Every
finite-dimensional inner product space is a Hilbert space, and so is the space of $n \times n$ matrices with the
trace inner product.
:::

The first infinite-dimensional Hilbert space is the space of square-summable sequences, the natural home for
coefficient sequences $(\langle e_k, u\rangle)_k$. The example defines it and sketches why it is complete, with the
details in @exr-hs-l2-cauchy.

::: {#exm-hs-l2-sequences}
#### The sequence space $\ell^2$

$\ell^2 = \{(a_n)_{n \geq 1} : \sum_n |a_n|^2 < \infty\}$ with $\langle a, b\rangle = \sum_n \bar a_n b_n$ is a
Hilbert space; the series converges absolutely by Cauchy-Schwarz on partial sums. Completeness: a Cauchy sequence
$a^{(m)}$ has Cauchy coordinates $a^{(m)}_n \to a_n$, and the limit sequence $a$ is in $\ell^2$ with $a^{(m)} \to
a$ (@exr-hs-l2-cauchy). The sequence $a_n = 1/n$ is in $\ell^2$ ($\sum 1/n^2 = \pi^2/6$, @sec-series), while
$a_n = 1/\sqrt n$ is not.
:::

The continuous functions with the integral inner product of @exm-ip-functions are the standard example of an
incomplete space: a Cauchy sequence of continuous functions can converge in norm towards a jump. The third example
exhibits such a sequence, and the completion is the space $L^2$ defined next.

::: {#exm-hs-incomplete}
#### Continuous functions are not complete in the $L^2$ norm

On $[-1, 1]$ let $f_n(x) = \max(-1, \min(1, nx))$, continuous and equal to the sign function outside
$[-1/n, 1/n]$. Then $\|f_m - f_n\|^2 \leq \int_{-1/n}^{1/n} 4\,dx = 8/n$ for $m > n$, a Cauchy sequence, but the
only candidate limit is the discontinuous $\operatorname{sign}(x)$, which is not in the space: the norm limit is
missing. The completion is $L^2(-1, 1)$ (@def-l2-space), in which $\operatorname{sign}$ is an element.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The completeness of $\ell^2$ is a model proof that reappears for every sequence space, and its two steps are to
identify a candidate limit coordinatewise and then to show that the convergence happens in the norm. The first
exercise asks for both steps.

::: {#exr-hs-l2-cauchy}
#### Completeness of $\ell^2$

Let $a^{(m)}$ be a Cauchy sequence in $\ell^2$. Show that each coordinate converges, $a^{(m)}_n \to a_n$, that
$a \in \ell^2$, and that $\|a^{(m)} - a\| \to 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|a^{(m)}_n - a^{(k)}_n| \leq \|a^{(m)} - a^{(k)}\|$, so each coordinate sequence is Cauchy in $\mathbb{C}$ and
converges, say to $a_n$. Given $\varepsilon$, choose $M$ with $\|a^{(m)} - a^{(k)}\| < \varepsilon$ for $m, k \geq
M$; for every finite $N$, $\sum_{n \leq N}|a^{(m)}_n - a^{(k)}_n|^2 < \varepsilon^2$, and letting $k \to \infty$
gives $\sum_{n \leq N}|a^{(m)}_n - a_n|^2 \leq \varepsilon^2$ for all $N$, hence $\|a^{(m)} - a\| \leq
\varepsilon$ for $m \geq M$. In particular $a^{(M)} - a \in \ell^2$, so $a = a^{(M)} - (a^{(M)} - a) \in \ell^2$,
and $a^{(m)} \to a$.
:::

Not every norm on a vector space comes from an inner product, and the parallelogram law of @exr-ip-polarisation is
the test. The second exercise applies it to the supremum norm and to the $\ell^1$ norm, which define complete
spaces (Banach spaces) that are not Hilbert spaces.

::: {#exr-hs-sup-norm-not-hilbert}
#### Norms that are not inner product norms

Show that the supremum norm $\|f\|_\infty = \sup|f|$ on continuous functions on $[0, 1]$ (@def-supremum) and the
norm $\|a\|_1 = \sum|a_n|$ on summable sequences violate the parallelogram law, so that neither comes from an inner
product.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Take $f(x) = 1$ and $g(x) = x$: $\|f + g\|_\infty = 2$, $\|f - g\|_\infty = 1$, so the left side of the law is $5$
while the right side is $2(1 + 1) = 4$. In $\ell^1$ take $a = (1, 0, 0, \dots)$, $b = (0, 1, 0, \dots)$: $\|a +
b\|_1^2 + \|a - b\|_1^2 = 4 + 4 = 8 \neq 2 + 2 = 4$. Since every inner product norm satisfies the law
(@exr-ip-polarisation), neither norm is induced by an inner product.
:::

The sequence of @exm-hs-incomplete converges in norm but not uniformly, and the two kinds of convergence must be
kept apart. The last exercise computes the norm distances explicitly and compares with uniform convergence
(@def-uniform-convergence).

::: {#exr-hs-l2-completeness-proof}
#### Norm convergence versus uniform convergence

For $f_n$ as in @exm-hs-incomplete compute $\|f_n - \operatorname{sign}\|^2$ exactly, show that $f_n \to
\operatorname{sign}$ in the $L^2$ norm, and explain why the convergence is not uniform.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
On $[0, 1/n]$, $f_n(x) - 1 = nx - 1$, and $\int_0^{1/n}(nx - 1)^2dx = 1/(3n)$; by symmetry $\|f_n -
\operatorname{sign}\|^2 = 2/(3n) \to 0$. The convergence is not uniform since $\sup_x|f_n(x) -
\operatorname{sign}(x)| = 1$ for every $n$ (approach $x = 0^+$), and indeed a uniform limit of continuous
functions would be continuous, which $\operatorname{sign}$ is not.
:::
::::

### The space $L^2$

The completion of the continuous functions in the integral norm is the space of square-integrable functions, and
describing it requires an integral more general than Riemann's. The definition below introduces the Lebesgue
integral informally, as the integral that handles limits of integrable functions, together with the identification
of functions that differ only on a negligible set.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-l2-space}
#### $L^2$ space

Let $X$ be an interval, a region of $\mathbb{R}^n$ or a surface with its volume element $d\mu$. The **Lebesgue
integral** $\int_X f\,d\mu$ extends the Riemann integral (@def-riemann-integral) to a larger class of functions
with the property that limits can be exchanged with the integral under mild conditions; every Riemann integrable
function is Lebesgue integrable with the same integral. A set is **null** (of **measure zero**) if it can be
covered by intervals of arbitrarily small total length, and functions that agree outside a null set are
**identified**. The space $L^2(X)$ consists of the (classes of) measurable functions with $\int_X|f|^2d\mu <
\infty$, with the inner product $\langle f, g\rangle = \int_X\bar f g\,d\mu$; it is a Hilbert space (the *
*Riesz-Fischer theorem**), and the continuous functions are dense in it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first instance is the circle, where the functions on $[0, 2\pi]$ with the integral inner product are
completed. The exponentials now form an orthonormal system in a Hilbert space, and the sign function excluded
in @exm-hs-incomplete is admitted.

::: {#exm-l2-circle}
#### $L^2(0, 2\pi)$ and the circle

$L^2(0, 2\pi)$, equivalently $L^2(S^1)$ for $2\pi$-periodic functions, contains every bounded Riemann integrable
function, including step functions and $\operatorname{sign}(x - \pi)$, and the exponentials $e^{inx}/\sqrt{2\pi}$
are an orthonormal system in it. The function $1/\sqrt x$ is in $L^2(0, 2\pi)$ only if $\int_0^{2\pi}dx/x$
converges, which it does not (@def-improper-integral); $x^{-1/4}$ is in $L^2$ since $\int_0^{2\pi}x^{-1/2}dx =
2\sqrt{2\pi}$.
:::

On the whole real line the inner product is an improper integral, and membership in $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ constrains
the decay at infinity. The second example is the Gaussian, the central element of the space, together with a
function that is bounded but not square-integrable.

::: {#exm-l2-real-line}
#### $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ and the Gaussian

$\psi(x) = e^{-x^2/2}$ is in $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ with $\|\psi\|^2 = \int e^{-x^2}dx = \sqrt\pi$ (the Gaussian
integral of @sec-riemann-integral), so $\pi^{-1/4}e^{-x^2/2}$ is a unit vector. The constant function $1$ and the
plane wave $e^{ikx}$ have $|f|^2 = 1$ and infinite integral: they are not in $L^2(\mathbb{R})$, a fact that
returns in @sec-unbounded-operators as the absence of eigenfunctions of the momentum operator. The function
$1/(1 + x^2)$ is in $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ (@exr-l2-membership).
:::

On a surface the volume element enters the inner product, and on the sphere it is $\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\varphi$.
The third example writes down $L^2(S^2)$, in which the spherical harmonics of @sec-harmonic-analysis form an
orthonormal system.

::: {#exm-l2-sphere}
#### $L^2(S^2)$

On the unit sphere with the area element $d\mu = \sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\varphi$, $\langle f, g\rangle =
\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi \bar f g\,\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\varphi$. The constant $1$ has $\|1\|^2 = 4\pi$, the area;
$\cos\theta$ has $\|\cos\theta\|^2 = 2\pi\int_0^\pi\cos^2\theta\sin\theta\,d\theta = 4\pi/3$, and $\langle 1,
\cos\theta\rangle = 0$. Normalised, $Y_{00} = 1/\sqrt{4\pi}$ and $Y_{10} = \sqrt{3/4\pi}\cos\theta$ are the first
spherical harmonics (@exr-l2-sphere-norm).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Deciding whether a function is square-integrable is a convergence test for an improper integral, local near
singularities and global at infinity. The first exercise runs Sage on four functions on $\mathbb{R}$ or on
$(0, 1)$.

::: {#exr-l2-membership}
#### Which functions are in $L^2$?

Decide, by hand and with Sage, which of $1/(1 + x^2)$, $1/\sqrt{1 + x^2}$, $\sin x/x$ on $\mathbb{R}$, and
$x^{-1/3}$, $x^{-1/2}$ on $(0, 1)$, belong to $L^2$, and compute the norms of those that do.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\int (1 + x^2)^{-2}dx = \pi/2$ (in $L^2$), $\int (1 + x^2)^{-1}dx = \pi$ (in $L^2$), $\int \sin^2x/x^2\,dx =
\pi$ (in $L^2$, although $\sin x/x$ is not absolutely integrable); $\int_0^1 x^{-2/3}dx = 3$ (in $L^2$) while
$\int_0^1 x^{-1}dx$ diverges ($x^{-1/2} \notin L^2(0, 1)$):

{{< sage exr-l2-membership >}}
:::

The identification of functions agreeing outside a null set is what makes $L^2$ a space of classes rather than of
functions, and the Dirichlet function is the standard illustration. The second exercise asks what it means for
this function to be the zero element, and connects with the Riemann integral.

::: {#exr-l2-dirichlet-function}
#### The Dirichlet function in $L^2$

The function $D(x) = 1$ for rational $x$ and $0$ for irrational $x$ on $[0, 1]$ is not Riemann integrable. Explain
why it is the zero element of $L^2(0, 1)$, why $\|D\| = 0$ is consistent with positive definiteness, and why the
value of an $L^2$ function at a single point is not defined.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The rationals in $[0, 1]$ are countable, $q_1, q_2, \dots$, and are covered by intervals of length
$\varepsilon 2^{-k}$ around $q_k$ with total length $\varepsilon$: a null set. $D$ agrees with $0$ outside it, so
$D$ and $0$ are identified and $\int D^2 = 0$. Positive definiteness holds for classes: $\|f\| = 0$ means $f = 0$
outside a null set, which is the zero class. A point is a null set, so changing $f$ at a point does not change its
class: $f(x_0)$ has no meaning for $f \in L^2$, only integrals of $f$ against other functions do. In
@sec-riemann-integral the same function appears as the example where upper and lower sums disagree.
:::

The normalisation constants of the spherical harmonics are integrals over the sphere with the correct area
element, and Sage computes them exactly. The last exercise does this for the three $l = 1$ harmonics and checks
their mutual orthogonality.

::: {#exr-l2-sphere-norm}
#### Normalising the $l = 1$ harmonics

Compute $\|\cos\theta\|^2$, $\|\sin\theta\,e^{i\varphi}\|^2$ and $\langle\cos\theta, \sin\theta\,e^{i\varphi}
\rangle$ in $L^2(S^2)$ with Sage, and show that $Y_{10} = \sqrt{3/4\pi}\cos\theta$ and $Y_{1, \pm1} =
\mp\sqrt{3/8\pi}\sin\theta\,e^{\pm i\varphi}$ are orthonormal.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\|\cos\theta\|^2 = 4\pi/3$, $\|\sin\theta\,e^{i\varphi}\|^2 = 2\pi\int_0^\pi\sin^3\theta\,d\theta = 8\pi/3$, and
the cross inner product vanishes because $\int_0^{2\pi}e^{i\varphi}d\varphi = 0$; dividing by the norms gives the
$Y_{1m}$, whose Gram matrix Sage returns as the identity:

{{< sage exr-l2-sphere-norm >}}
:::
::::

### Orthonormal bases

A finite orthonormal system spans a subspace; the question is when an infinite one spans, in the sense of limits,
the whole Hilbert space. The definition below answers it with the notion of an orthonormal basis and records
Parseval's identity, the infinite-dimensional Pythagorean theorem, which turns Bessel's inequality into an
equality.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-orthonormal-basis}
#### Orthonormal basis

An orthonormal system $(e_k)$ in a Hilbert space $H$ is an **orthonormal basis** if it is **complete**: the only
vector orthogonal to every $e_k$ is $0$. Equivalently, every $u \in H$ is the norm-convergent sum of its
**expansion** $u = \sum_k\langle e_k, u\rangle e_k$, and equivalently again **Parseval's identity** $\|u\|^2 =
\sum_k|\langle e_k, u\rangle|^2$ holds for all $u$; then also $\langle u, v\rangle = \sum_k\overline{\langle e_k,
u\rangle}\langle e_k, v\rangle$. A Hilbert space with a countable orthonormal basis is **separable**, and the map
$u \mapsto (\langle e_k, u\rangle)_k$ is then an isomorphism of $H$ onto $\ell^2$ preserving inner products. An
orthonormal basis of an infinite-dimensional space is not a basis in the sense of @def-basis, since infinite sums
are allowed.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The sequences with a single non-zero entry form the standard orthonormal basis of $\ell^2$, and every orthonormal
basis is modelled on it by the isomorphism in the definition. The first example checks completeness and Parseval
directly.

::: {#exm-onb-l2-sequences}
#### The standard basis of $\ell^2$

$\delta^{(k)} = (0, \dots, 0, 1, 0, \dots)$ with the $1$ in position $k$ form an orthonormal system in $\ell^2$, and
$\langle\delta^{(k)}, a\rangle = a_k$. If $a \perp \delta^{(k)}$ for all $k$ then every $a_k = 0$, so the system is
complete; Parseval's identity $\|a\|^2 = \sum|a_k|^2$ is the definition of the norm, and the expansion $a = \sum_k
a_k\delta^{(k)}$ converges in norm because the tail $\sum_{k > N}|a_k|^2 \to 0$.
:::

The exponentials are an orthonormal basis of $L^2(0, 2\pi)$; this is the completeness of the Fourier system, proved
in @sec-fourier-series and quoted here. Parseval's identity then turns an integral into a sum, and the example
evaluates $\sum 1/n^2$ this way.

::: {#exm-onb-fourier-parseval}
#### The Fourier basis and $\sum 1/n^2$

$e_n = e^{inx}/\sqrt{2\pi}$, $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, is an orthonormal basis of $L^2(-\pi, \pi)$ (@sec-fourier-series).
For $f(x) = x$, $\langle e_n, f\rangle = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\pi}^\pi xe^{-inx}dx = \sqrt{2\pi}\,i(-1)^n/n$
for $n \neq 0$ and $0$ for $n = 0$, so Parseval gives $\tfrac{2\pi^3}{3} = \|f\|^2 = 2\pi\sum_{n \neq 0}1/n^2 =
4\pi\sum_{n \geq 1}1/n^2$, that is, $\sum_{n \geq 1}1/n^2 = \pi^2/6$ (@exr-onb-parseval-x, @sec-series).
:::

The normalised Legendre polynomials are an orthonormal basis of $L^2(-1, 1)$, by the completeness part of the
Sturm-Liouville theorem (@thm-sturm-liouville) or by the density of polynomials. The third example states this and
shows how a function is expanded in them, with the figure as illustration.

::: {#exm-onb-legendre}
#### The Legendre basis of $L^2(-1, 1)$

$e_k = \sqrt{(2k + 1)/2}\,P_k$, $k \geq 0$, is an orthonormal basis of $L^2(-1, 1)$: polynomials are dense in the
continuous functions on $[-1, 1]$ (Weierstrass), which are dense in $L^2$, and the span of $e_0, \dots, e_n$ is the
polynomials of degree $\leq n$. The expansion of $e^x$ begins $e^x = \sinh 1\,P_0 + 3e^{-1}P_1 +
\tfrac52(e - 7e^{-1})P_2 + \dots$, and the sum of the first three terms is the projection shown in
@fig-gram-schmidt-projection (@prp-hilbert-space-computations).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The Fourier coefficients of $x$ and the resulting value of $\sum 1/n^2$ are a computation Sage does exactly, and the
partial sums of Parseval's identity show how fast the expansion converges. The first exercise carries this out and
repeats it for $x^2$, where the answer is $\sum 1/n^4$.

::: {#exr-onb-parseval-x}
#### Parseval for $x$ and $x^2$

With Sage, compute the Fourier coefficients of $f(x) = x$ and $g(x) = x^2$ on $(-\pi, \pi)$, verify Parseval's
identity in the form of the series $\sum 1/n^2 = \pi^2/6$ and $\sum 1/n^4 = \pi^4/90$, and check that the partial
sum over $|n| \leq 10$ already gives $\|f\|^2$ to within $10\%$ and $\|g\|^2$ to within $0.1\%$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|\langle e_n, f\rangle|^2 = 2\pi/n^2$ and, for $g$, $\langle e_0, g\rangle = \sqrt{2\pi}\,\pi^2/3$ with
$|\langle e_n, g\rangle|^2 = 8\pi/n^4$ for $n \neq 0$; the second series converges much faster because $g$ is
continuous as a periodic function while $f$ has a jump at $\pm\pi$:

{{< sage exr-onb-parseval-x >}}
:::

The three characterisations of an orthonormal basis in the definition are equivalent, and the equivalence is the
basic theorem on orthonormal systems. The second exercise asks for the proof, with completeness of the Hilbert
space used to make the expansion converge.

::: {#exr-onb-maximal-equivalence}
#### Three characterisations of an orthonormal basis

For an orthonormal system $(e_k)_{k \geq 1}$ in a Hilbert space, prove that the following are equivalent: (a) no
non-zero vector is orthogonal to all $e_k$; (b) $u = \sum_k\langle e_k, u\rangle e_k$ for all $u$; (c) $\|u\|^2 =
\sum_k|\langle e_k, u\rangle|^2$ for all $u$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) $\Rightarrow$ (b): by Bessel's inequality $\sum|\langle e_k, u\rangle|^2 \leq \|u\|^2$ converges, so the
partial sums $s_N = \sum_{k \leq N}\langle e_k, u\rangle e_k$ are Cauchy ($\|s_M - s_N\|^2 = \sum_{N < k \leq
M}|\langle e_k, u\rangle|^2$) and converge, by completeness, to some $s$. Then $\langle e_j, u - s\rangle =
\langle e_j, u\rangle - \langle e_j, u\rangle = 0$ for all $j$, so $u - s = 0$ by (a). (b) $\Rightarrow$ (c):
$\|u\|^2 = \lim\|s_N\|^2 = \lim\sum_{k \leq N}|\langle e_k, u\rangle|^2$ by continuity of the norm. (c)
$\Rightarrow$ (a): if $u \perp e_k$ for all $k$ then $\|u\|^2 = \sum 0 = 0$, so $u = 0$.
:::

Every separable Hilbert space is isomorphic to $\ell^2$, so "the" infinite-dimensional separable Hilbert space is
unique up to isomorphism; non-separable spaces exist but play no role here. The last exercise constructs the
isomorphism and shows why the plane waves cannot be an orthonormal system in $L^2(\mathbb{R})$.

::: {#exr-onb-separable}
#### $L^2$ is $\ell^2$ in disguise

Show that $U : L^2(-\pi, \pi) \to \ell^2(\mathbb{Z})$, $Uf = (\langle e_n, f\rangle)_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}$, is a
bijective linear map with $\langle Uf, Ug\rangle = \langle f, g\rangle$. Then explain why the family $\{e^{ikx}
: k \in \mathbb{R}\}$ cannot be an orthonormal basis of $L^2(\mathbb{R})$, although $\int e^{-ikx}e^{ik'x}dx$
"vanishes" for $k \neq k'$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$U$ is linear and preserves inner products by Parseval's identity in its polarised form, hence is injective; it is
surjective because for $a \in \ell^2(\mathbb{Z})$ the sum $\sum a_ne_n$ converges in $L^2$ (its partial sums are
Cauchy) to an $f$ with $Uf = a$. For the plane waves: they are not in $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ at all
(@exm-l2-real-line), and an orthonormal system in a separable space is countable, since the balls of radius
$1/2$ around its members are disjoint and a countable dense set must meet each; $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable. The
plane waves are instead a "continuous basis" in the sense of the Fourier transform (@sec-fourier-transform) and of
distributions (@sec-distributions).
:::
::::

### The Riesz representation theorem

A linear functional (@def-linear-functional) on a Hilbert space is a linear map to the scalars, and taking the
inner product with a fixed vector is one. The theorem below, quoted without proof, says that in a Hilbert space
there are no others among the continuous ones: the dual space (@def-dual-space) is the space itself, which is why
bra vectors and ket vectors can be identified.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-riesz-representation}
#### Riesz representation theorem

Let $H$ be a Hilbert space and $\varphi : H \to \mathbb{C}$ a linear functional that is **bounded**: $|\varphi(u)|
\leq C\|u\|$ for some constant $C$ and all $u$. Then there is a unique $v \in H$ with $\varphi(u) = \langle v,
u\rangle$ for all $u$, and the smallest constant $C$ equals $\|v\|$. Conversely every $u \mapsto \langle v,
u\rangle$ is bounded by Cauchy-Schwarz. The proof takes $v$ in the orthogonal complement of the kernel of
$\varphi$, which is a closed subspace of codimension one; the statement is quoted here and the outline is
@exr-riesz-proof-outline.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
In $\mathbb{C}^n$ the theorem is the statement that every linear functional is given by a row vector, and the
representing vector is its conjugate. The first example makes this explicit, including the correspondence of
norms.

::: {#exm-riesz-cn}
#### Functionals on $\mathbb{C}^n$

A linear functional on $\mathbb{C}^n$ is $\varphi(u) = \sum_k c_ku_k$ for some coefficients $c_k$
(@sec-linear-maps-dual), and $\varphi(u) = \langle v, u\rangle$ with $v_k = \bar c_k$. For $\varphi(u) = u_1 +
iu_2$ on $\mathbb{C}^2$ the representing vector is $v = (1, -i)$, and the best constant in $|\varphi(u)| \leq
C\|u\|$ is $\|v\| = \sqrt2$, attained at $u = v$.
:::

On $\ell^2$ the bounded functionals are the sums $\sum c_na_n$ with $c \in \ell^2$, and the theorem says that no
other bounded functional exists; the second example also shows a functional that is linear but not bounded. On a
space with an orthonormal basis, boundedness of a functional is a condition on its values on the basis.

::: {#exm-riesz-l2}
#### Functionals on $\ell^2$

For $c \in \ell^2$, $\varphi_c(a) = \sum_n\bar c_na_n = \langle c, a\rangle$ is bounded by $\|c\|$. Conversely a
bounded $\varphi$ has values $c_n = \overline{\varphi(\delta^{(n)})}$ with $\sum_{n \leq N}|c_n|^2 =
\varphi(\sum_{n \leq N}c_n\delta^{(n)}) \leq C(\sum_{n \leq N}|c_n|^2)^{1/2}$, so $\sum|c_n|^2 \leq C^2$ and $c \in
\ell^2$ (@exr-riesz-norm). The functional $\varphi(a) = \sum_n a_n$ is defined on the finite sequences but not
bounded: on $a = (1, \tfrac12, \dots, \tfrac1N, 0, \dots)$ it gives $H_N \to \infty$ while $\|a\| \leq \pi/\sqrt6$.
:::

The evaluation $f \mapsto f(x_0)$ is the most important linear functional on functions, and the third example
explains why it is not represented by any vector of $L^2$: the would-be representing function is the delta
function. This is where the Riesz theorem hands over to the theory of distributions.

::: {#exm-riesz-delta}
#### Evaluation is not bounded on $L^2$

On $L^2(-1, 1)$ the functional $f \mapsto f(0)$ is not even well defined, since $f(0)$ depends on the
representative (@exr-l2-dirichlet-function); on continuous functions it is defined but not bounded in the $L^2$
norm: $f_n(x) = \max(0, 1 - n|x|)$ has $f_n(0) = 1$ and $\|f_n\|^2 = 2/(3n) \to 0$. So there is no $g \in L^2$
with $f(0) = \int\bar gf\,dx$; the "function" $\delta(x)$ that would do it is a distribution
(@sec-distributions). The theorem does apply to $f \mapsto \int_{-1}^0f\,dx$, represented by the indicator
function of $[-1, 0]$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The norm of a functional, the smallest constant $C$, equals the norm of its representing vector, and the proof of
this half of the theorem is a Cauchy-Schwarz argument. The first exercise asks for it and for the computation in a
concrete case on $\ell^2$.

::: {#exr-riesz-norm}
#### The norm of a functional

Show that for $\varphi(u) = \langle v, u\rangle$ the smallest constant $C$ with $|\varphi(u)| \leq C\|u\|$ is
$\|v\|$, and find it for $\varphi(a) = \sum_{n \geq 1}a_n/n$ on $\ell^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Cauchy-Schwarz gives $|\langle v, u\rangle| \leq \|v\|\|u\|$, so $C = \|v\|$ works, and $u = v$ gives
$|\varphi(v)| = \|v\|^2 = \|v\|\|v\|$, so no smaller constant does. For $\varphi(a) = \sum a_n/n$ the representing
vector is $v = (1/n)_n$ with $\|v\| = \sqrt{\sum 1/n^2} = \pi/\sqrt6$, which is the norm of $\varphi$.
:::

The existence half of the theorem rests on the projection onto a closed subspace, which exists in a Hilbert space
by completeness. The second exercise asks the reader to assemble the argument from the kernel of $\varphi$ and
one vector orthogonal to it.

::: {#exr-riesz-proof-outline}
#### Outline of the proof

Assume that every closed subspace $K$ of $H$ has an orthogonal complement, $H = K \oplus K^\perp$. For a bounded
non-zero functional $\varphi$, let $K = \ker\varphi$ and pick a unit vector $w \in K^\perp$. Show that $K^\perp$ is
one-dimensional and that $v = \overline{\varphi(w)}\,w$ represents $\varphi$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$K$ is closed because $\varphi$ is continuous (bounded). For any $u$, the vector $\varphi(w)u - \varphi(u)w$ lies in
$K$, so it is orthogonal to $w$: $\varphi(w)\langle w, u\rangle - \varphi(u)\langle w, w\rangle = 0$, that is,
$\varphi(u) = \varphi(w)\langle w, u\rangle = \langle\overline{\varphi(w)}w, u\rangle$. In particular every $u \in
K^\perp$ satisfies $u = \langle w, u\rangle w$ (apply the identity $u = (u - \varphi(u)w/\varphi(w)) +
\varphi(u)w/\varphi(w)$ and note that the first term is in $K \cap K^\perp = 0$), so $K^\perp = \mathbb{C}w$.
Uniqueness: if $\langle v - v', u\rangle = 0$ for all $u$, take $u = v - v'$.
:::

For a functional given by an integral against a known function, the representing vector in a finite-dimensional
subspace is the projection of that function. The last exercise computes it in Sage for the functional
$f \mapsto \int_{-1}^1 x^3 f(x)\,dx$ restricted to the polynomials of degree at most $2$.

::: {#exr-riesz-sage-coefficients}
#### Representing a functional on polynomials

Let $V$ be the polynomials of degree $\leq 2$ in $L^2(-1, 1)$ and $\varphi(f) = \int_{-1}^1x^3f(x)\,dx$. Find
$v \in V$ with $\varphi(f) = \langle v, f\rangle$ for all $f \in V$ by expanding $x^3$ in the orthonormal Legendre
basis of $V$ with Sage, and check it on $f = 1, x, x^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$v$ is the orthogonal projection of $x^3$ onto $V$: $v = \sum_{k \leq 2}\langle e_k, x^3\rangle e_k = \tfrac35x$,
since $x^3$ is odd and $\langle x, x^3\rangle/\langle x, x\rangle = (2/5)/(2/3)$. The values $\varphi(1) = 0$,
$\varphi(x) = 2/5$, $\varphi(x^2) = 0$ agree with $\langle\tfrac35x, f\rangle$:

{{< sage exr-riesz-sage-coefficients >}}
:::
::::

### Worked computations

The computations of this section, Gram-Schmidt on monomials, the orthogonal projection in the plane and in
$L^2(-1, 1)$, and Parseval's identity for $f(x) = x$, are collected in one proposition. Each of them is a finite
computation with exact integrals and exact arithmetic.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-hilbert-space-computations}
#### Orthonormalisation and projection

Gram-Schmidt on $1, x, x^2, x^3$ in $L^2(-1, 1)$ gives $P_0, P_1, \tfrac23P_2, \tfrac25P_3$; the projection of
$(1, 2)$ onto the line spanned by $(2, 1)$ is $(\tfrac85, \tfrac45)$ with residual $(-\tfrac35, \tfrac65)$
orthogonal to the line; the $L^2(-1, 1)$ projection of $e^x$ onto polynomials of degree $\leq 2$ has a smaller
error than the Taylor polynomial of degree $2$; the partial Parseval sums of $f(x) = x$ on $(-\pi, \pi)$ increase
towards $\|f\|^2 = 2\pi^3/3$ and equal $4\pi\sum_{n \leq N}1/n^2$; and Cauchy-Schwarz holds with its sharp
constant for $(1, i, 0)$, $(1, 1, 1)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Exact computation (`figures/gram_schmidt_projection.sage`, symbolic integrals and exact
rational arithmetic).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The orthogonal projection onto a line is the first case of the formula $Pu = \sum\langle e_k, u\rangle e_k$, and
the figure shows it. The first example works through the numbers of the left panel.

::: {#exm-hsc-gram-schmidt-sage}
#### The left panel of the figure

With $v_1 = (2, 1)$, $e_1 = v_1/\sqrt5$ and $\langle e_1, v_2\rangle e_1 = \tfrac{4}{5}(2, 1) = (\tfrac85,
\tfrac45)$ for $v_2 = (1, 2)$; the residual $w_2 = (1, 2) - (\tfrac85, \tfrac45) = (-\tfrac35, \tfrac65)$ has
$\langle v_1, w_2\rangle = -\tfrac65 + \tfrac65 = 0$ and $e_2 = w_2/\|w_2\| = (-1, 2)/\sqrt5$. Sage's
`gram_schmidt` on the matrix with rows $v_1, v_2$ returns exactly $v_1$ and $w_2$.
:::

The right panel compares two quadratic approximations of $e^x$ on $[-1, 1]$: the Taylor polynomial, which is
best near $x = 0$, and the Legendre projection, which is best on average. The example gives the two polynomials
and the two errors.

::: {#exm-hsc-projection}
#### Legendre projection versus Taylor polynomial

The Taylor polynomial is $T_2 = 1 + x + x^2/2$ with $\|e^x - T_2\|^2 = \int_{-1}^1(e^x - 1 - x - x^2/2)^2dx
\approx 0.00899$. The projection is $Pe^x = \sinh 1 + 3e^{-1}x + \tfrac52(e - 7e^{-1})(\tfrac32x^2 - \tfrac12)
\approx 0.9963 + 1.1036x + 0.5367x^2$, with $\|e^x - Pe^x\|^2 \approx 0.00144$, about six times smaller
(@exr-hsc-best-approximation); near $x = 0$ the Taylor polynomial is nonetheless closer.
:::

Parseval's identity is a limit statement, and it is best seen through its partial sums, which
increase monotonically to the norm. The third example shows the numbers and relates the rate of convergence to the
jump of $f$.

::: {#exm-hsc-parseval-rate}
#### Partial Parseval sums for $f(x) = x$

$\sum_{|n| \leq N}|\langle e_n, f\rangle|^2 = 4\pi\sum_{n \leq N}1/n^2$ equals $4\pi \cdot 1 = 12.57$, $4\pi\cdot 1.
4636 = 18.39$ and $4\pi\cdot 1.5498 = 19.47$ for $N = 1, 5, 10$, against $\|f\|^2 = 2\pi^3/3 = 20.67$; the
missing tail $4\pi\sum_{n > N}1/n^2 \approx 4\pi/N$ decays slowly because the coefficients decay only like $1/n$,
the signature of the jump of the periodic extension of $x$ at $\pm\pi$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The projection formula is independent of which orthonormal basis of the subspace is used, a fact best believed
after a computation. The first exercise projects a vector of $\mathbb{R}^3$ onto a plane with two different
orthonormal bases of the plane.

::: {#exr-hsc-projection-plane}
#### Projection onto a plane

Project $u = (1, 2, 3)$ onto the plane $x + y + z = 0$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ using the orthonormal basis obtained by
Gram-Schmidt from $(1, -1, 0), (1, 0, -1)$, then using the one from $(0, 1, -1), (1, -1, 0)$, and check with Sage
that both give the same vector, equal to $u - \langle n, u\rangle n$ with $n = (1, 1, 1)/\sqrt3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Both give $Pu = (1, 2, 3) - 2(1, 1, 1) = (-1, 0, 1)$: the projection depends only on the subspace, and projecting
onto the plane is the same as removing the component along its normal:

{{< sage exr-hsc-projection-plane >}}
:::

The error of the Legendre projection in @exm-hsc-projection can be written without computing the projection
itself, by Pythagoras. The second exercise asks for this formula and uses it to show that adding $P_3$ to the
expansion reduces the error by a further large factor.

::: {#exr-hsc-best-approximation}
#### The error of a projection

Show that $\|u - P_nu\|^2 = \|u\|^2 - \sum_{k \leq n}|\langle e_k, u\rangle|^2$ for the projection onto $e_0,
\dots, e_n$, and use $\langle e_k, e^x\rangle$ for $k = 0, \dots, 3$ to compute $\|e^x - P_2e^x\|^2$ and $\|e^x -
P_3e^x\|^2$ to three significant figures.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By @exr-on-bessel-inequality, $\|u\|^2 = \|P_nu\|^2 + \|u - P_nu\|^2$ with $\|P_nu\|^2 = \sum_{k \leq n}|\langle
e_k, u\rangle|^2$. With $\|e^x\|^2 = \sinh 2 = 3.6269$ and $\langle e_k, e^x\rangle = \sqrt{(2k+1)/2}\int_{-1}^1
P_ke^xdx$: $\int P_0e^x = 2\sinh 1$, $\int P_1e^x = 2e^{-1}$, $\int P_2e^x = e - 7e^{-1}$, $\int P_3e^x = 37e^{-1} -
5e$, giving $|\langle e_k, e^x\rangle|^2 = 2.7622, 0.8120, 0.0512, 0.00142$; so $\|e^x - P_2e^x\|^2 \approx
3.6269 - 3.6254 = 0.00144$ and $\|e^x - P_3e^x\|^2 \approx 0.0000223$, a reduction by a factor of about $65$.
:::

Projection onto trigonometric polynomials is the partial Fourier sum, and for a function with a jump the error
decreases slowly, as @exm-hsc-parseval-rate showed. The last exercise asks Sage for the projections of the square
wave onto the first few modes and for the errors, which follow Parseval exactly.

::: {#exr-hsc-trig-projection}
#### Projecting the square wave

For $f = \operatorname{sign}(x)$ on $(-\pi, \pi)$, compute with Sage the projection $P_Nf$ onto
$\{e^{inx}/\sqrt{2\pi} : |n| \leq N\}$ for $N = 1, 3, 5$, the errors $\|f - P_Nf\|^2$, and check them against
$\|f\|^2 - \sum_{|n| \leq N}|\langle e_n, f\rangle|^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\langle e_n, f\rangle = -2i\sqrt{2/\pi}/n$ for odd $n$ and $0$ for even $n$, so $P_Nf = \tfrac4\pi\sum_{\text{odd }
n \leq N}\sin nx/n$ and $\|f - P_Nf\|^2 = 2\pi - \tfrac{16}{\pi}\sum_{\text{odd } n \leq N}1/n^2$, which is
$1.190$, $0.624$ and $0.421$ for $N = 1, 3, 5$:

{{< sage exr-hsc-trig-projection >}}
:::
::::

## Bounded operators {#sec-bounded-operators}

A bounded operator is a linear map of a Hilbert space to itself that stretches no vector by more than a fixed
factor; in finite dimensions every linear map is one. This section defines the operator norm, the adjoint and the
three classes of operators that quantum mechanics and spectral theory use constantly, self-adjoint, unitary and
projection operators, and ends with the commutator; the figure shows how an operator deforms the unit circle, and
the proposition checks the identities in Sage.

### The operator norm

A linear map (@def-linear-map) between inner product spaces may stretch different vectors by different factors, and
the largest stretching factor measures its size. The figure shows the image of the unit circle under three
operators, an ellipse, a circle and a segment, whose longest radius is this factor; the definition below names it.

![The unit circle of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and its images under a general matrix $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 &
1\end{pmatrix}$ (an ellipse whose semi-axes are the singular values $\sigma_1 = \|A\| \approx 2.29$ and $\sigma_2
\approx 0.87$, with $\sigma_1\sigma_2 = |\det A| = 2$), under a rotation $U$ (the circle itself, $\|U\| = 1$) and
under the orthogonal projection $P$ onto the diagonal (a segment, $\|P\| = 1$). Generated by
`figures/operator_norm_ellipse.sage`.](figures/operator_norm_ellipse.svg){#fig-operator-norm-ellipse width=95%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-bounded-operator}
#### Bounded operator

A linear map $A : H \to H$ on a Hilbert space is a **bounded operator** if its **operator norm** $\|A\| =
\sup_{u \neq 0}\|Au\|/\|u\| = \sup_{\|u\| = 1}\|Au\|$ is finite, so that $\|Au\| \leq \|A\|\,\|u\|$ for all $u$;
a linear map is bounded exactly when it is continuous. The bounded operators form a vector space $\mathcal{B}(H)$
with $\|A + B\| \leq \|A\| + \|B\|$, $\|\alpha A\| = |\alpha|\|A\|$, and the composition satisfies $\|AB\| \leq
\|A\|\,\|B\|$. In finite dimensions every linear map is bounded and $\|A\|$ is the largest **singular value** of
$A$, the square root of the largest eigenvalue of $A^\dagger A$, with $A^\dagger = \bar A^{\mathsf{T}}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The norm of a matrix is read off the ellipse into which it maps the unit circle: the longest semi-axis. The first
example computes it for the matrix of the figure, where the answer is not the largest entry nor the largest
eigenvalue.

::: {#exm-bo-matrix-norm}
#### The norm of a $2 \times 2$ matrix

For $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, $A^{\mathsf{T}}A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 2
\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $3 \pm \sqrt5$, so $\|A\| = \sqrt{3 + \sqrt5} = (1 + \sqrt5)/\sqrt2 \approx 2.288$
(@prp-bounded-operator-checks). This exceeds the eigenvalues $2$ and $1$ of $A$ itself: the vector $u = (1,
1)/\sqrt2$ is stretched to $\|Au\| = \|(3, 1)\|/\sqrt2 = \sqrt5 \approx 2.236$, and the best direction does
slightly better.
:::

Multiplying a function by a fixed bounded function is a bounded operator on $L^2$, and its norm is the largest
value of the multiplier. The second example is the position operator on an interval, which will be the model for
the continuous spectrum in @sec-spectral-theory.

::: {#exm-bo-multiplication}
#### Multiplication operators

For a bounded function $g$ on $X$, $(M_gf)(x) = g(x)f(x)$ is a bounded operator on $L^2(X)$ with $\|M_gf\|^2 =
\int|g|^2|f|^2 \leq (\sup|g|)^2\|f\|^2$, and $\|M_g\| = \sup|g|$ (up to null sets). On $L^2(0, 1)$ the position
operator $(xf)(x) = xf(x)$ has norm $1$, approached by functions concentrated near $x = 1$ but attained by none
(@exr-bo-norm-properties).
:::

The shift on $\ell^2$ moves every coordinate one place to the right, preserving the norm, and its adjoint will
turn out to move them to the left. The third example introduces this pair, the simplest operators without any
finite-dimensional analogue.

::: {#exm-bo-shift}
#### The shift on $\ell^2$

$S(a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots) = (0, a_1, a_2, \dots)$ satisfies $\|Sa\| = \|a\|$, so $\|S\| = 1$; the **backward
shift** $S^*(a_1, a_2, \dots) = (a_2, a_3, \dots)$ also has norm $1$, with $\|S^*a\| < \|a\|$ whenever $a_1 \neq
0$. The differentiation operator, by contrast, is not bounded on any natural domain in $L^2$
(@exr-bo-differentiation-unbounded), which is why @sec-unbounded-operators is needed.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Sage's `norm(2)` returns the operator norm of a matrix, and comparing it with the square root of the largest
eigenvalue of $A^\dagger A$ makes the definition concrete. The first exercise does this for two matrices, one of
which has the golden ratio as its norm.

::: {#exr-bo-norm-2x2}
#### Operator norms in Sage

Compute $\|A\|$ for $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1
\end{pmatrix}$ from the eigenvalues of $A^{\mathsf{T}}A$ and $B^{\mathsf{T}}B$, compare with Sage's `norm(2)`, and
show that $\|B\| = (1 + \sqrt5)/2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$B^{\mathsf{T}}B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$ has largest eigenvalue $(3 + \sqrt5)/2 = \varphi^2$
with $\varphi$ the golden ratio, so $\|B\| = \varphi \approx 1.618$; for $A$, $\|A\| = \sqrt{(30 + \sqrt{884})/2}
\approx 5.465$:

{{< sage exr-bo-norm-2x2 >}}
:::

The two inequalities quoted in the definition and the characterisation of the norm by matrix elements are short
consequences of Cauchy-Schwarz. The second exercise asks for them and for the statement that the norm of the
position operator on $(0, 1)$ is not attained.

::: {#exr-bo-norm-properties}
#### Properties of the operator norm

Prove $\|AB\| \leq \|A\|\|B\|$, prove $\|A\| = \sup\{|\langle v, Au\rangle| : \|u\| = \|v\| = 1\}$, and show that
the position operator on $L^2(0, 1)$ has norm $1$ but $\|xf\| < \|f\|$ for every $f \neq 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\|ABu\| \leq \|A\|\|Bu\| \leq \|A\|\|B\|\|u\|$. By Cauchy-Schwarz $|\langle v, Au\rangle| \leq \|Au\| \leq
\|A\|$ for unit $u, v$, and choosing $v = Au/\|Au\|$ gives $|\langle v, Au\rangle| = \|Au\|$, whose supremum over
unit $u$ is $\|A\|$. For the position operator, $\|xf\|^2 = \int_0^1x^2|f|^2dx < \int_0^1|f|^2dx$ because $x^2 <
1$ on $(0, 1)$ and $|f|^2$ is not the zero class; but $f_n = \sqrt n\,\mathbf{1}_{[1 - 1/n, 1]}$ has $\|f_n\| = 1$
and $\|xf_n\|^2 = n\int_{1 - 1/n}^1x^2dx = 1 - 1/n + 1/(3n^2) \to 1$, so the norm is $1$.
:::

Differentiation multiplies the mode $e^{inx}$ by $in$, so it stretches high modes without bound and cannot be a
bounded operator. The last exercise makes this precise on trigonometric polynomials and on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$.

::: {#exr-bo-differentiation-unbounded}
#### Differentiation is not bounded

Show that there is no constant $C$ with $\|f'\| \leq C\|f\|$ for all trigonometric polynomials $f$ on $(0, 2\pi)$,
and none with $\|f'\| \leq C\|f\|$ for all Gaussians $f(x) = e^{-ax^2}$, $a > 0$, on $\mathbb{R}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For $f = e^{inx}$, $\|f'\| = n\|f\|$, which exceeds $C\|f\|$ as soon as $n > C$. For $f = e^{-ax^2}$, $\|f\|^2 =
\sqrt{\pi/2a}$ and $\|f'\|^2 = 4a^2\int x^2e^{-2ax^2}dx = 4a^2\cdot\tfrac{1}{4a}\sqrt{\pi/2a} = a\sqrt{\pi/2a}$,
so $\|f'\|/\|f\| = \sqrt a \to \infty$ as $a \to \infty$: narrow Gaussians have steep slopes. In both cases the
ratio $\|f'\|/\|f\|$ is unbounded, so differentiation has no finite operator norm.
:::
::::

### The adjoint

Moving an operator from one slot of the inner product to the other produces, in general, a different operator;
for matrices this is the conjugate transpose already used above. The definition below introduces it for bounded
operators, where the Riesz representation theorem guarantees its existence.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-adjoint-operator}
#### Adjoint operator

The **adjoint** of a bounded operator $A$ is the unique bounded operator $A^\dagger$ with $\langle Au, v\rangle =
\langle u, A^\dagger v\rangle$ for all $u, v \in H$; it exists because for fixed $v$ the functional $u \mapsto
\langle v, Au\rangle$ is bounded and so, by @thm-riesz-representation, equals $\langle A^\dagger v, u\rangle$ for a
unique vector $A^\dagger v$. The adjoint satisfies $(A^\dagger)^\dagger = A$, $(AB)^\dagger = B^\dagger
A^\dagger$, $(\alpha A + B)^\dagger = \bar\alpha A^\dagger + B^\dagger$, $\|A^\dagger\| = \|A\|$ and
$\|A^\dagger A\| = \|A\|^2$. For a matrix in an orthonormal basis, $A^\dagger = \bar A^{\mathsf{T}}$, the
**conjugate transpose**. In Dirac's notation the operator $|u\rangle\langle v| : w \mapsto \langle v, w\rangle u$
has adjoint $|v\rangle\langle u|$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The conjugate transpose is the adjoint because the standard inner product on $\mathbb{C}^n$ conjugates the first
vector. The first example verifies the defining identity on a matrix with a complex entry, where the conjugation
matters.

::: {#exm-adj-matrix}
#### The conjugate transpose

For $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & i \\ 0 & 2\end{pmatrix}$, $A^\dagger = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -i & 2\end{pmatrix}$.
With $u = (1, 0)$ and $v = (0, 1)$: $Au = (1, 0)$, $\langle Au, v\rangle = 0$, and $A^\dagger v = (0, 2)$,
$\langle u, A^\dagger v\rangle = 0$; with $u = (0, 1)$, $v = (1, 0)$: $\langle Au, v\rangle = \overline{i}\cdot1 = -
i$ and $\langle u, A^\dagger v\rangle = \overline{1}\cdot(-i) = -i$. Without the conjugation the second pair
would give $i \neq -i$ (@exr-adj-sage-check).
:::

The adjoint of the shift is the backward shift, and the two compositions $S^\dagger S$ and $SS^\dagger$ differ,
which is impossible for square matrices. The second example is the first sign that infinite dimensions change
the algebra of operators.

::: {#exm-adj-shift}
#### The adjoint of the shift

$\langle Sa, b\rangle = \sum_{n \geq 2}\bar a_{n-1}b_n = \sum_{n \geq 1}\bar a_nb_{n+1} = \langle a, S^*b\rangle$
with $S^*b = (b_2, b_3, \dots)$: the adjoint $S^\dagger$ is the backward shift. $S^\dagger S = 1$, but $SS^\dagger
a = (0, a_2, a_3, \dots)$, so $SS^\dagger = 1 - P_1$ with $P_1$ the projection onto the first coordinate: a
one-sided inverse that is not two-sided (@exr-boc-shift-matrix).
:::

For multiplication and integral operators the adjoint is found by rewriting an integral, and the answer is to
conjugate the multiplier or to conjugate and transpose the kernel. The third example gives both rules, which
cover most operators met in practice.

::: {#exm-adj-multiplication}
#### Multiplication and integral operators

$\langle M_gf, h\rangle = \int\overline{gf}\,h = \int\bar f(\bar gh) = \langle f, M_{\bar g}h\rangle$, so
$M_g^\dagger = M_{\bar g}$. For an **integral operator** $(Kf)(x) = \int k(x, y)f(y)\,dy$ with a square-integrable
kernel, exchanging the order of integration gives $K^\dagger$ with kernel $k^\dagger(x, y) = \overline{k(y, x)}$
(@exr-adj-integral-operator), the continuous analogue of the conjugate transpose.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The algebraic rules for adjoints follow from the uniqueness in the definition, and the norm identities from
Cauchy-Schwarz. The first exercise asks for the three rules that are used most often.

::: {#exr-adj-properties}
#### Rules for adjoints

Prove $(AB)^\dagger = B^\dagger A^\dagger$, $(A^\dagger)^\dagger = A$ and $\|A^\dagger\| = \|A\|$, and deduce
$\|A^\dagger A\| = \|A\|^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\langle ABu, v\rangle = \langle Bu, A^\dagger v\rangle = \langle u, B^\dagger A^\dagger v\rangle$, and uniqueness
gives the first rule. Conjugating $\langle Au, v\rangle = \langle u, A^\dagger v\rangle$ gives $\langle v,
Au\rangle = \langle A^\dagger v, u\rangle$, which says $(A^\dagger)^\dagger = A$. Then $\|A^\dagger v\|^2 =
\langle A^\dagger v, A^\dagger v\rangle = \langle AA^\dagger v, v\rangle \leq \|A\|\|A^\dagger v\|\|v\|$, so
$\|A^\dagger v\| \leq \|A\|\|v\|$ and $\|A^\dagger\| \leq \|A\|$; by symmetry equality holds. Finally
$\|A^\dagger A\| \leq \|A\|^2$ by submultiplicativity, and $\|Au\|^2 = \langle u, A^\dagger Au\rangle \leq
\|A^\dagger A\|\|u\|^2$ gives the reverse inequality.
:::

With symbolic vectors Sage verifies the defining identity of the adjoint as a polynomial identity in the
components, not just at numerical points. The second exercise does this for a $3 \times 3$ complex matrix and
checks the product rule.

::: {#exr-adj-sage-check}
#### The adjoint identity in Sage

For $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & i & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1 - i \\ 0 & 3i & 1\end{pmatrix}$ and symbolic $u, v \in
\mathbb{C}^3$, check $\langle Au, v\rangle = \langle u, A^\dagger v\rangle$ with Sage, show that the identity
fails for the plain transpose, and verify $(AB)^\dagger = B^\dagger A^\dagger$ for $B = A^2 + iA$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Sage expands both sides into the same polynomial in the components of $u, v$ and their conjugates; the transpose
alone differs by terms proportional to $i$:

{{< sage exr-adj-sage-check >}}
:::

Integral operators are the infinite-dimensional matrices, with the kernel $k(x, y)$ playing the role of the entry
$A_{xy}$, and the rule for their adjoint follows from Fubini's theorem. The last exercise derives it and
identifies the self-adjoint kernels.

::: {#exr-adj-integral-operator}
#### The adjoint kernel

For $(Kf)(x) = \int_0^1k(x, y)f(y)\,dy$ on $L^2(0, 1)$ with continuous $k$, show that $K^\dagger$ has kernel
$\overline{k(y, x)}$, and conclude that $K$ is self-adjoint exactly when $k(x, y) = \overline{k(y, x)}$. Which of
$k = xy$, $k = x - y$, $k = i(x - y)$, $k = e^{i(x - y)}$ give self-adjoint operators?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\langle Kf, g\rangle = \int\overline{\int k(x, y)f(y)dy}\,g(x)dx = \int\bar f(y)\left(\int\overline{k(x, y)}
g(x)dx\right)dy = \langle f, K'g\rangle$ with $(K'g)(y) = \int\overline{k(x, y)}g(x)dx$, so $K^\dagger$ has
kernel $(y, x) \mapsto \overline{k(x, y)}$, that is, $k^\dagger(x, y) = \overline{k(y, x)}$. Self-adjointness means
$k(x, y) = \overline{k(y, x)}$: true for $xy$ (real symmetric), false for $x - y$ (antisymmetric), true for $i(x -
y)$ (since $\overline{i(y - x)} = i(x - y)$), and true for $e^{i(x - y)}$ (since $\overline{e^{i(y - x)}} =
e^{i(x - y)}$).
:::
::::

### Self-adjoint operators

Operators equal to their own adjoint are the infinite-dimensional Hermitian matrices, and they are the operators
whose expectation values $\langle u, Au\rangle$ are real. The definition below fixes the term and records the two
properties, reality and the decomposition of an arbitrary operator into self-adjoint parts, that make them
central.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-self-adjoint-operator}
#### Self-adjoint operator

A bounded operator is **self-adjoint** (or **Hermitian**) if $A^\dagger = A$, that is, $\langle Au, v\rangle =
\langle u, Av\rangle$ for all $u, v$. Then $\langle u, Au\rangle = \overline{\langle Au, u\rangle} =
\overline{\langle u, Au\rangle}$ is real for every $u$, and on a complex Hilbert space the converse holds
(@exr-sa-real-expectation). A self-adjoint $A$ is **positive**, $A \geq 0$, if $\langle u, Au\rangle \geq 0$ for
all $u$. Every bounded operator is uniquely $A = B + iC$ with $B = \tfrac12(A + A^\dagger)$ and $C =
\tfrac{1}{2i}(A - A^\dagger)$ self-adjoint, the analogue of real and imaginary parts.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The Pauli matrices are the basic Hermitian $2 \times 2$ matrices, and together with the identity they span all of
them with real coefficients. The first example records this, which is the reason they parametrise the observables
of a two-level system.

::: {#exm-sa-pauli}
#### Hermitian $2 \times 2$ matrices

$\sigma_1, \sigma_2, \sigma_3$ are Hermitian: $\sigma_2^\dagger = \overline{\sigma_2}^{\mathsf{T}} =
\begin{pmatrix} 0 & i \\ -i & 0\end{pmatrix}^{\mathsf{T}} = \sigma_2$. A matrix $a_0 1 + \sum_a a_a\sigma_a$ is
Hermitian exactly when all $a_\mu$ are real (@exr-ip-sage-matrices gave $a = (2, 2, 1, -1)$ for a Hermitian
example), and $\sigma_a^2 = 1$ makes each $\sigma_a$ a Hermitian matrix whose square is positive.
:::

A multiplication operator is self-adjoint exactly when its multiplier is real, and positive when the multiplier is
non-negative. The second example applies this to the position operator and to the potential-energy operators of
quantum mechanics, which are all of this type.

::: {#exm-sa-multiplication}
#### Real multiplication operators
