$M_g^\dagger = M_{\bar g}$ (@exm-adj-multiplication), so $M_g$ is self-adjoint exactly when $g$ is real, and then
$\langle f, M_gf\rangle = \int g|f|^2$ is real, positive if $g \geq 0$. The position operator on $L^2(0, 1)$ is
positive; multiplication by $\cos x$ on $L^2(0, 2\pi)$ is self-adjoint but not positive; multiplication by
$e^{ix}$ is not self-adjoint, and its decomposition $B + iC$ is $M_{\cos x} + iM_{\sin x}$.
:::

The operator $-i\,d/dx$ on smooth periodic functions is formally self-adjoint: integration by parts moves the
derivative across and the boundary terms cancel. The third example performs this computation, which is the model
for all differential operators in @sec-unbounded-operators, and shows that the eigenvalues it produces are real.

::: {#exm-sa-derivative-periodic}
#### $-i\,d/dx$ on periodic functions

On smooth $2\pi$-periodic $f, g$, $\langle -if', g\rangle = \int_0^{2\pi}\overline{(-if')}g\,dx =
i\int\bar f'g\,dx = i[\bar fg]_0^{2\pi} - i\int\bar fg'\,dx = \langle f, -ig'\rangle$, the boundary term vanishing
by periodicity. The operator is **symmetric**, and its eigenfunctions $e^{inx}$ have real eigenvalues $n$; it is
not bounded (@exr-bo-differentiation-unbounded), so the full definition of self-adjointness for it is deferred to
@def-unbounded-operator.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Reality of all expectation values characterises self-adjoint operators on complex spaces, and the proof is a
polarisation argument. The first exercise asks for it and for the counterexample showing that the statement fails
on real spaces.

::: {#exr-sa-real-expectation}
#### Real expectation values

Show that a bounded operator on a complex Hilbert space with $\langle u, Au\rangle \in \mathbb{R}$ for all $u$ is
self-adjoint, and that on $\mathbb{R}^2$ the rotation by $90^\circ$ has $\langle u, Au\rangle = 0$ for all $u$
without being symmetric.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Let $B = A - A^\dagger$; then $\langle u, Bu\rangle = \langle u, Au\rangle - \overline{\langle u, Au\rangle} = 0$
for all $u$. Polarising, $\langle u, Bv\rangle = \tfrac14\sum_k i^{-k}\langle u + i^kv, B(u + i^kv)\rangle = 0$ for
all $u, v$ (the identity of @exr-ip-polarisation holds for the form $\langle u, Bv\rangle$ by the same expansion),
so $B = 0$. On $\mathbb{R}^2$ the rotation $J = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$ has $\langle u,
Ju\rangle = -u_1u_2 + u_2u_1 = 0$ but $J^{\mathsf{T}} = -J \neq J$; complex scalars are needed for the
polarisation step.
:::

The decomposition into self-adjoint parts is unique and behaves like real and imaginary parts, but the two parts
need not commute. The second exercise computes the decomposition for a matrix and shows that $A$ is determined by
expectation values alone in the complex case.

::: {#exr-sa-decomposition}
#### Hermitian and anti-Hermitian parts

Decompose $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ as $B + iC$ with $B, C$ Hermitian, compute $[B, C]$,
and show that two bounded operators on a complex Hilbert space with the same expectation values $\langle u,
Au\rangle = \langle u, A'u\rangle$ for all $u$ are equal.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$B = \tfrac12(A + A^{\mathsf{T}}) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ and $C = \tfrac{1}{2i}(A -
A^{\mathsf{T}}) = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -i \\ i & 0\end{pmatrix} = \sigma_2$, both Hermitian; $[B, C] = BC - CB =
\begin{pmatrix} i & -i \\ i & -i\end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} -i & -i \\ i & i\end{pmatrix} = 2i\sigma_3 \neq
0$. If $\langle u, (A - A')u\rangle = 0$ for all $u$, the polarisation identity of the previous solution gives
$\langle u, (A - A')v\rangle = 0$ for all $u, v$, hence $A = A'$.
:::

Sage's `is_hermitian` decides the property for an explicit matrix, and symbolic vectors show the reality of
expectation values as an identity. The last exercise runs these checks on a tridiagonal Hermitian matrix that
returns in @sec-spectral-theory and decomposes a non-Hermitian one.

::: {#exr-sa-sage-random}
#### Hermitian checks in Sage

For $M = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & i & 0 \\ -i & 2 & i \\ 0 & -i & 2\end{pmatrix}$, check with Sage that $M$ is
Hermitian and that $\langle u, Mu\rangle$ is real for a symbolic $u \in \mathbb{C}^3$; then compute the Hermitian
and anti-Hermitian parts of $N = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4i\end{pmatrix}$ and verify that they add up to $N$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\langle u, Mu\rangle = 2\sum|u_k|^2 - 2\operatorname{Im}(\bar u_1u_2 + \bar u_2u_3)$, since $i(z - \bar z) = -
2\operatorname{Im}z$, visibly real; the parts of $N$ are $B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 5/2 \\ 5/2 & 0\end{pmatrix}$ and
$C = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & i/2 \\ -i/2 & 4\end{pmatrix}$:

{{< sage exr-sa-sage-random >}}
:::
::::

### Unitary operators

Operators that preserve all inner products, hence all lengths and angles, are the symmetries of a Hilbert space,
and they generalise rotations. The definition below gives the algebraic characterisation through the adjoint and
separates it from the weaker notion of an isometry, which in infinite dimensions is genuinely different.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-unitary-operator}
#### Unitary operator

A bounded operator $U$ is **unitary** if $U^\dagger U = UU^\dagger = 1$, that is, $U$ is invertible with $U^{-1}
= U^\dagger$. Equivalently, $U$ is surjective and preserves inner products, $\langle Uu, Uv\rangle = \langle u,
v\rangle$, or surjective and preserves norms, $\|Uu\| = \|u\|$ (@exr-un-norm-one). An operator with $U^\dagger U
= 1$ alone is an **isometry**; in finite dimensions every isometry is unitary. A unitary has $\|U\| = 1$, maps
orthonormal bases to orthonormal bases, and the unitaries of $H$ form a group under composition, $U(n)$ for $H =
\mathbb{C}^n$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Rotations of the plane and the diagonal phase matrices are the unitaries one can draw, and the exponential of
$i$ times a Pauli matrix produces both. The first example records these, with the Lie groups of @sec-lie-groups
in the background.

::: {#exm-un-rotation}
#### Rotations and phases

$R_\theta = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta\end{pmatrix}$ satisfies
$R_\theta^{\mathsf{T}}R_\theta = 1$: it is unitary (orthogonal) and maps the unit circle to itself
(@fig-operator-norm-ellipse). The diagonal matrix $e^{i\theta\sigma_3} = \operatorname{diag}(e^{i\theta},
e^{-i\theta})$ is unitary with $\det = 1$, an element of $SU(2) \subset U(2)$, and $e^{i\theta\sigma_2} =
\cos\theta + i\sin\theta\,\sigma_2 = R_\theta$ (@exr-un-sage-exp).
:::

On function spaces the basic unitaries are multiplication by a phase and translation, and the Fourier transform
itself. The second example lists them; the unitarity of the Fourier transform is Plancherel's theorem of
@sec-fourier-transform.

::: {#exm-un-phase}
#### Phases, translations and the Fourier transform

Multiplication by $e^{i\alpha(x)}$ with real $\alpha$ is unitary on $L^2(X)$, since $M_{e^{i\alpha}}^\dagger =
M_{e^{-i\alpha}}$ is its inverse. Translation $(T_af)(x) = f(x - a)$ is unitary on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$, as
$\int|f(x - a)|^2dx = \int|f|^2dx$ and $T_a^{-1} = T_{-a}$. The Fourier transform $\hat f(k) = (2\pi)^{-1/2}\int
f(x)e^{-ikx}dx$ is unitary on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$: $\|\hat f\| = \|f\|$ is Plancherel's theorem
(@sec-fourier-transform), and it turns $T_a$ into multiplication by $e^{-ika}$.
:::

The shift is an isometry that is not unitary, since its range misses the first coordinate, while the two-sided
shift on $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z})$ is unitary. The third example contrasts the two and identifies the bilateral shift
with a multiplication operator through the Fourier isomorphism.

::: {#exm-un-shift-isometry}
#### Isometries that are not unitary

The shift $S$ on $\ell^2$ has $S^\dagger S = 1$ but $SS^\dagger = 1 - P_1 \neq 1$ (@exm-adj-shift): an isometry
whose range is the proper closed subspace $\{a_1 = 0\}$, so not unitary. The **bilateral shift** $(Va)_n =
a_{n-1}$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z})$ is unitary, with $V^{-1} = V^\dagger$ the left shift; under the isomorphism
$L^2(-\pi, \pi) \cong \ell^2(\mathbb{Z})$ of @exr-onb-separable it becomes multiplication by $e^{ix}$
(@exr-un-fourier-plancherel).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The equivalence of the three characterisations in the definition is the unitary counterpart of
@exr-sa-real-expectation, with polarisation again doing the work. The first exercise asks for it and for the
location of the eigenvalues of a unitary.

::: {#exr-un-norm-one}
#### Characterising unitaries

Prove that a surjective bounded operator preserving norms preserves inner products and is unitary, that $\|U\| =
1$, and that every eigenvalue of a unitary operator has modulus $1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $\|Uu\| = \|u\|$ for all $u$, polarisation (@exr-ip-polarisation) expresses $\langle Uu, Uv\rangle$ through
norms $\|U(u + i^kv)\| = \|u + i^kv\|$, so $\langle Uu, Uv\rangle = \langle u, v\rangle$, that is, $\langle u,
(U^\dagger U - 1)v\rangle = 0$ for all $u, v$ and $U^\dagger U = 1$. Surjectivity with injectivity (norm
preservation) makes $U$ invertible, and $U^{-1} = U^\dagger U U^{-1} = U^\dagger$, so also $UU^\dagger = 1$.
$\|U\| = \sup\|Uu\|/\|u\| = 1$. If $Uu = \lambda u$ with $u \neq 0$ then $\|u\| = \|Uu\| = |\lambda|\|u\|$, so
$|\lambda| = 1$.
:::

The exponential of $i$ times a Hermitian matrix is unitary, a fact that @sec-spectral-theory proves in general and
that Sage can check symbolically in small cases. The second exercise does this for $e^{i\theta\sigma_2}$ and for
the discrete Fourier transform matrix.

::: {#exr-un-sage-exp}
#### Unitaries from exponentials

With Sage, compute $U(\theta) = e^{i\theta\sigma_2}$ in closed form, verify $U^\dagger U = 1$ for symbolic
$\theta$ and $U(\theta)U(\varphi) = U(\theta + \varphi)$, and check that the $4 \times 4$ matrix $F_{jk} =
e^{2\pi ijk/4}/2$ is unitary with $F^4 = 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$e^{i\theta\sigma_2} = \cos\theta\,1 + i\sin\theta\,\sigma_2 = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & \sin\theta \\ -
\sin\theta & \cos\theta\end{pmatrix}$, a rotation, since $\sigma_2^2 = 1$ splits the series into even and odd
powers; the group law is the addition formula for sines and cosines, and $F$ is the discrete Fourier transform,
unitary by the geometric sum $\sum_j e^{2\pi ij(k - l)/4} = 4\delta_{kl}$:

{{< sage exr-un-sage-exp >}}
:::

The Fourier isomorphism $L^2(-\pi, \pi) \to \ell^2(\mathbb{Z})$ is unitary, and under it multiplication by
$e^{ix}$ becomes the bilateral shift. The last exercise verifies both statements, giving a first instance of the
principle that a unitary change of basis turns a multiplication operator into a shift and vice versa.

::: {#exr-un-fourier-plancherel}
#### Multiplication by $e^{ix}$ is a shift

Show that $Uf = (\langle e_n, f\rangle)_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}$, $e_n = e^{inx}/\sqrt{2\pi}$, is unitary from
$L^2(-\pi, \pi)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z})$, and that $UM_{e^{ix}}U^{-1}$ is the bilateral shift $(a_n) \mapsto
(a_{n-1})$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$U$ preserves inner products by Parseval's identity (@exr-onb-separable) and is surjective, hence unitary. For the
shift, $(UM_{e^{ix}}f)_n = \langle e_n, e^{ix}f\rangle = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int e^{-inx}e^{ix}f\,dx = \langle
e_{n-1}, f\rangle = (Uf)_{n-1}$, so $UM_{e^{ix}}U^{-1}$ maps $(a_n)$ to $(a_{n-1})$: the bilateral shift. Its
inverse, the left shift, corresponds to multiplication by $e^{-ix}$, and both are unitary because $|e^{\pm ix}|
= 1$.
:::
::::

### Orthogonal projections

The projection onto a subspace was defined in @def-orthonormal-system through an orthonormal basis of the
subspace; as an operator it is characterised by two equations. The definition below gives this characterisation
and the Dirac notation for rank-one projections, which is the notation of quantum mechanics.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-orthogonal-projection}
#### Orthogonal projection

An **orthogonal projection** is a bounded operator $P$ with $P^2 = P$ and $P^\dagger = P$. Its range $K = PH$ is
a closed subspace, $Pu$ is the point of $K$ closest to $u$, and $1 - P$ is the projection onto the **orthogonal
complement** $K^\perp = \{v : \langle v, k\rangle = 0 \text{ for all } k \in K\}$, so that $H = K \oplus K^\perp$.
Conversely every closed subspace is the range of exactly one orthogonal projection. If $e_1, e_2, \dots$ is an
orthonormal basis of $K$ then $P = \sum_k|e_k\rangle\langle e_k|$, where $|e\rangle\langle e| : u \mapsto \langle
e, u\rangle e$ is the projection onto the line $\mathbb{C}e$ for a unit vector $e$; $\|P\| = 1$ unless $P = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The projection onto a line in $\mathbb{C}^2$ is a $2 \times 2$ matrix of rank one, and for the eigenvectors of a
Pauli matrix it is a simple combination of that Pauli matrix and the identity. The first example computes it and
checks the two defining equations.

::: {#exm-proj-line}
#### Projection onto a line in $\mathbb{C}^2$

For $e = (1, i)/\sqrt2$, $P = |e\rangle\langle e|$ has entries $P_{jk} = e_j\bar e_k$: $P = \tfrac12
\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -i \\ i & 1\end{pmatrix} = \tfrac12(1 + \sigma_2)$. Then $P^\dagger = P$ and $P^2 = \tfrac14(1 +
2\sigma_2 + \sigma_2^2) = \tfrac12(1 + \sigma_2) = P$; the complementary projection $1 - P = \tfrac12(1 -
\sigma_2)$ projects onto $(1, -i)/\sqrt2$, and $\sigma_2 = P - (1 - P)$.
:::

For each Pauli matrix the two projections onto its eigenvectors add up to the identity and multiply to zero,
and the matrix itself is their difference weighted by its eigenvalues. The second example writes this out for
$\sigma_3$; it is the spectral decomposition of @sec-spectral-theory in its smallest case.

::: {#exm-proj-complement-sum}
#### Complementary projections and $\sigma_3$

$P_\pm = \tfrac12(1 \pm \sigma_3)$ are $\operatorname{diag}(1, 0)$ and $\operatorname{diag}(0, 1)$, the projections
onto the eigenvectors $(1, 0)$ and $(0, 1)$ of $\sigma_3$. They satisfy $P_+ + P_- = 1$, $P_+P_- = 0$, $P_\pm^2 =
P_\pm$ and $\sigma_3 = (+1)P_+ + (-1)P_-$: the matrix is the sum of its eigenvalues times the projections onto its
eigenspaces (@exr-proj-sum-commuting).
:::

Truncating a Fourier series is an orthogonal projection, and letting the truncation grow gives a sequence of
projections converging to the identity vector by vector but not in norm. The third example states this
distinction, which is typical of infinite dimensions.

::: {#exm-proj-fourier-truncation}
#### Fourier truncation

$P_N = \sum_{|n| \leq N}|e_n\rangle\langle e_n|$ on $L^2(-\pi, \pi)$ is the projection onto the trigonometric
polynomials of degree $\leq N$ (@exm-on-exponentials). For every $f$, $P_Nf \to f$ in norm as $N \to \infty$
(completeness of the Fourier basis), but $\|1 - P_N\| = 1$ for every $N$, as $(1 - P_N)e_{N+1} = e_{N+1}$: the
convergence $P_N \to 1$ is **strong**, not in operator norm.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The matrix of a projection onto a subspace is $EE^\dagger$ when $E$ has orthonormal columns spanning it, and Sage
builds it from any spanning set via Gram-Schmidt. The first exercise constructs such a matrix in $\mathbb{C}^3$,
checks the defining equations and reads off the eigenvalues.

::: {#exr-proj-formula}
#### The matrix of a projection

Find the matrix $P$ of the orthogonal projection onto $\operatorname{span}\{(1, 1, 0), (0, 1, i)\}$ in
$\mathbb{C}^3$ with Sage, check $P^2 = P = P^\dagger$, and find its eigenvalues and $\operatorname{tr}P$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With orthonormal columns $e_1, e_2$ of $E$, $P = EE^\dagger = |e_1\rangle\langle e_1| + |e_2\rangle\langle e_2|$;
the eigenvalues are $1, 1, 0$ and the trace equals the dimension of the range:

{{< sage exr-proj-formula >}}
:::

The properties listed in the definition follow from the two equations $P^2 = P = P^\dagger$ alone. The second
exercise asks for the derivations, which are short but instructive about how the adjoint and idempotence
interact.

::: {#exr-proj-norm-and-complement}
#### From the two equations

From $P^2 = P = P^\dagger$ deduce: $\langle u, Pu\rangle = \|Pu\|^2$, hence $\|Pu\| \leq \|u\|$ and $\|P\| = 1$
if $P \neq 0$; $1 - P$ is an orthogonal projection; and the range of $P$ is $\{u : Pu = u\}$, which is closed.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\langle u, Pu\rangle = \langle u, P^2u\rangle = \langle P^\dagger u, Pu\rangle = \|Pu\|^2$, and by
Cauchy-Schwarz $\|Pu\|^2 \leq \|u\|\|Pu\|$, so $\|Pu\| \leq \|u\|$; on the range $Pu = u$, so $\|P\| = 1$. $(1 -
P)^2 = 1 - 2P + P^2 = 1 - P$ and $(1 - P)^\dagger = 1 - P$. If $u = Pv$ then $Pu = P^2v = u$, so the range is
contained in the fixed set, and conversely fixed vectors are in the range; the fixed set is the kernel of the
bounded operator $1 - P$, hence closed.
:::

Sums and products of projections are projections only under a commutation condition, and the condition has a
geometric meaning. The last exercise asks for the two criteria and tests them on the projections onto two
lines of the plane.

::: {#exr-proj-sum-commuting}
#### Sums and products of projections

Let $P, Q$ be orthogonal projections. Show that $PQ$ is an orthogonal projection if and only if $PQ = QP$, and that
$P + Q$ is one if and only if $PQ = 0$. For $P$ the projection onto $(1, 0)$ and $Q$ onto $(1, 1)/\sqrt2$ in
$\mathbb{R}^2$, compute $PQ$ and $QP$ and interpret.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $PQ = QP$ then $(PQ)^\dagger = QP = PQ$ and $(PQ)^2 = PQPQ = P^2Q^2 = PQ$; conversely a self-adjoint $PQ$ has
$PQ = (PQ)^\dagger = QP$. For the sum, $(P + Q)^2 = P + Q + PQ + QP$ equals $P + Q$ iff $PQ + QP = 0$; multiplying
by $P$ on the left and right gives $PQ + PQP = 0$ and $PQP + QP = 0$, so $PQ = QP$ and then $2PQ = 0$. With $P =
\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}$ and $Q = \tfrac12\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, $PQ =
\tfrac12\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix} \neq QP = \tfrac12\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0
\end{pmatrix}$: projecting onto the diagonal and then onto the horizontal axis is not a projection, as the two lines
are neither equal nor orthogonal.
:::
::::

### Commutators

Two operators may be applied in either order, and the difference between the two orders measures how far they
are from commuting. The definition below names this difference and lists its algebraic rules; its importance is
that commuting self-adjoint operators can be diagonalised simultaneously, while non-commuting ones cannot.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-commutator}
#### Commutator

The **commutator** of two bounded operators is $[A, B] = AB - BA$, and $A, B$ **commute** if $[A, B] = 0$. It is
bilinear and antisymmetric, satisfies the **Jacobi identity** $[A, [B, C]] + [B, [C, A]] + [C, [A, B]] = 0$ and
the **Leibniz rule** $[A, BC] = [A, B]C + B[A, C]$, and $[A, B]^\dagger = [B^\dagger, A^\dagger]$; for
self-adjoint $A, B$ the commutator is anti-self-adjoint and $i[A, B]$ is self-adjoint. In finite dimensions
$\operatorname{tr}[A, B] = 0$. The **anticommutator** is $\{A, B\} = AB + BA$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The Pauli matrices have the commutation relations of angular momentum, and these relations are the Lie algebra
$\mathfrak{su}(2)$ of @sec-lie-algebras. The first example records them together with the anticommutators, which
make the Pauli matrices a Clifford algebra as well.

::: {#exm-comm-pauli}
#### Pauli commutators

$[\sigma_1, \sigma_2] = \sigma_1\sigma_2 - \sigma_2\sigma_1 = i\sigma_3 - (-i\sigma_3) = 2i\sigma_3$, and
cyclically $[\sigma_a, \sigma_b] = 2i\varepsilon_{abc}\sigma_c$; the matrices $J_a = \sigma_a/2$ then satisfy
$[J_a, J_b] = i\varepsilon_{abc}J_c$, the relations of @sec-weights-su2. The anticommutators are $\{\sigma_a,
\sigma_b\} = 2\delta_{ab}$, so $\sigma_a\sigma_b = \delta_{ab} + i\varepsilon_{abc}\sigma_c$
(@exr-comm-pauli-sage).
:::

Operators that are diagonal in the same basis commute, and so do multiplication operators by different functions.
The second example records this, together with the fact that an operator commutes with every function of itself,
which the functional calculus of @sec-spectral-theory will make precise.

::: {#exm-comm-diagonal}
#### Commuting operators

Diagonal matrices commute, since $(DD')_{jk} = d_jd'_j\delta_{jk}$ is symmetric in $D, D'$; multiplication
operators commute, $M_gM_h = M_{gh} = M_hM_g$; and any $A$ commutes with its powers and polynomials, $[A, p(A)]
= 0$. Conversely two Hermitian matrices commute exactly when they have a common orthonormal eigenbasis
(@exr-sth-commuting-simultaneous), the finite-dimensional form of simultaneous diagonalisation.
:::

Multiplication by $x$ and differentiation do not commute, and their commutator is the identity: this is the
algebraic core of the canonical commutation relation of @sec-unbounded-operators. The third example computes it
on smooth functions and uses the trace to show that it cannot hold for matrices.

::: {#exm-comm-position-derivative}
#### $[d/dx, x\rbrack  = 1$

On smooth functions, $\tfrac{d}{dx}(xf) - x\tfrac{df}{dx} = f + xf' - xf' = f$, so $[\tfrac{d}{dx}, x] = 1$; with
$p = -i\,d/dx$ this reads $[x, p] = i$. No pair of $n \times n$ matrices satisfies $[X, P] = i\,1$, since
$\operatorname{tr}[X, P] = \operatorname{tr}XP - \operatorname{tr}PX = 0$ while $\operatorname{tr}(i\,1) = in$
(@prp-bounded-operator-checks): the relation forces infinite dimensions and unbounded operators.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The Jacobi identity and the Leibniz rule follow by expanding both sides, and the adjoint rule follows from
$(AB)^\dagger = B^\dagger A^\dagger$. The first exercise asks for all three and for the self-adjointness of
$i[A, B]$.

::: {#exr-comm-jacobi}
#### Rules for commutators

Prove the Jacobi identity, the Leibniz rule $[A, BC] = [A, B]C + B[A, C]$, and $[A, B]^\dagger = [B^\dagger,
A^\dagger]$; deduce that $i[A, B]$ is self-adjoint when $A$ and $B$ are.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Expanding, $[A, [B, C]] = ABC - ACB - BCA + CBA$; the cyclic sum contains each of the six orderings of $A, B, C$
once with $+$ and once with $-$, so it vanishes. $[A, B]C + B[A, C] = ABC - BAC + BAC - BCA = [A, BC]$. $(AB -
BA)^\dagger = B^\dagger A^\dagger - A^\dagger B^\dagger = [B^\dagger, A^\dagger]$. For self-adjoint $A, B$ this
gives $[A, B]^\dagger = [B, A] = -[A, B]$, and $(i[A, B])^\dagger = -i[A, B]^\dagger = i[A, B]$.
:::

Sage multiplies the Pauli matrices exactly, so the whole table of commutators and anticommutators is a short
computation. The second exercise asks for the table and for extracting the structure constants from it.

::: {#exr-comm-pauli-sage}
#### The Pauli algebra in Sage

Compute all $[\sigma_a, \sigma_b]$ and $\{\sigma_a, \sigma_b\}$ with Sage, verify $\sigma_a\sigma_b = \delta_{ab}1 +
i\varepsilon_{abc}\sigma_c$, and check the Jacobi identity for $(\sigma_1, \sigma_2, \sigma_3)$ and for
$(\sigma_1, \sigma_1\sigma_2, \sigma_3)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The structure constants are read off by taking the trace inner product of $[\sigma_a, \sigma_b]$ with $\sigma_c$,
which gives $2i\varepsilon_{abc}\cdot 2$:

{{< sage exr-comm-pauli-sage >}}
:::

For projections the commutator measures the angle between the subspaces, and it vanishes exactly when the
subspaces are compatible. The last exercise computes it for two lines in the plane and shows that it is always an
anti-Hermitian matrix of a specific form.

::: {#exr-comm-projections}
#### Commutators of projections

For the projections $P_\theta$ onto $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$ and $P_0$ onto $(1, 0)$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$, compute
$[P_0, P_\theta]$, show that it vanishes exactly for $\theta \in \{0, \pi/2\}$ modulo $\pi$, and find the norm of
$i[P_0, P_\theta]$ as a function of $\theta$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$P_\theta = \begin{pmatrix} c^2 & cs \\ cs & s^2\end{pmatrix}$ with $c = \cos\theta$, $s = \sin\theta$, and
$P_0P_\theta = \begin{pmatrix} c^2 & cs \\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}$, $P_\theta P_0 = \begin{pmatrix} c^2 & 0 \\ cs &
0\end{pmatrix}$, so $[P_0, P_\theta] = cs\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{pmatrix} = \tfrac12\sin 2\theta\,J$.
It vanishes iff $\sin 2\theta = 0$, that is, the lines coincide or are perpendicular. $iJ$ is Hermitian with
eigenvalues $\pm1$, so $\|i[P_0, P_\theta]\| = \tfrac12|\sin 2\theta|$, maximal at $45^\circ$.
:::
::::

### Worked computations

The norm of the matrix of the figure can be compared with its singular values, the adjoint identity can be tested
on general vectors, and the projection, the rotation, the Pauli commutators and the trace of a commutator can all
be computed explicitly. The proposition collects these computations.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-bounded-operator-checks}
#### Norms, adjoints and commutators of explicit operators

For $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, $\|A\| = \sqrt{3 + \sqrt5}$ is the largest singular value,
the semi-axes of the ellipse $A(S^1)$ are the singular values and their product is $|\det A| = 2$; $\langle Au,
v\rangle = \langle u, A^\dagger v\rangle$ holds identically for symbolic $u, v \in \mathbb{C}^3$ and a complex
$3 \times 3$ matrix; $P = \tfrac12\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ satisfies $P^2 = P = P^\dagger$
with $\|P\| = 1$; the rotation $R_\theta$ satisfies $R_\theta^{\mathsf{T}}R_\theta = 1$ and preserves $\|u\|$ for
symbolic $u$; $[\sigma_a, \sigma_b] = 2i\varepsilon_{abc}\sigma_c$; and $\operatorname{tr}[A, B] = 0$ for symbolic
$3 \times 3$ matrices.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Exact computation (`figures/operator_norm_ellipse.sage`, exact algebraic numbers and
symbolic matrices).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The ellipse in the figure is determined by the singular value decomposition of $A$: its axes point along the
images of the eigenvectors of $A^{\mathsf{T}}A$. The first example reads the geometry of the left panel from the
computation.

::: {#exm-boc-ellipse}
#### The ellipse of a matrix

$A^{\mathsf{T}}A$ has eigenvectors $v_\pm$ for the eigenvalues $3 \pm \sqrt5$, and $Av_\pm$ are orthogonal with
lengths $\sigma_\pm = \sqrt{3 \pm \sqrt5} \approx 2.288, 0.874$: the unit circle is mapped to the ellipse with
these semi-axes, and the area scales by $\sigma_+\sigma_- = \sqrt{9 - 5} = 2 = |\det A|$. The direction stretched
most is $v_+ \approx (0.85, 0.53)$, not the eigenvector $(1, 0)$ of $A$ for its largest eigenvalue $2$.
:::

A unitary maps the unit sphere onto itself, and in two real dimensions the only such maps are rotations and
reflections. The second example contrasts this with a non-unitary matrix of norm $1$, whose image of the circle
touches the circle only at the stretched direction.

::: {#exm-boc-unitary-circle}
#### Circles onto circles

$R_\theta$ maps the unit circle onto itself and $\|R_\theta u\| = \|u\|$ for every $u$, since
$R_\theta^{\mathsf{T}}R_\theta = 1$. The matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1/2\end{pmatrix}$ also has norm $1$ but is not
unitary: its ellipse has semi-axes $1$ and $\tfrac12$ and meets the unit circle only at $(\pm1, 0)$. A norm-one
operator is unitary exactly when it preserves every length, not just the largest.
:::

The vanishing trace of a commutator is the obstruction to realising $[x, p] = i$ with matrices, and it holds
identically for general $3 \times 3$ matrices with symbolic entries. The third example records the computation and its consequence
for the operators of @sec-unbounded-operators.

::: {#exm-boc-pauli-check}
#### No finite-dimensional canonical pair

With $A, B$ generic $3 \times 3$ symbolic matrices, Sage expands $\operatorname{tr}(AB - BA)$ to $0$, since
$\operatorname{tr}AB = \sum_{jk}A_{jk}B_{kj} = \operatorname{tr}BA$. Hence $[X, P] = i\,1$ has no matrix
solution in any dimension $n$, and the truncated ladder operators of @exr-boc-heisenberg-trace show how the
relation fails at the truncation: the commutator is $1$ except for one diagonal entry equal to $1 - n$, which
restores the zero trace.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The singular values of a matrix are the lengths of the semi-axes of its ellipse, and Sage computes them through
$A^{\mathsf{T}}A$ or the singular value decomposition. The first exercise asks for them, for the norm of the
inverse and for the condition number of the matrix of the figure.

::: {#exr-boc-singular-values}
#### Singular values and the inverse

For $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ compute the singular values exactly with Sage, check
$\sigma_1\sigma_2 = |\det A|$, show that $\|A^{-1}\| = 1/\sigma_2$, and compute the condition number $\|A\|\,
\|A^{-1}\|$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\sigma_{1,2} = \sqrt{3 \pm \sqrt5} = (\sqrt5 \pm 1)/\sqrt2$; $A^{-1}$ has singular values $1/\sigma_2 >
1/\sigma_1$, so $\|A^{-1}\| = 1/\sigma_2 = \sigma_1/2$ and the condition number is $\sigma_1^2/2 = (3 + \sqrt5)/2
\approx 2.618$:

{{< sage exr-boc-singular-values >}}
:::

The truncation $S_N$ of the shift to $N$ coordinates is a matrix whose products with its transpose are two
different projections, and the behaviour of the infinite shift is read off by letting $N \to \infty$. The second
exercise computes these products and the norms.

::: {#exr-boc-shift-matrix}
#### The truncated shift

Let $S_N$ be the $N \times N$ matrix with $1$ on the first subdiagonal and $0$ elsewhere. Compute $S_N^{\mathsf{T}}
S_N$ and $S_NS_N^{\mathsf{T}}$, their norms, and $S_N^N$; explain how the infinite shift $S$ differs.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$S_N^{\mathsf{T}}S_N = \operatorname{diag}(1, \dots, 1, 0)$ and $S_NS_N^{\mathsf{T}} = \operatorname{diag}(0, 1,
\dots, 1)$, both projections of rank $N - 1$ and norm $1$; $S_N^N = 0$ (nilpotent), so $S_N$ has only the
eigenvalue $0$. The infinite shift has $S^\dagger S = 1$ exactly, since no coordinate is lost, $SS^\dagger = 1 -
P_1$, and $S^n \neq 0$ for all $n$ with $\|S^n\| = 1$; it has no eigenvalues at all, as $Sa = \lambda a$ forces
$a_1 = 0$ and then all $a_n = 0$ (@exm-sp-shift).
:::

The truncated ladder operators are the standard finite approximations to a canonical pair, and their commutator
shows exactly how the trace obstruction manifests itself. The last exercise builds them in Sage and inspects
the commutator.

::: {#exr-boc-heisenberg-trace}
#### Truncated ladder operators

Let $a$ be the $N \times N$ matrix with $a_{n, n+1} = \sqrt n$ ($n = 1, \dots, N - 1$) and $0$ elsewhere. With
Sage, compute $[a, a^\dagger]$ for $N = 5$, check that $\operatorname{tr}[a, a^\dagger] = 0$ and
$\operatorname{tr}[A, B] = 0$ for symbolic $3 \times 3$ matrices, and compute $x = (a + a^\dagger)/\sqrt2$,
$p = i(a^\dagger - a)/\sqrt2$ and $[x, p]$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[a, a^\dagger] = \operatorname{diag}(1, 1, 1, 1, 1 - N)$: the relation $[a, a^\dagger] = 1$ holds on the first
$N - 1$ basis vectors and fails on the last by exactly the amount that makes the trace vanish; $[x, p] =
i[a, a^\dagger]$ is $i$ on the same subspace:

{{< sage exr-boc-heisenberg-trace >}}
:::
::::

## Spectral theory {#sec-spectral-theory}

The spectrum of an operator is the set of numbers $\lambda$ for which $A - \lambda$ fails to be invertible; for a
matrix these are the eigenvalues, and for operators on infinite-dimensional spaces the set may also contain a
continuous part without eigenvectors. This section defines eigenvalues and the spectrum, proves the spectral
theorem for Hermitian matrices, quotes it for compact self-adjoint operators, and builds the functional calculus
that defines $f(A)$, in particular the unitary $e^{iA}$; the figure shows the eigenvectors and the exponential of a
symmetric matrix.

### Eigenvalues

A vector that an operator merely rescales is the simplest thing an operator can do, and the rescaling factor is the
number attached to it. The definition below fixes the terms, including the multiplicity of an eigenvalue and the
eigenspace, in a form that applies equally to matrices and to operators on function spaces.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-operator-eigenvalue}
#### Eigenvalue of an operator

A number $\lambda \in \mathbb{C}$ is an **eigenvalue** of an operator $A$ if $Au = \lambda u$ for some non-zero
**eigenvector** $u$; the **eigenspace** $\ker(A - \lambda)$ is the set of all such $u$ together with $0$, and its
dimension is the **multiplicity** of $\lambda$. For a self-adjoint operator every eigenvalue is real and eigenvectors
of distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal; for a unitary operator every eigenvalue has modulus $1$
(@exr-ev-selfadjoint-real-orthogonal). An $n \times n$ matrix has at least one and at most $n$ eigenvalues, the
roots of its **characteristic polynomial** $\det(A - \lambda)$; an operator on an infinite-dimensional space may
have none at all.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The Pauli matrix $\sigma_1$ exchanges the two coordinates, and its eigenvectors are the vectors unchanged or
negated by the exchange. The first example finds them and checks the orthogonality promised by the definition.

::: {#exm-ev-pauli-x}
#### Eigenvectors of $\sigma_1$

$\sigma_1(a, b) = (b, a)$ equals $\lambda(a, b)$ iff $b = \lambda a$ and $a = \lambda b$, so $\lambda^2 = 1$: the
eigenvalues are $\pm1$ with eigenvectors $(1, 1)/\sqrt2$ and $(1, -1)/\sqrt2$, orthogonal and of multiplicity one.
Similarly $\sigma_2$ has eigenvectors $(1, \pm i)/\sqrt2$ (@exm-on-rotated-basis) and $\sigma_3$ has $(1, 0)$,
$(0, 1)$, all for the eigenvalues $\pm1$.
:::

The second derivative on periodic functions has the exponentials as eigenfunctions, with eigenvalues that grow
without bound and come in pairs. The second example records this, the model for the Laplacian of
@sec-unbounded-operators, and notes the multiplicities.

::: {#exm-ev-derivative-modes}
#### Eigenfunctions of $-d^2/dx^2$

On smooth $2\pi$-periodic functions, $-\tfrac{d^2}{dx^2}e^{inx} = n^2e^{inx}$: the eigenvalues are $n^2$, $n = 0,
1, 2, \dots$, with eigenspace spanned by $e^{inx}$ and $e^{-inx}$ (equivalently $\cos nx$ and $\sin nx$) of
multiplicity $2$ for $n \geq 1$, and the constants for $n = 0$. The eigenvalues are real and the eigenfunctions
orthogonal (@exm-ip-functions), as the operator is symmetric.
:::

Multiplication by $x$ on $L^2(0, 1)$ is bounded and self-adjoint but has no eigenvalue whatsoever, since an
eigenfunction would have to be concentrated at a single point. The third example proves this and introduces the
approximate eigenvectors that replace eigenvectors in the next definition.

::: {#exm-ev-multiplication-none}
#### The position operator has no eigenvalues

If $xf(x) = \lambda f(x)$ in $L^2(0, 1)$ then $(x - \lambda)f(x) = 0$ for almost every $x$, and since $x - \lambda
\neq 0$ except at one point, $f = 0$ almost everywhere, that is, $f$ is the zero class. For every $\lambda \in
[0, 1]$ there are nonetheless **approximate eigenvectors**, $f_n = \sqrt n\,\mathbf{1}_{[\lambda, \lambda + 1/n]}$
with $\|f_n\| = 1$ and $\|(x - \lambda)f_n\|^2 = n\int_\lambda^{\lambda + 1/n}(x - \lambda)^2dx = 1/(3n^2) \to 0$
(@exm-sp-multiplication).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
A real symmetric tridiagonal matrix is the standard test case for eigenvalue computations, and Sage returns its
eigenvalues and eigenvectors exactly as algebraic numbers. The first exercise asks for them and for the check that
the eigenvectors are orthogonal.

::: {#exr-ev-sage-3x3}
#### Eigenvalues of a tridiagonal matrix

Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$
with Sage, check that the eigenvectors are mutually orthogonal, and verify $\operatorname{tr}A = \sum\lambda$ and
$\det A = \prod\lambda$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The characteristic polynomial is $(2 - \lambda)((2 - \lambda)^2 - 2)$, so $\lambda = 2, 2 \pm \sqrt2$ with
eigenvectors $(1, 0, -1)$, $(1, \pm\sqrt2, 1)$; the sum is $6 = \operatorname{tr}A$ and the product $2\cdot 2 = 4
= \det A$:

{{< sage exr-ev-sage-3x3 >}}
:::

The reality of eigenvalues of self-adjoint operators and the orthogonality of their eigenvectors are two-line
arguments with the inner product, and the same arguments handle unitaries. The second exercise asks for all four
statements.

::: {#exr-ev-selfadjoint-real-orthogonal}
#### Eigenvalues of self-adjoint and unitary operators

Prove that the eigenvalues of a self-adjoint operator are real, that eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are
orthogonal, and that the same orthogonality holds for a unitary operator, whose eigenvalues have modulus $1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $Au = \lambda u$ with $u \neq 0$ and $A^\dagger = A$: $\lambda\|u\|^2 = \langle u, Au\rangle = \langle Au,
u\rangle = \bar\lambda\|u\|^2$, so $\lambda$ is real. If also $Av = \mu v$ with $\mu \neq \lambda$: $\lambda\langle
v, u\rangle = \langle v, Au\rangle = \langle Av, u\rangle = \mu\langle v, u\rangle$, so $\langle v, u\rangle = 0$.
For unitary $U$ with $Uu = \lambda u$, $Uv = \mu v$: $\langle v, u\rangle = \langle Uv, Uu\rangle = \bar\mu\lambda
\langle v, u\rangle$, and $|\lambda| = |\mu| = 1$ (@exr-un-norm-one) gives $\bar\mu\lambda = \lambda/\mu \neq 1$,
hence $\langle v, u\rangle = 0$.
:::

The shift and its adjoint show the two extremes possible in infinite dimensions: one has no eigenvalues, the other
has a whole disc of them. The last exercise asks for both, with explicit eigenvectors for the backward shift.

::: {#exr-ev-shift-adjoint}
#### Eigenvalues of the shifts

Show that the shift $S$ on $\ell^2$ has no eigenvalue, and that every $\lambda$ with $|\lambda| < 1$ is an
eigenvalue of the backward shift $S^\dagger$, with eigenvector $(1, \lambda, \lambda^2, \dots)$. What happens for
$|\lambda| = 1$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$Sa = \lambda a$ reads $(0, a_1, a_2, \dots) = (\lambda a_1, \lambda a_2, \dots)$. If $\lambda = 0$ then all $a_n
= 0$; if $\lambda \neq 0$ then $a_1 = 0$ and $a_{n+1} = \lambda^{-1}\cdot 0 = 0$ inductively, so $a = 0$: no
eigenvalues. For $S^\dagger$, $S^\dagger(1, \lambda, \lambda^2, \dots) = (\lambda, \lambda^2, \dots) = \lambda(1,
\lambda, \dots)$, and the vector is in $\ell^2$ iff $\sum|\lambda|^{2n} < \infty$ iff $|\lambda| < 1$. For
$|\lambda| = 1$ the geometric sequence is not square-summable and $\lambda$ is not an eigenvalue, although it lies in
the spectrum (@exm-sp-shift).
:::
::::

### The spectrum

An eigenvalue makes $A - \lambda$ non-injective; in infinite dimensions $A - \lambda$ can also fail to be invertible
by having a range that is too small or an inverse that is unbounded. The definition below collects all such
$\lambda$ into the spectrum, which is the set that replaces the list of eigenvalues.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-spectrum}
#### Spectrum

The **spectrum** $\sigma(A)$ of a bounded operator is the set of $\lambda \in \mathbb{C}$ for which $A - \lambda$
has no bounded inverse; its complement is the **resolvent set**, on which the **resolvent** $R(\lambda) = (A -
\lambda)^{-1}$ is defined. The spectrum is a closed non-empty subset of the disc $|\lambda| \leq \|A\|$
(@exr-sp-spectrum-closed-bounded). It contains the eigenvalues (the **point spectrum**) and every **approximate
eigenvalue**, a $\lambda$ with unit vectors $u_n$ such that $\|(A - \lambda)u_n\| \to 0$; the rest is the
**continuous spectrum**. For a self-adjoint operator $\sigma(A) \subset \mathbb{R}$ and every point of the
spectrum is an approximate eigenvalue; for a unitary operator $\sigma(U)$ lies on the unit circle
(@exr-sp-unitary-circle).
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For a matrix the spectrum is exactly the set of eigenvalues, and the resolvent is a matrix of rational functions
of $\lambda$ with poles there. The first example computes it for the matrix of @fig-operator-norm-ellipse.

::: {#exm-sp-matrix}
#### The resolvent of a matrix

For $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, $(A - \lambda)^{-1} = \frac{1}{(2 - \lambda)(1 - \lambda)}
\begin{pmatrix} 1 - \lambda & -1 \\ 0 & 2 - \lambda\end{pmatrix}$ exists for $\lambda \neq 1, 2$: $\sigma(A) =
\{1, 2\}$, the eigenvalues, and the resolvent has simple poles there with $\|R(\lambda)\| \to \infty$ as $\lambda$
approaches the spectrum (@exr-sp-resolvent-2x2). In finite dimensions the spectrum is always the point spectrum,
since a non-injective or non-surjective matrix is both.
:::

The position operator on $L^2(0, 1)$ has spectrum the whole interval $[0, 1]$ and no eigenvalues: every point is an
approximate eigenvalue. The second example proves this, giving the first purely continuous spectrum.

::: {#exm-sp-multiplication}
#### The continuous spectrum of the position operator

For $\lambda \notin [0, 1]$, $(x - \lambda)^{-1}$ is a bounded function on $(0, 1)$, so $M_{(x - \lambda)^{-1}}$
is the bounded inverse of $M_x - \lambda$. For $\lambda \in [0, 1]$ the approximate eigenvectors of
@exm-ev-multiplication-none show that $(M_x - \lambda)^{-1}$, if it existed, would have $\|(M_x - \lambda)^{-1}
g_n\| \geq 3n^2$ for the unit vectors $g_n = (x - \lambda)f_n/\|(x - \lambda)f_n\|$, so it is not bounded. Hence
$\sigma(M_x) = [0, 1]$, entirely continuous spectrum; for a general real $g$, $\sigma(M_g)$ is the (essential)
range of $g$.
:::

The shift has the closed unit disc as spectrum with no eigenvalues, and the bilateral shift has only the unit
circle. The third example assembles this from the eigenvalues of $S^\dagger$ and the identification of the
bilateral shift with a multiplication operator.

::: {#exm-sp-shift}
#### Spectra of the shifts

$\|S\| = 1$ gives $\sigma(S) \subset \{|\lambda| \leq 1\}$. Every $|\lambda| < 1$ is an eigenvalue of $S^\dagger$
(@exr-ev-shift-adjoint), so $S^\dagger - \lambda$ is not injective, hence $S - \bar\lambda = (S^\dagger -
\lambda)^\dagger$ is not invertible (an invertible operator has an invertible adjoint); since the spectrum is
closed, $\sigma(S) = \{|\lambda| \leq 1\}$, with empty point spectrum. The bilateral shift is unitarily equivalent to
$M_{e^{ix}}$ on $L^2(-\pi, \pi)$ (@exr-un-fourier-plancherel), whose spectrum is the range of $e^{ix}$, the unit
circle.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Sage inverts $A - \lambda$ symbolically, which displays the poles of the resolvent and allows the growth of its norm
near the spectrum to be measured. The first exercise does this for two matrices and checks the resolvent identity.

::: {#exr-sp-resolvent-2x2}
#### Resolvents in Sage

Compute $(A - \lambda)^{-1}$ for $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ and for $\sigma_1$ with Sage,
verify the **resolvent identity** $R(\lambda) - R(\mu) = (\lambda - \mu)R(\lambda)R(\mu)$, and compute $\|R(2 +
\varepsilon)\|$ for $\varepsilon = 10^{-1}, 10^{-2}, 10^{-3}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The resolvent of $\sigma_1$ is $(1 - \lambda^2)^{-1}\begin{pmatrix} -\lambda & -1 \\ -1 & -\lambda\end{pmatrix}$
with poles at $\pm1$; near $\lambda = 2$ the norm of the resolvent of $A$ grows like $1/\varepsilon$, the sign of a
simple pole:

{{< sage exr-sp-resolvent-2x2 >}}
:::

That the spectrum is bounded by the norm and closed follows from two geometric series for inverses. The second
exercise asks for both, the Neumann series for $(1 - B)^{-1}$ being the key tool.

::: {#exr-sp-spectrum-closed-bounded}
#### The spectrum is compact

Show that $\|B\| < 1$ implies that $1 - B$ is invertible with $(1 - B)^{-1} = \sum_{n \geq 0}B^n$; deduce that
$|\lambda| > \|A\|$ lies in the resolvent set, and that the resolvent set is open (so the spectrum is closed).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The partial sums of $\sum B^n$ are Cauchy in operator norm since $\|B^n\| \leq \|B\|^n$, and $\mathcal{B}(H)$ is
complete, so the series converges to some $C$ with $(1 - B)C = \lim(1 - B^{N+1}) = 1 = C(1 - B)$. For $|\lambda| >
\|A\|$ write $A - \lambda = -\lambda(1 - A/\lambda)$ with $\|A/\lambda\| < 1$. If $\lambda_0$ is in the resolvent
set and $|\lambda - \lambda_0| < 1/\|R(\lambda_0)\|$, then $A - \lambda = (A - \lambda_0)(1 - (\lambda -
\lambda_0)R(\lambda_0))$ is a product of invertibles, so a neighbourhood of $\lambda_0$ is in the resolvent set.
:::

Self-adjoint operators have real spectrum and unitaries have spectrum on the circle; both statements come from
lower bounds on $\|(A - \lambda)u\|$. The last exercise derives the bounds and explains why a lower bound plus a
dense range gives a bounded inverse.

::: {#exr-sp-unitary-circle}
#### Real and unimodular spectra

For self-adjoint $A$ show $\|(A - \lambda)u\| \geq |\operatorname{Im}\lambda|\,\|u\|$. Granting that an operator
$B$ with $\|Bu\| \geq c\|u\|$ ($c > 0$) and $B^\dagger$ with the same property is invertible with $\|B^{-1}\| \leq
1/c$, conclude $\sigma(A) \subset \mathbb{R}$. Show similarly that a unitary $U$ has $\sigma(U) \subset \{|\lambda|
= 1\}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $\lambda = a + ib$, $\|(A - \lambda)u\|^2 = \|(A - a)u\|^2 + b^2\|u\|^2 - 2b\operatorname{Im}\langle (A -
a)u, u\rangle$, and the last term vanishes because $\langle (A - a)u, u\rangle$ is real; so $\|(A - \lambda)u\|
\geq |b|\|u\|$, and the same for $(A - \lambda)^\dagger = A - \bar\lambda$. For $b \neq 0$ the granted criterion
gives invertibility, so non-real $\lambda$ are in the resolvent set. For $U$: if $|\lambda| > 1$, $U - \lambda$ is
invertible by the Neumann series ($\|U\| = 1$); if $|\lambda| < 1$, $U - \lambda = U(1 - \lambda U^\dagger)$ with
$\|\lambda U^\dagger\| < 1$ is also invertible.
:::
::::

### The spectral theorem for Hermitian matrices

A Hermitian matrix can be diagonalised by a unitary change of basis, and this is the single most used fact of
linear algebra in quantum mechanics. The figure shows what it means geometrically for a symmetric $2 \times 2$
matrix, and the theorem below states and proves it, with the decomposition into eigenprojections as the form that
generalises.

![Left: the symmetric matrix $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$ maps the unit circle to an ellipse
whose axes lie along the orthonormal eigenvectors $(1, 1)/\sqrt2$ and $(1, -1)/\sqrt2$ and have lengths equal to the
eigenvalues $3$ and $1$. Right: the eigenvalues $3$ and $1$ on the real line and the eigenvalues $e^{3i}$ and
$e^{i}$ of the unitary $e^{iA}$ on the unit circle; the dotted arcs trace $e^{3it}$ and $e^{it}$ for $0 \leq t \leq
1$. Generated by `figures/hermitian_spectrum.sage`.](figures/hermitian_spectrum.svg){#fig-hermitian-spectrum
width=95%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-spectral-theorem-hermitian}
#### Spectral theorem for Hermitian matrices

A Hermitian $n \times n$ matrix $A$ has real eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n$ (with multiplicity) and an
orthonormal basis of eigenvectors $e_1, \dots, e_n$. Equivalently $A = UDU^\dagger$ with $U$ the unitary matrix
whose columns are the $e_k$ and $D = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_k)$, or $A = \sum_\lambda\lambda P_\lambda$ with
$P_\lambda$ the orthogonal projection onto the eigenspace of $\lambda$, where $\sum_\lambda P_\lambda = 1$ and
$P_\lambda P_\mu = 0$ for $\lambda \neq \mu$ (the **spectral decomposition**). *Proof.* By induction on $n$. The
characteristic polynomial has a root $\lambda_1 \in \mathbb{C}$, real by @exr-ev-selfadjoint-real-orthogonal, with
a unit eigenvector $e_1$. The orthogonal complement $K = e_1^\perp$ is invariant under $A$: for $v \perp e_1$,
$\langle e_1, Av\rangle = \langle Ae_1, v\rangle = \lambda_1\langle e_1, v\rangle = 0$. The restriction of $A$ to
$K$ is Hermitian on an $(n - 1)$-dimensional space, so by induction $K$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis $e_2, \dots,
e_n$, and $e_1, \dots, e_n$ is the required basis. The matrix forms follow by writing $u = \sum_k\langle e_k,
u\rangle e_k$ and applying $A$. The same statement holds for **normal** matrices ($AA^\dagger = A^\dagger A$),
in particular for unitary matrices, with complex eigenvalues (@exr-sth-normal-matrices).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The Pauli matrices are the simplest case, where the two eigenprojections are $\tfrac12(1 \pm \sigma)$. The first
example also treats a general linear combination $\mathbf{n}\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma$, whose eigenvalues are $\pm$
the length of $\mathbf{n}$.

::: {#exm-sth-pauli-decomposition}
#### Spectral decomposition of $\mathbf{n}\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma$

$\sigma_1 = (+1)P_+ + (-1)P_-$ with $P_\pm = \tfrac12(1 \pm \sigma_1)$, the projections onto $(1, \pm1)/\sqrt2$,
and $P_+ + P_- = 1$, $P_+P_- = 0$. For real $\mathbf{n} = (n_1, n_2, n_3)$, $(\mathbf{n}\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma)^2
= |\mathbf{n}|^2\,1$ by the anticommutation relations (@exm-comm-pauli), so the eigenvalues are $\pm|\mathbf{n}|$
and the eigenprojections are $P_\pm = \tfrac12(1 \pm \hat{\mathbf{n}}\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma)$ with
$\hat{\mathbf{n}} = \mathbf{n}/|\mathbf{n}|$: the general $2 \times 2$ Hermitian matrix $a_0 + \mathbf{a}\cdot
\boldsymbol\sigma$ has eigenvalues $a_0 \pm |\mathbf{a}|$.
:::

The tridiagonal matrix of @exr-ev-sage-3x3 has three distinct eigenvalues, and normalising its eigenvectors gives
the unitary $U$ of the theorem explicitly. The second example writes it down, which the Sage exercise below
checks.

::: {#exm-sth-3x3}
#### A $3 \times 3$ example

For $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$ the orthonormal eigenvectors are
$e_1 = (1, \sqrt2, 1)/2$, $e_2 = (1, 0, -1)/\sqrt2$, $e_3 = (1, -\sqrt2, 1)/2$ for $\lambda = 2 + \sqrt2, 2, 2 -
\sqrt2$, and $A = UDU^{\mathsf{T}}$ with these as the columns of $U$; equivalently $A = \sum_k\lambda_k|e_k\rangle
\langle e_k|$ (@exr-sth-sage-decomposition). The complex Hermitian matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 2 & i & 0 \\ -i & 2 & i
\\ 0 & -i & 2\end{pmatrix}$ has the same eigenvalues with eigenvectors $(1, \pm i\sqrt2, -1)/2$, $(1, 0, 1)/\sqrt2$
(@prp-spectral-decompositions).
:::

A rotation of the plane has no real eigenvector, but as a unitary matrix it is diagonalised over $\mathbb{C}$ by
the eigenvectors of $\sigma_2$. The third example shows this, the case of the theorem for normal matrices in which
complex eigenvalues are unavoidable.

::: {#exm-sth-unitary}
#### Diagonalising a rotation

$R_\theta = e^{i\theta\sigma_2}$ (@exr-un-sage-exp) is unitary, hence normal, and its eigenvectors are those of
$\sigma_2$, $(1, \pm i)/\sqrt2$, with eigenvalues $e^{\pm i\theta}$: $R_\theta = e^{i\theta}P_+ +
e^{-i\theta}P_-$ with $P_\pm = \tfrac12(1 \pm \sigma_2)$. Over $\mathbb{R}$ the rotation has no eigenvectors for
$\theta \notin \pi\mathbb{Z}$; the complex eigenvalues have modulus $1$ as every eigenvalue of a unitary must.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Sage's `eigenmatrix_right` returns $D$ and a matrix of eigenvectors; normalising the columns gives the unitary of
the theorem. The first exercise constructs it for the $3 \times 3$ example and verifies the three forms of the
decomposition.

::: {#exr-sth-sage-decomposition}
#### The decomposition in Sage

For $A$ of @exm-sth-3x3, obtain $D$ and the normalised eigenvector matrix $U$ in Sage, and check $U^\dagger U = 1$,
$A = UDU^\dagger$, $A = \sum_k\lambda_k|e_k\rangle\langle e_k|$ and $\sum_k|e_k\rangle\langle e_k| = 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The eigenvectors returned are $(1, \pm\sqrt2, 1)$ and $(1, 0, -1)$; dividing by their norms $2$ and $\sqrt2$ gives
an orthogonal $U$, and the three identities hold exactly in $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2)$:

{{< sage exr-sth-sage-decomposition >}}
:::

Two Hermitian matrices can be diagonalised in the same basis exactly when they commute, which is the mathematical
content of "compatible observables". The second exercise asks for the proof, through the invariance of
eigenspaces.

::: {#exr-sth-commuting-simultaneous}
#### Simultaneous diagonalisation

Show that Hermitian matrices $A, B$ with $[A, B] = 0$ have a common orthonormal eigenbasis, and that conversely
matrices with a common eigenbasis commute. Find a common eigenbasis of $\sigma_3$ and $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\
0 & 5\end{pmatrix}$, and explain why $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_3$ have none.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $Au = \lambda u$ then $A(Bu) = BAu = \lambda Bu$, so $B$ maps each eigenspace $E_\lambda$ of $A$ into itself;
$B$ restricted to $E_\lambda$ is Hermitian and has an orthonormal eigenbasis by the theorem, and the union over
$\lambda$ of these bases is an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of both $A$ and $B$. Conversely, if $A = UDU^\dagger$
and $B = UD'U^\dagger$ then $AB = UDD'U^\dagger = BA$ since diagonal matrices commute. $\sigma_3$ and
$\operatorname{diag}(1, 5)$ are both diagonal in the standard basis. $[\sigma_1, \sigma_3] = -2i\sigma_2 \neq 0$,
so no common eigenbasis exists; indeed the eigenvectors $(1, \pm1)/\sqrt2$ of $\sigma_1$ are not eigenvectors of
$\sigma_3$.
:::

The theorem for normal matrices reduces to the Hermitian case by splitting $A$ into commuting Hermitian and
anti-Hermitian parts. The last exercise asks for this reduction and applies it to unitaries.

::: {#exr-sth-normal-matrices}
#### Normal matrices

Show that $A$ is normal iff its parts $B = \tfrac12(A + A^\dagger)$, $C = \tfrac{1}{2i}(A - A^\dagger)$ commute,
deduce the spectral theorem for normal matrices from @exr-sth-commuting-simultaneous, and conclude that every
unitary matrix is $U = \sum_k e^{i\theta_k}|e_k\rangle\langle e_k|$ with real $\theta_k$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[B, C] = \tfrac{1}{4i}[A + A^\dagger, A - A^\dagger] = \tfrac{1}{4i}(-[A, A^\dagger] + [A^\dagger, A]) =
\tfrac{1}{2i}(A^\dagger A - AA^\dagger)$, which vanishes iff $A$ is normal. Then $B$ and $C$ have a common
orthonormal eigenbasis $e_k$ with $Be_k = b_ke_k$, $Ce_k = c_ke_k$, and $Ae_k = (b_k + ic_k)e_k$. A unitary is normal
($U^\dagger U = 1 = UU^\dagger$), so $U = \sum_k\lambda_k|e_k\rangle\langle e_k|$ with $|\lambda_k| = 1$, that is,
$\lambda_k = e^{i\theta_k}$.
:::
::::

### Compact operators

Operators on infinite-dimensional spaces that behave most like matrices are those that squeeze bounded sets into
sets with compact closure (@def-compact). The definition below introduces them, with the finite-rank operators and
their norm limits as the examples that cover every case met in this chapter.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-compact-operator}
#### Compact operator

A bounded operator $A$ on $H$ is **compact** if the image of the unit ball has compact closure, equivalently if
every bounded sequence $u_n$ has a subsequence along which $Au_n$ converges in norm. Operators of **finite rank**
(finite-dimensional range) are compact, norm limits of compact operators are compact, and on a Hilbert space every
compact operator is a norm limit of finite-rank operators. An operator with $\sum_k\|Ae_k\|^2 < \infty$ for an
orthonormal basis $(e_k)$ is **Hilbert-Schmidt**, and Hilbert-Schmidt operators are compact; an integral operator
with kernel $k \in L^2(X \times X)$ is Hilbert-Schmidt with $\sum_k\|Ae_k\|^2 = \int\int|k(x, y)|^2dx\,dy$. The
identity on an infinite-dimensional space is not compact.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A matrix, a projection onto a finite-dimensional subspace and the rank-one operator $|u\rangle\langle v|$ are
compact for the simplest reason: their range is finite-dimensional. The first example records this and the
non-compactness of the identity.

::: {#exm-co-finite-rank}
#### Finite rank and the identity

$|u\rangle\langle v|$ has range $\mathbb{C}u$, and a projection onto an $n$-dimensional subspace has an
$n$-dimensional range: both are compact, as bounded sets in finite dimensions have compact closure. The identity on
$\ell^2$ is not: the orthonormal sequence $\delta^{(n)}$ is bounded, but $\|\delta^{(m)} - \delta^{(n)}\| = \sqrt2$
for $m \neq n$, so no subsequence of $1\cdot\delta^{(n)}$ converges (@exr-co-identity-not-compact).
:::

A diagonal operator is compact exactly when its diagonal entries tend to zero, because it is then the norm limit
of its truncations. The second example gives the argument, which is the model for the spectral theorem of the next
subsection.

::: {#exm-co-diagonal}
#### Diagonal operators

Let $De_n = \lambda_ne_n$ for an orthonormal basis with $\lambda_n \to 0$, and $D_N = \sum_{n \leq N}\lambda_n |
e_n\rangle\langle e_n|$ its finite-rank truncation. Then $\|D - D_N\| = \sup_{n > N}|\lambda_n| \to 0$, so $D$
is compact. For $\lambda_n = 1/n$, $D$ is even Hilbert-Schmidt ($\sum 1/n^2 < \infty$); for $\lambda_n =
1/\sqrt n$ it is compact but not Hilbert-Schmidt; for $\lambda_n = 1$ it is the identity.
:::

Integral operators with square-integrable kernels are the infinite matrices with square-summable entries, and the
Green's operator of a boundary value problem is the prime example. The third example is the Green's operator of
$-d^2/dx^2$ on $[0, 1]$ with Dirichlet conditions (@sec-greens-functions).

::: {#exm-co-integral-operator}
#### The Green's operator of $-d^2/dx^2$

$(Gf)(x) = \int_0^1g(x, y)f(y)\,dy$ with $g(x, y) = \min(x, y) - xy$ solves $-u'' = f$, $u(0) = u(1) = 0$
(@sec-greens-functions). The kernel is real, symmetric and bounded, so $G$ is self-adjoint and Hilbert-Schmidt with
$\int_0^1\int_0^1g^2\,dx\,dy = 1/90$ (@exr-co-hilbert-schmidt-norm), hence compact. Its eigenfunctions are
$\sqrt2\sin n\pi x$ with eigenvalues $1/(n\pi)^2 \to 0$, and $1/90 = \sum_n 1/(n\pi)^4$ is Parseval's identity for
the kernel.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Non-compactness of the identity, and more generally of any projection of infinite rank, is proved with an
orthonormal sequence. The first exercise asks for these proofs and for the observation that an invertible operator
is never compact in infinite dimensions.

::: {#exr-co-identity-not-compact}
#### Which projections are compact?

Show that an orthogonal projection is compact iff its range is finite-dimensional, and that no invertible bounded
operator on an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space is compact.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If the range $K$ is infinite-dimensional, pick an orthonormal sequence $e_n$ in $K$ (Gram-Schmidt on any
independent sequence): $Pe_n = e_n$ has no convergent subsequence since $\|e_m - e_n\| = \sqrt2$, so $P$ is not
compact; if $K$ is finite-dimensional, $P$ has finite rank. If $A$ is invertible and compact, then $1 = A^{-1}A$
would map bounded sequences to sequences with convergent subsequences (apply $A$, extract, then apply the bounded
$A^{-1}$), making the identity compact, which it is not in infinite dimensions.
:::

The Hilbert-Schmidt norm of the Green's kernel is a double integral that Sage evaluates exactly, and comparing it
with the sum of squared eigenvalues confirms the eigenvalues. The second exercise does this and computes the
kernel's expansion coefficients.

::: {#exr-co-hilbert-schmidt-norm}
#### The Hilbert-Schmidt norm of the Green's kernel

With Sage, compute $\int_0^1\int_0^1(\min(x, y) - xy)^2\,dx\,dy$, compare with $\sum_{n \geq 1}1/(n\pi)^4$, and
check $\int_0^1\int_0^1 g(x, y)\,\sqrt2\sin n\pi x\,\sqrt2\sin m\pi y\,dx\,dy = \delta_{mn}/(n\pi)^2$ for $m, n \leq
3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Both quantities equal $1/90$, since $\sum 1/n^4 = \pi^4/90$ (@exr-onb-parseval-x); the matrix elements of $G$ in the
sine basis are diagonal with entries $1/(n\pi)^2$:

{{< sage exr-co-hilbert-schmidt-norm >}}
:::

That a norm limit of finite-rank operators is compact is the statement which makes the diagonal and
Hilbert-Schmidt examples work, and its proof is a diagonal argument on subsequences. The last exercise asks for it
and for the Hilbert-Schmidt case.

::: {#exr-co-limit-of-finite-rank}
#### Limits of finite-rank operators

Prove that if $\|A - A_N\| \to 0$ with each $A_N$ of finite rank, then $A$ is compact. Deduce that a Hilbert-Schmidt
operator is compact by taking $A_N = AP_N$ with $P_N$ the projection onto $e_1, \dots, e_N$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Let $u_n$ be bounded by $M$. Since $A_1$ has finite rank, $A_1u_n$ has a convergent subsequence; along it $A_2u_n$
has a convergent subsequence, and so on. The diagonal subsequence $u_{n_k}$ makes every $A_Nu_{n_k}$ converge. Then
$\|Au_{n_j} - Au_{n_k}\| \leq 2M\|A - A_N\| + \|A_Nu_{n_j} - A_Nu_{n_k}\|$, and choosing $N$ large and then $j,
k$ large makes this small: $Au_{n_k}$ is Cauchy, hence convergent. For Hilbert-Schmidt $A$, $\|A - AP_N\|^2 \leq
\|A(1 - P_N)\|^2 \leq \sum_{k > N}\|Ae_k\|^2 \to 0$ (expand $u = \sum\langle e_k, u\rangle e_k$ and use
Cauchy-Schwarz), and $AP_N$ has finite rank.
:::
::::

### The spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators

Compact self-adjoint operators are the operators for which the matrix spectral theorem survives word for word,
with countably many eigenvalues tending to zero. The theorem below, quoted without proof, states this; the proof
mimics the matrix case, using compactness to produce the first eigenvector as a maximiser of $|\langle u,
Au\rangle|$.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-spectral-theorem-compact}
#### Spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators

Let $A$ be a compact self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space $H$. Then $H$ has an orthonormal basis of
eigenvectors of $A$; the non-zero eigenvalues are real, each of finite multiplicity, and form a finite set or a
sequence $\lambda_k \to 0$; $\|A\| = \max_k|\lambda_k|$ is attained; and $A = \sum_k\lambda_k|e_k\rangle\langle
e_k|$ with convergence in operator norm. For an integral operator with Hermitian kernel $k \in L^2(X \times X)$ the
kernel itself expands as $k(x, y) = \sum_k\lambda_ke_k(x)\overline{e_k(y)}$ in $L^2(X \times X)$ (the
**Hilbert-Schmidt theorem**). The theorem is quoted; the first eigenvalue is characterised in @exr-stc-min-max.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For a diagonal operator with $\lambda_n \to 0$ the theorem is visible from the definition, and the bilateral shift
shows what is lost without compactness. The first example makes the comparison.

::: {#exm-stc-diagonal}
#### Diagonal operators and the shift

$D = \sum_n\lambda_n|e_n\rangle\langle e_n|$ with $\lambda_n \to 0$ real is compact self-adjoint (@exm-co-diagonal),
and the theorem reproduces its definition: eigenvalues $\lambda_n$, eigenbasis $e_n$, norm $\max|\lambda_n|$. The
bilateral shift $V$ is normal but not compact, and its spectrum, the unit circle, contains no eigenvalue at all
(@exm-sp-shift): without compactness the spectrum need not consist of eigenvalues.
:::

The Green's operator of @exm-co-integral-operator is compact self-adjoint, and the theorem gives the Fourier sine
expansion of its kernel. The second example writes it out; the identity is a Fourier series of
@sec-fourier-series.

::: {#exm-stc-greens-operator}
#### The Green's kernel as an eigenfunction expansion

For $g(x, y) = \min(x, y) - xy$ on $[0, 1]^2$, $Ge_n = e_n/(n\pi)^2$ with $e_n = \sqrt2\sin n\pi x$
(@exr-stc-kernel-eigen), and the Hilbert-Schmidt theorem gives $\min(x, y) - xy = \sum_{n \geq 1}\frac{2\sin n\pi x
\sin n\pi y}{n^2\pi^2}$. At $x = y = \tfrac12$ this reads $\tfrac14 = \tfrac{2}{\pi^2}\sum_{n \text{ odd}}1/n^2$,
that is, $\sum_{n \text{ odd}}1/n^2 = \pi^2/8$, consistent with $\sum 1/n^2 = \pi^2/6$.
:::

The Laplacian on a compact space is unbounded, but its inverse on the complement of the constants is compact, and
the theorem applied to the inverse gives the Laplacian a discrete spectrum. The third example states this
principle, which @sec-unbounded-operators uses for the circle, the sphere and the torus.

::: {#exm-stc-inverse-laplacian}
#### Discrete spectra from compact inverses

If an operator $L$ (such as $-d^2/dx^2$ with Dirichlet conditions, or $-\Delta$ on a compact surface restricted to
functions of mean zero) has a compact self-adjoint inverse $G$, then $Ge_k = \mu_ke_k$ with $\mu_k \to 0$ gives
$Le_k = \mu_k^{-1}e_k$: $L$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with eigenvalues $\lambda_k = 1/\mu_k \to \infty$, each of
finite multiplicity. This is how the Sturm-Liouville theorem (@thm-sturm-liouville, @exr-stc-sturm-liouville-link)
and the discreteness of the Laplacian's spectrum on compact spaces (@thm-laplacian-discrete-spectrum) are proved.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The eigenvalue equation $Ge_n = e_n/(n\pi)^2$ is an integral identity that Sage verifies exactly, and the partial
sums of the kernel expansion can be compared with the kernel. The first exercise does both.

::: {#exr-stc-kernel-eigen}
#### Eigenfunctions of the Green's operator

With Sage, verify $\int_0^1(\min(x, y) - xy)\sin n\pi y\,dy = \sin n\pi x/(n\pi)^2$ for $n = 1, 2, 3$, and compare
the partial sums $\sum_{n \leq N}2\sin n\pi x\sin n\pi y/(n\pi)^2$ at $(x, y) = (\tfrac13, \tfrac12)$ for $N = 1,
3, 10$ with $\min(x, y) - xy = \tfrac16$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Splitting the integral at $y = x$ and integrating by parts twice gives the eigenvalue equation; the partial sums are
$0.1755$ for $N = 1$ and $N = 3$ (the $n = 2, 3$ terms vanish at these points) and $0.1649$ for $N = 10$, approaching
$1/6 = 0.1667$:

{{< sage exr-stc-kernel-eigen >}}
:::

The largest eigenvalue of a compact self-adjoint operator is the maximum of the Rayleigh quotient, and the
expansion in eigenvectors proves it in two lines. The second exercise asks for this and for the characterisation
of the next eigenvalue.

::: {#exr-stc-min-max}
#### The Rayleigh quotient

For $A = \sum_k\lambda_k|e_k\rangle\langle e_k|$ compact self-adjoint with $\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq \dots
\geq 0$, show that $\lambda_1 = \max_{\|u\| = 1}\langle u, Au\rangle$, attained at $e_1$, and that $\lambda_2 =
\max\{\langle u, Au\rangle : \|u\| = 1, u \perp e_1\}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $u = \sum c_ke_k$ and $\sum|c_k|^2 = 1$, $\langle u, Au\rangle = \sum_k\lambda_k|c_k|^2 \leq
\lambda_1\sum|c_k|^2 = \lambda_1$, with equality for $u = e_1$. If $u \perp e_1$ then $c_1 = 0$ and $\sum_{k \geq
2}\lambda_k|c_k|^2 \leq \lambda_2$, with equality at $e_2$. Iterating gives the **min-max characterisation** of all
eigenvalues, and for the Green's operator $\lambda_1 = 1/\pi^2$ is the maximum of $\int\int g(x, y)\bar u(x)u(y)$
over unit $u$.
:::

The Sturm-Liouville theorem of @sec-sturm-liouville was quoted; its proof is the spectral theorem for the Green's
operator. The last exercise asks the reader to trace each clause of that theorem to a clause of the one above.

::: {#exr-stc-sturm-liouville-link}
#### Sturm-Liouville from the spectral theorem

Assume that a regular Sturm-Liouville operator $L$ has a Green's operator $G$ that is compact, self-adjoint and
injective on $L^2$. Deduce from @thm-spectral-theorem-compact that the eigenvalues of $L$ are real, form a sequence
$|\lambda_n| \to \infty$, have orthogonal eigenfunctions, and that the eigenfunctions are complete.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$G$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis $e_n$ with real eigenvalues $\mu_n \to 0$; injectivity excludes $\mu_n = 0$, so
every $e_n$ satisfies $Le_n = \mu_n^{-1}e_n =: \lambda_ne_n$ with real $\lambda_n$ and $|\lambda_n| = 1/|\mu_n|
\to \infty$. Eigenfunctions for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal by @exr-ev-selfadjoint-real-orthogonal applied
to $G$. Completeness of the $e_n$ in $L^2$ is the statement that they form an orthonormal basis, which the theorem
asserts; so every $f \in L^2$ is the norm limit of its expansion $\sum\langle e_n, f\rangle e_n$, the completeness
clause of @thm-sturm-liouville.
:::
::::

### The functional calculus

Once an operator is diagonal, any function can be applied to it by applying the function to the diagonal. The
definition below turns this into the functional calculus, whose most important instance is the unitary $e^{itA}$
generated by a self-adjoint $A$, and quotes Stone's theorem, which says that all one-parameter unitary groups arise
this way.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-functional-calculus}
#### Functional calculus

For a self-adjoint operator with spectral decomposition $A = \sum_k\lambda_kP_k$ (a Hermitian matrix or a compact
self-adjoint operator) and a function $f$ on the spectrum, $f(A) = \sum_kf(\lambda_k)P_k$. This **functional
calculus** agrees with the algebraic definition for polynomials, satisfies $(fg)(A) = f(A)g(A)$, $f(A)^\dagger =
\bar f(A)$, $\|f(A)\| = \max_k|f(\lambda_k)|$, and $\sigma(f(A)) = f(\sigma(A))$ (the **spectral mapping
theorem**); for a multiplication operator, $f(M_g) = M_{f \circ g}$. In particular $e^{itA}$ is unitary for real
$t$ with $e^{itA}e^{isA} = e^{i(t + s)A}$, and $\sqrt A = \sum\sqrt{\lambda_k}P_k$ is the positive square root of a
positive $A$. For a general bounded self-adjoint operator the same calculus exists with the sum replaced by an
integral over the spectrum (the general spectral theorem, quoted); **Stone's theorem** (quoted) states that every
strongly continuous family of unitaries with $U(t)U(s) = U(t + s)$ is $U(t) = e^{itA}$ for a unique self-adjoint,
possibly unbounded, $A$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The exponential of $i\theta$ times a Pauli matrix is computed from the two eigenprojections, and the result is the
formula behind @exr-un-sage-exp. The first example derives it for a general direction $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$.

::: {#exm-fc-exp-pauli}
#### $e^{i\theta\,\hat{\mathbf{n}}\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma}$

With $\hat{\mathbf{n}}\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma = P_+ - P_-$ (@exm-sth-pauli-decomposition), $e^{i\theta\hat{\mathbf
n}\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma} = e^{i\theta}P_+ + e^{-i\theta}P_- = \cos\theta(P_+ + P_-) + i\sin\theta(P_+ - P_-) =
\cos\theta\,1 + i\sin\theta\,\hat{\mathbf{n}}\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma$, a unitary with eigenvalues $e^{\pm
i\theta}$ and determinant $1$. These are the elements of $SU(2)$, and $\theta \mapsto e^{i\theta\hat{\mathbf
n}\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma}$ is the one-parameter subgroup generated by $\hat{\mathbf{n}}\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma$
(@sec-exponential).
:::

A positive matrix has a unique positive square root, computed from its spectral decomposition, and the square root
of $A^\dagger A$ gives every matrix a polar decomposition. The second example computes $\sqrt A$ for the matrix of
the figure and states the polar decomposition.

::: {#exm-fc-sqrt}
#### Square roots

For $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix} = 3P_+ + 1P_-$ with $P_\pm = \tfrac12(1 \pm \sigma_1)$,
$\sqrt A = \sqrt3P_+ + P_- = \tfrac{\sqrt3 + 1}{2}1 + \tfrac{\sqrt3 - 1}{2}\sigma_1$, and indeed $(\sqrt A)^2 =
3P_+ + P_- = A$ (@prp-spectral-decompositions). For any matrix $B$, $|B| = \sqrt{B^\dagger B}$ is positive with
$\||B|u\| = \|Bu\|$, and $B = U|B|$ for a unitary $U$ (the **polar decomposition**); the singular values of $B$ are
the eigenvalues of $|B|$ (@exr-boc-singular-values).
:::

For a multiplication operator the functional calculus is composition of functions, and the spectral mapping
theorem is then the statement that the range of $f \circ g$ is $f$ of the range of $g$. The third example records
this and the consequence that $e^{itM_x}$ is multiplication by a phase.

::: {#exm-fc-multiplication}
#### Functions of multiplication operators

$f(M_g) = M_{f \circ g}$: $e^{itM_x}$ on $L^2(0, 1)$ is multiplication by $e^{itx}$, unitary with spectrum
$\{e^{itx} : x \in [0, 1]\}$, an arc of the circle, which is $f(\sigma(M_x))$ for $f(\lambda) = e^{it\lambda}$. For
the Fourier-transformed picture, $e^{itp}$ with $p = -i\,d/dx$ on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ is multiplication by $e^{itk}$
on $\hat f(k)$, which is the translation $f(x) \mapsto f(x + t)$ (@sec-fourier-transform): momentum generates
translations (@exr-sd-stone-glimpse).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Sage computes $e^{iA}$ either from the spectral decomposition or by its built-in matrix exponential, and the two
must agree. The first exercise compares them for the matrix of the figure, checks unitarity and verifies the square
root.

::: {#exr-fc-sage-exp}
#### $e^{iA}$ and $\sqrt A$ in Sage

For $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$, compute $e^{iA}$ in Sage from $U\operatorname{diag}
(e^{3i}, e^{i})U^\dagger$ and from the matrix exponential, check that they agree and are unitary with eigenvalues
$e^{3i}, e^{i}$, and verify $(\sqrt A)^2 = A$ for $\sqrt A = \tfrac{\sqrt3 + 1}{2}1 + \tfrac{\sqrt3 - 1}{2}
\sigma_1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$e^{iA} = e^{2i}(\cos 1\,1 + i\sin 1\,\sigma_1)$, since $A = 2\cdot1 + \sigma_1$ with commuting summands; its
determinant is $e^{4i} = e^{i\operatorname{tr}A}$:

{{< sage exr-fc-sage-exp >}}
:::

The unitarity of $e^{itA}$ and its group law follow from the functional calculus, and its derivative is $iAe^{itA}$,
which is the Schrödinger equation in disguise. The second exercise asks for these three facts.

::: {#exr-fc-exp-unitary-proof}
#### The unitary group $e^{itA}$

For Hermitian $A$ prove that $(e^{itA})^\dagger = e^{-itA}$, that $e^{itA}$ is unitary, that $e^{itA}e^{isA} =
e^{i(t + s)A}$, and that $\tfrac{d}{dt}e^{itA} = iAe^{itA}$; conclude that $u(t) = e^{-itA}u_0$ solves $i\,du/dt =
Au$ with $u(0) = u_0$ and $\|u(t)\| = \|u_0\|$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(\sum e^{it\lambda_k}P_k)^\dagger = \sum e^{-it\lambda_k}P_k = e^{-itA}$ since $P_k^\dagger = P_k$ and $\lambda_k$
is real. Then $e^{itA}e^{-itA} = \sum_{j, k}e^{it(\lambda_j - \lambda_k)}P_jP_k = \sum_kP_k = 1$ using $P_jP_k =
\delta_{jk}P_k$, and the same computation gives $e^{itA}e^{isA} = \sum e^{i(t + s)\lambda_k}P_k$. Differentiating
termwise, $\tfrac{d}{dt}\sum e^{it\lambda_k}P_k = \sum i\lambda_ke^{it\lambda_k}P_k = iA\,e^{itA}$. Hence $u(t) =
e^{-itA}u_0$ has $i\,du/dt = Au$, and $\|u(t)\| = \|u_0\|$ because $e^{-itA}$ is unitary.
:::

The resolvent of a diagonalisable operator is a sum of eigenprojections weighted by $(\lambda_k - z)^{-1}$, and
the projections can be recovered from it either by a contour integral or by Lagrange interpolation. The last
exercise asks for both formulas.

::: {#exr-fc-resolvent-and-projection}
#### Eigenprojections from the resolvent

For $A = \sum_k\lambda_kP_k$ with distinct $\lambda_k$, show that $(A - z)^{-1} = \sum_k(\lambda_k - z)^{-1}P_k$
for $z \notin \sigma(A)$, that $P_k = -\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{\gamma_k}(A - z)^{-1}dz$ for a small circle
$\gamma_k$ around $\lambda_k$, and that $P_k = \prod_{j \neq k}\frac{A - \lambda_j}{\lambda_k - \lambda_j}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(A - z)\sum_k(\lambda_k - z)^{-1}P_k = \sum_k(\lambda_k - z)(\lambda_k - z)^{-1}P_k = \sum_kP_k = 1$, using
$(A - z)P_k = (\lambda_k - z)P_k$. Integrating over $\gamma_k$, only the term $j = k$ has a pole inside, and
$\oint(\lambda_k - z)^{-1}dz = -2\pi i$ (@thm-residue), giving the contour formula. For the product, apply it to
the spectral decomposition: $\prod_{j \neq k}(A - \lambda_j)/(\lambda_k - \lambda_j) = \sum_m\prod_{j \neq
k}\frac{\lambda_m - \lambda_j}{\lambda_k - \lambda_j}P_m$, and the coefficient is $1$ for $m = k$ and $0$ for $m
\neq k$ (one factor vanishes): this is Lagrange interpolation of the indicator function of $\lambda_k$.
:::
::::

### Worked computations

The spectral decomposition of the symmetric matrix of the figure and of a complex Hermitian $3 \times 3$ matrix
can be carried out exactly, and their exponentials and polynomials then follow from the functional calculus. The
proposition records the results.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-spectral-decompositions}
#### Spectral decompositions of explicit Hermitian matrices

$A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $3, 1$ with orthonormal eigenvectors
$(1, \pm1)/\sqrt2$, $A = 3P_+ + P_-$, $e^{iA} = e^{2i}(\cos 1 + i\sin 1\,\sigma_1)$ is unitary with eigenvalues
$e^{3i}, e^{i}$, and $(\sqrt3P_+ + P_-)^2 = A$; the semi-axes of $A(S^1)$ are $3$ and $1$ along the eigenvectors.
$M = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & i & 0 \\ -i & 2 & i \\ 0 & -i & 2\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $2 \pm \sqrt2, 2$ with
orthonormal eigenvectors forming a unitary $U$, $M = UDU^\dagger$, $p(M) = \sum_kp(\lambda_k)P_k$ for $p(x) = x^3 -
2x + 1$, and $e^{iM}$ is unitary with $\det e^{iM} = e^{6i}$.
:::
