:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For a symmetric matrix the ellipse of @sec-bounded-operators has its axes along the eigenvectors and the singular
values are the absolute eigenvalues. The first example reads this off the left panel of the figure and contrasts it
with the non-symmetric matrix of @fig-operator-norm-ellipse.

::: {#exm-sd-figure}
#### The ellipse of a symmetric matrix

$A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$ stretches $(1, 1)/\sqrt2$ by $3$ and $(1, -1)/\sqrt2$ by $1$,
so $A(S^1)$ is the ellipse with these axes and $\|A\| = 3$, the largest eigenvalue: for Hermitian $A$,
$A^\dagger A = A^2$ has eigenvalues $\lambda_k^2$ and the singular values are $|\lambda_k|$. For the non-symmetric
$\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ the axes were along neither eigenvector and the norm exceeded both
eigenvalues (@exm-bo-matrix-norm).
:::

The unitary $e^{itA}$ moves each eigenvalue of $A$ around the unit circle at its own angular speed, and the right
panel of the figure shows the two resulting arcs. The second example writes the matrix as a function of $t$.

::: {#exm-sd-exp-rotation}
#### The curve $t \mapsto e^{itA}$

$e^{itA} = e^{3it}P_+ + e^{it}P_- = e^{2it}(\cos t\,1 + i\sin t\,\sigma_1)$ for $A = 2 + \sigma_1$: a curve in
$U(2)$ starting at $1$, with eigenvalues $e^{3it}$ and $e^{it}$ tracing the circle at speeds $3$ and $1$. At $t =
2\pi$ both return to $1$, so $e^{2\pi iA} = 1$: the group $\{e^{itA}\}$ is periodic because the eigenvalues of $A$
are integers, and would be dense in a torus for incommensurable eigenvalues.
:::

The trace and determinant of $f(A)$ are the sum and product of $f(\lambda_k)$, which gives identities such as
$\det e^{iA} = e^{i\operatorname{tr}A}$. The third example lists the values for the two matrices of the proposition
and previews the traces of @sec-traces-heat-kernels.

::: {#exm-sd-trace-det}
#### Traces and determinants of $f(A)$

$\operatorname{tr}f(A) = \sum_kf(\lambda_k)$ and $\det f(A) = \prod_kf(\lambda_k)$, since $f(A)$ is diagonal in
the eigenbasis. For $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$: $\operatorname{tr}e^{iA} = e^{3i} + e^{i}$,
$\det e^{iA} = e^{4i} = e^{i\operatorname{tr}A}$, $\operatorname{tr}\sqrt A = \sqrt3 + 1$; for $M$ of the
proposition, $\det e^{iM} = e^{i(2 + \sqrt2 + 2 + 2 - \sqrt2)} = e^{6i}$. The heat traces $\operatorname{tr}e^{-tA}
= \sum_ke^{-t\lambda_k}$ of @sec-traces-heat-kernels are the same identity for infinite spectra.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
A Hermitian tridiagonal matrix with $\pm i$ off the diagonal has eigenvalues involving the golden ratio, which Sage
finds exactly. The first exercise asks for its decomposition and for the trace of $e^{iA}$ in two ways.

::: {#exr-sd-sage-4x4}
#### A $4 \times 4$ Hermitian matrix

For $A$ the $4 \times 4$ matrix with $1$ on the diagonal, $i$ on the superdiagonal and $-i$ on the subdiagonal,
find the eigenvalues with Sage and express them through $\varphi = (1 + \sqrt5)/2$, build the unitary $U$ of
eigenvectors, check $U^\dagger U = 1$ and $A = UDU^\dagger$, and verify $\operatorname{tr}e^{iA} =
\sum_ke^{i\lambda_k}$ numerically.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The eigenvalues are $1 + 2\cos(k\pi/5)$, $k = 1, \dots, 4$, that is, $1 \pm \varphi$ and $1 \pm 1/\varphi$; the
eigenvalues of a tridiagonal Toeplitz matrix with entries $(c, a, b)$ are $a + 2\sqrt{bc}\cos(k\pi/(n + 1))$ and here
$bc = (i)(-i) = 1$:

{{< sage exr-sd-sage-4x4 >}}
:::

Two polynomials that agree on the spectrum define the same operator, and this is the reason the functional calculus
is well defined and the Cayley-Hamilton theorem holds. The second exercise asks for these consequences.

::: {#exr-sd-polynomial-identity}
#### Polynomials agreeing on the spectrum

For a Hermitian matrix $A$ show that $p(A) = q(A)$ whenever $p(\lambda_k) = q(\lambda_k)$ for all eigenvalues, that
the characteristic polynomial satisfies $\chi_A(A) = 0$ (Cayley-Hamilton), and that $f(A)$ for any $f$ equals $p(A)$
for the interpolation polynomial $p$ with $p(\lambda_k) = f(\lambda_k)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$p(A) = \sum_kp(\lambda_k)P_k = \sum_kq(\lambda_k)P_k = q(A)$. $\chi_A(\lambda_k) = 0$ for every eigenvalue, so
$\chi_A(A) = \sum_k0\cdot P_k = 0$. The Lagrange polynomial $p = \sum_kf(\lambda_k)\prod_{j \neq k}(x -
\lambda_j)/(\lambda_k - \lambda_j)$ has $p(\lambda_k) = f(\lambda_k)$, so $f(A) = \sum f(\lambda_k)P_k = p(A)$; for
$A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$ and $f = \exp$, $p(x) = \tfrac{e^3 - e}{2}x + \tfrac{3e -
e^3}{2}$ and $e^A = p(A)$.
:::

Stone's theorem identifies the generator of a unitary group, and two cases can be worked out by hand: a rotation
group in the plane and the translation group on the line. The last exercise asks for both generators.

::: {#exr-sd-stone-glimpse}
#### Generators of unitary groups

Find the Hermitian $A$ with $R_t = \begin{pmatrix} \cos t & \sin t \\ -\sin t & \cos t\end{pmatrix} = e^{itA}$,
and show formally that the translations $(T_af)(x) = f(x - a)$ on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ satisfy $T_a = e^{-iap}$ with $p
= -i\,d/dx$ by expanding $f(x - a)$ in a Taylor series.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\tfrac{d}{dt}R_t|_{t = 0} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{pmatrix} = i\sigma_2$, so $A = \sigma_2$ and
$R_t = e^{it\sigma_2}$ (@exr-un-sage-exp), with eigenvalues $e^{\pm it}$ on the eigenvectors $(1, \pm i)/\sqrt2$.
For translations, $f(x - a) = \sum_n\frac{(-a)^n}{n!}f^{(n)}(x) = e^{-a\,d/dx}f(x) = e^{-ia(-i\,d/dx)}f(x) =
e^{-iap}f(x)$ for analytic $f$; Stone's theorem makes this rigorous on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ with $p$ the self-adjoint
momentum operator of @sec-unbounded-operators, and the Fourier transform turns $e^{-iap}$ into multiplication by
$e^{-iak}$ (@exm-fc-multiplication).
:::
::::

## Compact and Fredholm operators {#sec-fredholm-operators}

Compact operators behave like matrices, and an operator that is invertible up to finite-dimensional errors behaves like
a matrix between spaces of different dimension. This part extends the compact operators of @def-compact-operator to
Banach spaces, proves the Fredholm alternative for equations $(1 - K)u = f$ with compact $K$, defines Fredholm operators
and their index, the difference between the number of solutions and the number of conditions, and shows that the index
is stable under compact and small perturbations and constant along continuous paths. Toeplitz operators and their
winding numbers are the model computation; the index of the Dirac operator in the later chapters is an index in exactly
this sense. The sources are @arcozzi2025 [Ch. 4] and @waterstraat2016 [Ch. 1].

### Compact operators

An operator is compact when it maps bounded sets into sets that are almost finite-dimensional. Integral operators are
the historical examples, and the figure shows how fast the singular values of two of them, the Volterra operator and the
Green's operator of $-d^2/dx^2$, decrease, compared with the identity, whose singular values are all $1$.

![The singular values $s_k$ (square roots of the eigenvalues of $T^*T$) on $L^2(0, 1)$ of the Volterra operator $Vf(x) =
\int_0^xf$, $s_k = \tfrac{2}{(2k - 1)\pi}$, and of the Green's operator $G$ of $-d^2/dx^2$ with Dirichlet conditions, $s_k
= \tfrac1{k^2\pi^2}$, against $k$ on logarithmic axes; the points are the singular values of $200 \times 200$
discretisations. Both tend to zero, as for every compact operator. Generated by
`figures/fa2-compact-singular-values.sage`.](figures/fa2-compact-singular-values.svg){#fig-fa2-compact-singular-values width=60%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-compact-banach-operator}
#### Compact operator between Banach spaces

A linear operator $T : X \to Y$ between Banach spaces is **compact** if the image of the unit ball has compact closure in
$Y$, equivalently if every bounded sequence $(x_n)$ has a subsequence along which $Tx_n$ converges @arcozzi2025 [Sec.
4.1.2]; @waterstraat2016 [Def. 1.1.4]. Compact operators are bounded; they form a closed subspace $\mathcal{K}(X, Y)$ of
$\mathcal{B}(X, Y)$, and products of compact and bounded operators are compact @waterstraat2016 [Lemma 1.1.5]. Operators
of finite rank and their norm limits are compact, and on a Hilbert space every compact operator is such a limit
@arcozzi2025 [Thm. 4.3]. A compact operator maps weakly convergent sequences to norm convergent ones @arcozzi2025 [Thm.
4.1]. On a Hilbert space this is @def-compact-operator.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The Volterra operator is compact on $C[0, 1]$ because it maps bounded functions to Lipschitz functions. The first example
applies the Arzelà-Ascoli theorem to it @arcozzi2025 [Thm. 4.8].

::: {#exm-fan-volterra-compact}
#### The Volterra operator

For $\|f\|_\infty \leq 1$, $Vf(x) = \int_0^xf$ satisfies $|Vf(x)| \leq 1$ and $|Vf(x) - Vf(y)| \leq |x - y|$. The set $V(B)$
is bounded and equicontinuous, hence has compact closure in $C[0, 1]$ by Arzelà-Ascoli: $V$ is compact. On $L^2(0, 1)$ it
is compact too, being Hilbert-Schmidt with kernel $\mathbf{1}_{t \leq x}$ @arcozzi2025 [Thm. 4.10].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Diagonal operators on the sequence spaces are compact exactly when their entries tend to zero. The second example proves
this on $\ell^p$ @arcozzi2025 [Exercise 4.1].

::: {#exm-fan-diagonal-compact}
#### Diagonal operators on $\ell^p$

$D = \operatorname{diag}(d_1, d_2, \dots)$ with $d_n \to 0$ is the norm limit of its finite-rank truncations $D_N$, since
$\|D - D_N\| = \sup_{n > N}|d_n| \to 0$ (@exm-fan-multiplication-lp), hence compact. If $|d_n| \geq c > 0$ along a
subsequence, $D\delta^{(n)} = d_n\delta^{(n)}$ has no convergent subsequence ($\|d_m\delta^{(m)} - d_n\delta^{(n)}\|_p \geq
c$), so $D$ is not compact.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Integral operators with continuous kernels are compact on every reasonable space of functions. The third example states
this and computes one example of finite rank.

::: {#exm-fan-continuous-kernel}
#### Continuous kernels

If $k$ is continuous on $[0, 1]^2$, $Kf(x) = \int_0^1k(x, y)f(y)\,dy$ is compact from $C[0, 1]$ to itself and from $L^p$ to
$L^p$, $1 \leq p < \infty$, by uniform continuity of $k$ and Arzelà-Ascoli @arcozzi2025 [Thm. 4.8]. A separated kernel $k(x,
y) = \sum_{j \leq N}a_j(x)b_j(y)$ gives a finite-rank operator: for $k = 1 + xy$, $Kf = (\int f)\cdot 1 + (\int yf)\cdot x$ has
rank $2$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The identity of an infinite-dimensional space is not compact, and the reason is a lemma of F. Riesz. The fourth example
states it @arcozzi2025 [Lemma 4.1, Cor. 4.1].

::: {#exm-fan-riesz-lemma}
#### The unit ball is not compact

For a proper closed subspace $Y$ of a Banach space and $0 < \alpha < 1$ there is a unit vector $z$ with $d(z, Y) \geq \alpha$
(**Riesz's lemma**). Applied to $Y_n = \operatorname{span}\{x_1, \dots, x_n\}$ it gives unit vectors with $\|x_m - x_n\|
\geq \tfrac12$, so the unit ball is compact only in finite dimensions, and a compact operator on an infinite-dimensional
space is never invertible, nor even surjective @arcozzi2025 [Prop. 4.1].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
In $C[0, 1]$ the unit vectors of the lemma can be written down. The first exercise does so with tents.

::: {#exr-fan-tents}
#### Tents in $C[0, 1\rbrack$

Let $h_n$ be the tent of height $1$ supported on $[2^{-n - 1}, 2^{-n}]$. Show $\|h_n\|_\infty = 1$ and $\|h_m - h_n\|_\infty
= 1$ for $m \neq n$, and conclude that the unit ball of $C[0, 1]$ is not compact. What is $Vh_n$ in norm?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The supports have disjoint interiors, so $|h_m - h_n|$ reaches $1$ at the top of each tent. No subsequence is Cauchy,
so the unit ball is not compact. $Vh_n(x) = \int_0^xh_n$ grows from $0$ to the area $\tfrac12\cdot 2^{-n - 1}$ of the
tent, so $\|Vh_n\|_\infty = 2^{-n - 2} \to 0$: the compact operator $V$ sends this non-convergent sequence to a convergent
one.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Norm limits of compact operators are compact, which is what makes $\mathcal{K}(X, Y)$ closed. The second exercise asks for
the $\varepsilon/3$ proof.

::: {#exr-fan-compact-closed}
#### Limits of compact operators

Let $T_n \to T$ in norm with $T_n$ compact. Show that $T(B)$ is totally bounded: cover it by finitely many balls of radius
$\varepsilon$ using a finite $\varepsilon/3$-net of $T_n(B)$ with $\|T - T_n\| < \varepsilon/3$. Conclude that $T$ is
compact.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Choose $n$ with $\|T - T_n\| < \varepsilon/3$ and points $y_1, \dots, y_m$ with $T_n(B) \subset\bigcup B(y_j,
\varepsilon/3)$. For $x \in B$, $\|Tx - y_j\| \leq \|Tx - T_nx\| + \|T_nx - y_j\| < \tfrac23\varepsilon$ for some $j$, so
$T(B)$ is totally bounded. In the complete space $Y$ a totally bounded set has compact closure.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The singular values of the Volterra operator can be found by solving the eigenvalue problem for $V^*V$, which is a
boundary value problem. The third exercise does this and compares with a discretisation.

::: {#exr-fan-volterra-singular-values}
#### Singular values of the Volterra operator

Show $V^*g(x) = \int_x^1g$ and that $V^*Vf = \mu f$ becomes $-\mu f'' = f$ with $f'(0) = 0$, $f(1) = 0$. Solve it to find
$\mu_k = \tfrac{4}{(2k - 1)^2\pi^2}$. With Sage, compare with the singular values of the matrix $h\,(\mathbf{1}_{i \geq
j})$, $h = 1/N$, for $N = 200$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\langle g, Vf\rangle = \int_0^1\bar g(x)\int_0^xf = \int_0^1f(t)\overline{\int_t^1g}\,dt$ gives $V^*$ @arcozzi2025 [Thm.
4.10]. With $u = V^*Vf$, $u' = -Vf$ and $u'' = -f$, with $u(1) = 0$ and $u'(0) = -Vf(0) = 0$. So $\mu f = u$ gives $-\mu
f'' = f$, $f'(0) = 0 = f(1)$, solved by $f = \cos(\omega x)$ with $\cos\omega = 0$, $\omega = (k - \tfrac12)\pi$, and $\mu
= \omega^{-2}$:

{{< sage exr-fan-volterra-singular-values >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Compact operators on an infinite-dimensional space are never invertible, but away from zero their spectrum is as simple
as that of a matrix. The theorem below states this; it is the Banach-space form of the spectral facts of
@thm-spectral-theorem-compact, without self-adjointness.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-riesz-schauder}
#### Spectrum of a compact operator

Let $K$ be a compact operator on an infinite-dimensional Banach space $X$. Then $0 \in \sigma(K)$; every $\lambda \in
\sigma(K) \setminus \{0\}$ is an eigenvalue of finite multiplicity; and $\sigma(K) \setminus \{0\}$ is finite or a sequence
tending to $0$ (**Riesz-Schauder**) @arcozzi2025 [Prop. 4.1, Thm. 4.5]. More generally, a closed operator with a compact
resolvent has a discrete spectrum of eigenvalues of finite type @waterstraat2016 [Thm. 1.3.5].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The Volterra operator is compact with spectrum $\{0\}$, so it has no eigenvalues at all: the theorem says nothing about
$\lambda = 0$. The first example proves this @arcozzi2025 [Thm. 4.10].

::: {#exm-fan-volterra-spectrum}
#### The spectrum of the Volterra operator

If $Vf = \lambda f$ with $\lambda \neq 0$, then $f$ is continuous, hence $C^1$, with $f = \lambda f'$ and $f(0) = 0$, so
$f = Ce^{x/\lambda} = 0$. For $\lambda = 0$, $Vf = 0$ gives $f = 0$. So $V$ has no eigenvalues, and by the theorem
$\sigma(V) = \{0\}$, consistent with the spectral radius $\lim\|V^n\|^{1/n} = 0$ of @exr-fan-volterra-powers.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

For a diagonal operator the theorem can be read off. The second example does so and shows the role of $0$ as the only
possible accumulation point.

::: {#exm-fan-diagonal-spectrum}
#### Diagonal operators

For $D = \operatorname{diag}(1, \tfrac12, \tfrac13, \dots)$ on $\ell^p$, $\sigma(D) = \{1, \tfrac12, \tfrac13, \dots\} \cup
\{0\}$; each $\tfrac1n$ is an eigenvalue of multiplicity $1$, and $0$ is in the spectrum without being an eigenvalue,
because $D^{-1} = \operatorname{diag}(n)$ is unbounded.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A rank-one operator has at most one non-zero eigenvalue, given by a pairing. The third example computes it, which is the
building block of the Fredholm determinants of @sec-traces-heat-kernels.

::: {#exm-fan-rank-one-spectrum}
#### Rank one

$Kx = \varphi(x)u$ with $u \in X$, $\varphi \in X^*$ has range $\mathbb{C}u$. If $Kx = \lambda x$ with $\lambda \neq 0$,
then $x \propto u$ and $\lambda = \varphi(u)$. So $\sigma(K) = \{0, \varphi(u)\}$. For the kernel $k(x, y) = xy$ on $[0, 1]$,
$u = x$, $\varphi(f) = \int yf$ and $\lambda = \int_0^1y^2dy = \tfrac13$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The powers of the Volterra operator have explicit kernels, and their norms tend to zero faster than any geometric
sequence. The first exercise computes them.

::: {#exr-fan-volterra-powers}
#### Powers of the Volterra operator

Show by induction $V^nf(x) = \int_0^x\tfrac{(x - t)^{n - 1}}{(n - 1)!}f(t)\,dt$ and $\|V^n\|_{C \to C} = \tfrac1{n!}$. Deduce
$\|V^n\|^{1/n} \to 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$V^{n + 1}f(x) = \int_0^x\int_0^s\tfrac{(s - t)^{n - 1}}{(n - 1)!}f(t)\,dt\,ds = \int_0^xf(t)\int_t^x\tfrac{(s - t)^{n -
1}}{(n - 1)!}ds\,dt = \int_0^x\tfrac{(x - t)^n}{n!}f(t)\,dt$. The norm is $\max_x\int_0^x\tfrac{(x - t)^{n - 1}}{(n - 1)!}dt =
\tfrac1{n!}$, attained at $f = 1$, $x = 1$. Since $n! \geq (n/e)^n$, $\|V^n\|^{1/n} \leq e/n \to 0$.

Sage checks the induction step and the norms $1/n!$:

{{< sage exr-fan-volterra-powers >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A kernel built from finitely many Fourier modes gives a finite-rank operator whose eigenvalues are its Fourier
coefficients. The second exercise computes them for a convolution kernel on the circle.

::: {#exr-fan-cosine-kernel}
#### A convolution kernel on the circle

Find the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of $Kf(x) = \int_0^{2\pi}\cos(x - y)f(y)\,dy$ on $C[0, 2\pi]$, and check that
$\sigma(K) = \{0, \pi\}$ with $\pi$ of multiplicity $2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\cos(x - y) = \cos x\cos y + \sin x\sin y$, so $Kf = (\int\cos y\,f)\cos x + (\int\sin y\,f)\sin x$ has rank $2$. On $\cos$:
$\int_0^{2\pi}\cos^2 = \pi$ and $\int\sin\cos = 0$, so $K\cos = \pi\cos$; similarly $K\sin = \pi\sin$. Every $f$ orthogonal
to $\cos$ and $\sin$ is in the kernel, so $\sigma(K) = \{0, \pi\}$.

Sage applies $K$ to several functions and diagonalises a discretisation:

{{< sage exr-fan-cosine-kernel >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The theorem also excludes non-zero spectral values that are not eigenvalues. The third exercise shows that a compact
operator on an infinite-dimensional space cannot be onto, which gives $0 \in \sigma(K)$ @arcozzi2025 [Prop. 4.1].

::: {#exr-fan-compact-not-onto}
#### Compact operators are not onto

Let $K$ be compact on an infinite-dimensional Banach space and suppose $K$ onto. Use the open mapping theorem
(@thm-open-mapping) to find a ball in $K(\bar B)$, and derive a contradiction with @exm-fan-riesz-lemma.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By the open mapping theorem $K(B) \supset B(0, \eta)$, so $\overline{K(\bar B)}$, which is compact, contains the closed ball
$\bar B(0, \eta/2)$. A closed subset of a compact set is compact, so a closed ball would be compact, which happens only in
finite dimensions. Hence $K$ is not onto, and $0 \in \sigma(K)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### The Fredholm alternative

For a compact $K$, the equation $u - Ku = f$ behaves like a square linear system: it is uniquely solvable for every $f$
unless the homogeneous equation has non-trivial solutions, and then it is solvable exactly when $f$ satisfies finitely many
conditions. The theorem below states this classical result, the origin of the whole theory in Fredholm's work on integral
equations.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-fredholm-alternative}
#### Fredholm alternative

Let $K$ be a compact operator on a Banach space $X$ and $\lambda \neq 0$. Then $\ker(\lambda - K)$ is finite-dimensional,
the range of $\lambda - K$ is closed, and $\dim\ker(\lambda - K) = \dim\ker(\lambda - K')$ for the transpose $K' \in
\mathcal{B}(X^*)$. Either $\lambda - K$ is invertible, so that $(\lambda - K)u = f$ has exactly one solution for every $f$,
or $(\lambda - K)u = 0$ has non-zero solutions; in the second case $(\lambda - K)u = f$ is solvable if and only if
$\varphi(f) = 0$ for every $\varphi \in \ker(\lambda - K')$ @arcozzi2025 [Thm. 4.4, Cor. 4.2]. On a Hilbert space $K'$ is
the adjoint $K^*$ and the condition reads $f \perp \ker(\bar\lambda - K^*)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A separated kernel turns the integral equation into a linear system for finitely many numbers. The first example solves
the rank-one case completely.

::: {#exm-fan-rank-one-equation}
#### A rank-one integral equation

$u(x) - \lambda\int_0^1xy\,u(y)\,dy = f(x)$ forces $u = f + \lambda cx$ with $c = \int_0^1yu$. Multiplying by $y$ and
integrating, $c = \int yf + \tfrac\lambda3c$. For $\lambda \neq 3$, $c = \tfrac{\int yf}{1 - \lambda/3}$ and the solution is
unique. For $\lambda = 3$ the equation is solvable iff $\int_0^1yf(y)\,dy = 0$, that is, $f \perp x$, the eigenfunction of the
symmetric kernel, and then $u = f + Cx$ for every $C$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In finite dimensions the theorem is the rank-nullity theorem for square matrices. The second example states it in the form
that the theorem generalises.

::: {#exm-fan-alternative-matrices}
#### Square matrices

For an $n \times n$ matrix $A$, $\dim\ker A = n - \operatorname{rank}A = \dim\ker A^{\mathsf T}$, and $Ax = b$ is solvable iff
$b \perp \ker A^{\mathsf T}$ (in the real case). For $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{pmatrix}$, $\ker A^{\mathsf T}$
is spanned by $(2, -1)$, so $Ax = (1, 2)$ is solvable and $Ax = (1, 0)$ is not.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Without compactness the alternative fails, and the shift gives an operator $1 - T$ that is injective without being onto.
The third example shows the failure.

::: {#exm-fan-alternative-fails}
#### Failure for non-compact operators

On $\ell^2$, $1 - S$ is injective: $(1 - S)a = 0$ gives $a_1 = 0$ and $a_n = a_{n - 1}$, so $a = 0$. Its adjoint $1 - S^*$ is
injective too, since $(1, 1, \dots) \notin \ell^2$. Yet $1 - S$ is not onto: $(1 - S)a = \delta^{(1)}$ forces $a = (1, 1,
\dots)$. The range is dense but not closed, which is what the theorem rules out for $1 - K$ with $K$ compact.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Volterra equations of the second kind are always uniquely solvable, since $\sigma(V) = \{0\}$. The fourth example solves one
explicitly.

::: {#exm-fan-volterra-equation}
#### A Volterra equation

$u - \mu Vu = f$ with $f \in C^1$ gives $u' - \mu u = f'$, $u(0) = f(0)$, hence $u(x) = f(x) + \mu\int_0^xe^{\mu(x - t)}f(t)\,dt$
for every $\mu \in \mathbb{C}$: the resolvent kernel is $\mu e^{\mu(x - t)}\mathbf{1}_{t \leq x} = \sum_{n \geq 1}\mu^n
\tfrac{(x - t)^{n - 1}}{(n - 1)!}$, the Neumann series of @exr-fan-volterra-powers summed.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
A kernel of rank two leads to a $2 \times 2$ system whose determinant vanishes at the exceptional values. The first exercise
solves it with Sage.

::: {#exr-fan-degenerate-kernel}
#### A rank-two kernel

For $u(x) - \lambda\int_0^1(1 + xy)u(y)\,dy = f(x)$, write $u = f + \lambda(a + bx)$, derive the linear system for $a$, $b$,
and find the values of $\lambda$ where it is singular. With Sage, solve for $f = 1$ and general $\lambda$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$a = \int u$ and $b = \int yu$ give $(1 - \lambda)a - \tfrac\lambda2b = \int f$ and $-\tfrac\lambda2a + (1 - \tfrac\lambda3)b
= \int yf$. The determinant is $1 - \tfrac43\lambda + \tfrac1{12}\lambda^2$, vanishing at $\lambda = 8 \pm 2\sqrt{13}$; these
are the reciprocals of the two non-zero eigenvalues of the kernel:

{{< sage exr-fan-degenerate-kernel >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

For finite-rank $K$ the theorem is pure linear algebra, and the first step of the general proof reduces to it. The second
exercise proves the finite-rank case @arcozzi2025 [proof of Thm. 4.4].

::: {#exr-fan-alternative-finite-rank}
#### The finite-rank case

Let $Kx = \sum_{j \leq n}\varphi_j(x)u_j$. Show that $x - Kx = f$ is equivalent to $x = f + \sum c_ju_j$ with $c - Mc = (\varphi_i
(f))_i$, $M_{ij} = \varphi_i(u_j)$, and deduce the alternative from the corresponding statement for the matrix $1 - M$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
If $x - Kx = f$ then $x = f + \sum_jc_ju_j$ with $c_j = \varphi_j(x)$, and applying $\varphi_i$ gives $c_i = \varphi_i(f) +
\sum_jM_{ij}c_j$. Conversely each solution $c$ gives a solution $x$. So the equation is uniquely solvable for all $f$ iff
$1 - M$ is invertible; otherwise the homogeneous equation has solutions $\sum c_ju_j$ with $c \in \ker(1 - M)$, and solvability
is a finite set of linear conditions on $(\varphi_i(f))$, those of $\ker(1 - M)^{\mathsf T}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The second-kind Volterra equation has a solution for every right-hand side, which the third exercise checks on an example. It
also shows the resolvent kernel at work.

::: {#exr-fan-volterra-solve}
#### Solving a Volterra equation

Solve $u(x) - 2\int_0^xu(t)\,dt = 1$ on $[0, 1]$ in two ways: by the formula of @exm-fan-volterra-equation and by summing the
Neumann series $\sum_n2^nV^n1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The formula gives $u = 1 + 2\int_0^xe^{2(x - t)}dt = 1 + (e^{2x} - 1) = e^{2x}$. The series gives $\sum_n2^n\tfrac{x^n}{n!} =
e^{2x}$, since $V^n1 = x^n/n!$. Check: $e^{2x} - 2\cdot\tfrac{e^{2x} - 1}{2} = 1$.

Sage carries out both methods and the check:

{{< sage exr-fan-volterra-solve >}}
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

### Fredholm operators and the index

An operator is Fredholm when its kernel and cokernel are finite-dimensional, so that it is invertible up to finitely many
dimensions. Its index counts solutions minus conditions; the figure shows the curves whose winding numbers give the indices
of Toeplitz operators, the main example of the section.

![The curves $\theta \mapsto \varphi(e^{i\theta})$ for the symbols $\varphi(z) = z$, $z^2$, $z - \tfrac12$, $z^{-1}$ and $2 + z$,
with their winding numbers about $0$: $1, 2, 1, -1, 0$. The Toeplitz operators with these symbols have indices $-1, -2,
-1, 1, 0$. Generated by `figures/fa2-winding-number.sage`.](figures/fa2-winding-number.svg){#fig-fa2-winding-number width=95%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-fredholm-operator}
#### Fredholm operator

A bounded operator $T : X \to Y$ between Banach spaces is a **Fredholm operator** if its kernel $\ker T$ is finite-dimensional
and its range $\operatorname{ran}T$ has finite codimension; the range is then closed @waterstraat2016 [Lemma 1.1.11, Lemma
1.2.15]. Its **index** is $\operatorname{ind}T = \dim\ker T - \operatorname{codim}\operatorname{ran}T$. The same definition
applies to closed operators $T : D(T) \subset X \to Y$ @waterstraat2016 [Def. 1.2.14]. On Hilbert spaces
$\operatorname{codim}\operatorname{ran}T = \dim\ker T^*$, so $\operatorname{ind}T = \dim\ker T - \dim\ker T^*$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Matrices between spaces of different dimensions are Fredholm, and their index depends only on the dimensions. The first example
computes it from the rank-nullity theorem.

::: {#exm-fan-matrix-index}
#### Matrices

$T : \mathbb{C}^n \to \mathbb{C}^m$ has $\dim\ker T = n - r$ and $\operatorname{codim}\operatorname{ran}T = m - r$ with $r$ the
rank, so $\operatorname{ind}T = n - m$, whatever the matrix. In finite dimensions the index carries no information about the
operator; in infinite dimensions it does.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The shifts are the simplest operators of non-zero index in infinite dimensions. The second example computes their indices
from their kernels and ranges.

::: {#exm-fan-shift-index}
#### Shifts

On $\ell^2$, $S$ is injective with range $\{a : a_1 = 0\}$ of codimension $1$, so $\operatorname{ind}S = -1$; $S^*$ is onto with
kernel $\mathbb{C}\delta^{(1)}$, so $\operatorname{ind}S^* = 1$; and $\operatorname{ind}S^k = -k$. The equation $Sa = b$ is
solvable iff $b_1 = 0$, one condition and no free parameter.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Differentiation is Fredholm between spaces of different smoothness, and its index depends on the boundary conditions. The
third example compares the interval and the circle @waterstraat2016 [Ex. 1.2.16].

::: {#exm-fan-derivative-index}
#### Differentiation

$d/dx : C^1[0, 1] \to C[0, 1]$ is bounded for the $C^1$ norm, onto ($u = \int_0^xv$) with kernel the constants: index $1$. On
the circle, $d/dx : C^1(S^1) \to C(S^1)$ has the constants as kernel and the functions of mean zero as range, of codimension
$1$: index $0$. With the condition $u(0) = 0$ on the interval the kernel disappears and the index is $0$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Perturbations of the identity by compact operators are Fredholm of index zero, which is the Fredholm alternative restated. The
fourth example records it.

::: {#exm-fan-identity-plus-compact}
#### Identity plus compact

For $K$ compact and $\lambda \neq 0$, @thm-fredholm-alternative gives $\dim\ker(\lambda - K) = \dim\ker(\lambda - K') =
\operatorname{codim}\operatorname{ran}(\lambda - K) < \infty$, so $\lambda - K$ is Fredholm of index $0$. Operators of the form
$\lambda - K$ are the Fredholm operators of index zero that the integral equations of the previous section produce.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The index is additive under composition, which the first exercise checks on shifts. The general product formula is part of
@thm-index-stability.

::: {#exr-fan-shift-products}
#### Products of shifts

Compute $\ker$ and $\operatorname{ran}$ of $S^m(S^*)^n$ on $\ell^2$, and show $\operatorname{ind}S^m(S^*)^n = n - m =
\operatorname{ind}S^m + \operatorname{ind}(S^*)^n$. Show $S^*S = 1$ but $SS^* = 1 - |\delta^{(1)}\rangle\langle\delta^{(1)}|$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(S^*)^n$ drops the first $n$ entries: kernel of dimension $n$, onto. $S^m$ then prepends $m$ zeros: injective, range of
codimension $m$. So $\dim\ker = n$, $\operatorname{codim}\operatorname{ran} = m$, index $n - m$. $S^*Sa = a$, while $SS^*a = (0,
a_2, a_3, \dots)$, which is $a$ minus its projection on $\delta^{(1)}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A first-order differential operator on the circle has index zero, and its kernel can be computed. The second exercise does
this for $d/dx + a(x)$.

::: {#exr-fan-first-order-circle}
#### A first-order operator on the circle

For continuous $2\pi$-periodic $a$, let $T = d/dx + a : C^1(S^1) \to C(S^1)$. Show that $\ker T$ is spanned by $e^{-A(x)}$, $A(x) =
\int_0^xa$, if $\int_0^{2\pi}a = 0$, and is zero otherwise. For $a = c$ constant, show that $T$ is invertible iff $c \notin
i\mathbb{Z}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$u' + au = 0$ gives $u = Ce^{-A}$, periodic iff $A(2\pi) = 0$. For constant $a = c$, on Fourier modes $Te^{inx} = (in + c)e^{inx}$,
which vanishes for some $n$ iff $c = -in$. Otherwise $u' + cu = f$ has the
solution $u(x) = e^{-cx}(C + \int_0^xe^{ct}f(t)\,dt)$, which is periodic for exactly one $C$, since $e^{2\pi c} \neq 1$; so
$T$ is bijective. In general $T_t = d/dx + ta$ is a continuous path from $d/dx$, of index $0$ (@exm-fan-derivative-index), so
every $T$ has index $0$ (@thm-index-stability).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A Fredholm operator has a closed range, and the second half of the definition can be weakened to the existence of a closed
complement. The third exercise proves the key lemma @waterstraat2016 [Lemma 1.1.11].

::: {#exr-fan-finite-codim-closed}
#### Finite codimension implies closed range

Let $T \in \mathcal{B}(X, Y)$ and let $V \subset Y$ be a finite-dimensional subspace with $Y = \operatorname{ran}T \oplus V$.
Show that $\tilde T : X/\ker T \times V \to Y$, $([x], v) \mapsto Tx + v$, is a bounded bijection, and use the inverse
mapping theorem to show that $\operatorname{ran}T$ is closed.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$X/\ker T$ is a Banach space and $V$ is complete, so the domain is a Banach space; $\tilde T$ is bounded, injective because
$Tx + v = 0$ forces $v = 0$ and $x \in \ker T$, and onto by hypothesis. By @thm-open-mapping, $\tilde T^{-1}$ is bounded, so
$\tilde T$ maps the closed subspace $X/\ker T \times \{0\}$ onto a closed set, which is $\operatorname{ran}T$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

The Toeplitz operators are compressions of multiplication operators to the non-negative Fourier modes, and their index is the
winding number of the symbol with a minus sign. The theorem below states this, the simplest index theorem: an analytic index
on the left, a topological invariant on the right.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-toeplitz-index}
#### Index of a Toeplitz operator

Let $\varphi : S^1 \to \mathbb{C}$ be continuous, with Fourier coefficients $\hat\varphi(n)$, and let $T_\varphi$ act on
$\ell^2(\{0, 1, 2, \dots\})$ by the matrix $(T_\varphi)_{jk} = \hat\varphi(j - k)$, that is, multiplication by $\varphi$
followed by the projection onto the non-negative modes (the **Toeplitz operator** with **symbol** $\varphi$). If $\varphi$ has no
zero on $S^1$, then $T_\varphi$ is Fredholm and $\operatorname{ind}T_\varphi = -\operatorname{wind}(\varphi)$, where
$\operatorname{wind}(\varphi) = \tfrac1{2\pi i}\oint\tfrac{d\varphi}{\varphi}$ is the winding number about $0$; moreover
$T_\varphi T_\psi - T_{\varphi\psi}$ is compact. The identification of a Fredholm index with a winding number is proved for the
edge operators of chiral lattice models by @zhou2024bulkedge [Sec. III A, eq. 27], where the orientation of the edge fixes the
sign.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Monomial symbols give the shifts, and the theorem reduces to @exm-fan-shift-index. The first example records this and
checks the sign convention of the theorem.

::: {#exm-fan-toeplitz-monomials}
#### Monomial symbols

$\varphi(z) = z^k$ has $\hat\varphi(n) = \delta_{nk}$, so $T_{z^k} = S^k$ for $k \geq 0$ and $T_{z^{-k}} = (S^*)^k$. The winding
numbers are $\pm k$ and the indices $\mp k$, as computed directly. The constant symbol $1$ gives the identity, of index $0$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The symbol $z - a$ winds around zero exactly when $|a| < 1$, and the operator $S - a$ changes accordingly. The second example
computes kernel and cokernel.

::: {#exm-fan-toeplitz-affine}
#### The symbol $z - a$

$T_{z - a} = S - a$. For $|a| > 1$ it is invertible ($\|S\| = 1 < |a|$, Neumann series), index $0$, and $z - a$ does not wind.
For $|a| < 1$, $S - a$ is injective, and $\ker(S^* - \bar a)$ is spanned by $(1, \bar a, \bar a^2, \dots) \in \ell^2$, so the
cokernel has dimension $1$: index $-1 = -\operatorname{wind}(z - a)$. For $|a| = 1$ the symbol vanishes on $S^1$, and $S - a$
is not Fredholm.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A positive symbol has winding number zero, and its Toeplitz operator is invertible. The third example gives a tridiagonal
one, which is the Hamiltonian of a particle hopping on a half-line.

::: {#exm-fan-toeplitz-tridiagonal}
#### A tridiagonal Toeplitz operator

$\varphi(e^{i\theta}) = 3 + e^{i\theta} + e^{-i\theta} = 3 + 2\cos\theta \geq 1$ gives the tridiagonal matrix with $3$ on the
diagonal and $1$ beside it, $T_\varphi = 3 + S + S^*$. It is self-adjoint with $\langle a, T_\varphi a\rangle \geq \|a\|^2$, hence
invertible, index $0 = -\operatorname{wind}\varphi$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The kernel of the adjoint of $S - a$ is a geometric sequence, which is the edge state of the half-line. The first exercise
computes it and its normalisation.

::: {#exr-fan-edge-state}
#### The cokernel of $S - a$

For $|a| < 1$ solve $(S^* - \bar a)x = 0$ on $\ell^2$, normalise the solution, and show that $\operatorname{ran}(S - a) =
\{b : \sum_n a^{n - 1}b_n = 0\}$. Why does the solution disappear for $|a| \geq 1$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(S^*x)_n = x_{n + 1} = \bar ax_n$ gives $x_n = \bar a^{n - 1}x_1$, of norm $|x_1|(1 - |a|^2)^{-1/2}$; normalised, $x_1 = (1 -
|a|^2)^{1/2}$. The range of $S - a$ is closed (Fredholm) and equals $\ker(S^* - \bar a)^\perp = \{b : \sum a^{n - 1}b_n = 0\}$.
For $|a| \geq 1$ the geometric sequence is not square summable, so the kernel of $S^* - \bar a$ is $0$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Winding numbers of rational symbols are counted by the argument principle (@thm-residue). The second exercise computes one and
checks the integral with Sage.

::: {#exr-fan-winding-numbers}
#### Winding numbers by the argument principle

Compute $\operatorname{wind}(\varphi)$ for $\varphi(z) = z^2(z - \tfrac12)/(z - 3)$ by counting zeros and poles in the unit disc,
and give $\operatorname{ind}T_\varphi$. With Sage, evaluate $\tfrac1{2\pi i}\oint\varphi'/\varphi\,dz$ numerically on the unit
circle.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\varphi'/\varphi = \tfrac2z + \tfrac1{z - 1/2} - \tfrac1{z - 3}$, and inside the disc the residues are $2$ and $1$, while the
pole $3$ lies outside: $\operatorname{wind}\varphi = 3$ and $\operatorname{ind}T_\varphi = -3$:

{{< sage exr-fan-winding-numbers >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Toeplitz operators do not multiply like their symbols, but the defect is compact. The third exercise computes it for the
simplest pair.

::: {#exr-fan-toeplitz-semicommutator}
#### The semicommutator

Show $T_{\bar z}T_z = 1 = T_{\bar zz}$ but $T_zT_{\bar z} = 1 - |\delta^{(0)}\rangle\langle\delta^{(0)}|$ (indexing from $0$).
Check that both products have index $0 = \operatorname{ind}T_z + \operatorname{ind}T_{\bar z}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$T_z = S$ and $T_{\bar z} = S^*$, so $T_{\bar z}T_z = S^*S = 1$ and $T_zT_{\bar z} = SS^*$ is the projection that kills the
$0$-th mode (@exr-fan-shift-products). The difference $T_zT_{\bar z} - T_{z\bar z}$ has rank one, hence is compact. $1$ has index
$0$, and $1 - P$ with $P$ a rank-one projection has a one-dimensional kernel and cokernel, index $0$; both equal $-1 + 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### Stability of the index

The dimension of the kernel of an operator can jump under small perturbations, but the index cannot. The theorem below states
the stability properties that make the index a topological invariant; they are the reason why index theorems compute
something robust.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-index-stability}
#### Stability of the Fredholm index

Let $T : X \to Y$ be Fredholm. (i) There is $\gamma > 0$ such that $T + B$ is Fredholm with $\dim\ker(T + B) \leq \dim\ker T$
and $\operatorname{ind}(T + B) = \operatorname{ind}T$ whenever $\|B\| < \gamma$ @waterstraat2016 [Thm. 1.2.17]. (ii) For compact
$K$, $T + K$ is Fredholm with $\operatorname{ind}(T + K) = \operatorname{ind}T$ @waterstraat2016 [Thm. 1.2.18]. (iii) The
index is constant along any norm-continuous path of Fredholm operators. (iv) If $S : Y \to Z$ is Fredholm, $\operatorname{ind}
(ST) = \operatorname{ind}S + \operatorname{ind}T$. (v) (**Atkinson**) $T$ is Fredholm if and only if it is invertible modulo
compact operators: $RT - 1$ and $TR - 1$ are compact for some bounded $R$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The dimension of the kernel is only upper semicontinuous, and it can drop while the index stays fixed. The first example shows
the jump in the simplest family.

::: {#exm-fan-kernel-jump}
#### Jumping kernels

$T_t = \operatorname{diag}(t, 1, 1, \dots)$ on $\ell^2$ is Fredholm for every $t$, with index $0$. At $t = 0$ kernel and cokernel
are both one-dimensional; for $t \neq 0$ both vanish. The jump happens in kernel and cokernel together, as the stability of the
index requires, and $\dim\ker$ can only drop under small perturbations.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Along the family $S - a$ the index is $-1$ inside the disc and $0$ outside, and the change happens where the operator stops being
Fredholm. The second example traces the family.

::: {#exm-fan-index-path}
#### Crossing the unit circle

$a \mapsto S - a$ is norm continuous. For $|a| < 1$ it is Fredholm of index $-1$, for $|a| > 1$ of index $0$
(@exm-fan-toeplitz-affine). Part (iii) of the theorem forces any path from inside to outside to pass through non-Fredholm
operators, and indeed $S - a$ with $|a| = 1$ has a dense, non-closed range.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Compact perturbations of the identity have index zero, which recovers the Fredholm alternative from part (ii). The third example
also applies part (ii) to a Toeplitz operator.

::: {#exm-fan-compact-perturbation}
#### Compact perturbations

$1 + K$ has index $\operatorname{ind}1 = 0$ for every compact $K$. The rank-one perturbation $S + \tfrac12|\delta^{(1)}\rangle
\langle\delta^{(5)}|$ of the shift has index $-1$, though its kernel and cokernel may differ from those of $S$. The tridiagonal
operator of @exm-fan-toeplitz-tridiagonal, changed in finitely many matrix entries, keeps index $0$.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The product formula can be checked on matrices and shifts. The first exercise proves it in finite dimensions, where it is a count
of dimensions.

::: {#exr-fan-product-formula-matrices}
#### The product formula for matrices

For $T : \mathbb{C}^n \to \mathbb{C}^m$ and $S : \mathbb{C}^m \to \mathbb{C}^p$, verify $\operatorname{ind}(ST) = \operatorname{ind}S +
\operatorname{ind}T$ using @exm-fan-matrix-index. Then check it for $S^*\cdot S^2$ on $\ell^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\operatorname{ind}(ST) = n - p = (m - p) + (n - m)$. On $\ell^2$, $S^*S^2 = S$ has index $-1 = 1 + (-2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

The kernel of $S^* - \lambda$ is one-dimensional on the whole open disc, which shows that the dimension of the kernel can be
locally constant as well. The second exercise computes the index of $S^* - \lambda$ and identifies where the family leaves the
Fredholm operators.

::: {#exr-fan-backward-shift-family}
#### The family $S^* - \lambda$

For $|\lambda| < 1$, find $\ker(S^* - \lambda)$ and show $S^* - \lambda$ is onto, so the index is $1$. For $|\lambda| > 1$ show it
is invertible. Which part of the theorem explains that the index is constant on the open disc?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$x_{n + 1} = \lambda x_n$ gives the one-dimensional kernel spanned by $(1, \lambda, \lambda^2, \dots)$. The adjoint $S - \bar\lambda$
is injective (@exm-fan-toeplitz-affine), and the range of a Fredholm operator is closed, so $S^* - \lambda$ is onto: index $1$.
For $|\lambda| > 1$ the Neumann series inverts it. The disc is connected and $\lambda \mapsto S^* - \lambda$ is continuous, so
part (iii) makes the index constant there.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Atkinson's characterisation gives a quick proof that Toeplitz operators with non-vanishing symbols are Fredholm. The third
exercise carries it out with the compact semicommutator of @thm-toeplitz-index.

::: {#exr-fan-atkinson-toeplitz}
#### Toeplitz operators are Fredholm

Let $\varphi$ be continuous without zeros. Using that $T_\varphi T_\psi - T_{\varphi\psi}$ is compact, show that $R =
T_{1/\varphi}$ inverts $T_\varphi$ modulo compacts, and conclude with part (v). Use parts (iii) and (iv) to show that
$\operatorname{ind}T_\varphi$ depends only on the homotopy class of $\varphi$ in $C(S^1, \mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\})$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$T_{1/\varphi}T_\varphi - 1 = T_{1/\varphi}T_\varphi - T_1$ and $T_\varphi T_{1/\varphi} - 1$ are compact, so $T_\varphi$ is
Fredholm by Atkinson. $\|T_\varphi - T_\psi\| \leq \|\varphi - \psi\|_\infty$, so a homotopy of non-vanishing symbols gives a
norm-continuous path of Fredholm operators, along which the index is constant. Homotopy classes of such symbols are labelled by
the winding number, which is how @thm-toeplitz-index reduces to the monomials of @exm-fan-toeplitz-monomials.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

### Exercises

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
These exercises combine compact operators, the Fredholm alternative and the index. The last one is a small index theorem with a
topological answer.

A boundary value problem becomes an integral equation of the second kind through the Green's function, and the Fredholm
alternative then gives its solvability. The first integrative exercise treats the resonant string.

::: {#exr-fan-resonant-string}
#### The resonant string

Show that $-u'' - \mu u = f$, $u(0) = u(1) = 0$ is equivalent to $u - \mu Gu = Gf$ with the Green's operator $G$ of
@exm-co-integral-operator, and that for $\mu = \pi^2$ it is solvable iff $\int_0^1f(x)\sin\pi x\,dx = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$G$ inverts $-d^2/dx^2$ with Dirichlet conditions, so applying $G$ to $-u'' = \mu u + f$ gives $u = \mu Gu + Gf$, and conversely.
$G$ is compact self-adjoint with eigenvalues $1/(n\pi)^2$ and eigenfunctions $\sin n\pi x$. For $\mu = \pi^2$, $\ker(1 - \pi^2G)$ is
spanned by $\sin\pi x$, and by @thm-fredholm-alternative $u - \pi^2Gu = Gf$ is solvable iff $\langle\sin\pi x, Gf\rangle =
\pi^{-2}\langle\sin\pi x, f\rangle = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The index of a Fredholm operator does not change under compact perturbations, even when the perturbation changes the kernel. The
second integrative exercise computes the kernel and cokernel of a perturbed shift.

::: {#exr-fan-perturbed-shift}
#### A perturbed shift

Let $T = S + c\,|\delta^{(1)}\rangle\langle\delta^{(1)}|$ on $\ell^2$. Find $\ker T$ and $\ker T^*$ for every $c$, and check that the
index is always $-1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$Ta = (ca_1, a_1, a_2, \dots)$, which vanishes only for $a = 0$: $\ker T = 0$. $T^*b = (b_2 + \bar cb_1, b_3, b_4, \dots)$ vanishes iff
$b_n = 0$ for $n \geq 3$ and $b_2 = -\bar cb_1$, a one-dimensional space. So the index is $0 - 1 = -1$ for every $c$, as part (ii) of
@thm-index-stability predicts.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The index of a Toeplitz operator can be computed from a finite matrix when the symbol is a polynomial. The third integrative
exercise does so for a quadratic symbol by factoring it.

::: {#exr-fan-toeplitz-quadratic}
#### A quadratic symbol

For $\varphi(z) = (z - \tfrac12)(z - 2)$, find the winding number, write $T_\varphi$ as a polynomial in $S$, and find its kernel and
cokernel. Why do the finite truncations of $T_\varphi$ not show the cokernel?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Only the zero $\tfrac12$ lies inside the disc, so $\operatorname{wind}\varphi = 1$ and $\operatorname{ind}T_\varphi = -1$. $T_\varphi =
(S - \tfrac12)(S - 2)$; $S - 2$ is invertible, and $S - \tfrac12$ is injective with cokernel spanned by $(1, \tfrac12, \tfrac14, \dots)$
(@exr-fan-edge-state). So $\ker T_\varphi = 0$, and $T_\varphi^* = (S^* - 2)(S^* - \tfrac12)$ with $S^* - 2$ invertible, so $\ker T_\varphi^* =
\ker(S^* - \tfrac12)$ is spanned by $(2^{-n})_{n \geq 0}$. The truncations are lower triangular with $\hat\varphi(0) = 1$ on the
diagonal, hence invertible: the cokernel lives at infinity, in the tail that every truncation cuts off.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
