## Unbounded operators and the Laplacian {#sec-unbounded-operators}

Differentiation is not a bounded operator, and neither are the position and momentum operators of quantum
mechanics or the Laplacian; they are defined only on a dense subspace, their domain, and the choice of domain is
part of the definition. This section introduces unbounded operators and their domains, the canonical commutation
relation $[x, p] = i$, self-adjoint extensions in outline, and the Laplacian on the circle, the sphere and the
torus, whose spectrum on a compact space is discrete; the figure shows the eigenfunctions and the spectra.

### Domains

An operator that cannot be defined on every vector of $H$ must come with the subspace on which it is defined, and
notions such as symmetric and self-adjoint must be reconsidered with domains in view. The definition below does
this, and records that the spectral theorem survives for self-adjoint unbounded operators.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-unbounded-operator}
#### Unbounded operator

An **operator** on $H$ is a linear map $A : D(A) \to H$ defined on a dense subspace $D(A)$, its **domain**; it is
**bounded** if $\|Au\| \leq C\|u\|$ on $D(A)$, in which case it extends to all of $H$, and **unbounded**
otherwise. It is **symmetric** if $\langle Au, v\rangle = \langle u, Av\rangle$ for all $u, v \in D(A)$. The
**adjoint** $A^\dagger$ has domain $D(A^\dagger) = \{v : u \mapsto \langle v, Au\rangle \text{ is bounded on }
D(A)\}$ and is defined there by @thm-riesz-representation, so that $\langle Au, v\rangle = \langle u, A^\dagger
v\rangle$ for $u \in D(A)$, $v \in D(A^\dagger)$; $A$ is **self-adjoint** if $A^\dagger = A$ including the equality
of domains $D(A^\dagger) = D(A)$. A symmetric operator has $D(A) \subseteq D(A^\dagger)$ and is self-adjoint only
when its domain is large enough. Eigenvectors are required to lie in the domain, and the spectrum is defined as in
@def-spectrum. For self-adjoint $A$ the spectrum is real, the spectral theorem and the functional calculus extend
(quoted), and $e^{itA}$ is a unitary group on all of $H$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The derivative on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ is the first example, defined on smooth functions vanishing outside a bounded
set or on the Schwartz space; it is symmetric when multiplied by $-i$, and its self-adjoint version has the largest
possible domain. The example introduces the Sobolev space on which that version lives.

::: {#exm-ub-derivative-domain}
#### $-i\,d/dx$ on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$

$p = -i\,d/dx$ with domain $C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ (smooth, zero outside a bounded set) is symmetric by
integration by parts, the boundary terms vanishing at infinity, and unbounded (@exr-bo-differentiation-unbounded).
It is not self-adjoint on this domain: $D(p^\dagger)$ is the much larger **Sobolev space** $H^1(\mathbb{R}) =
\{f \in L^2 : f' \in L^2\}$ with $f'$ in the sense of distributions (@sec-distributions). Extending $p$ to
$H^1(\mathbb{R})$ makes it self-adjoint, with spectrum $\mathbb{R}$ and no eigenvalues (@exr-ccr-fourier-conjugation).
:::

Multiplication by $x$ on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ is unbounded because the line is infinite, and its natural domain is the
set of functions for which $xf$ is still square-integrable. The second example checks membership for a Gaussian
and for a slowly decaying function, and notes that this operator is self-adjoint without further ado.

::: {#exm-ub-multiplication-domain}
#### The position operator on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$

$(xf)(x) = xf(x)$ with the maximal domain $D(x) = \{f \in L^2(\mathbb{R}) : xf \in L^2(\mathbb{R})\}$ is
self-adjoint (@exr-ub-symmetric-adjoint), unbounded, with spectrum $\mathbb{R}$ and no eigenvalues
(@exm-ev-multiplication-none with $(0, 1)$ replaced by $\mathbb{R}$). The Gaussian $e^{-x^2/2}$ is in the domain;
$f = 1/(1 + |x|)$ is in $L^2$ but not in $D(x)$, since $|xf|^2 \to 1$ at infinity is not integrable. In the Fourier
picture (@sec-fourier-transform), $x$ becomes $i\,d/dk$ and $p$ becomes multiplication by $k$.
:::

The second derivative on periodic functions is the Laplacian of the circle, and its domain question is settled by
the Fourier isomorphism, under which it becomes multiplication by $n^2$ on sequences. The third example describes
this, which is the pattern for all Laplacians on compact spaces.

::: {#exm-ub-laplacian-domain}
#### $-d^2/dx^2$ on the circle

On $L^2(S^1) = L^2(-\pi, \pi)$ with periodic functions, $-d^2/dx^2$ on smooth periodic functions is symmetric and
positive, since $\langle f, -g''\rangle = \int\bar f'g'\,dx$ after one integration by parts without boundary terms.
Under $U : f \mapsto (\langle e_n, f\rangle)_n$ of @exr-un-fourier-plancherel it becomes the multiplication
operator $(a_n) \mapsto (n^2a_n)$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z})$, self-adjoint on the domain $\{a : \sum n^4|a_n|^2 <
\infty\}$, which pulls back to the periodic Sobolev space $H^2(S^1)$ (@exr-ub-unbounded-norm). Its spectrum is
$\{n^2\}$, discrete, with the eigenfunctions $e^{inx}$ as an orthonormal basis.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
In the Fourier picture the domain of the derivative is a decay condition on the coefficients, and whether a given
function belongs to it is decided by a series. The first exercise asks Sage to compute the relevant partial sums for
two functions on the circle, one with a jump and one with a kink.

::: {#exr-ub-unbounded-norm}
#### Domains in the Fourier picture

For $f(x) = x$ and $g(x) = \pi^2 - x^2$ on $(-\pi, \pi)$ extended periodically, compute with Sage the partial sums
$\sum_{|n| \leq N}n^2|\langle e_n, f\rangle|^2$ and $\sum_{|n| \leq N}n^2|\langle e_n, g\rangle|^2$ and
$\sum_{|n| \leq N}n^4|\langle e_n, g\rangle|^2$ for $N = 10, 100, 1000$, and decide which of $f, g$ lie in the
domains of $-i\,d/dx$ and of $-d^2/dx^2$ on the circle.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|\langle e_n, f\rangle|^2 = 2\pi/n^2$, so $\sum n^2|\langle e_n, f\rangle|^2 = \sum 2\pi$ diverges: the
periodised $f$ has a jump at $\pm\pi$ and is not in the domain of the derivative. $|\langle e_n, g\rangle|^2 =
8\pi/n^4$, so $\sum n^2 \cdot 8\pi/n^4$ converges (to $8\pi^3/3$ over both signs of $n$) but $\sum n^4\cdot 8\pi/n^4$
diverges: the periodised $g$ is continuous with a kink at $\pm\pi$, in $H^1$ but not in $H^2$:

{{< sage exr-ub-unbounded-norm >}}
:::

An everywhere-defined symmetric operator is automatically bounded, which is why unbounded symmetric operators must
have restricted domains; and a symmetric operator always sits inside its adjoint. The second exercise asks for
the second statement and for the proof that a bounded symmetric operator is self-adjoint.

::: {#exr-ub-closed-graph}
#### Symmetric operators and their adjoints

Show that for a symmetric operator $D(A) \subseteq D(A^\dagger)$ with $A^\dagger = A$ on $D(A)$, and that a
bounded symmetric operator defined on all of $H$ is self-adjoint. Explain, using @exm-sa-derivative-periodic, why
$-i\,d/dx$ on smooth periodic functions is symmetric but has a strictly larger adjoint domain.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For $v \in D(A)$ the functional $u \mapsto \langle v, Au\rangle = \langle Av, u\rangle$ is bounded by
$\|Av\|\|u\|$, so $v \in D(A^\dagger)$ and $A^\dagger v = Av$ by uniqueness in the Riesz theorem. If $A$ is bounded
on $H$, then $D(A^\dagger) = H = D(A)$, since every $u \mapsto \langle v, Au\rangle$ is bounded, and $A^\dagger = A$
there. For $-i\,d/dx$ on smooth periodic functions, any $v \in H^1(S^1)$ (for example a continuous piecewise linear
periodic function) makes $u \mapsto \langle v, -iu'\rangle = \langle -iv', u\rangle$ bounded, so $v \in
D(A^\dagger)$ without being smooth; the self-adjoint version is the extension to $H^1(S^1)$.
:::

The position operator with its maximal domain is self-adjoint, and the proof is a direct computation of the
adjoint's domain. The last exercise asks for it, which is the simplest instance of showing $D(A^\dagger) = D(A)$.

::: {#exr-ub-symmetric-adjoint}
#### Self-adjointness of the position operator

Let $x$ act on $D(x) = \{f \in L^2(\mathbb{R}) : xf \in L^2(\mathbb{R})\}$. Show that $x$ is symmetric and that
$D(x^\dagger) = D(x)$, so that $x$ is self-adjoint.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Symmetry: $\langle xf, g\rangle = \int\overline{xf}g = \int\bar f(xg) = \langle f, xg\rangle$ since $x$ is real.
If $v \in D(x^\dagger)$, there is $w = x^\dagger v \in L^2$ with $\int\bar v\,xu = \int\bar w\,u$ for all $u \in
D(x)$; taking $u$ supported in a bounded set (where $D(x)$ contains all of $L^2$) gives $xv = w$ on every bounded
set, hence $xv = w \in L^2$ and $v \in D(x)$. Together with $D(x) \subseteq D(x^\dagger)$ (@exr-ub-closed-graph) this
gives equality of domains, and $x^\dagger = x$.
:::
::::

### The canonical commutation relation

Position and momentum on the line are the pair of unbounded self-adjoint operators whose commutator is the
identity, the relation that @exm-comm-position-derivative showed to be impossible for matrices. The definition
below fixes the operators, their common domain and the relation, with $\hbar = 1$.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-canonical-commutation-relation}
#### Canonical commutation relation

On the **Schwartz space** $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}) \subset L^2(\mathbb{R})$ of smooth functions decaying, with all
their derivatives, faster than any power, the **position operator** $(xf)(x) = xf(x)$ and the **momentum operator**
$(pf)(x) = -if'(x)$ (units with $\hbar = 1$) are symmetric, map $\mathcal{S}$ into itself, and satisfy the
**canonical commutation relation** $[x, p] = i$ on $\mathcal{S}$: $(xp - px)f = -ixf' + i(xf)' = if$. Both extend
to self-adjoint operators on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ with spectrum $\mathbb{R}$ and no eigenvalues, and the Fourier
transform $\mathcal{F}$ exchanges them, $\mathcal{F}p\mathcal{F}^{-1}$ is multiplication by $k$. For a unit vector
$\psi$, $\langle x\rangle = \langle\psi, x\psi\rangle$ is the **expectation value** and $(\Delta x)^2 = \langle (x -
\langle x\rangle)^2\rangle$ the **variance**, and the relation implies the **uncertainty inequality** $\Delta x\,
\Delta p \geq \tfrac12$ (@exr-hso-uncertainty).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The relation itself is a one-line computation with the product rule, valid for every differentiable
function. The first example records it and the related commutators with functions of $x$.

::: {#exm-ccr-direct}
#### $[x, p\rbrack f = if$

For $f \in \mathcal{S}$: $(px)f = -i(xf)' = -if - ixf'$ and $(xp)f = -ixf'$, so $[x, p]f = -ixf' + if + ixf' =
if$ (@prp-laplacian-spectra). More generally $[g(x), p] = ig'(x)$ for smooth $g$, by the same product rule, and
$[x, p^2] = 2ip$ by the Leibniz rule of @def-commutator; these are the identities behind Ehrenfest's theorem in
quantum mechanics.
:::

Gaussians are the states for which the uncertainty inequality is an equality, and the variances are computed by
two integrals. The second example computes them for a Gaussian of width $s$, showing that narrow position means
wide momentum.

::: {#exm-ccr-gaussian-uncertainty}
#### Gaussian wave packets

For $\psi_s(x) = (2\pi s^2)^{-1/4}e^{-x^2/4s^2}$, a unit vector with $\langle x\rangle = \langle p\rangle = 0$:
$(\Delta x)^2 = \int x^2|\psi_s|^2dx = s^2$ and $(\Delta p)^2 = \int|\psi_s'|^2dx = 1/(4s^2)$, so $\Delta x\,
\Delta p = \tfrac12$ exactly (@prp-laplacian-spectra): Gaussians saturate the uncertainty inequality, and shrinking
$s$ trades position spread for momentum spread. The Fourier transform of $\psi_s$ is a Gaussian of width $1/(2s)$
in $k$ (@sec-fourier-transform), which is the same statement.
:::

The combinations $a = (x + ip)/\sqrt2$ and $a^\dagger = (x - ip)/\sqrt2$ turn the canonical commutation relation
into $[a, a^\dagger] = 1$, and they generate the eigenfunctions of $x^2 + p^2$ from the Gaussian. The third example
introduces them; the full theory is in @sec-harmonic-oscillator.

::: {#exm-ccr-ladder}
#### Ladder operators

$a = (x + ip)/\sqrt2$ and $a^\dagger = (x - ip)/\sqrt2$ satisfy $[a, a^\dagger] = \tfrac12[x + ip, x - ip] =
\tfrac12(-i[x, p] + i[p, x]) = -i\cdot i = 1$, and $\tfrac12(x^2 + p^2) = a^\dagger a + \tfrac12$. The Gaussian
$\psi_0 = \pi^{-1/4}e^{-x^2/2}$ satisfies $a\psi_0 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(x\psi_0 + \psi_0') = 0$, and $\psi_n \propto
(a^\dagger)^n\psi_0$ are eigenfunctions of $\tfrac12(x^2 + p^2)$ with eigenvalues $n + \tfrac12$
(@exr-ccr-sage): the Hermite functions, an orthonormal basis of $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ (@sec-sturm-liouville). The
truncated matrices of @exr-boc-heisenberg-trace are these operators in the basis $\psi_n$, cut off at $n = N - 1$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The commutation relation, the annihilation of the Gaussian and the eigenvalue equations for the first Hermite
functions are symbolic computations that Sage performs exactly. The first exercise runs them.

::: {#exr-ccr-sage}
#### Ladder operators on functions

With Sage, verify $[x, p]f = if$ for a symbolic $f$, $a\psi_0 = 0$ for $\psi_0 = \pi^{-1/4}e^{-x^2/2}$, and
$\tfrac12(x^2 + p^2)\psi_n = (n + \tfrac12)\psi_n$ for $\psi_n = (a^\dagger)^n\psi_0/\sqrt{n!}$, $n = 0, 1, 2, 3$;
check that $\psi_0, \dots, \psi_3$ are orthonormal in $L^2(\mathbb{R})$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\psi_1 = \sqrt2\,x\psi_0$, $\psi_2 = (2x^2 - 1)\psi_0/\sqrt2$, $\psi_3 = (2x^3 - 3x)\psi_0/\sqrt3$, the Hermite
polynomials times the Gaussian; the eigenvalue equations and the Gram matrix are exact:

{{< sage exr-ccr-sage >}}
:::

The Fourier transform turns $p$ into multiplication by $k$, which identifies its spectrum, and the plane waves are
approximate eigenvectors made square-integrable by a Gaussian envelope. The second exercise asks for both.

::: {#exr-ccr-fourier-conjugation}
#### The spectrum of the momentum operator

Using $\widehat{f'}(k) = ik\hat f(k)$ (@sec-fourier-transform), show that $\mathcal{F}p\mathcal{F}^{-1}$ is
multiplication by $k$ on $L^2(\mathbb{R}, dk)$, so $\sigma(p) = \mathbb{R}$ with no eigenvalues. Then show
directly that $\psi_L(x) = e^{ikx}e^{-x^2/2L^2}$ satisfies $\|(p - k)\psi_L\|/\|\psi_L\| = 1/(L\sqrt2)$, so $k$ is
an approximate eigenvalue.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\widehat{pf} = -i\cdot ik\hat f = k\hat f$, so under the unitary $\mathcal{F}$ the operator $p$ becomes $M_k$,
whose spectrum is the range $\mathbb{R}$ of $k$ and which has no eigenvalues (@exm-sp-multiplication); the
"eigenfunctions" $e^{ikx}$ are not in $L^2$ (@exm-l2-real-line). Directly, $(p - k)\psi_L = -i\psi_L' - k\psi_L =
(ix/L^2)\psi_L$, so $\|(p - k)\psi_L\|^2 = L^{-4}\int x^2e^{-x^2/L^2}dx = L^{-4}\cdot\tfrac{L^3\sqrt\pi}{2}$ and
$\|\psi_L\|^2 = L\sqrt\pi$, whose ratio is $1/(2L^2)$; the ratio of norms is $1/(L\sqrt2) \to 0$ as $L \to
\infty$.
:::

In the basis of Hermite functions the operators $x$, $p$ and $\tfrac12(x^2 + p^2)$ are infinite matrices, and their
truncations show how the spectrum $n + \tfrac12$ emerges. The last exercise builds them in Sage and compares with
the exact values.

::: {#exr-ccr-truncated-ladder}
#### The oscillator in the truncated ladder basis

With the $N \times N$ truncation $a$ of @exr-boc-heisenberg-trace for $N = 6$, form $x = (a + a^\dagger)/\sqrt2$,
$p = i(a^\dagger - a)/\sqrt2$ and $H = \tfrac12(x^2 + p^2)$ in Sage; compute the eigenvalues of $H$, compare with
$n + \tfrac12$, and check that $e^{i\theta a^\dagger a}\,a\,e^{-i\theta a^\dagger a} = e^{-i\theta}a$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$H = a^\dagger a + \tfrac12[a, a^\dagger]$ is diagonal with entries $n + \tfrac12$ for $n < N - 1$ and $(N - 1) +
\tfrac12(1 - N) = (N - 1)/2$ in the last slot, the truncation artefact; the conjugation identity holds exactly since
$a^\dagger a$ is diagonal with integer entries and $a$ lowers the index by one:

{{< sage exr-ccr-truncated-ladder >}}
:::
::::

### Self-adjoint extensions

A symmetric operator on a small domain can often be enlarged to a self-adjoint operator in several ways, each with
its own spectrum; for differential operators on an interval these ways are boundary conditions. The definition
below introduces the notion and quotes von Neumann's criterion for existence and uniqueness.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-self-adjoint-extension}
#### Self-adjoint extension

A **self-adjoint extension** of a symmetric operator $A$ is a self-adjoint operator $B$ with $D(B) \supseteq D(A)$
and $B = A$ on $D(A)$. A symmetric operator may have none, exactly one or infinitely many; it is **essentially
self-adjoint** if its closure is self-adjoint, equivalently if the extension is unique. Von Neumann's criterion
(quoted): with the **deficiency indices** $n_\pm = \dim\ker(A^\dagger \mp i)$, self-adjoint extensions exist iff
$n_+ = n_-$, the extension is unique iff $n_+ = n_- = 0$, and for $n_+ = n_- = n > 0$ the extensions are
parametrised by the unitary group $U(n)$. For a differential operator on an interval the extensions are the
self-adjoint **boundary conditions**, and different conditions give different spectra.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The momentum operator on a bounded interval has a circle's worth of self-adjoint extensions, one for each phase
relating the values at the two ends. The first example describes them with their eigenfunctions, and the periodic
one is the operator of @exm-sa-derivative-periodic.

::: {#exm-sae-periodic}
#### Twisted periodic conditions

$-i\,d/dx$ on $C_c^\infty(0, 2\pi)$ has $n_+ = n_- = 1$: $\ker(A^\dagger \mp i)$ is spanned by $e^{\pm x}$. Its
self-adjoint extensions are indexed by $\alpha \in [0, 2\pi)$, with domain $\{f \in H^1(0, 2\pi) : f(2\pi) =
e^{i\alpha}f(0)\}$; the boundary term $-i[\bar fg]_0^{2\pi}$ vanishes on it (@exr-sae-boundary-form). The
eigenfunctions are $e^{i(n + \alpha/2\pi)x}$ with eigenvalues $n + \alpha/2\pi$, $n \in \mathbb{Z}$
(@exr-sae-spectrum-twisted): the spectrum is the integers shifted by $\alpha/2\pi$, and $\alpha = 0$ is the periodic
case.
:::

On a half-line the two deficiency indices differ, so the momentum operator has no self-adjoint extension at all,
while the position operator is unproblematic. The second example records this, the standard illustration that
not every symmetric operator is an observable.

::: {#exm-sae-half-line}
#### No momentum on the half-line

$-i\,d/dx$ on $C_c^\infty(0, \infty) \subset L^2(0, \infty)$ is symmetric, and $\ker(A^\dagger - i)$ is spanned by
$e^{-x}$ (square-integrable) while $\ker(A^\dagger + i)$ would be spanned by $e^{x}$, which is not: $n_+ = 1$, $n_-
= 0$, and no self-adjoint extension exists. The position operator on $L^2(0, \infty)$, by contrast, is self-adjoint
on its maximal domain exactly as in @exr-ub-symmetric-adjoint; and $-d^2/dx^2$ on the half-line has a
one-parameter family of extensions, the conditions $f'(0) = \kappa f(0)$.
:::

The Laplacian on an interval has a four-parameter family of extensions, and the familiar boundary conditions are
special members whose spectra differ already in the lowest eigenvalue. The third example lists Dirichlet, Neumann
and periodic conditions with their spectra.

::: {#exm-sae-laplacian-interval}
#### Boundary conditions for $-d^2/dx^2$ on $(0, \pi)$

$-d^2/dx^2$ on $C_c^\infty(0, \pi)$ has $n_+ = n_- = 2$ ($\ker(A^\dagger \mp i)$ is spanned by $e^{\pm\sqrt{\mp
i}\,x}$, two solutions each), so the extensions form a four-parameter family. **Dirichlet** $f(0) = f(\pi) = 0$:
eigenfunctions $\sin nx$, eigenvalues $n^2$, $n \geq 1$. **Neumann** $f'(0) = f'(\pi) = 0$: $\cos nx$, eigenvalues
$n^2$, $n \geq 0$, including $0$. **Periodic** $f(0) = f(\pi)$, $f'(0) = f'(\pi)$: $e^{2inx}$, eigenvalues $4n^2$
with multiplicity $2$ for $n \neq 0$. The same symbol $-d^2/dx^2$ thus names three different self-adjoint operators
(@exr-sae-dirichlet-neumann, @sec-sturm-liouville).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The twisted eigenfunctions, their eigenvalues and their orthogonality are exact computations, as is the vanishing
of the boundary term on the twisted domain. The first exercise asks Sage for all of them.

::: {#exr-sae-spectrum-twisted}
#### The twisted spectrum in Sage

For $\alpha \in [0, 2\pi)$ and $f_n(x) = e^{i(n + \alpha/2\pi)x}$, check with Sage that $-if_n' = (n +
\alpha/2\pi)f_n$, that $f_n(2\pi) = e^{i\alpha}f_n(0)$, that $\langle f_m, f_n\rangle = 2\pi\delta_{mn}$ on $(0,
2\pi)$, and that for $\alpha = \pi$ the spectrum is the half-integers.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The orthogonality integral is $\int_0^{2\pi}e^{i(n - m)x}dx$, independent of $\alpha$; for $\alpha = \pi$ the
eigenvalues are $n + \tfrac12$, the antiperiodic spectrum:

{{< sage exr-sae-spectrum-twisted >}}
:::

Dirichlet, Neumann and Robin conditions all make $-d^2/dx^2$ symmetric, and the proof is to check that the boundary
terms of the two integrations by parts cancel. The second exercise asks for this and for the eigenvalues under
Robin conditions in a special case.

::: {#exr-sae-dirichlet-neumann}
#### Symmetric boundary conditions

Show that $-d^2/dx^2$ is symmetric on smooth functions on $[0, \pi]$ satisfying Dirichlet, Neumann or **Robin**
conditions $f'(0) = \kappa f(0)$, $f'(\pi) = -\kappa f(\pi)$ with real $\kappa$, and that for Dirichlet conditions
the eigenvalues are exactly $n^2$, $n \geq 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Two integrations by parts give $\langle -f'', g\rangle - \langle f, -g''\rangle = [-\bar f'g + \bar fg']_0^\pi$.
Under Dirichlet conditions both $f, g$ vanish at the ends; under Neumann both derivatives vanish; under Robin
conditions $-\bar f'g + \bar fg' = -\kappa\bar fg + \kappa\bar fg = 0$ at $0$ and similarly at $\pi$ (real
$\kappa$ is essential). For Dirichlet eigenfunctions, $-f'' = \lambda f$ has solutions $A\sin\sqrt\lambda x +
B\cos\sqrt\lambda x$; $f(0) = 0$ forces $B = 0$ and $f(\pi) = 0$ forces $\sin\sqrt\lambda\pi = 0$, so $\lambda =
n^2$ ($\lambda \leq 0$ gives only the zero solution by positivity of the operator).
:::

The boundary form $\langle Af, g\rangle - \langle f, Ag\rangle$ is the obstruction to self-adjointness, and a
self-adjoint extension is a maximal domain on which it vanishes. The last exercise computes it for the momentum
operator on an interval and shows why the phase condition is the right one.

::: {#exr-sae-boundary-form}
#### The boundary form of $-i\,d/dx$

For $f, g \in H^1(0, 2\pi)$ compute $\langle -if', g\rangle - \langle f, -ig'\rangle$. Show that it vanishes for all
$f, g$ in $D_\alpha = \{f(2\pi) = e^{i\alpha}f(0)\}$, that it does not vanish for all $f, g$ in $D = \{f(0) =
0\}$ or in $\{f(0) = 2f(2\pi)\}$, and interpret.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Integration by parts gives $\langle -if', g\rangle - \langle f, -ig'\rangle = i\int\bar f'g + i\int\bar fg' =
i[\bar fg]_0^{2\pi} = i(\overline{f(2\pi)}g(2\pi) - \overline{f(0)}g(0))$. On $D_\alpha$ this is $i(e^{-i\alpha}
e^{i\alpha} - 1)\overline{f(0)}g(0) = 0$. On $\{f(0) = 0\}$ it is $i\overline{f(2\pi)}g(2\pi)$, non-zero for
functions not vanishing at $2\pi$: the condition is too weak (the adjoint has the smaller domain $\{f(0) = f(2\pi)
= 0\}$, and the operator is symmetric but not self-adjoint). On $\{f(0) = 2f(2\pi)\}$ it is $i(1 - 4)\overline{
f(2\pi)}g(2\pi) \neq 0$: the condition is not even symmetric, since $|2| \neq 1$. Only unimodular phases work,
which is the $U(1)$ of von Neumann's criterion.
:::
::::

### The Laplacian on compact spaces

The Laplacian of a curved space is the divergence of the gradient, built from the metric (@def-metric), and on a
compact space without boundary it is a symmetric operator with no boundary conditions to choose. The figure shows
its eigenfunctions on the circle and the spectra on the circle, the sphere and the torus; the definition below
writes the operator in coordinates.

![Left: the eigenfunctions $\cos n\theta$, $\sin n\theta$ of the Laplacian on the circle for $n = 1, 2, 3$. The
three bar charts show the spectra of $-\Delta$ on the unit circle (eigenvalues $n^2$, multiplicity $2$ for $n \geq
1$), on the unit sphere (eigenvalues $l(l + 1)$, multiplicity $2l + 1$) and on the square torus (eigenvalues
$m^2 + n^2$, multiplicity the number of representations as a sum of two squares), bar height being the
multiplicity. Generated by `figures/laplacian_spectra.sage`.](figures/laplacian_spectra.svg){#fig-laplacian-spectra
width=100%}

{{< interactive laplacian_spectra 460 >}}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-laplace-beltrami}
#### Laplace-Beltrami operator

On a Riemannian manifold with metric $g_{ij}$ in coordinates $y^i$ (@sec-metrics), the **Laplace-Beltrami
operator** on functions is $\Delta f = \frac{1}{\sqrt g}\partial_i\left(\sqrt g\,g^{ij}\partial_jf\right)$, with
$g = \det(g_{ij})$ and $g^{ij}$ the inverse metric; it is the divergence of the gradient and reduces to
$\sum_i\partial_i^2$ in flat coordinates. On a compact manifold $M$ without boundary, with $L^2(M)$ defined by the
volume element $\sqrt g\,d^ny$, **Green's identity** $\langle f, -\Delta h\rangle = \int_Mg^{ij}\,\overline{
\partial_if}\,\partial_jh\,\sqrt g\,d^ny$ shows that $-\Delta$ is symmetric and positive on smooth functions, with
$\Delta f = 0$ only for constants when $M$ is connected. Scaling the metric by $R^2$ scales $\Delta$ by $R^{-2}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
On a circle of radius $R$ the Laplacian is the second derivative in the angle, divided by $R^2$, and the
exponentials are its eigenfunctions. The first example records the spectrum with its multiplicities, which is the
Fourier series of @sec-fourier-series read as spectral theory.

::: {#exm-lb-circle}
#### The circle

On $S^1_R$ with $ds^2 = R^2d\theta^2$, $\Delta = R^{-2}\partial_\theta^2$ and $-\Delta e^{in\theta} = (n^2/R^2)
e^{in\theta}$: the eigenvalues are $n^2/R^2$, $n \geq 0$, with multiplicity $2$ for $n \geq 1$ (spanned by
$e^{\pm in\theta}$, or by $\cos n\theta$, $\sin n\theta$ as in @fig-laplacian-spectra) and $1$ for $n = 0$. The
eigenfunctions $e^{in\theta}/\sqrt{2\pi R}$ are an orthonormal basis of $L^2(S^1_R)$ (@exr-lb-circle-eigen).
:::

On the round sphere the Laplacian in spherical coordinates is the angular part of the flat Laplacian of
$\mathbb{R}^3$, and the spherical harmonics of @sec-harmonic-analysis are its eigenfunctions. The second example
states the spectrum, with multiplicities equal to the dimensions of the $SO(3)$ representations of
@sec-weights-su2.

::: {#exm-lb-sphere}
#### The sphere

On $S^2_R$ with $ds^2 = R^2(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2)$, $\sqrt g = R^2\sin\theta$ and $\Delta =
\frac{1}{R^2}\left[\frac{1}{\sin\theta}\partial_\theta(\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta) + \frac{1}{\sin^2\theta}
\partial_\varphi^2\right]$. The spherical harmonics satisfy $-\Delta Y_{lm} = \frac{l(l + 1)}{R^2}Y_{lm}$, $l \geq
0$, $-l \leq m \leq l$ (@prp-laplacian-spectra, @exr-lb-sphere-ylm): the eigenvalue $l(l + 1)/R^2$ has multiplicity
$2l + 1$, the dimension of the spin-$l$ representation, and the $Y_{lm}$ are an orthonormal basis of $L^2(S^2_R)$
(@sec-harmonic-analysis).
:::

On a torus the Laplacian is flat and the eigenfunctions are products of exponentials, but the multiplicities are
irregular because they count the ways an integer is a sum of two squares. The third example gives the spectrum for
a rectangular torus and the arithmetic of the square case.

::: {#exm-lb-torus}
#### The torus

On $T^2 = S^1_{R_1} \times S^1_{R_2}$ with $ds^2 = R_1^2d\theta^2 + R_2^2d\varphi^2$, $\Delta = R_1^{-2}
\partial_\theta^2 + R_2^{-2}\partial_\varphi^2$ and $-\Delta e^{i(m\theta + n\varphi)} = (m^2/R_1^2 + n^2/R_2^2)
e^{i(m\theta + n\varphi)}$, $m, n \in \mathbb{Z}$. For $R_1 = R_2 = 1$ the eigenvalue $N$ has multiplicity $r_2(N)$,
the number of pairs $(m, n)$ with $m^2 + n^2 = N$: $r_2(1) = 4$, $r_2(2) = 4$, $r_2(3) = 0$, $r_2(5) = 8$, $r_2(25) =
12$ (@exr-lb-torus-multiplicity); for incommensurable $R_1^2/R_2^2$ the multiplicities are only $1$, $2$ or $4$
(@exr-ls-torus-rectangular).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
That the exponentials are the only eigenfunctions on the circle, and that no negative eigenvalues occur, follows
from solving the eigenvalue equation with periodicity. The first exercise asks for this and for the positivity
argument from Green's identity.

::: {#exr-lb-circle-eigen}
#### The complete spectrum of the circle

Show that every smooth $2\pi$-periodic solution of $-f'' = \lambda f$ has $\lambda = n^2$ for some integer $n \geq
0$, with $f$ in the span of $e^{\pm in\theta}$, and use Green's identity to show $\lambda \geq 0$ directly.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By Green's identity $\lambda\|f\|^2 = \langle f, -f''\rangle = \|f'\|^2 \geq 0$, so $\lambda \geq 0$; $\lambda = 0$
forces $f' = 0$, constant $f$. For $\lambda = \mu^2 > 0$ the solutions of $f'' = -\mu^2f$ are $Ae^{i\mu\theta} +
Be^{-i\mu\theta}$ (@sec-odes), periodic iff $e^{2\pi i\mu} = 1$, that is $\mu = n \in \mathbb{Z}_{> 0}$; so the
eigenvalues are $n^2$ with the two-dimensional eigenspaces stated. Completeness of the eigenfunctions is the
completeness of the Fourier system (@sec-fourier-series).
:::

The eigenvalue equation for the spherical harmonics is a differential identity that Sage verifies symbolically,
and their orthonormality is an integral over the sphere. The second exercise runs both checks through the
spherical Laplacian.

::: {#exr-lb-sphere-ylm}
#### Spherical harmonics as eigenfunctions

With Sage, verify $-\Delta Y_{lm} = l(l + 1)Y_{lm}$ on the unit sphere for all $l \leq 3$ using the explicit
Laplacian in spherical coordinates, check orthonormality $\langle Y_{lm}, Y_{l'm'}\rangle = \delta_{ll'}
\delta_{mm'}$ for $l, l' \leq 2$, and count the eigenfunctions for each eigenvalue.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Sage's `spherical_harmonic(l, m, theta, phi)` gives the $Y_{lm}$; the Laplacian annihilates $Y_{00}$ and gives
$-2, -6, -12$ times $Y_{lm}$ for $l = 1, 2, 3$, with $1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16$ eigenfunctions up to $l = 3$:

{{< sage exr-lb-sphere-ylm >}}
:::

The multiplicities on the square torus are an arithmetic function, and Sage counts them by listing lattice points
on circles. The last exercise asks for the counts up to $N = 30$ and for the pattern behind the zeros.

::: {#exr-lb-torus-multiplicity}
#### Counting lattice points

With Sage, compute the multiplicity $r_2(N)$ of each eigenvalue $N \leq 30$ of $-\Delta$ on the square torus, list the
eigenvalues with multiplicity $8$ and $12$, and explain why $N = 3, 6, 7, 11$ do not occur.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$r_2(N) = 8$ for $N = 5, 10, 13, 17, 20, 26, 29$ and $r_2(25) = 12$ ($25 = 25 + 0 = 9 + 16$ in two essentially
different ways); an integer is a sum of two squares iff every prime $\equiv 3 \pmod 4$ divides it to an even power,
which excludes $3, 6, 7, 11$:

{{< sage exr-lb-torus-multiplicity >}}
:::
::::

### Discreteness of the spectrum

The three examples share a feature that holds on every compact space: the eigenvalues form a sequence tending to
infinity with finite multiplicities, and the eigenfunctions form an orthonormal basis. The theorem below, quoted
without proof, states this; the mechanism is that the inverse of $-\Delta$ is a compact operator, so that
@thm-spectral-theorem-compact applies as in @exm-stc-inverse-laplacian.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-laplacian-discrete-spectrum}
#### Discrete spectrum of the Laplacian on a compact manifold

Let $M$ be a compact connected Riemannian manifold without boundary. The operator $-\Delta$, extended from smooth
functions to its natural domain in $L^2(M)$, is self-adjoint and non-negative, and its spectrum is **discrete**: the
eigenvalues form a sequence $0 = \lambda_0 < \lambda_1 \leq \lambda_2 \leq \dots \to \infty$, each of finite
multiplicity, with $\lambda_0 = 0$ belonging to the constants. The eigenfunctions $\varphi_k$ can be chosen to form
an orthonormal basis of $L^2(M)$, so that every $f \in L^2(M)$ has the **mode expansion** $f = \sum_k\langle
\varphi_k, f\rangle\varphi_k$, and **Weyl's law** gives the growth: the number $N(\lambda)$ of eigenvalues
$\leq \lambda$ satisfies $N(\lambda) \sim \frac{\operatorname{Vol}(M)}{(4\pi)^{d/2}\Gamma(d/2 + 1)}\lambda^{d/2}$
for $d = \dim M$. The theorem is quoted; its proof applies @thm-spectral-theorem-compact to the Green's operator of
$-\Delta$ on the complement of the constants, which is compact by Rellich's theorem.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
On the circle the theorem is the theory of Fourier series, and Weyl's law counts the integers $n$ with $n^2/R^2 \leq
\lambda$. The first example checks the constant in Weyl's law in this case.

::: {#exm-ds-circle-fourier}
#### Weyl's law on the circle

For $S^1_R$, $N(\lambda) = \#\{n \in \mathbb{Z} : n^2 \leq R^2\lambda\} = 2\lfloor R\sqrt\lambda\rfloor + 1 \sim
2R\sqrt\lambda$. Weyl's law with $d = 1$, $\operatorname{Vol} = 2\pi R$, $\Gamma(3/2) = \sqrt\pi/2$ gives
$\frac{2\pi R}{\sqrt{4\pi}\cdot\sqrt\pi/2}\lambda^{1/2} = 2R\sqrt\lambda$, in agreement. The mode expansion is the
Fourier series, and the finite multiplicities are the pairs $\pm n$.
:::

On the sphere the eigenvalues $l(l + 1)$ have multiplicities $2l + 1$, so counting them is a sum of odd numbers, a
perfect square. The second example verifies Weyl's law for the sphere and records the mode expansion in spherical
harmonics.

::: {#exm-ds-sphere-harmonics}
#### Weyl's law on the sphere

For the unit sphere, $N(\lambda) = \sum_{l(l + 1) \leq \lambda}(2l + 1) = (L + 1)^2$ with $L$ the largest $l$
allowed, and $L(L + 1) \leq \lambda$ gives $(L + 1)^2 \sim \lambda$. Weyl's law with $d = 2$, $\operatorname{Vol} =
4\pi$, $\Gamma(2) = 1$ gives $\frac{4\pi}{4\pi}\lambda = \lambda$. The mode expansion $f(\theta, \varphi) =
\sum_{l, m}\langle Y_{lm}, f\rangle Y_{lm}$ is the expansion in spherical harmonics of @sec-harmonic-analysis, and
on the torus it is the double Fourier series (@exr-ds-weyl-counting).
:::

The practical content of the theorem is that a function of time and of a point on a compact space can be expanded
in the modes, turning a partial differential equation into countably many ordinary ones with discrete frequencies.
The third example carries this out for the wave equation on $\mathbb{R} \times M$.

::: {#exm-ds-field-decomposition}
#### Fields on a compact space decompose into modes

Let $\phi(t, y)$ on $\mathbb{R} \times M$ satisfy the wave equation $\partial_t^2\phi = \Delta_M\phi$
(@sec-pdes). Expanding $\phi(t, \cdot) = \sum_kc_k(t)\varphi_k$ in the eigenbasis gives $\ddot c_k = -\lambda_kc_k$,
so $c_k(t) = a_ke^{i\sqrt{\lambda_k}t} + b_ke^{-i\sqrt{\lambda_k}t}$: the field is a sum of independent oscillators
with the discrete frequencies $\omega_k = \sqrt{\lambda_k}$, one for each eigenfunction (counted with
multiplicity). On the circle $\omega_n = |n|/R$, on the sphere $\omega_l = \sqrt{l(l + 1)}/R$; the zero mode $k =
0$ has $\ddot c_0 = 0$. Compactness of $M$ is what makes the frequencies discrete, and the heat equation separates
the same way with $c_k(t) = c_k(0)e^{-\lambda_kt}$ (@exr-ds-heat-decay).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Weyl's law on the torus counts lattice points in a disc, and the error term is the Gauss circle problem. The first
exercise asks Sage for the counts and their comparison with the leading term.

::: {#exr-ds-weyl-counting}
#### Lattice points in a disc

For the square torus, compute $N(\lambda) = \#\{(m, n) : m^2 + n^2 \leq \lambda\}$ with Sage for $\lambda = 10^2,
10^3, 10^4$, compare with Weyl's prediction $\pi\lambda$, and check that the relative error decreases.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Weyl's law with $d = 2$ and $\operatorname{Vol}(T^2) = 4\pi^2$ gives $N(\lambda) \sim \pi\lambda$, the area of the
disc of radius $\sqrt\lambda$; the counts are $317, 3149, 31417$ against $314.2, 3141.6, 31415.9$, with relative
errors $0.9\%$, $0.2\%$, $0.003\%$:

{{< sage exr-ds-weyl-counting >}}
:::

Separation of variables in the eigenbasis is the general method, and energy conservation for the wave equation
follows from it mode by mode. The second exercise asks for the derivation and for the conserved energy.

::: {#exr-ds-mode-equation}
#### Separation in the eigenbasis

Derive $\ddot c_k = -\lambda_kc_k$ from $\partial_t^2\phi = \Delta_M\phi$ and the mode expansion, justify the
termwise differentiation formally, and show that $E = \sum_k(|\dot c_k|^2 + \lambda_k|c_k|^2)$ is conserved and
equals $\int_M(|\partial_t\phi|^2 + g^{ij}\overline{\partial_i\phi}\partial_j\phi)\sqrt g\,d^ny$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$c_k(t) = \langle\varphi_k, \phi(t, \cdot)\rangle$, so $\ddot c_k = \langle\varphi_k, \partial_t^2\phi\rangle =
\langle\varphi_k, \Delta\phi\rangle = \langle\Delta\varphi_k, \phi\rangle = -\lambda_kc_k$ by symmetry of
$\Delta$ (differentiation under the inner product is justified for smooth $\phi$ by @thm-differentiation-under-integral).
Then $\tfrac{d}{dt}(|\dot c_k|^2 + \lambda_k|c_k|^2) = 2\operatorname{Re}(\bar{\dot c}_k\ddot c_k + \lambda_k\bar
c_k\dot c_k) = 0$. By Parseval, $\sum|\dot c_k|^2 = \|\partial_t\phi\|^2$ and $\sum\lambda_k|c_k|^2 = \langle\phi,
-\Delta\phi\rangle = \int g^{ij}\overline{\partial_i\phi}\partial_j\phi\sqrt g$ by Green's identity.
:::

For the heat equation the modes decay exponentially at rates given by the eigenvalues, so the solution converges
to its mean value, and the first non-zero eigenvalue sets the rate. The last exercise asks for this and for the
rate on the three model spaces.

::: {#exr-ds-heat-decay}
#### Heat flow on a compact space

Show that the solution of $\partial_tu = \Delta u$ on $M$ with $u(0, \cdot) = f$ is $u(t) = \sum_ke^{-\lambda_kt}
\langle\varphi_k, f\rangle\varphi_k$, that $u(t) \to \bar f = \operatorname{Vol}(M)^{-1}\int_Mf$ in $L^2$ as $t \to
\infty$ with $\|u(t) - \bar f\| \leq e^{-\lambda_1t}\|f - \bar f\|$, and give $\lambda_1$ for $S^1_R$, $S^2_R$ and
the square torus of side $2\pi R$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Writing $u = \sum c_k(t)\varphi_k$, the equation gives $\dot c_k = -\lambda_kc_k$, so $c_k(t) = e^{-\lambda_kt}c_k(0)$
with $c_k(0) = \langle\varphi_k, f\rangle$. The $k = 0$ term is $\langle\varphi_0, f\rangle\varphi_0 = \bar f$ with
$\varphi_0 = \operatorname{Vol}^{-1/2}$, and $\|u(t) - \bar f\|^2 = \sum_{k \geq 1}e^{-2\lambda_kt}|c_k(0)|^2
\leq e^{-2\lambda_1t}\|f - \bar f\|^2$. $\lambda_1 = 1/R^2$ on the circle, $2/R^2$ on the sphere ($l = 1$) and
$1/R^2$ on the torus ($(m, n) = (\pm1, 0), (0, \pm1)$, multiplicity $4$).
:::
::::

### Worked computations

The eigenvalue equations on the circle, the sphere and the torus, the multiplicities, the canonical commutation
relation on a general function, the Gaussian uncertainty product and Weyl's law on the torus are all explicit
computations with the Laplace-Beltrami operator. The proposition records them.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-laplacian-spectra}
#### Spectra of the Laplacian on the circle, the sphere and the torus

With the Laplace-Beltrami operator: on $S^1_R$, $-\Delta e^{in\theta} = (n^2/R^2)e^{in\theta}$
for $n \leq 4$; on $S^2_R$, $-\Delta Y_{lm} = (l(l + 1)/R^2)Y_{lm}$ for all $l \leq 3$, the $Y_{lm}$ with $l \leq 2$
are orthonormal, and the multiplicities are $2l + 1$; on $T^2$ with radii $R_1, R_2$, $-\Delta e^{i(m\theta +
n\varphi)} = (m^2/R_1^2 + n^2/R_2^2)e^{i(m\theta + n\varphi)}$, and on the square torus the multiplicities of the
eigenvalues $N \leq 30$ are the lattice-point counts $r_2(N)$ with $r_2(25) = 12$, while $N(10^4) = 31417$ is within
$0.01\%$ of $\pi\cdot10^4$. Moreover $[x, p]f = if$ for a symbolic $f$ and the Gaussian $\psi_s$ has $(\Delta x)^2
(\Delta p)^2 = \tfrac14$.
:::

**Sage.** Exact computation (`figures/laplacian_spectra.sage`, SageManifolds `laplacian`, symbolic

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The three bar charts of the figure are three growth patterns for the same kind of spectrum: quadratic eigenvalues
with constant multiplicity, quadratic eigenvalues with linearly growing multiplicity, and all sums of two squares
with arithmetic multiplicities. The first example reads them against Weyl's law.

::: {#exm-ls-figure}
#### Reading the spectra

On the circle the eigenvalues $n^2$ thin out ($N(\lambda) \sim 2\sqrt\lambda$) but each has multiplicity $2$; on
the sphere $l(l + 1)$ also thins out, but the multiplicity $2l + 1$ grows so that $N(\lambda) \sim \lambda$; on
the torus every sum of two squares occurs, with $N(\lambda) \sim \pi\lambda$. In two dimensions $N(\lambda)$ grows
linearly in both cases, with slope $\operatorname{Vol}/4\pi$: $1$ for the unit sphere, $\pi$ for the square
torus of area $4\pi^2$, exactly as Weyl's law predicts.
:::

All eigenvalues scale as $1/R^2$ with the size of the space, so a small compact space has a large gap between the
zero mode and the first excited mode. The second example records this scaling and the gaps, which is the
quantitative form of "compactness makes frequencies discrete".

::: {#exm-ls-radius-scaling}
#### Scaling with the radius

Since $\Delta_R = R^{-2}\Delta_1$, the spectrum of $-\Delta$ on $S^1_R$ is $\{n^2/R^2\}$, on $S^2_R$ it is
$\{l(l + 1)/R^2\}$ and on the torus $\{m^2/R_1^2 + n^2/R_2^2\}$ (@exr-ls-radius-sage): the spectral gap
$\lambda_1$ is $1/R^2$, $2/R^2$ and $\min(R_1, R_2)^{-2}$ respectively, and the frequencies $\omega_k =
\sqrt{\lambda_k}$ of @exm-ds-field-decomposition scale as $1/R$. The zero mode is the only one that survives as
$R \to 0$ at fixed frequency, while all others become arbitrarily stiff.
:::

The multiplicities on the circle and the sphere are the dimensions of the irreducible representations of their
isometry groups, because the Laplacian commutes with isometries and so acts on each irreducible piece by a scalar.
The third example states this connection to @sec-representations-schur and contrasts the torus.

::: {#exm-ls-multiplicity-count}
#### Multiplicities as dimensions of representations

The isometries of $S^2$ form $SO(3)$ and commute with $\Delta$, so each eigenspace is a representation of $SO(3)$;
the eigenspace of $l(l + 1)$ is the irreducible spin-$l$ representation of dimension $2l + 1$ (@sec-weights-su2,
@sec-harmonic-analysis). On the circle the isometry group $SO(2)$ has one-dimensional irreducibles $e^{\pm
in\theta}$, and the multiplicity $2$ comes from the reflection $\theta \mapsto -\theta$ pairing $n$ with $-n$. On
the torus the group $U(1)^2$ is abelian, all irreducibles are one-dimensional, and the multiplicities $r_2(N)$ are
accidental coincidences of eigenvalues rather than dimensions of irreducibles.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
SageManifolds builds the Laplace-Beltrami operator from a metric, and with a symbolic radius the scaling of the
eigenvalues is checked directly. The first exercise asks for the sphere and the torus with general radii.

::: {#exr-ls-radius-sage}
#### Laplacians with a symbolic radius

Using SageManifolds, define the metrics of $S^2_R$ and of $T^2$ with radii $R_1, R_2$, and check $-\Delta Y_{lm} =
(l(l + 1)/R^2)Y_{lm}$ for $l \leq 2$ and $-\Delta e^{i(m\theta + n\varphi)} = (m^2/R_1^2 + n^2/R_2^2)e^{i(m\theta +
n\varphi)}$ for symbolic radii.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The metric components are $R^2$ and $R^2\sin^2\theta$ on the sphere and $R_1^2$, $R_2^2$ on the torus; `laplacian()`
returns the operator of @def-laplace-beltrami and the eigenvalue equations hold as symbolic identities in $R, R_1,
R_2$:

{{< sage exr-ls-radius-sage >}}
:::

The three-sphere is a compact group, $SU(2)$, and its Laplacian spectrum follows from representation theory: the
eigenvalues are $k(k + 2)$ with multiplicity $(k + 1)^2$. The second exercise asks for the derivation from the
Peter-Weyl theorem in outline and for the check of Weyl's law.

::: {#exr-ls-s3-spectrum}
#### The spectrum of $S^3$

Granting that $L^2(SU(2))$ decomposes under left and right translations into $\bigoplus_j V_j \otimes V_j^*$ with
$\dim V_j = 2j + 1$ (Peter-Weyl, @sec-harmonic-analysis) and that $-\Delta$ acts on the $j$-th summand as the
Casimir $4j(j + 1)$ for the round unit metric, show that the eigenvalues of $-\Delta$ on $S^3 = SU(2)$ are $k(k +
2)$, $k = 2j = 0, 1, 2, \dots$, with multiplicity $(k + 1)^2$, and check Weyl's law $N(\lambda) \sim
\lambda^{3/2}/3$ against $\operatorname{Vol}(S^3) = 2\pi^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $k = 2j$, $4j(j + 1) = k(k + 2)$ and $\dim(V_j \otimes V_j^*) = (2j + 1)^2 = (k + 1)^2$. Then $N(\lambda) =
\sum_{k(k + 2) \leq \lambda}(k + 1)^2 \approx \sum_{k \leq \sqrt\lambda}(k + 1)^2 \sim \lambda^{3/2}/3$. Weyl's
law with $d = 3$: $\frac{2\pi^2}{(4\pi)^{3/2}\Gamma(5/2)}\lambda^{3/2} = \frac{2\pi^2}{8\pi^{3/2}\cdot
3\sqrt\pi/4}\lambda^{3/2} = \frac{2\pi^2}{6\pi^2}\lambda^{3/2} = \lambda^{3/2}/3$, in agreement. The eigenvalues
$0, 3, 8, 15, \dots$ with multiplicities $1, 4, 9, 16, \dots$ are those of @sec-harmonic-analysis.
:::

A rectangular torus with incommensurable radii has no accidental degeneracies, and Sage makes the contrast with
the square torus visible by listing the lowest eigenvalues. The last exercise does this for two choices of
$R_2^2/R_1^2$.

::: {#exr-ls-torus-rectangular}
#### Rectangular tori

With Sage, list the ten lowest eigenvalues $m^2 + n^2/\rho$ of the torus with $R_1 = 1$, $R_2^2 = \rho$ and their
multiplicities for $\rho = 1$, $\rho = 2$ and $\rho = \pi$; identify an accidental degeneracy for $\rho = 2$ and
explain why for $\rho = \pi$ the multiplicities are only $1$, $2$ or $4$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For $\rho = 2$, $(m, n) = (\pm2, \pm1)$ and $(0, \pm3)$ both give $9/2 = 4 + 1/2 = 9/2$, a multiplicity $4 + 2 = 6$
not explained by the sign symmetries (and $(\pm3, 0)$, $(\pm1, \pm4)$ both give $9$). For irrational $\rho$, $m^2 + n^2/\rho = m'^2 + n'^2/\rho$ forces $m^2 = m'^2$ and $n^2 =
n'^2$, so only the sign choices $(\pm m, \pm n)$ coincide: multiplicity $1$ for $(0, 0)$, $2$ if one index
vanishes, $4$ otherwise:

{{< sage exr-ls-torus-rectangular >}}
:::
::::

## Sobolev spaces {#sec-sobolev-spaces}

Differential operators are unbounded on $L^2$, but they become bounded between spaces that measure smoothness in a
square-integrable way. This part defines weak derivatives, the Sobolev spaces $H^s$ on the torus through Fourier
coefficients and on $\mathbb{R}^n$ through the Fourier transform, and proves the three facts the book uses: functions with
more than $n/2$ derivatives in $L^2$ are continuous (the Sobolev embedding), the Laplacian gains two derivatives (elliptic
regularity), and on a compact space a gain of smoothness is a compact operator (the Rellich theorem), which makes the
spectra of elliptic operators discrete. The Fourier conventions are those of @def-fourier-coefficient and
@def-fourier-transform; the compact-resolvent argument is that of @waterstraat2016 [Thm. 1.3.5].

### Weak derivatives

A function with a corner has no classical derivative at the corner, but integration by parts against smooth test functions
still defines one. The figure shows such a weak derivative, and a continuous function that has none.

![Left: $|x|$ on $[-1, 1]$ (blue) and its weak derivative $\operatorname{sgn}x$ (orange); $\int|x|\varphi' = -\int
\operatorname{sgn}x\,\varphi$ for every test function. Right: the Cantor function, continuous, non-decreasing from $0$ to
$1$ and constant on each removed interval, so its classical derivative is $0$ almost everywhere; it has no weak derivative,
since that would have to be $0$, and the function is not constant. Generated by
`figures/fa2-weak-derivative.sage`.](figures/fa2-weak-derivative.svg){#fig-fa2-weak-derivative width=95%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-weak-derivative}
#### Weak derivative

Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be open and $f, g$ locally integrable on $\Omega$. Then $g$ is the **weak derivative**
$\partial^\alpha f$ of $f$ for a multi-index $\alpha$ if $\int_\Omega f\,\partial^\alpha\varphi\,dx = (-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega
g\varphi\,dx$ for every test function $\varphi \in C^\infty_c(\Omega)$ (@def-test-function). The weak derivative is unique
almost everywhere when it exists, it agrees with the classical derivative for $C^{|\alpha|}$ functions, and it is the
distributional derivative of @def-distributional-derivative when that distribution is a function. The **Sobolev space**
$W^{k, p}(\Omega)$ consists of the $f \in L^p$ whose weak derivatives of order $\leq k$ lie in $L^p$, with norm $(\sum_{|\alpha|
\leq k}\|\partial^\alpha f\|_p^p)^{1/p}$; $H^k = W^{k, 2}$.
:::

:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A function with a corner has a weak derivative with a jump. The first example computes it for the absolute value of the
figure.

::: {#exm-fan-abs-weak}
#### The absolute value

For $\varphi \in C^\infty_c(-1, 1)$, $\int_{-1}^1|x|\varphi' = \int_0^1x\varphi' - \int_{-1}^0x\varphi' = -\int_0^1\varphi +
\int_{-1}^0\varphi = -\int\operatorname{sgn}x\,\varphi$, integrating by parts on each half (the boundary terms vanish at $0$
because $|x| = 0$ there). So $|x|' = \operatorname{sgn}x$ weakly, and $|x| \in W^{1, p}(-1, 1)$ for every $p$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A jump cannot be differentiated weakly: its distributional derivative is a point mass. The second example shows this for the
step function.

::: {#exm-fan-step-no-weak}
#### The step function

For $H = \mathbf{1}_{x > 0}$ on $(-1, 1)$, $\int H\varphi' = -\varphi(0)$, so a weak derivative $g$ would satisfy $\int g\varphi =
\varphi(0)$ for every test function. Testing with $\varphi$ supported away from $0$ forces $g = 0$ almost everywhere, and
then $\varphi(0) = 0$ for all $\varphi$, a contradiction. The distributional derivative is $\delta$ (@def-dirac-delta), which
is not a function.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Continuity does not guarantee a weak derivative, and the Cantor function of the figure shows it. The third example gives the
argument.

::: {#exm-fan-cantor-function}
#### The Cantor function

The Cantor function $c$ is continuous and constant on each interval removed in the construction of the Cantor set
(@exm-fan-cantor), whose complement has measure zero; so $c' = 0$ almost everywhere. If $c$ had a weak derivative $g$, then
$g = 0$ (it would equal $c'$ where $c$ is locally constant, which is almost everywhere), and a function with zero weak
derivative is constant (@exr-fan-zero-weak-derivative). But $c(0) = 0 \neq 1 = c(1)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In several variables a function may be unbounded and still have square-integrable weak derivatives. The fourth example
treats powers of $|x|$ on the unit ball.

::: {#exm-fan-radial-powers}
#### Radial powers

On the unit ball $B \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, $f(x) = |x|^{-a}$ with $0 < a < n - 1$ has the weak gradient $-a|x|^{-a - 2}x$ (the
classical one away from $0$; the singular point does not contribute because $|x|^{-a}$ times the area $|x|^{n - 1}$ of small
spheres tends to $0$). So $f \in W^{1, p}(B)$ iff $(a + 1)p < n$. For $n = 3$, $p = 2$: $|x|^{-a} \in H^1(B)$ for $a < \tfrac12$,
an unbounded function with square-integrable gradient.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
A function with zero weak derivative on an interval is constant, the weak form of a basic fact of calculus. The first exercise
proves it by testing against derivatives of test functions.

::: {#exr-fan-zero-weak-derivative}
#### Zero weak derivative

Let $f \in L^1(a, b)$ with $\int f\varphi' = 0$ for all $\varphi \in C^\infty_c(a, b)$. Fix $\psi_0 \in C^\infty_c$ with $\int\psi_0
= 1$. Show that every $\psi \in C^\infty_c$ is $\varphi' + (\int\psi)\psi_0$ for some test function $\varphi$, and conclude that $f
= c$ almost everywhere with $c = \int f\psi_0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\psi - (\int\psi)\psi_0$ has integral $0$ and compact support, so its primitive $\varphi(x) = \int_a^x(\psi - (\int\psi)\psi_0)$
is a test function. Then $\int f\psi = \int f\varphi' + (\int\psi)\int f\psi_0 = c\int\psi$, so $\int(f - c)\psi = 0$ for all test
functions, hence $f = c$ almost everywhere.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Weak derivatives of piecewise polynomials are computed piece by piece, as long as the function is continuous at the joins.
The second exercise iterates this for $x|x|$.

::: {#exr-fan-x-abs-x}
#### Iterated weak derivatives

Compute the weak derivatives of $f(x) = x|x|$ on $(-1, 1)$ of orders $1$, $2$ and $3$, when they exist, and decide for which
$k$ and $p$ the function lies in $W^{k, p}(-1, 1)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$f$ is $C^1$ with $f' = 2|x|$, which by @exm-fan-abs-weak has the weak derivative $f'' = 2\operatorname{sgn}x$. The third
derivative would be $4\delta$, not a function (@exm-fan-step-no-weak). So $f \in W^{2, p}$ for every $p$ and $f \notin W^{3,
p}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The integrability of radial powers is a one-dimensional integral in polar coordinates. The third exercise computes the
$H^1$ norm in the example.

::: {#exr-fan-radial-h1}
#### A radial $H^1$ function

For $f = |x|^{-a}$ on the unit ball of $\mathbb{R}^3$, compute $\int_B|\nabla f|^2$ and $\int_Bf^2$ in polar coordinates, and
show that both are finite exactly for $a < \tfrac12$ and $a < \tfrac32$ respectively.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|\nabla f|^2 = a^2r^{-2a - 2}$, so $\int_B|\nabla f|^2 = 4\pi a^2\int_0^1r^{-2a}dr = \tfrac{4\pi a^2}{1 - 2a}$ for $a < \tfrac12$
(and infinite otherwise), and $\int_Bf^2 = 4\pi\int_0^1r^{2 - 2a}dr = \tfrac{4\pi}{3 - 2a}$ for $a < \tfrac32$.

Sage computes both integrals and shows the divergence of the gradient integral at $a \geq \tfrac12$ through a small cutoff:

{{< sage exr-fan-radial-h1 >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### Sobolev spaces on the torus

On the torus, a derivative multiplies the $k$-th Fourier coefficient by $ik$, so the smoothness of a function is read from the
decay of its coefficients. The figure compares three functions on the circle, and the definition below turns the decay rate
into a scale of Hilbert spaces.

![Moduli of the Fourier coefficients $|c_k|$ against $k$ on logarithmic axes, for the square wave ($\propto k^{-1}$, in
$H^s$ for $s < \tfrac12$), the triangle wave $|x|$ on $[-\pi, \pi]$ ($\propto k^{-2}$, in $H^s$ for $s < \tfrac32$) and
$e^{\cos x}$ (faster than any power, in every $H^s$). Odd $k$ only for the first two, whose even coefficients vanish.
Generated by `figures/fa2-sobolev-torus.sage`.](figures/fa2-sobolev-torus.svg){#fig-fa2-sobolev-torus width=60%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-sobolev-torus}
#### Sobolev space on the torus

Let $T^n = (\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z})^n$ and, for $f \in L^2(T^n)$, $c_k = (2\pi)^{-n}\int_{T^n}fe^{-ik\cdot x}dx$, $k \in
\mathbb{Z}^n$. For real $s$, the **Sobolev space** $H^s(T^n)$ consists of the $f$ with
$$
\|f\|_{H^s}^2 = (2\pi)^n\sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}^n}(1 + |k|^2)^s|c_k|^2 < \infty,
$$
a Hilbert space with the corresponding inner product; for $s < 0$ its elements are distributions with these coefficients.
$H^0 = L^2$ isometrically by Parseval, $H^s \subset H^t$ for $s > t$, and for integer $s = m \geq 0$, $H^m(T^n)$ is the space of
$L^2$ functions with weak derivatives of order $\leq m$ in $L^2$, with an equivalent norm.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The square wave is discontinuous, but its coefficients decay like $1/k$, so it has "almost half a derivative". The first
example decides its membership.

::: {#exm-fan-square-wave-hs}
#### The square wave

The $2\pi$-periodic $f = \operatorname{sgn}x$ on $(-\pi, \pi)$ has $c_k = \tfrac{2}{i\pi k}$ for odd $k$ and $0$ for even $k$.
Then $\sum_{k\ \mathrm{odd}}(1 + k^2)^s\tfrac{4}{\pi^2k^2}$ converges iff $2s - 2 < -1$, that is, $f \in H^s$ iff $s < \tfrac12$.
A jump costs half a derivative in the $L^2$ scale.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The triangle wave is continuous with a corner, and gains one more power of decay. The second example places it in the scale.

::: {#exm-fan-triangle-hs}
#### The triangle wave

The $2\pi$-periodic extension of $|x|$ on $[-\pi, \pi]$ has $c_0 = \tfrac\pi2$ and $c_k = -\tfrac{2}{\pi k^2}$ for odd $k$ (and $0$
for even $k \neq 0$). So $|x| \in H^s$ iff $s < \tfrac32$: it has one weak derivative in $L^2$ (the square wave, by
@exm-fan-abs-weak) and half a derivative more.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Negative Sobolev spaces contain distributions, and the delta function is the standard example. The third example finds its
place on $T^n$.

::: {#exm-fan-delta-hs}
#### The delta function

$\delta$ at $0 \in T^n$ has $c_k = (2\pi)^{-n}$ for all $k$, so $\|\delta\|_{H^s}^2 = (2\pi)^{-n}\sum_k(1 + |k|^2)^s$, finite iff $2s
< -n$. So $\delta \in H^s(T^n)$ exactly for $s < -\tfrac n2$: on the circle for $s < -\tfrac12$, on $T^3$ for $s < -\tfrac32$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
For integer order the Fourier norm is a norm of derivatives, which the first exercise checks for $s = 1$ on the circle. The
identity is Parseval's theorem applied to $f$ and $f'$.

::: {#exr-fan-h1-norm-circle}
#### The $H^1$ norm on the circle

Show that $\|f\|_{H^1}^2 = \|f\|_2^2 + \|f'\|_2^2$ on $T^1$ for $f \in C^1$, using $c_k(f') = ikc_k(f)$. Compute $\|\sin x +
\tfrac12\cos 2x\|_{H^1}^2$ both ways.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$2\pi\sum(1 + k^2)|c_k|^2 = 2\pi\sum|c_k|^2 + 2\pi\sum|ikc_k|^2 = \|f\|_2^2 + \|f'\|_2^2$ by Parseval (@thm-parseval). For $f =
\sin x + \tfrac12\cos2x$: $\|f\|_2^2 = \pi + \tfrac\pi4$, $f' = \cos x - \sin2x$ with $\|f'\|_2^2 = 2\pi$; total $\tfrac{13\pi}4$.
In coefficients: $|c_{\pm1}| = \tfrac12$, $|c_{\pm2}| = \tfrac14$, and $2\pi(2\cdot 2\cdot\tfrac14 + 2\cdot 5\cdot\tfrac1{16}) =
2\pi(1 + \tfrac58) = \tfrac{13\pi}4$.

Sage computes the norm both ways:

{{< sage exr-fan-h1-norm-circle >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The coefficients of the triangle wave are a standard Fourier computation. The second exercise asks for it and for the
borderline sum.

::: {#exr-fan-triangle-coefficients}
#### Coefficients of the triangle wave

Compute $c_k$ for $|x|$ on $[-\pi, \pi]$ and verify $\|\,|x|\,\|_{H^1}^2 = \|x\|_2^2 + \|\operatorname{sgn}x\|_2^2 = \tfrac{2\pi^3}3 +
2\pi$ from the coefficients, using $\sum_{k\ \mathrm{odd}}k^{-2} = \tfrac{\pi^2}8$ and $\sum_{k\ \mathrm{odd}}k^{-4} =
\tfrac{\pi^4}{96}$ (sums over positive and negative odd $k$ double these).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$c_k = \tfrac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^\pi|x|e^{-ikx}dx = \tfrac1\pi\int_0^\pi x\cos kx\,dx = \tfrac{(-1)^k - 1}{\pi k^2}$. Then
$2\pi\sum_k|c_k|^2 = 2\pi(\tfrac{\pi^2}4 + 2\cdot\tfrac4{\pi^2}\cdot\tfrac{\pi^4}{96}) = \tfrac{\pi^3}{2} + \tfrac{\pi^3}6 =
\tfrac{2\pi^3}3$ and $2\pi\sum_kk^2|c_k|^2 = 2\pi\cdot 2\cdot\tfrac{4}{\pi^2}\cdot\tfrac{\pi^2}8 = 2\pi$, which add up as stated.

Sage computes the coefficients and the two sums:

{{< sage exr-fan-triangle-coefficients >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

On the circle, $H^1$ functions are Hölder continuous of order $\tfrac12$, a direct consequence of Cauchy-Schwarz. The third
exercise proves it.

::: {#exr-fan-holder-half}
#### $H^1$ functions are Hölder

For $f \in C^1(T^1)$ show $|f(x) - f(y)| \leq |x - y|^{1/2}\|f'\|_2$, and extend it to $f \in H^1$ by density. Show that the
exponent $\tfrac12$ is sharp using $f(x) = |x|^{1/2 + \varepsilon}$ near $0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|f(x) - f(y)| = |\int_y^xf'| \leq |x - y|^{1/2}(\int_y^x|f'|^2)^{1/2}$. For $H^1$ functions, approximate by trigonometric
polynomials in $H^1$; the bound passes to the limit and shows that the limit is continuous. For $f = |x|^\beta$ near $0$,
$f' \in L^2$ iff $2\beta - 2 > -1$, that is $\beta > \tfrac12$, and $|f(x) - f(0)| = |x|^\beta$; so every exponent above $\tfrac12$
is realised and $\tfrac12$ cannot be improved.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

On the torus, square-summable derivatives of more than half the dimension control the supremum. The theorem below states this;
the proof is Cauchy-Schwarz on the Fourier series, which converges absolutely.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-sobolev-embedding-torus}
#### Sobolev embedding on the torus

If $s > \tfrac n2$, every $f \in H^s(T^n)$ has an absolutely and uniformly convergent Fourier series, is continuous, and
$\|f\|_\infty \leq C_{n, s}\|f\|_{H^s}$ with $C_{n, s}^2 = (2\pi)^{-n}\sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}^n}(1 + |k|^2)^{-s}$. If $s > \tfrac n2 +
m$, then $f \in C^m(T^n)$. For $s > \tfrac n2$, $H^s(T^n)$ is an algebra: $\|fg\|_{H^s} \leq C\|f\|_{H^s}\|g\|_{H^s}$. At $s =
\tfrac n2$ the embedding into continuous functions fails.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
On the circle with $s = 1$ the constant is a classical sum. The first example evaluates it and finds the function for
which the bound is an equality.

::: {#exm-fan-sobolev-constant}
#### The constant on the circle

For $n = 1$, $s = 1$: $C^2 = \tfrac1{2\pi}\sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}\tfrac1{1 + k^2} = \tfrac1{2\pi}\pi\coth\pi = \tfrac12\coth\pi$, so
$\|f\|_\infty \leq 0.7084\,\|f\|_{H^1}$ on $T^1$. Equality holds for $f$ with $c_k \propto (1 + k^2)^{-1}$, that is, the periodic
Green's function of $1 - d^2/dx^2$, $f(x) = \cosh(x - \pi)$ on $[0, 2\pi]$, at $x = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

At $s = \tfrac n2$ the theorem fails, and a lacunary-type logarithmic series shows it. The second example gives a function in
$H^{1/2}(T^1)$ that is unbounded.

::: {#exm-fan-critical-unbounded}
#### Unbounded at the critical exponent

$f(x) = \sum_{k \geq 2}\tfrac{\cos kx}{k\log k}$ has $\sum_k(1 + k^2)^{1/2}\tfrac1{k^2\log^2k} \approx \sum\tfrac1{k\log^2k} <
\infty$, so $f \in H^{1/2}(T^1)$, but $f(0) = \sum_k\tfrac1{k\log k} = \infty$ (integral test) and the partial sums at $0$ grow
like $\log\log N$. In two dimensions, $\log\log(1/|x|)$ near $0$ is the analogous unbounded $H^1$ function.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The theorem counts derivatives precisely: $\tfrac n2$ derivatives for continuity, one more for each classical derivative. The
third example checks this on a series with coefficients $k^{-3}$.

::: {#exm-fan-derivative-count}
#### Counting derivatives

$f(x) = \sum_{k \geq 1}\tfrac{\cos kx}{k^3}$ lies in $H^s$ for $s < \tfrac52$. The theorem gives $f \in C^1$ (as $s > \tfrac12 + 1$
is possible) but not $C^2$; indeed $f'' = -\sum\tfrac{\cos kx}{k} = \log|2\sin\tfrac x2|$, which is unbounded at $0$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The proof of the theorem is one application of Cauchy-Schwarz to the Fourier series. The first exercise asks for it and
for the condition $s > \tfrac n2$.

::: {#exr-fan-embedding-proof}
#### Proof of the embedding

Show $\sum_k|c_k| \leq (\sum_k(1 + |k|^2)^{-s})^{1/2}(\sum_k(1 + |k|^2)^s|c_k|^2)^{1/2}$, that the first sum is finite iff $s > \tfrac
n2$ (compare with $\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}(1 + |\xi|^2)^{-s}d\xi$), and deduce the theorem's bound and continuity.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Write $|c_k| = (1 + |k|^2)^{-s/2}\cdot(1 + |k|^2)^{s/2}|c_k|$ and apply Cauchy-Schwarz. The sum $\sum(1 + |k|^2)^{-s}$ is comparable
to $\int(1 + |\xi|^2)^{-s}d\xi = |S^{n - 1}|\int_0^\infty\tfrac{r^{n - 1}}{(1 + r^2)^s}dr$, finite iff $2s - n + 1 > 1$. The series
$\sum c_ke^{ik\cdot x}$ then converges absolutely and uniformly, so its sum is continuous, and $|f(x)| \leq \sum|c_k| \leq C_{n,
s}\|f\|_{H^s}$ with the factors of $2\pi$ as in the definition.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The sum $\sum 1/(1 + k^2)$ is evaluated by the Fourier series of a hyperbolic cosine. The second exercise computes the
constant of the first example.

::: {#exr-fan-coth-sum}
#### The sum $\sum 1/(1 + k^2)$

Show $\sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}\tfrac1{1 + k^2} = \pi\coth\pi$ from the Fourier series of $\cosh(x - \pi)$ on $[0, 2\pi]$, and check
the value and the constant $C_{1, 1}$ with Sage.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$g(x) = \cosh(x - \pi)$ on $[0, 2\pi]$ has $c_k = \tfrac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\cosh(x - \pi)e^{-ikx}dx = \tfrac{\sinh\pi}{\pi(1 + k^2)}$.
At $x = 0$ the (convergent) series gives $\cosh\pi = \tfrac{\sinh\pi}\pi\sum\tfrac1{1 + k^2}$, which is the identity:

{{< sage exr-fan-coth-sum >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The algebra property of $H^s$ for $s > \tfrac n2$ is what makes non-linear field equations tractable in Sobolev spaces. The third
exercise proves it on the circle for $s = 1$.

::: {#exr-fan-h1-algebra}
#### $H^1(T^1)$ is an algebra

For $f, g \in H^1(T^1)$, use $(fg)' = f'g + fg'$ and the embedding $\|g\|_\infty \leq C\|g\|_{H^1}$ to show $\|fg\|_{H^1} \leq
2C\|f\|_{H^1}\|g\|_{H^1}$ with $C = C_{1, 1}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\|fg\|_2^2 + \|(fg)'\|_2^2 \leq \|f\|_\infty^2\|g\|_2^2 + 2\|f\|_\infty^2\|g'\|_2^2 + 2\|g\|_\infty^2\|f'\|_2^2$, using
$|a + b|^2 \leq 2|a|^2 + 2|b|^2$. The first two terms are at most $2\|f\|_\infty^2\|g\|_{H^1}^2 \leq 2C^2\|f\|_{H^1}^2\|g\|_{H^1}^2$,
the last at most $2C^2\|g\|_{H^1}^2\|f\|_{H^1}^2$. So $\|fg\|_{H^1}^2 \leq 4C^2\|f\|_{H^1}^2\|g\|_{H^1}^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
