## Traces, determinants and heat kernels {#sec-traces-heat-kernels}

The trace of a matrix is the sum of its eigenvalues, and for an operator on an infinite-dimensional space the sum
may or may not converge; when it does for $e^{-t(-\Delta)}$, the resulting function of $t$ encodes the spectrum of
the Laplacian and, through its small-$t$ behaviour, the geometry of the space. This section defines trace-class
operators and determinants, the heat kernel and heat trace, quotes the small-$t$ asymptotics, and introduces zeta
regularisation with the Casimir energy as its application in outline; the figure shows the heat trace of the
circle against its leading asymptotics.

### Trace class

Summing the diagonal entries of an infinite matrix may give a different answer in a different basis, or no answer
at all, unless the entries decay fast enough. The definition below isolates the operators for which the trace is
well defined and basis independent, with the eigenvalue sum as the formula that matters.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-trace-class}
#### Trace class

For a positive operator $A \geq 0$ the **trace** $\operatorname{tr}A = \sum_k\langle e_k, Ae_k\rangle \in [0,
\infty]$ is independent of the orthonormal basis $(e_k)$ (@exr-tc-basis-independence). A bounded operator $A$ is *
*trace class** if $\|A\|_1 = \operatorname{tr}|A| < \infty$ with $|A| = \sqrt{A^\dagger A}$; then
$\operatorname{tr}A = \sum_k\langle e_k, Ae_k\rangle$ converges absolutely, is basis independent, and satisfies
$|\operatorname{tr}A| \leq \|A\|_1$ and $\operatorname{tr}(AB) = \operatorname{tr}(BA)$ for bounded $B$. Trace-class
operators are Hilbert-Schmidt, hence compact; a compact self-adjoint operator is trace class iff
$\sum_k|\lambda_k| < \infty$, and then $\operatorname{tr}A = \sum_k\lambda_k$. An integral operator on a compact
space with a continuous kernel that is trace class has $\operatorname{tr}K = \int k(x, x)\,dx$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For matrices the trace is the sum of the diagonal entries and of the eigenvalues, and its cyclic property is the
reason it is basis independent. The first example records these facts and the trace of a projection.

::: {#exm-tc-matrix}
#### Traces of matrices

For an $n \times n$ matrix, $\operatorname{tr}A = \sum_jA_{jj} = \sum_k\lambda_k$ (from $A = UDU^\dagger$ and
$\operatorname{tr}(UDU^\dagger) = \operatorname{tr}(DU^\dagger U) = \operatorname{tr}D$), and $\operatorname{tr}
(AB) = \sum_{jk}A_{jk}B_{kj} = \operatorname{tr}(BA)$. The trace of an orthogonal projection is the dimension of its
range (eigenvalues $1$ and $0$), $\operatorname{tr}\sigma_a = 0$, and $\operatorname{tr}e^{iA} = \sum
e^{i\lambda_k}$ as in @exm-sd-trace-det (@exr-tc-trace-cyclic).
:::

A diagonal operator is trace class exactly when its diagonal is absolutely summable, and the Green's operator of
@exm-co-integral-operator is an example whose trace can be computed in two ways. The second example compares the
eigenvalue sum with the integral of the kernel along the diagonal.

::: {#exm-tc-diagonal}
#### Diagonal operators and the Green's operator

$De_n = \lambda_ne_n$ is trace class iff $\sum|\lambda_n| < \infty$: $\lambda_n = 1/n^2$ gives
$\operatorname{tr}D = \pi^2/6$, while $\lambda_n = 1/n$ is Hilbert-Schmidt but not trace class (the harmonic
series diverges, @sec-series). The Green's operator $G$ with kernel $g(x, y) = \min(x, y) - xy$ has eigenvalues
$1/(n\pi)^2$ and $\operatorname{tr}G = \sum_n1/(n\pi)^2 = 1/6$, which equals $\int_0^1g(x, x)\,dx = \int_0^1(x -
x^2)\,dx = 1/6$ (@exr-tc-trace-cyclic): the trace formula for kernels.
:::

The heat operator on the circle is trace class for every positive time, with a trace given by a rapidly convergent
series, but at time zero it degenerates to the identity. The third example introduces this trace, the main object
of the rest of the section.

::: {#exm-tc-heat-circle}
#### The heat operator on the circle

$e^{t\Delta}$ on $L^2(S^1)$ has eigenvalues $e^{-tn^2}$ on $e^{in\theta}$ (@def-functional-calculus extended to the
unbounded $\Delta$), and $\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}e^{-tn^2} < \infty$ for $t > 0$: the operator is trace class with
$\operatorname{tr}e^{t\Delta} = \sum_ne^{-tn^2} = 1 + 2e^{-t} + 2e^{-4t} + \dots$, the **heat trace**. At $t = 0$
the operator is the identity, not trace class, and the trace diverges as $t \to 0$ like $\sqrt{\pi/t}$
(@thm-heat-trace-asymptotics, @fig-heat-trace-circle).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The cyclic property, the trace of a projection and the two computations of $\operatorname{tr}G$ are exact in Sage.
The first exercise asks for them, including a product of three matrices where only cyclic permutations agree.

::: {#exr-tc-trace-cyclic}
#### Traces in Sage

With Sage, check $\operatorname{tr}(AB) = \operatorname{tr}(BA)$ and $\operatorname{tr}(ABC) =
\operatorname{tr}(CAB) \neq \operatorname{tr}(BAC)$ for explicit $3 \times 3$ matrices, verify
$\operatorname{tr}P = 2$ for the projection of @exr-proj-formula, and compute $\operatorname{tr}G$ both as
$\sum_n1/(n\pi)^2$ and as $\int_0^1g(x, x)\,dx$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The trace is invariant under cyclic permutations only; with non-commuting $A, B, C$ the transposition $A
\leftrightarrow B$ changes it. Both computations of $\operatorname{tr}G$ give $1/6$:

{{< sage exr-tc-trace-cyclic >}}
:::

Basis independence of the trace of a positive operator is proved by inserting a second orthonormal basis and
exchanging the order of two non-negative sums. The second exercise asks for this proof through the square root of
$A$.

::: {#exr-tc-basis-independence}
#### Basis independence of the trace

For $A \geq 0$ with square root $\sqrt A$, show that $\sum_k\langle e_k, Ae_k\rangle = \sum_k\|\sqrt Ae_k\|^2 =
\sum_j\|\sqrt Af_j\|^2$ for any two orthonormal bases $(e_k)$, $(f_j)$, and deduce that $\operatorname{tr}A$ is
basis independent and that $\operatorname{tr}(U^\dagger AU) = \operatorname{tr}A$ for unitary $U$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\langle e_k, Ae_k\rangle = \langle\sqrt Ae_k, \sqrt Ae_k\rangle = \|\sqrt Ae_k\|^2$. By Parseval in the basis
$(f_j)$, $\|\sqrt Ae_k\|^2 = \sum_j|\langle f_j, \sqrt Ae_k\rangle|^2 = \sum_j|\langle\sqrt Af_j, e_k\rangle|^2$
(self-adjointness of $\sqrt A$), and summing over $k$ and exchanging the sums of non-negative terms gives
$\sum_j\|\sqrt Af_j\|^2$ by Parseval in the basis $(e_k)$. Hence the trace is basis independent; $U^\dagger AU$
has the diagonal entries $\langle Ue_k, AUe_k\rangle$, which is the trace of $A$ in the orthonormal basis $(Ue_k)$.
:::

Trace class is strictly stronger than Hilbert-Schmidt, and absolute convergence of the diagonal sum is what makes
the trace well defined. The last exercise asks for the inclusion and for the absolute convergence through the polar
decomposition.

::: {#exr-tc-hilbert-schmidt-vs-trace}
#### Trace class versus Hilbert-Schmidt

Show that a compact self-adjoint operator with $\sum|\lambda_k| < \infty$ has $\sum\lambda_k^2 < \infty$, that the
diagonal operator with $\lambda_n = 1/n$ is Hilbert-Schmidt but not trace class, and that for trace-class $A =
U|A|$ (polar decomposition) the series $\sum_k\langle e_k, Ae_k\rangle$ converges absolutely with
$|\operatorname{tr}A| \leq \operatorname{tr}|A|$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\sum\lambda_k^2 \leq (\max|\lambda_k|)\sum|\lambda_k| < \infty$. For $\lambda_n = 1/n$, $\sum 1/n^2 = \pi^2/6$ but
$\sum 1/n = \infty$. With $A = U|A|$, $\langle e_k, Ae_k\rangle = \langle|A|^{1/2}U^\dagger e_k, |A|^{1/2}
e_k\rangle$, so $|\langle e_k, Ae_k\rangle| \leq \||A|^{1/2}U^\dagger e_k\|\,\||A|^{1/2}e_k\|$ and by
Cauchy-Schwarz over $k$, $\sum_k|\langle e_k, Ae_k\rangle| \leq (\sum_k\||A|^{1/2}U^\dagger e_k\|^2)^{1/2}
(\sum_k\||A|^{1/2}e_k\|^2)^{1/2} \leq \operatorname{tr}|A|$, using $\sum_k\||A|^{1/2}U^\dagger e_k\|^2 =
\operatorname{tr}(U|A|U^\dagger) \leq \operatorname{tr}|A|$ (the trace of $U|A|U^\dagger$ equals that of $|A|$ when
$U$ is unitary, and is bounded by it for a partial isometry).
:::
::::

### Determinants

The determinant of a matrix is the product of its eigenvalues, and for an operator of the form $1 + A$ with $A$
trace class the infinite product converges. The definition below introduces this Fredholm determinant and the
formula $\det e^A = e^{\operatorname{tr}A}$ that ties it to the trace.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-fredholm-determinant}
#### Fredholm determinant

For a trace-class operator $A$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_k$ (with multiplicity), the **Fredholm determinant** is
$\det(1 + A) = \prod_k(1 + \lambda_k)$, absolutely convergent because $\sum|\lambda_k| < \infty$
(@exr-fd-product-convergence). It satisfies $\det((1 + A)(1 + B)) = \det(1 + A)\det(1 + B)$, $\det(1 + A) \neq 0$
iff $1 + A$ is invertible, $\det e^A = e^{\operatorname{tr}A}$, and for $\|A\| < 1$ the expansion $\log\det(1 + zA)
= \sum_{m \geq 1}\frac{(-1)^{m + 1}}{m}z^m\operatorname{tr}(A^m)$, so that $\operatorname{tr}A$ is the derivative
of $\det(1 + zA)$ at $z = 0$. For a compact self-adjoint $A$ of trace class, $z \mapsto \det(1 - zA) = \prod_k(1 -
z\lambda_k)$ is an entire function whose zeros are the reciprocals of the eigenvalues.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For a matrix the Fredholm determinant is the ordinary one, and the identity $\det e^A = e^{\operatorname{tr}A}$
follows from triangularisation. The first example records it on an explicit matrix and gives the expansion of the
determinant in traces.

::: {#exm-fd-matrix}
#### Determinants of matrices

For $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{pmatrix}$, $\det e^A = e^{\operatorname{tr}A} = e^5$ although $e^A$
itself has transcendental entries (@exr-fd-sage-det-exp); in general $e^A = Ue^TU^{-1}$ with $T$ upper triangular
gives $\det e^A = \prod e^{T_{kk}} = e^{\sum T_{kk}}$. For $2 \times 2$ matrices $\det(1 + zA) = 1 +
z\operatorname{tr}A + z^2\det A$, and the series $\log\det(1 + zA) = z\operatorname{tr}A - \tfrac{z^2}{2}
\operatorname{tr}A^2 + \dots$ reproduces $\det A = \tfrac12((\operatorname{tr}A)^2 - \operatorname{tr}A^2)$.
:::

The Fredholm determinant of the Green's operator is Euler's product for the sine, and its zeros are the eigenvalues
of the Dirichlet Laplacian. The second example states this identity, the model for the determinants of
differential operators defined by zeta regularisation below.

::: {#exm-fd-sine-product}
#### The sine as a Fredholm determinant

For the Green's operator $G$ with eigenvalues $1/(n\pi)^2$ (@exm-co-integral-operator), $\det(1 - zG) =
\prod_{n \geq 1}\left(1 - \frac{z}{n^2\pi^2}\right) = \frac{\sin\sqrt z}{\sqrt z}$, Euler's product for the sine
(@sec-analytic-continuation), an entire function of $z$ with zeros at $z = n^2\pi^2$, the eigenvalues of
$-d^2/dx^2$ with Dirichlet conditions on $(0, 1)$. The coefficient of $z$ is $-\operatorname{tr}G = -1/6$, which
is the Taylor coefficient of $\sin\sqrt z/\sqrt z = 1 - z/6 + z^2/120 - \dots$ (@exr-fd-sine-product-sage).
:::

The determinant of $-\Delta$ itself cannot be a Fredholm determinant, since the eigenvalues grow; the way out is
to define it through the derivative of the spectral zeta function, as in @def-zeta-regularisation. The third
example previews this by rewriting $\log\det$ as a trace of a logarithm.

::: {#exm-fd-det-exp-trace}
#### $\log\det = \operatorname{tr}\log$

For a positive matrix, $\log\det A = \sum_k\log\lambda_k = \operatorname{tr}\log A$, and formally $\sum_k\log
\lambda_k = -\frac{d}{ds}\sum_k\lambda_k^{-s}\big|_{s = 0}$. For $-\Delta$ on a compact space the sum $\sum\log
\lambda_k$ diverges, but $\zeta_\Delta(s) = \sum\lambda_k^{-s}$ converges for large $\operatorname{Re}s$ and
continues analytically to $s = 0$, which is how $\det{}_\zeta(-\Delta) = e^{-\zeta_\Delta'(0)}$ is defined; for
the Dirichlet operator on $(0, \pi)$ this gives $\det{}_\zeta = 2\pi$ (@exm-zr-det-dirichlet).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Sage verifies $\det e^A = e^{\operatorname{tr}A}$ symbolically and expands $\log\det(1 + zA)$ in traces of powers.
The first exercise asks for both and for the product formula over the eigenvalues.

::: {#exr-fd-sage-det-exp}
#### $\det e^A$ and the trace expansion in Sage

For $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{pmatrix}$ check $\det e^A = e^{\operatorname{tr}A}$ symbolically,
verify $\det(1 + A) = \prod(1 + \lambda_k)$, and compare the Taylor expansion of $\log\det(1 + zA)$ to order $z^4$
with $\sum_{m \leq 4}\frac{(-1)^{m + 1}}{m}z^m\operatorname{tr}(A^m)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\det e^A = e^5$ exactly; $\det(1 + A) = 4 = (1 + \lambda_1)(1 + \lambda_2)$ with $\lambda_{1, 2} = (5 \pm
\sqrt{33})/2$; the two expansions agree term by term:

{{< sage exr-fd-sage-det-exp >}}
:::

An infinite product $\prod(1 + \lambda_k)$ converges absolutely exactly when $\sum|\lambda_k|$ does, which is why
the Fredholm determinant needs trace class and not merely Hilbert-Schmidt. The second exercise asks for this and
for the regularised determinant that works for Hilbert-Schmidt operators.

::: {#exr-fd-product-convergence}
#### Convergence of the product

Show that for $\lambda_k \to 0$ the product $\prod_k(1 + \lambda_k)$ converges absolutely (that is, $\sum|\log(1 +
\lambda_k)| < \infty$) iff $\sum|\lambda_k| < \infty$; show that $\prod(1 + 1/n)$ diverges; and show that
$\prod_k(1 + \lambda_k)e^{-\lambda_k}$ converges whenever $\sum\lambda_k^2 < \infty$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For $|\lambda| \leq \tfrac12$, $\tfrac12|\lambda| \leq |\log(1 + \lambda)| \leq \tfrac32|\lambda|$, so the two
series converge or diverge together. $\prod_{n \leq N}(1 + 1/n) = \prod_{n \leq N}\tfrac{n + 1}{n} = N + 1 \to
\infty$, in line with $\sum 1/n = \infty$. Finally $\log((1 + \lambda)e^{-\lambda}) = \log(1 + \lambda) - \lambda =
-\lambda^2/2 + O(\lambda^3)$, bounded by $C\lambda^2$ for small $\lambda$, so the series of logarithms converges
when $\sum\lambda_k^2 < \infty$: this is the **regularised determinant** $\det{}_2(1 + A)$ of a Hilbert-Schmidt
operator.
:::

Euler's product converges slowly, and the partial products can be compared with $\sin\sqrt z/\sqrt z$ at a few
points; the coefficients of the expansion give the traces of powers of $G$. The last exercise does this in Sage.

::: {#exr-fd-sine-product-sage}
#### Euler's product in Sage

Compute $\prod_{n \leq N}(1 - z/(n^2\pi^2))$ for $N = 10, 100, 1000$ at $z = 1$ and $z = \pi^2/4$ and compare with
$\sin\sqrt z/\sqrt z$; expand $\sin\sqrt z/\sqrt z$ to order $z^2$ and deduce $\operatorname{tr}G = 1/6$ and
$\operatorname{tr}G^2 = 1/90$ from the coefficients.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
At $z = \pi^2/4$ the product tends to $\sin(\pi/2)/(\pi/2) = 2/\pi$. From $\log\prod(1 - z\lambda_n) = -z\sum
\lambda_n - \tfrac{z^2}{2}\sum\lambda_n^2 - \dots$ and $\log(\sin\sqrt z/\sqrt z) = -z/6 - z^2/180 - \dots$ one
reads $\operatorname{tr}G = 1/6$ and $\operatorname{tr}G^2 = 1/90$, the Hilbert-Schmidt norm of
@exr-co-hilbert-schmidt-norm:

{{< sage exr-fd-sine-product-sage >}}
:::
::::

### Heat kernels

The functional calculus applied to the Laplacian with the function $e^{-t\lambda}$ gives the solution operator of
the heat equation, and this operator has a kernel built from the eigenfunctions. The definition below introduces
the heat kernel and the heat trace, which the figure plots for the circle.

![Left: the heat trace $Z(t) = \operatorname{tr}e^{t\Delta} = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}e^{-tn^2}$ of the unit circle
against its small-$t$ asymptotics $\sqrt{\pi/t}$ and its large-$t$ limit $1$ (the zero mode). Right: the difference
$Z(t) - \sqrt{\pi/t}$ on a logarithmic scale against the first correction $2\sqrt{\pi/t}\,e^{-\pi^2/t}$ from the
Poisson summation formula; the asymptotics is exponentially accurate. Generated by
`figures/heat_trace_circle.sage`.](figures/heat_trace_circle.svg){#fig-heat-trace-circle width=95%}

{{< interactive heat_trace_circle 460 >}}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-heat-kernel}
#### Heat kernel

Let $-\Delta$ on a compact manifold $M$ have the orthonormal eigenbasis $\varphi_k$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_k$
(@thm-laplacian-discrete-spectrum). The **heat operator** $e^{t\Delta} = \sum_ke^{-t\lambda_k}|\varphi_k\rangle
\langle\varphi_k|$, $t > 0$, solves the heat equation: $u(t) = e^{t\Delta}f$ satisfies $\partial_tu = \Delta u$,
$u(0) = f$ (@def-heat-equation). It is the integral operator with the **heat kernel** $K_t(x, y) =
\sum_ke^{-t\lambda_k}\varphi_k(x)\overline{\varphi_k(y)}$, a smooth function for $t > 0$ with $K_t(x, \cdot) \to
\delta_x$ as $t \to 0$ and the **semigroup property** $\int_MK_t(x, z)K_s(z, y)\,dz = K_{t + s}(x, y)$. The **heat
trace** is $Z(t) = \operatorname{tr}e^{t\Delta} = \sum_ke^{-t\lambda_k} = \int_MK_t(x, x)\,dx$, finite for every
$t > 0$ by Weyl's law, so $e^{t\Delta}$ is trace class.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
On the real line, which is not compact, the heat kernel is the Gaussian and the heat operator is not trace class,
since the integral of the kernel along the diagonal diverges. The first example records this, the continuous
spectrum showing up as an infinite trace.

::: {#exm-hk-real-line}
#### The line: the Gaussian kernel

On $L^2(\mathbb{R})$, $K_t(x, y) = (4\pi t)^{-1/2}e^{-(x - y)^2/4t}$ solves $\partial_tK = \partial_x^2K$ with
$K_t \to \delta$ (@sec-pdes), and $e^{t\partial_x^2}$ is multiplication by $e^{-tk^2}$ in the Fourier picture, with
continuous spectrum $(0, 1]$. It is not trace class: $K_t(x, x) = (4\pi t)^{-1/2}$ is constant and $\int_{\mathbb{R}}
K_t(x, x)\,dx = \infty$. Compactness of the space is what makes the heat trace finite.
:::

On the circle the heat kernel is a Fourier series, and the Poisson summation formula rewrites it as a sum over
images of the Gaussian kernel of the line. The second example gives both forms, which produce the two regimes of
the figure.

::: {#exm-hk-circle}
#### The circle: Fourier and image sums

On $S^1$ with $\varphi_n = e^{in\theta}/\sqrt{2\pi}$, $K_t(\theta, \theta') = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sum_{n \in
\mathbb{Z}}e^{-tn^2}e^{in(\theta - \theta')}$, and by the **Poisson summation formula** (@exr-hk-poisson-summation)
$K_t(\theta, \theta') = \sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}(4\pi t)^{-1/2}e^{-(\theta - \theta' - 2\pi k)^2/4t}$: the kernel of
the line summed over the images $\theta' + 2\pi k$. The heat trace is $Z(t) = \sum_ne^{-tn^2} = \sqrt{\pi/t}\sum_k
e^{-\pi^2k^2/t}$ (@prp-heat-trace-values): the first form shows $Z(t) \to 1$ as $t \to \infty$, the second
$Z(t) \sim \sqrt{\pi/t}$ as $t \to 0$ with exponentially small corrections.
:::

On the sphere the addition theorem for spherical harmonics collapses the sum over $m$ to a Legendre polynomial of
the angle between the two points, and the heat trace is a sum over $l$ alone. The third example writes both down.

::: {#exm-hk-sphere}
#### The sphere

On the unit $S^2$, $\sum_{m = -l}^lY_{lm}(x)\overline{Y_{lm}(y)} = \frac{2l + 1}{4\pi}P_l(\cos\gamma)$ with $\gamma$
the angle between $x$ and $y$ (the addition theorem, @sec-harmonic-analysis), so $K_t(x, y) = \sum_{l \geq 0}
\frac{2l + 1}{4\pi}e^{-tl(l + 1)}P_l(\cos\gamma)$ and $Z(t) = \sum_{l \geq 0}(2l + 1)e^{-tl(l + 1)}$. There is no
closed form, but $Z(t) = \frac1t + \frac13 + \frac{t}{15} + O(t^2)$ as $t \to 0$ (@exm-hta-sphere,
@exr-hta-sphere-numeric), and $Z(t) \to 1$ as $t \to \infty$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The Fourier form of the circle kernel can be checked against the heat equation and the semigroup property mode by
mode, and the Poisson summation identity can be tested to high precision numerically. The first exercise does all
three in Sage.

::: {#exr-hk-circle-pde}
#### The circle kernel in Sage

With Sage, check that each term $e^{-tn^2}e^{in(\theta - \theta')}$ of the circle kernel solves $\partial_tK =
\partial_\theta^2K$ and that the modes satisfy the semigroup property under the $L^2$ inner product; then evaluate
$\sum_{|n| \leq 60}e^{-tn^2}$ and $\sqrt{\pi/t}\sum_{|k| \leq 10}e^{-\pi^2k^2/t}$ for $t = 1/10, 1/2, 1$ to twenty
digits.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The semigroup property is $\sum_n e^{-tn^2}e^{-sn^2}|\varphi_n\rangle\langle\varphi_n| = \sum_ne^{-(t + s)n^2} |
\varphi_n\rangle\langle\varphi_n|$, which holds because the modes are orthonormal; the two Poisson sums agree to
all twenty digits:

{{< sage exr-hk-circle-pde >}}
:::

The semigroup property and the positivity of the kernel on the diagonal follow from the spectral expansion, and the
identity $Z(t) = \int K_t(x, x)$ is the trace formula for kernels. The second exercise asks for these derivations.

::: {#exr-hk-semigroup}
#### Properties of the heat operator

Show that $e^{t\Delta}e^{s\Delta} = e^{(t + s)\Delta}$, that $\|e^{t\Delta}\| = 1$ with $e^{t\Delta}\varphi_0 =
\varphi_0$ for the constant mode, that $K_t(x, x) = \sum_ke^{-t\lambda_k}|\varphi_k(x)|^2 \geq 0$, and that
$\int_MK_t(x, x)\,dx = Z(t)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$e^{t\Delta}e^{s\Delta} = \sum_{j, k}e^{-t\lambda_j - s\lambda_k}|\varphi_j\rangle\langle\varphi_j|\varphi_k\rangle
\langle\varphi_k| = \sum_ke^{-(t + s)\lambda_k}|\varphi_k\rangle\langle\varphi_k|$ by orthonormality. The
eigenvalues $e^{-t\lambda_k}$ lie in $(0, 1]$ with $e^{-t\lambda_0} = 1$, so the norm is $1$ and the constant
mode is fixed. Setting $y = x$ in the kernel gives the non-negative sum. Integrating, $\int|\varphi_k|^2 = 1$ gives
$\int K_t(x, x)\,dx = \sum_ke^{-t\lambda_k} = Z(t)$, and the exchange of sum and integral is justified by the
positivity of the terms.
:::

The Poisson summation formula is the Fourier series of a periodised function evaluated at zero, and for the Gaussian
it is the identity between the two forms of the circle kernel. The last exercise asks for the derivation and for
the resulting functional equation of the theta function.

::: {#exr-hk-poisson-summation}
#### Poisson summation

For a rapidly decaying $f$ on $\mathbb{R}$ with Fourier transform $\hat f(k) = \int f(x)e^{-ikx}dx$, let $F(x) =
\sum_nf(x + 2\pi n)$. Compute the Fourier coefficients of the $2\pi$-periodic $F$, evaluate the series at $x = 0$,
and deduce $\sum_nf(2\pi n) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sum_k\hat f(k)$; apply it to $f(x) = e^{-tx^2/4\pi^2}$ to obtain
$\theta(t) = \sum_ne^{-tn^2} = \sqrt{\pi/t}\,\theta(\pi^2/t)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$c_k = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}F(x)e^{-ikx}dx = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sum_n\int_{2\pi n}^{2\pi(n + 1)}f(y)e^{-iky}dy =
\frac{1}{2\pi}\hat f(k)$, using $e^{-ik\cdot 2\pi n} = 1$. Then $F(0) = \sum_kc_k$, that is, $\sum_nf(2\pi n) =
\frac{1}{2\pi}\sum_k\hat f(k)$ (convergence of the Fourier series at $0$ holds for smooth $F$, @sec-fourier-series).
For $f(x) = e^{-tx^2/4\pi^2}$, $f(2\pi n) = e^{-tn^2}$ and $\hat f(k) = \sqrt{4\pi^3/t}\,e^{-\pi^2k^2/t}$ (Gaussian
transform, @sec-fourier-transform), giving $\theta(t) = \sqrt{\pi/t}\sum_ke^{-\pi^2k^2/t} = \sqrt{\pi/t}\,
\theta(\pi^2/t)$.
:::
::::

### Small-time asymptotics

As $t \to 0$ the heat kernel concentrates near the diagonal and only sees the local geometry, so the heat trace has
an expansion in powers of $t$ whose coefficients are integrals of curvature invariants. The theorem below, quoted,
states the first two coefficients; they determine the dimension, the volume and the total scalar curvature of the
space.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-heat-trace-asymptotics}
#### Heat trace asymptotics

On a compact Riemannian manifold $M$ of dimension $d$ without boundary, the heat trace of $-\Delta$ has the
asymptotic expansion $Z(t) = \operatorname{tr}e^{t\Delta} \sim (4\pi t)^{-d/2}\left(a_0 + a_1t + a_2t^2 +
\dots\right)$ as $t \to 0^+$, with $a_0 = \operatorname{Vol}(M)$, $a_1 = \frac16\int_MR\,d\mathrm{vol}$ for the
scalar curvature $R$ (@def-scalar-curvature), and every $a_k$ the integral of a polynomial in the curvature and its
derivatives (the **Minakshisundaram-Pleijel expansion**, quoted). For flat $M$ all $a_k$ with $k \geq 1$ vanish and
the corrections are exponentially small. Weyl's law of @thm-laplacian-discrete-spectrum follows from the leading
term by a Tauberian argument (@exr-hta-weyl-law).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
On the circle the theorem gives $\sqrt{\pi/t}$ for the unit radius, and the Poisson formula shows that this is exact
up to exponentially small terms. The first example checks the constant and reads the figure.

::: {#exm-hta-circle}
#### The circle

With $d = 1$ and $\operatorname{Vol}(S^1_R) = 2\pi R$: $Z(t) \sim (4\pi t)^{-1/2}\cdot 2\pi R = R\sqrt{\pi/t}$,
and the circle being flat, all $a_k = 0$ for $k \geq 1$. Indeed for $R = 1$ Poisson summation gives $Z(t) =
\sqrt{\pi/t}(1 + 2e^{-\pi^2/t} + 2e^{-4\pi^2/t} + \dots)$ exactly, so $Z(t) - \sqrt{\pi/t} \approx
2\sqrt{\pi/t}e^{-\pi^2/t}$, which is $10^{-42}$ at $t = 0.1$ and still only $0.00018$ at $t = 1$
(@fig-heat-trace-circle, right).
:::

On a flat torus the leading term is the area over $4\pi t$, again exact up to exponentially small terms, and the
heat trace factorises into two circle traces. The second example records this and compares with Weyl's law.

::: {#exm-hta-torus}
#### The torus

For $T^2$ with radii $R_1, R_2$, $Z(t) = \sum_{m, n}e^{-t(m^2/R_1^2 + n^2/R_2^2)} = \theta(t/R_1^2)\theta(t/R_2^2)
\sim \frac{\pi R_1R_2}{t} = \frac{\operatorname{Vol}(T^2)}{4\pi t}$ with $\operatorname{Vol} = 4\pi^2R_1R_2$
(@exr-htv-torus-trace). The coefficient of $1/t$ is $\operatorname{Vol}/4\pi$, the slope of Weyl's law $N(\lambda)
\sim \operatorname{Vol}\,\lambda/4\pi$ of @exm-ls-figure, and the flatness makes all further power corrections
vanish.
:::

On the unit sphere the curvature contributes a constant term, and the expansion begins $1/t + 1/3 + t/15$; the
constant $1/3$ is the Gauss-Bonnet integral $\int R/6 = 4\pi\chi/6$ divided by $4\pi$. The third example works out
the coefficients and their geometric meaning.

::: {#exm-hta-sphere}
#### The sphere and Gauss-Bonnet

For the unit $S^2$, $d = 2$, $\operatorname{Vol} = 4\pi$ and $R = 2$ (@prp-sphere-curvature), so $a_0 = 4\pi$,
$a_1 = \frac16\cdot 2\cdot 4\pi = \frac{4\pi}{3}$ and $Z(t) \sim \frac{1}{4\pi t}(4\pi + \tfrac{4\pi}{3}t + \dots)
= \frac1t + \frac13 + \dots$; the next coefficient gives $t/15$ (@exr-hta-sphere-numeric). For any closed surface
$a_1 = \frac16\int R = \frac13\int K = \frac{2\pi\chi}{3}$ by Gauss-Bonnet (@prp-gauss-bonnet-examples), so the
constant term of $Z(t)$ is $\chi(M)/6$: $1/3$ for the sphere and $0$ for the torus, as found.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The sphere expansion has no closed form but is tested numerically by summing the series for small $t$, and the
remainder after three terms should be of order $t^2$. The first exercise asks Sage for this test.

::: {#exr-hta-sphere-numeric}
#### The sphere heat trace numerically

Compute $Z(t) = \sum_{l \leq 300}(2l + 1)e^{-tl(l + 1)}$ for $t = 0.2, 0.1, 0.05, 0.025$ with Sage, subtract
$\frac1t + \frac13 + \frac{t}{15}$, and check that the remainder is $\approx \frac{4t^2}{315}$, the next term of the
expansion.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The remainders divided by $t^2$ approach $4/315 \approx 0.0127$ as $t$ decreases, confirming the expansion $Z(t) =
\frac1t + \frac13 + \frac{t}{15} + \frac{4t^2}{315} + \dots$:

{{< sage exr-hta-sphere-numeric >}}
:::

The leading term of the heat trace determines the growth of the eigenvalue counting function: this is a Tauberian
theorem, and the heuristic behind it is a Laplace transform. The second exercise asks for the heuristic and its
verification on the circle and the sphere.

::: {#exr-hta-weyl-law}
#### From the heat trace to Weyl's law

Writing $Z(t) = \int_0^\infty e^{-t\lambda}\,dN(\lambda)$ with $N$ the eigenvalue counting function, show that
$N(\lambda) = C\lambda^{d/2}$ gives $Z(t) = C\,\Gamma(d/2 + 1)\,t^{-d/2}$, and match with $Z(t) \sim
\operatorname{Vol}(M)(4\pi t)^{-d/2}$ to recover the constant of Weyl's law. Check on $S^1$ ($N \sim 2\sqrt\lambda$)
and on $S^2$ ($N \sim \lambda$).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\int_0^\infty e^{-t\lambda}\,d(C\lambda^{d/2}) = C\tfrac d2\int_0^\infty\lambda^{d/2 - 1}e^{-t\lambda}d\lambda =
C\tfrac d2\Gamma(d/2)t^{-d/2} = C\Gamma(d/2 + 1)t^{-d/2}$. Matching gives $C = \operatorname{Vol}/((4\pi)^{d/2}
\Gamma(d/2 + 1))$, the constant of @thm-laplacian-discrete-spectrum (Karamata's Tauberian theorem makes the
converse rigorous). Circle: $C = 2$, $d = 1$: $Z \sim 2\Gamma(3/2)t^{-1/2} = \sqrt{\pi/t}$. Sphere: $C = 1$, $d =
2$: $Z \sim \Gamma(2)/t = 1/t$. Both agree with the expansions above.
:::

The heat trace of a space determines its dimension, volume and total curvature, which is the start of the question
whether the spectrum determines the geometry. The last exercise asks what the first terms reveal and gives a case
where they do not decide.

::: {#exr-hta-dimension-from-trace}
#### Hearing dimension, volume and curvature

Explain how $d$, $\operatorname{Vol}(M)$ and $\int_MR$ are read off from $Z(t)$ as $t \to 0$, and compute the first
two terms for the sphere of radius $R$ and for the flat torus of the same area $4\pi R^2$; which spectral quantity
distinguishes them?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$d$ is twice the exponent of the leading power $t^{-d/2}$, $\operatorname{Vol}$ is $(4\pi)^{d/2}$ times its
coefficient, and $\int R = 6a_1$ is read from the next term. For $S^2_R$: $\lambda_l = l(l + 1)/R^2$ and $Z(t) = \sum_l(2l + 1)e^{-tl(l + 1)/R^2}$ with $Z(t) \sim \frac{R^2}{t} + \frac13 + \dots$ (scalar curvature $2/R^2$ integrated over
$4\pi R^2$ gives $8\pi$, $a_1 = 4\pi/3$). For the torus of area $4\pi R^2$: $Z(t) \sim \frac{R^2}{t} + 0 + \dots$.
The leading terms coincide, as they must for equal volumes, and the constant term $\chi/6$ ($1/3$ versus $0$)
distinguishes them: the heat trace hears the Euler characteristic of a surface. Isospectral but non-isometric
manifolds exist in higher dimensions, so the full spectrum does not determine the geometry.
:::
::::

### Zeta regularisation

Sums over the spectrum such as $\sum_k\lambda_k$ or $\sum_k\log\lambda_k$ diverge, but the function $\sum_k
\lambda_k^{-s}$ converges for large $s$ and continues analytically to the values of $s$ at which the divergent sums
would sit. The definition below assigns values to such sums in this way and connects the procedure to the heat
trace.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-zeta-regularisation}
#### Zeta regularisation

For an operator with discrete spectrum $0 < \lambda_1 \leq \lambda_2 \leq \dots$ (zero modes excluded) satisfying
Weyl's law in dimension $d$, the **spectral zeta function** $\zeta_A(s) = \sum_k\lambda_k^{-s}$ converges for
$\operatorname{Re}s > d/2$ and extends to a meromorphic function of $s$, regular at $s = 0$ and at the negative
integers, through the Mellin transform $\zeta_A(s) = \frac{1}{\Gamma(s)}\int_0^\infty t^{s - 1}(Z(t) - \dim\ker
A)\,dt$ and the heat trace asymptotics (@exr-zr-heat-kernel-link). The **zeta-regularised sum** of the eigenvalues
is $\sum_k\lambda_k := \zeta_A(-1)$, and the **zeta-regularised determinant** is $\det{}_\zeta A := e^{-\zeta_A'(0)}$,
formalising $\sum\log\lambda_k = -\zeta_A'(0)$. For $\lambda_k = k$ the spectral zeta function is Riemann's
$\zeta(s)$ (@def-zeta-function), and $\zeta(-1) = -\tfrac{1}{12}$, $\zeta(0) = -\tfrac12$, $\zeta(-3) =
\tfrac{1}{120}$, $\zeta'(0) = -\tfrac12\log 2\pi$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The regularised value of $1 + 2 + 3 + \dots$ is $-1/12$, and a cutoff shows what this means: the divergence is a
pure power of the cutoff and the finite remainder is $-1/12$. The first example makes this comparison, which is the
form in which the value is used in physics.

::: {#exm-zr-sum-n}
#### $1 + 2 + 3 + \dots = -1/12$

$\zeta(-1) = -1/12$ is the analytic continuation of $\sum n^{-s}$ to $s = -1$ (Sage returns it exactly from
Bernoulli numbers, $\zeta(-n) = -B_{n + 1}/(n + 1)$, @exr-htv-bernoulli). With an exponential cutoff, $\sum_{n \geq
1}ne^{-\varepsilon n} = \frac{e^\varepsilon}{(e^\varepsilon - 1)^2} = \frac{1}{\varepsilon^2} - \frac{1}{12} +
\frac{\varepsilon^2}{240} + \dots$ (@prp-heat-trace-values): the divergent part $1/\varepsilon^2$ depends on the
cutoff and the finite part is $-1/12$. Likewise $\sum_{n \geq 1}e^{-\varepsilon n} = \frac1\varepsilon - \frac12 +
\dots$ has finite part $\zeta(0) = -\tfrac12$ (@exr-zr-abel-regularisation).
:::

The Dirichlet Laplacian on an interval has spectral zeta function $\zeta(2s)$, and its regularised determinant is a
pure number. The second example computes it, the simplest determinant of a differential operator.

::: {#exm-zr-det-dirichlet}
#### The determinant of $-d^2/dx^2$ on $(0, \pi)$

With Dirichlet conditions the eigenvalues are $n^2$ (@exm-sae-laplacian-interval), so $\zeta_A(s) = \sum n^{-2s} =
\zeta(2s)$, $\zeta_A'(0) = 2\zeta'(0) = -\log 2\pi$, and $\det{}_\zeta(-d^2/dx^2) = e^{\log 2\pi} = 2\pi$
(@exr-zr-sage-values). On an interval of length $L$ the eigenvalues are $(n\pi/L)^2$, $\zeta_A(s) = (L/\pi)^{2s}
\zeta(2s)$, and $\det{}_\zeta = e^{-2\log(L/\pi)\zeta(0) - 2\zeta'(0)} = (L/\pi)\cdot 2\pi = 2L$: the determinant
scales with the length, as $\zeta_A(0) = \zeta(0) = -\tfrac12$ dictates.
:::

On the circle the zero mode is removed and each non-zero eigenvalue is doubled; the regularised sums of even powers
vanish and the determinant is $4\pi^2$. The third example records these values and the regularised sum of
$|n|$, which is the Casimir energy of the circle.

::: {#exm-zr-circle}
#### The circle

For $-\Delta$ on the unit circle with the zero mode removed, $\zeta_\Delta(s) = \sum_{n \neq 0}(n^2)^{-s} =
2\zeta(2s)$. Then $\det{}_\zeta(-\Delta') = e^{-4\zeta'(0)} = (2\pi)^2 = 4\pi^2$; the regularised sum of the
eigenvalues is $2\zeta(-2) = 0$, as $\zeta$ vanishes at the negative even integers; and for the frequencies
$\omega_n = |n| = \sqrt{\lambda_n}$, $\sum_{n \neq 0}|n| = 2\zeta(-1) = -\tfrac16$, the value that enters the
Casimir energy of a periodic field (@exr-hso-circle-zeta).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Sage knows the Riemann zeta function exactly at the integers and numerically elsewhere, and it expands cutoff sums
symbolically. The first exercise asks for the values used above and for the Dirichlet determinant.

::: {#exr-zr-sage-values}
#### Zeta values in Sage

With Sage, evaluate $\zeta(-1)$, $\zeta(0)$, $\zeta(-3)$ exactly and $\zeta'(0)$ numerically against
$-\tfrac12\log 2\pi$, expand $\sum_{n \geq 1}e^{-\varepsilon n}$ and $\sum_{n \geq 1}n^3e^{-\varepsilon n}$ in
$\varepsilon$ to identify their finite parts with $\zeta(0)$ and $\zeta(-3)$, and compute $\det{}_\zeta(-d^2/dx^2)
= e^{-2\zeta'(0)}$ on $(0, \pi)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The finite parts are $-\tfrac12$ and $\tfrac{1}{120}$, matching $\zeta(0)$ and $\zeta(-3)$, and $e^{-2\zeta'(0)} =
2\pi$ to all digits computed:

{{< sage exr-zr-sage-values >}}
:::

The Mellin transform ties the spectral zeta function to the heat trace, and the heat asymptotics then locate the
poles of $\zeta_A$ and give $\zeta_A(0)$. The second exercise asks for the derivation and for the check on the
circle.

::: {#exr-zr-heat-kernel-link}
#### Zeta function from the heat trace

Using $\lambda^{-s} = \frac{1}{\Gamma(s)}\int_0^\infty t^{s - 1}e^{-t\lambda}dt$, derive the Mellin formula for
$\zeta_A(s)$. Inserting $Z(t) - \dim\ker A \sim (4\pi t)^{-d/2}\sum_ka_kt^k$ for small $t$, show that $\zeta_A$
has at most simple poles at $s = d/2 - k$ and that $\zeta_A(0) = \frac{a_{d/2}}{(4\pi)^{d/2}} - \dim\ker A$ for
even $d$, $\zeta_A(0) = -\dim\ker A$ for odd $d$; verify $\zeta_\Delta(0) = -1$ on the circle.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Summing the Gamma-function identity over the non-zero eigenvalues gives $\zeta_A(s) = \frac{1}{\Gamma(s)}
\int_0^\infty t^{s - 1}\sum_ke^{-t\lambda_k}dt = \frac{1}{\Gamma(s)}\int_0^\infty t^{s - 1}(Z(t) - \dim\ker A)dt$,
convergent for $\operatorname{Re}s > d/2$. Splitting the integral at $t = 1$, the part over $(1, \infty)$ is entire;
over $(0, 1)$ each term $a_kt^{k - d/2}$ integrates to $\frac{a_k}{(4\pi)^{d/2}(s + k - d/2)}$, a simple pole at
$s = d/2 - k$, while the subtracted $-\dim\ker A$ gives $-\dim\ker A/s$. Dividing by $\Gamma(s)$, which has a
simple zero at $s = 0$ with $1/\Gamma(s) \sim s$, the value at $s = 0$ is the residue of the pole at $s = 0$: the
term $k = d/2$ (present only for even $d$) contributes $a_{d/2}/(4\pi)^{d/2}$ and the kernel term $-\dim\ker A$.
On the circle, $d = 1$, $\dim\ker = 1$: $\zeta_\Delta(0) = -1 = 2\zeta(0)$, consistent with $\zeta_\Delta(s) =
2\zeta(2s)$.
:::

The finite part of a cutoff sum does not depend on the shape of the cutoff function, which is what makes the
regularised value meaningful. The last exercise proves this with the Euler-Maclaurin formula for the class of
cutoffs $g(\varepsilon n)$.

::: {#exr-zr-abel-regularisation}
#### Universality of the finite part

Let $g$ be smooth with $g(0) = 1$ and rapidly decaying. Using the Euler-Maclaurin formula $\sum_{n \geq 1}f(n) =
\int_0^\infty f\,dx - \tfrac12f(0) - \tfrac{1}{12}f'(0) + \tfrac{1}{720}f'''(0) - \dots$ with $f(x) = x\,g(\varepsilon
x)$, show that $\sum_{n \geq 1}n\,g(\varepsilon n) = \frac{C_g}{\varepsilon^2} - \frac{1}{12} + O(\varepsilon)$ with
$C_g = \int_0^\infty xg(x)dx$, so the finite part is $-1/12$ for every such $g$; identify $C_g$ for $g = e^{-x}$ and
$g = e^{-x^2}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\int_0^\infty xg(\varepsilon x)dx = \varepsilon^{-2}\int_0^\infty yg(y)dy = C_g/\varepsilon^2$; $f(0) = 0$; $f'(x) =
g(\varepsilon x) + \varepsilon xg'(\varepsilon x)$ gives $f'(0) = g(0) = 1$; and $f'''(0) = 3\varepsilon^2g''(0) =
O(\varepsilon^2)$, with all higher derivatives at $0$ carrying higher powers of $\varepsilon$. So the sum is
$C_g/\varepsilon^2 - 1/12 + O(\varepsilon^2)$, and the finite part $-\tfrac{1}{12} = \zeta(-1)$ is independent of
$g$. $C_g = 1$ for $e^{-x}$ (matching @exm-zr-sum-n) and $C_g = \tfrac12$ for $e^{-x^2}$. The same argument applied to
$f(x) = g(\varepsilon x)$ gives the finite part $-\tfrac12 f(0) = -\tfrac12$ for $\sum g(\varepsilon n)$, that is, $\zeta(0)$.
:::
::::

### The Casimir energy in outline

A quantised field confined to a finite region has a zero-point energy $\tfrac12\sum\omega_k$ over its modes, which
diverges; zeta regularisation extracts a finite part that depends on the size of the region and produces a
measurable force. The proposition below states the result for an interval and quotes it for parallel plates, as an
outline of how the regularised sums of this section enter physics.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-casimir-energy}
#### Casimir energy

For a massless scalar field on an interval of length $L$ with Dirichlet conditions at both ends, the modes have
frequencies $\omega_n = n\pi/L$ (@exm-sae-laplacian-interval, $\omega_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}$ as in
@exm-ds-field-decomposition), and the zero-point energy $E = \tfrac12\sum_n\omega_n$ has the zeta-regularised value
$E(L) = \frac{\pi}{2L}\zeta(-1) = -\frac{\pi}{24L}$ (units $\hbar = c = 1$), giving the attractive **Casimir force**
$F = -\frac{dE}{dL} = -\frac{\pi}{24L^2}$ between the ends. With a cutoff, $E_\varepsilon = \frac{L}{2\pi
\varepsilon^2} - \frac{\pi}{24L} + O(\varepsilon^2)$: the divergent part is proportional to $L$, a bulk energy
density independent of the boundaries, and only the finite part gives an $L$-dependent force. For the
electromagnetic field between parallel conducting plates at separation $a$ the same method gives $E/A = -
\frac{\pi^2\hbar c}{720a^3}$ and $F/A = -\frac{\pi^2\hbar c}{240a^4}$ (Casimir, quoted; @exr-ce-plates). The
statement is an outline: the field quantisation that produces $\tfrac12\sum\omega_n$ is the subject of
@sec-quantum-field-theory.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The cutoff computation makes the structure of the result visible: the divergence is a bulk term, and the finite
part is the zeta value. The first example carries it out with the exponential cutoff of @exm-zr-sum-n.

::: {#exm-ce-interval}
#### The cutoff computation on the interval

$E_\varepsilon = \frac{\pi}{2L}\sum_{n \geq 1}ne^{-\varepsilon n\pi/L} = \frac{\pi}{2L}\left[\frac{L^2}{\pi^2
\varepsilon^2} - \frac{1}{12} + \frac{\pi^2\varepsilon^2}{240L^2} + \dots\right] = \frac{L}{2\pi\varepsilon^2} -
\frac{\pi}{24L} + O(\varepsilon^2)$ (@exr-ce-cutoff). The term $L/(2\pi\varepsilon^2)$ is an energy per unit length
times $L$, the same inside and outside any boundary and so without effect on forces between boundaries; the
remainder $-\pi/(24L)$ is the Casimir energy, and @exr-zr-abel-regularisation shows that it does not depend on
the cutoff function.
:::

The sign and the magnitude of the force depend on the boundary conditions and on the dimension, and in one
dimension the computation can be repeated for other conditions. The second example contrasts Dirichlet, periodic
and mixed conditions, the last giving a repulsive force.

::: {#exm-ce-force}
#### Dependence on the boundary conditions

Dirichlet (or Neumann) conditions give $E = -\pi/(24L)$ and an attractive force $-\pi/(24L^2)$. For a field on a
circle of circumference $L$ (periodic conditions), $\omega_n = 2\pi|n|/L$ for $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $E =
\frac{\pi}{L}\sum_{n \neq 0}|n| = \frac{2\pi}{L}\zeta(-1) = -\frac{\pi}{6L}$, four times larger
(@exr-hso-circle-zeta). For mixed conditions, Dirichlet at one end and Neumann at the other, $\omega_n = (n +
\tfrac12)\pi/L$ and $E = \frac{\pi}{2L}\zeta_H(-1, \tfrac12) = +\frac{\pi}{48L}$ with the Hurwitz zeta function
$\zeta_H(s, a) = \sum_{n \geq 0}(n + a)^{-s}$: the force is repulsive (@exr-ce-mixed).
:::

Between parallel plates the modes have a continuous transverse momentum and a discrete normal one, and the
regularised sum over both gives Casimir's $a^{-3}$ law. The third example states the numbers and the size of the
effect at micrometre separations.

::: {#exm-ce-plates}
#### Parallel plates

For the electromagnetic field (two polarisations) between plates of area $A$ at separation $a$, $E/A = -\frac{\pi^2
\hbar c}{720a^3}$ and the pressure is $F/A = -\frac{\pi^2\hbar c}{240a^4}$; a single scalar field with Dirichlet
conditions gives half of this (@exr-ce-plates). Numerically $\pi^2\hbar c/240 = 1.3\times10^{-27}\,\mathrm{J\,m}$,
so at $a = 1\,\mu\mathrm{m}$ the pressure is $1.3\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{Pa}$, measurable and measured; the
$a^{-4}$ law follows from dimensional analysis alone once $\hbar c$ is the only scale.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The cutoff expansion of the interval energy is a Taylor series that Sage computes, and the finite part can be
compared with a different cutoff. The first exercise asks for the expansion with exponential and Gaussian cutoffs.

::: {#exr-ce-cutoff}
#### Cutoffs in Sage

With Sage, expand $E_\varepsilon = \frac{\pi}{2L}\sum_{n \geq 1}ne^{-\varepsilon n\pi/L}$ in $\varepsilon$ to
order $\varepsilon^2$ and read off the bulk term and the Casimir energy; then evaluate $\frac{\pi}{2L}\sum_n
ne^{-\varepsilon^2n^2}$ numerically for $L = 1$ and $\varepsilon = 0.1, 0.05$, subtract the bulk term
$\frac{\pi}{2L}\cdot\frac{1}{2\varepsilon^2}$, and compare with $-\pi/24$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The exponential cutoff gives $\frac{L}{2\pi\varepsilon^2} - \frac{\pi}{24L} + \frac{\pi^3\varepsilon^2}{480L^3}$;
with the Gaussian cutoff the bulk term is $\frac{\pi}{4L\varepsilon^2}$ (as $C_g = \tfrac12$) and the remainder approaches
$-\pi/24 = -0.1309$ with an error of order $\varepsilon^2$ ($1.3\times10^{-4}$ at $\varepsilon = 0.1$, $3\times10^{-5}$ at
$\varepsilon = 0.05$):

{{< sage exr-ce-cutoff >}}
:::

Mixed boundary conditions shift the spectrum by a half-integer, and the Hurwitz zeta function evaluates the
regularised sum; Sage has it built in. The second exercise computes the repulsive Casimir energy and checks the
Hurwitz value against Bernoulli polynomials.

::: {#exr-ce-mixed}
#### Mixed conditions and the Hurwitz zeta function

With Sage, evaluate $\zeta_H(-1, \tfrac12)$ and compare with $-B_2(\tfrac12)/2$ for the Bernoulli polynomial
$B_2(x) = x^2 - x + \tfrac16$; deduce $E = \frac{\pi}{2L}\sum_{n \geq 0}(n + \tfrac12) = \frac{\pi}{48L}$ for the
Dirichlet-Neumann interval, and check the identity $\sum_{n \geq 0}(n + \tfrac12)^{-s} = (2^s - 1)\zeta(s)$ at
$s = -1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\zeta_H(-1, \tfrac12) = -B_2(\tfrac12)/2 = -(\tfrac14 - \tfrac12 + \tfrac16)/2 = \tfrac{1}{24}$, so $E =
\frac{\pi}{48L} > 0$ and $F = -dE/dL = \frac{\pi}{48L^2}$ is repulsive; the identity gives $(2^{-1} - 1)\zeta(-1) =
-\tfrac12\cdot(-\tfrac{1}{12}) = \tfrac{1}{24}$ as well:

{{< sage exr-ce-mixed >}}
:::

The parallel-plate result combines a continuous integral over transverse momenta with a discrete sum, and zeta
regularisation of both gives the $a^{-3}$ law with the value $\zeta(-3) = 1/120$. The last exercise asks for this
derivation in outline.

::: {#exr-ce-plates}
#### Casimir's $a^{-3}$ law

For a scalar field with Dirichlet conditions on two plates at separation $a$, the modes are $e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot
\mathbf{x}_\perp}\sin(n\pi z/a)$ with $\omega = \sqrt{k^2 + (n\pi/a)^2}$. Using the regularised integral
$\int\frac{d^2k}{(2\pi)^2}(k^2 + m^2)^{-s} = \frac{m^{2 - 2s}}{4\pi(s - 1)}$ at $s = -\tfrac12$, show that
$\frac{E}{A} = \frac12\sum_n\int\frac{d^2k}{(2\pi)^2}\omega = -\frac{\pi^2}{12a^3}\sum_nn^3 = -\frac{\pi^2}{1440a^3}$,
and that two polarisations give Casimir's $-\pi^2/(720a^3)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
At $s = -\tfrac12$ the regularised integral is $\frac{m^3}{4\pi(-3/2)} = -\frac{m^3}{6\pi}$ with $m = n\pi/a$, so
$\frac{E}{A} = \frac12\sum_n\left(-\frac{n^3\pi^3}{6\pi a^3}\right) = -\frac{\pi^2}{12a^3}\sum_{n \geq 1}n^3 = -
\frac{\pi^2}{12a^3}\zeta(-3) = -\frac{\pi^2}{12a^3}\cdot\frac{1}{120} = -\frac{\pi^2}{1440a^3}$. The
electromagnetic field has two polarisations, each contributing this amount, giving $-\pi^2/(720a^3)$ and the
pressure $-\pi^2/(240a^4)$; restoring units multiplies by $\hbar c$. The analytic continuation of the
$k$-integral from $\operatorname{Re}s > 1$ to $s = -\tfrac12$ is the same mechanism as $\zeta(-3)$, applied to the
continuous part of the spectrum.
:::
::::

### Worked computations

The Poisson summation formula for the circle heat trace, the leading asymptotics on the circle and the sphere, the
zeta values, the cutoff expansion and the trace and determinant identities of the section can all be evaluated
explicitly. The proposition collects them.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-heat-trace-values}
#### Heat traces and zeta values

The circle heat trace $Z(t) = \sum_ne^{-tn^2}$ equals $\sqrt{\pi/t}\sum_ke^{-\pi^2k^2/t}$ to $10^{-18}$ at $t =
\tfrac{1}{10}, \tfrac12, 1$, and $Z(t) - \sqrt{\pi/t}$ is within $1\%$ of $2\sqrt{\pi/t}e^{-\pi^2/t}$ at $t = 0.2, 0.4,
\dots, 1$; the sphere heat trace $\sum_l(2l + 1)e^{-tl(l + 1)}$ differs from $\frac1t + \frac13 + \frac{t}{15}$ by less than
$0.02t^2$ for $t \leq 0.2$; $\zeta(-1) = -\tfrac{1}{12}$, $\zeta(0) = -\tfrac12$, $\zeta(-3) = \tfrac{1}{120}$
exactly and $\zeta'(0) = -\tfrac12\log 2\pi$ to $25$ digits; $\sum_{n \geq 1}ne^{-\varepsilon n} = \varepsilon^{-2} -
\tfrac{1}{12} + \tfrac{\varepsilon^2}{240} + O(\varepsilon^4)$; $\operatorname{tr}(AB) = \operatorname{tr}(BA)$
and $\det e^A = e^{\operatorname{tr}A}$ for an explicit $3 \times 3$ matrix; and $\operatorname{tr}G = \sum
1/(n\pi)^2 = \int_0^1(x - x^2)dx = \tfrac16$ with $\sin\sqrt z/\sqrt z = 1 - z/6 + \dots$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Exact computation (`figures/heat_trace_circle.sage`, exact zeta values and symbolic
series, with the Poisson identity tested at high precision).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The two panels of the figure show the two regimes of the circle heat trace: the zero mode dominates for large $t$
and the Weyl term for small $t$, with an exponentially small crossover. The first example reads the numbers.

::: {#exm-htv-figure}
#### Reading the figure

At $t = 3$, $Z(t) = 1 + 2e^{-3} + \dots = 1.0996$, essentially the zero mode; at $t = 0.1$, $Z(t) = 5.6050 =
\sqrt{10\pi}$ to twelve digits, the Weyl term alone; the Weyl term $\sqrt{\pi/t}$ falls below the large-$t$ limit
$1$ at $t = \pi$, where neither approximation is good. The right panel shows that the deviation from the Weyl term
is $2\sqrt{\pi/t}e^{-\pi^2/t}$, invisible on a linear scale below $t = 0.5$ (about $10^{-8}$) and only
$1.8\times10^{-4}$ at $t = 1$.
:::

The Poisson summation formula is an exact identity, so the asymptotic statement of the theorem is, for the circle, a
convergent expansion in exponentially small terms. The second example states this as the functional equation of the
theta function.

::: {#exm-htv-poisson}
#### The theta function

$\theta(t) = \sum_ne^{-tn^2}$ satisfies $\theta(t) = \sqrt{\pi/t}\,\theta(\pi^2/t)$ (@exr-hk-poisson-summation),
and since $\theta(\pi^2/t) = 1 + 2e^{-\pi^2/t} + \dots \to 1$ as $t \to 0$, the small-$t$ expansion of $Z(t) =
\theta(t)$ is $\sqrt{\pi/t}(1 + 2e^{-\pi^2/t} + 2e^{-4\pi^2/t} + \dots)$ with no power corrections at all. The same
identity relates the two regimes of the torus trace $\theta(t/R_1^2)\theta(t/R_2^2)$ (@exr-htv-torus-trace) and
underlies the modular invariance of theta functions.
:::

The exact zeta values at negative integers come from Bernoulli numbers, and the values at positive even integers from
the same numbers with powers of $\pi$. The third example records the formulas that Sage uses and that the exercises
check.

::: {#exm-htv-zeta}
#### Zeta values from Bernoulli numbers

$\zeta(-n) = -\frac{B_{n + 1}}{n + 1}$ for $n \geq 1$ and $\zeta(2n) = \frac{(-1)^{n + 1}B_{2n}(2\pi)^{2n}}{2(2n)!}$,
with $B_2 = \tfrac16$, $B_4 = -\tfrac{1}{30}$, $B_6 = \tfrac{1}{42}$: $\zeta(-1) = -\tfrac{1}{12}$, $\zeta(-3) =
\tfrac{1}{120}$, $\zeta(-5) = -\tfrac{1}{252}$, $\zeta(2) = \tfrac{\pi^2}{6}$ (@exm-onb-fourier-parseval),
$\zeta(4) = \tfrac{\pi^4}{90}$ (@exr-onb-parseval-x); $\zeta(0) = -\tfrac12$ and $\zeta(-2n) = 0$ because $B_{2n +
1} = 0$ (@exr-htv-bernoulli). These are the values that appear in regularised sums, Casimir energies and the
expansion of the cutoff sums.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The torus heat trace is the product of two circle traces, and both regimes are visible numerically. The first
exercise computes it and its leading term for two tori of equal area.

::: {#exr-htv-torus-trace}
#### The torus heat trace

With Sage, compute $Z_{T^2}(t) = \sum_{|m|, |n| \leq 60}e^{-t(m^2/R_1^2 + n^2/R_2^2)}$ for $(R_1, R_2) = (1, 1)$
and $(2, \tfrac12)$ at $t = 0.1, 0.5, 2$, check $Z_{T^2}(t) = \theta(t/R_1^2)\theta(t/R_2^2)$, and compare with
the leading term $\pi R_1R_2/t$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Both tori have area $4\pi^2$ and leading term $\pi/t$, but their traces differ at finite $t$ (the second has the
small eigenvalue $1/4$); the factorisation holds to machine precision:

{{< sage exr-htv-torus-trace >}}
:::

The functional equation of the theta function converts large-$t$ information into small-$t$ information and vice
versa, and it fixes the asymptotics in both directions. The second exercise asks for these consequences and for
the modular reading of the identity.

::: {#exr-htv-theta-functional-equation}
#### Two regimes from one identity

From $\theta(t) = \sqrt{\pi/t}\,\theta(\pi^2/t)$ and the definition of $\theta$, derive $\theta(t) \to 1$ as $t \to
\infty$, $\theta(t) \sim \sqrt{\pi/t}$ as $t \to 0$ with the error $2\sqrt{\pi/t}e^{-\pi^2/t}(1 + O(e^{-3\pi^2/t}))$,
and show that $t^{1/4}\theta(t)$ is invariant under $t \mapsto \pi^2/t$. Why is the small-$t$ limit "hard" from
the definition but "easy" from the identity?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
From the definition, $\theta(t) = 1 + 2\sum_{n \geq 1}e^{-tn^2} \to 1$ as $t \to \infty$, the terms decaying
exponentially. Applying the identity, $\theta(t) = \sqrt{\pi/t}(1 + 2e^{-\pi^2/t} + 2e^{-4\pi^2/t} + \dots)$, so
$\theta(t) - \sqrt{\pi/t} = 2\sqrt{\pi/t}e^{-\pi^2/t}(1 + e^{-3\pi^2/t} + \dots)$. Multiplying the identity by
$t^{1/4}$: $t^{1/4}\theta(t) = \pi^{1/2}t^{-1/4}\theta(\pi^2/t) = (\pi^2/t)^{1/4}\theta(\pi^2/t)$, invariant. For
small $t$ the series $\sum e^{-tn^2}$ converges slowly (about $1/\sqrt t$ terms matter), while the dual series needs
one term: the identity exchanges the two regimes, which is the content of modular invariance.
:::

Sage's `bernoulli` gives the Bernoulli numbers, and the two formulas of @exm-htv-zeta can be checked against
`zeta` for a range of integers. The last exercise does this and adds the vanishing at negative even integers.

::: {#exr-htv-bernoulli}
#### Bernoulli numbers and zeta values

With Sage, verify $\zeta(-n) = -B_{n + 1}/(n + 1)$ for $n = 1, \dots, 9$, $\zeta(2n) = (-1)^{n + 1}B_{2n}
(2\pi)^{2n}/(2(2n)!)$ for $n = 1, \dots, 4$, and $\zeta(-2n) = 0$ for $n = 1, \dots, 4$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
All identities hold exactly, with $B_3 = B_5 = \dots = 0$ producing the trivial zeros:

{{< sage exr-htv-bernoulli >}}
:::
::::

## Banach and C\*-algebras {#sec-banach-algebras}

Bounded operators can be added, multiplied and normed, and many of their properties depend only on these operations. A Banach
algebra abstracts them; a C\*-algebra adds the adjoint and the identity $\|a^*a\| = \|a\|^2$ that holds for operators on a Hilbert
space. This part defines both, proves that every element of a Banach algebra has a non-empty compact spectrum whose radius is
$\lim\|a^n\|^{1/n}$, and constructs the continuous functional calculus of self-adjoint elements, which is how functions of
observables are defined in quantum mechanics. The outline follows @arcozzi2025 [Sec. 6.1] and @landsman1998 [Sec. 2.1-2.5 and
2.8], with numerical examples from @izaac2018computational [Ch. 7].

### Banach algebras

In a Banach algebra the geometric series converges whenever the ratio has norm less than one, exactly as for numbers. The figure
shows the partial sums of $\sum A^k$ for two matrices, one of norm less than one and one whose norm is larger but whose powers
still decay, and the definition below names the setting.

![The error $\|(1 - A)^{-1} - \sum_{k < N}A^k\|$ against $N$ for $A_1 = \tfrac12\sigma_1$ ($\|A_1\| = \tfrac12$, geometric decay
$2^{1 - N}$) and $A_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1/2 & 4 \\ 0 & 1/2\end{pmatrix}$ ($\|A_2\| > 4$, but $A_2^k \to 0$): the error of the second series
decreases slowly at first, is still above $1$ at $N = 7$, and then decays at the rate $N2^{-N}$ set by the spectral radius
$\tfrac12$. Generated by
`figures/fa2-neumann-series.sage`.](figures/fa2-neumann-series.svg){#fig-fa2-neumann-series width=60%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-banach-algebra}
#### Banach algebra

A **Banach algebra** is a complex Banach space $\mathcal{A}$ with an associative bilinear product satisfying $\|ab\| \leq
\|a\|\,\|b\|$; it is **unital** if it has a unit $1$ with $\|1\| = 1$ @arcozzi2025 [Sec. 6.1.1]; @landsman1998 [Def. 2.1.8].
An element $a$ is **invertible** if $ab = ba = 1$ for some $b = a^{-1}$; a left and a right inverse, when both exist, coincide.
Every Banach algebra without unit embeds in the unital algebra $\mathcal{A} \oplus \mathbb{C}$ with the norm $\|a + z\| = \|a\| +
|z|$ @arcozzi2025 [Exercise 6.1]; @landsman1998 [Prop. 2.2.1].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The bounded operators on a Banach space form the model Banach algebra, and the shift shows that one-sided inverses need not be
inverses. The first example records both facts @arcozzi2025 [Sec. 6.1.1].

::: {#exm-fan-operator-algebra}
#### Bounded operators

$\mathcal{B}(X)$ with composition and the operator norm is a unital Banach algebra (@def-bounded-linear-map). In
$\mathcal{B}(\ell^2)$, $S^*S = 1$ but $SS^* \neq 1$: $S$ has the left inverse $S^*$ and no right inverse, since it is not onto.
The $n \times n$ matrices with the operator norm are the finite-dimensional case.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Continuous functions with the pointwise product form a commutative Banach algebra in which invertibility is decided pointwise.
The second example states it.

::: {#exm-fan-ck-algebra}
#### $C(K)$

$C(K)$ with pointwise operations and the supremum norm is a commutative unital Banach algebra, $\|fg\|_\infty \leq
\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_\infty$. A function $f$ is invertible iff it has no zero on $K$, the inverse being $1/f$, continuous on the
compact set $K$. So $x$ is invertible in $C[1, 2]$ but not in $C[0, 1]$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Convolution of summable sequences gives the algebra of absolutely convergent Fourier series. The third example describes this
**Wiener algebra** @arcozzi2025 [Sec. 6.1.1, item 3].

::: {#exm-fan-wiener-algebra}
#### The Wiener algebra

$\ell^1(\mathbb{Z})$ with $(a * b)_n = \sum_ma_mb_{n - m}$ is a commutative unital Banach algebra, $\|a * b\|_1 \leq
\|a\|_1\|b\|_1$, with unit $\delta^{(0)}$. Under $a \mapsto \hat a(\theta) = \sum_na_ne^{in\theta}$ it becomes the algebra of
absolutely convergent Fourier series with pointwise product, $\widehat{a * b} = \hat a\hat b$. By **Wiener's lemma**, $a$ is
invertible in $\ell^1(\mathbb{Z})$ iff $\hat a$ has no zero.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The unitisation makes every Banach algebra unital, and its norm is checked in the first exercise @arcozzi2025 [Exercise 6.1]. The construction
is what allows the spectrum to be defined in non-unital algebras.

::: {#exr-fan-unitisation}
#### Adding a unit

On $\mathcal{A} \oplus \mathbb{C}$ with $(a + z)(b + w) = ab + zb + wa + zw$ and $\|a + z\| = \|a\| + |z|$, show that the norm is
submultiplicative and that $\|1\| = 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\|(a + z)(b + w)\| \leq \|ab\| + |z|\,\|b\| + |w|\,\|a\| + |zw| \leq \|a\|\,\|b\| + |z|\,\|b\| + |w|\,\|a\| + |z|\,|w| = (\|a\| +
|z|)(\|b\| + |w|)$, and $1 = 0 + 1$ has norm $1$. Completeness follows from that of $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathbb{C}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Commuting elements whose product is invertible are both invertible, and the shift shows that commutation is needed. The second
exercise proves this @arcozzi2025 [Thm. 6.1].

::: {#exr-fan-commuting-inverse}
#### Products of commuting elements

If $ab = ba$ and $ab$ is invertible, show that $(ab)^{-1}a$ is a left and $a(ab)^{-1}$ a right inverse of $b$, so $b$ is invertible.
Why does $S^*S = 1$ not contradict this?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(ab)^{-1}ab = 1$ shows that $(ab)^{-1}a$ is a left inverse of $b$, and $ba(ab)^{-1} = ab(ab)^{-1} = 1$ that $a(ab)^{-1}$ is a right
inverse; the two coincide, so $b$ is invertible, and similarly $a$. For the shift, $S^*$ and $S$ do not commute ($SS^* \neq S^*S$), so
the hypothesis fails.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Not every natural norm on matrices is submultiplicative, and the third exercise shows that the largest entry fails. It also shows
how to repair it.

::: {#exr-fan-max-entry-norm}
#### A norm that is not submultiplicative

Show that $\|A\|_{\max} = \max_{ij}|A_{ij}|$ on $n \times n$ matrices is a norm but not submultiplicative, using $J = \begin{pmatrix} 1
& 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, and that $n\|A\|_{\max}$ is submultiplicative.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$J^2 = 2J$, so $\|J^2\|_{\max} = 2 > 1 = \|J\|_{\max}^2$. For the scaled norm, $|(AB)_{ij}| \leq \sum_k|A_{ik}||B_{kj}| \leq
n\|A\|_{\max}\|B\|_{\max}$, so $n\|AB\|_{\max} \leq (n\|A\|_{\max})(n\|B\|_{\max})$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

The geometric series of an element of norm less than one converges, and its sum is the inverse of one minus the element. The theorem
below states this and its consequence that invertibility survives small perturbations.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-neumann-series}
#### Neumann series

In a unital Banach algebra, if $\|a\| < 1$ then $1 - a$ is invertible, $(1 - a)^{-1} = \sum_{n \geq 0}a^n$ (the **Neumann series**),
and $\|(1 - a)^{-1}\| \leq (1 - \|a\|)^{-1}$. If $a$ is invertible and $\|b - a\| < \|a^{-1}\|^{-1}$, then $b$ is invertible; so the
invertible elements form an open set, on which $a \mapsto a^{-1}$ is continuous @arcozzi2025 [Thm. 6.2]; @landsman1998 [Lemmas
2.2.4 and 2.2.5]. The series converges more generally whenever $\|a^n\|^{1/n}$ is eventually less than one.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For a matrix of small norm the series can be summed by hand. The first example sums it for a multiple of a Pauli matrix.

::: {#exm-fan-neumann-pauli}
#### A Pauli matrix

For $a = t\sigma_1$ with $|t| < 1$, $a^2 = t^2$, so $\sum a^n = (1 + t\sigma_1)\sum t^{2n} = \tfrac{1 + t\sigma_1}{1 - t^2}$, which is
$(1 - t\sigma_1)^{-1}$; the bound $(1 - |t|)^{-1}$ is attained, since $\|(1 - t\sigma_1)^{-1}\| = \max_\pm|1 \mp t|^{-1}$. For $t = \tfrac12$
this is @exr-fan-neumann-matrix.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Integral equations of the second kind with a small coupling are solved by the Neumann series, which physicists call the Born series.
The second example applies it to a rank-one kernel and compares with the exact solution.

::: {#exm-fan-born-series}
#### The Born series

For $Kf(x) = \int_0^1xyf(y)\,dy$ on $L^2(0, 1)$, $\|K\| = \int_0^1x^2dx = \tfrac13$ and $K^n = 3^{1 - n}K$. The series $\sum\lambda^nK^n$
converges for $|\lambda| < 3$ to $1 + \tfrac{\lambda}{1 - \lambda/3}K$, which is the exact resolvent of @exm-fan-rank-one-equation.
The radius of convergence $3$ is the first value where the equation stops being uniquely solvable.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A matrix can have norm larger than one and still have a convergent Neumann series, as the figure shows. The third example computes
the powers of the second matrix of the figure.

::: {#exm-fan-neumann-nonnormal}
#### Large norm, small powers

$A = \tfrac12 + 4N$ with $N = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}$, $N^2 = 0$, has $A^k = 2^{-k} + 4k2^{1 - k}N$, so $\|A^k\| \to 0$
although $\|A\| > 4$. The Neumann series converges to $(1 - A)^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 16 \\ 0 & 2\end{pmatrix}$, and the partial
sums approach it only after the transient visible in the figure.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise asks for the proof of the theorem. The perturbation statement follows from the Neumann series by factoring out
$a$.

::: {#exr-fan-neumann-proof}
#### Proof of the theorem

Show that $\sum a^n$ converges if $\|a\| < 1$ (@thm-absolute-series) and that $(1 - a)\sum_{n \leq N}a^n = 1 - a^{N + 1}$. For the
perturbation, write $b = a(1 - a^{-1}(a - b))$. Show also that $\|b^{-1} - a^{-1}\| \leq \tfrac{\|a^{-1}\|^2\|b - a\|}{1 -
\|a^{-1}\|\,\|b - a\|}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\sum\|a^n\| \leq \sum\|a\|^n < \infty$, and the telescoping identity gives $(1 - a)\sum a^n = 1$ in the limit, similarly on the other
side; the norm bound follows from the geometric sum. With $c = a^{-1}(a - b)$, $\|c\| \leq \|a^{-1}\|\,\|b - a\| < 1$, so $b = a(1 -
c)$ is invertible with $b^{-1} = (1 - c)^{-1}a^{-1}$. Then $b^{-1} - a^{-1} = ((1 - c)^{-1} - 1)a^{-1} = \sum_{n \geq 1}c^na^{-1}$, of
norm at most $\tfrac{\|c\|}{1 - \|c\|}\|a^{-1}\|$, which gives the bound and the continuity of inversion.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Inverting a matrix by its Neumann series is an iteration, and Sage shows its convergence. The second exercise computes the inverse
of $1 - A$ for the non-normal matrix of the figure.

::: {#exr-fan-neumann-nonnormal-sage}
#### The non-normal series in Sage

For $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1/2 & 4 \\ 0 & 1/2\end{pmatrix}$, compute $(1 - A)^{-1}$ exactly, the partial sums $\sum_{k < N}A^k$ for $N =
5, 10, 20, 40$, and the norm of the error. At which $N$ does the error first drop below $1$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(1 - A)^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 16 \\ 0 & 2\end{pmatrix}$. The error is $\sum_{k \geq N}A^k$, whose off-diagonal entry is $8\sum_{k \geq
N}k2^{-k} = 8(N + 1)2^{1 - N}$, so it decays like $N2^{-N}$:

{{< sage exr-fan-neumann-nonnormal-sage >}}
:::

The Born series of the rank-one kernel can be summed in closed form, which the third exercise asks for. It shows that the series
diverges exactly where the solution stops being unique.

::: {#exr-fan-born-sum}
#### Summing the Born series

With $K$ as in @exm-fan-born-series, show $K^n = 3^{1 - n}K$, sum $\sum_n\lambda^nK^nf$ for $f = 1$, and compare with the solution of
@exm-fan-rank-one-equation. What happens at $|\lambda| = 3$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$K^2f = x\int y^2\int zf = \tfrac13Kf$, so $K^n = 3^{1 - n}K$. For $f = 1$, $Kf = \tfrac x2$ and $\sum_{n \geq 0}\lambda^nK^n1 = 1 +
\tfrac x2\sum_{n \geq 1}\lambda^n3^{1 - n} = 1 + \tfrac{\lambda x/2}{1 - \lambda/3}$, matching $c = \tfrac{1/2}{1 - \lambda/3}$ in the
example. At $|\lambda| = 3$ the series diverges; at $\lambda = 3$ the equation has no solution for $f = 1$, as $\int y\cdot 1 \neq 0$.

Sage computes the powers of $K$, sums the series and solves the equation directly:

{{< sage exr-fan-born-sum >}}
:::

### Spectrum and spectral radius

The spectrum of an element of a Banach algebra is the set of numbers $\lambda$ for which $\lambda - a$ cannot be inverted. The figure
shows how $\|a^n\|^{1/n}$ converges to the largest modulus in the spectrum, for matrices and for the Volterra operator, and the
definition below introduces the spectrum.

![$\|a^n\|^{1/n}$ against $n$ for the matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 1/2 & 4 \\ 0 & 1/2\end{pmatrix}$ (spectral radius $\tfrac12$), the matrix
$\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 9 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 2\end{pmatrix}$ of @izaac2018computational [Problem P7.6] (eigenvalues $3, -3, 2$,
spectral radius $3$) and the Volterra operator on $C[0, 1]$, $\|V^n\| = 1/n!$ (spectral radius $0$). The dashed lines are the
limits. Generated by `figures/fa2-spectral-radius.sage`.](figures/fa2-spectral-radius.svg){#fig-fa2-spectral-radius width=60%}

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-algebra-spectrum}
#### Spectrum in a Banach algebra

Let $\mathcal{A}$ be a unital Banach algebra and $a \in \mathcal{A}$. The **resolvent set** $\rho(a)$ is the set of $\lambda \in
\mathbb{C}$ for which $\lambda - a$ is invertible, the **spectrum** is $\sigma(a) = \mathbb{C} \setminus \rho(a)$, the **resolvent** is
$R_\lambda(a) = (\lambda - a)^{-1}$, holomorphic on $\rho(a)$, and the **spectral radius** is $r(a) = \max\{|\lambda| : \lambda \in
\sigma(a)\}$ @arcozzi2025 [Sec. 6.1.2, 6.1.5]; @landsman1998 [Def. 2.2.2]. The spectrum is a non-empty compact subset of the disc
$|\lambda| \leq \|a\|$ @arcozzi2025 [Thms. 6.3 and 6.4]; @landsman1998 [Thm. 2.2.3]. For $\mathcal{A} = \mathcal{B}(H)$ it is the
spectrum of @def-spectrum.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
In $C(K)$ the spectrum of a function is its set of values. The first example derives this from the invertibility criterion of
@exm-fan-ck-algebra.

::: {#exm-fan-spectrum-ck}
#### Functions

$\lambda - f$ is invertible in $C(K)$ iff $f(x) \neq \lambda$ for all $x$, so $\sigma(f) = f(K)$, a compact set, and $r(f) =
\|f\|_\infty$. For $f(\theta) = e^{i\theta}$ on the circle, $\sigma(f)$ is the unit circle; for $f(x) = x^2$ on $[-1, 1]$ it is $[0,
1]$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

For a multiplication operator on $L^2$ the spectrum is the essential range of the multiplier, a measure-theoretic version of the
previous example. The second example states it @arcozzi2025 [Sec. 6.1.3].

::: {#exm-fan-spectrum-multiplication}
#### Multiplication operators

For $g \in L^\infty$, $\sigma(M_g)$ is the **essential range** of $g$, the set of $w$ with $\mu\{|g - w| < \varepsilon\} > 0$ for every
$\varepsilon > 0$. For $g(x) = x$ on $L^2(0, 1)$ it is $[0, 1]$, with no eigenvalues; for $g = \mathbf{1}_{[0, 1/2]}$ it is $\{0, 1\}$,
both eigenvalues of infinite multiplicity.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The spectrum depends on the algebra in which inverses are sought, and it can only shrink when the algebra grows. The third example
compares the coordinate $z$ in two algebras of functions.

::: {#exm-fan-spectrum-depends}
#### The spectrum depends on the algebra

In $C(S^1)$ the function $z = e^{i\theta}$ has spectrum the unit circle. In the **disc algebra** $A(\bar D)$ of continuous functions
on the closed disc holomorphic inside, restricted to the circle (a closed subalgebra of $C(S^1)$), $\lambda - z$ with $|\lambda| < 1$
is not invertible, since its inverse would be holomorphic with a pole at $\lambda$; so $\sigma_{A(\bar D)}(z)$ is the closed disc.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The spectrum is never empty, because the resolvent would otherwise be an entire function vanishing at infinity. The first exercise
carries out this argument @arcozzi2025 [Thm. 6.4].

::: {#exr-fan-spectrum-nonempty}
#### Non-emptiness of the spectrum

Suppose $\sigma(a) = \emptyset$. For $\varphi \in \mathcal{A}^*$ show that $\lambda \mapsto \varphi((\lambda - a)^{-1})$ is entire and
tends to $0$ as $|\lambda| \to \infty$, using the series $(\lambda - a)^{-1} = \sum a^n\lambda^{-n - 1}$. Conclude with Liouville's
theorem (@cor-liouville) and Hahn-Banach (@thm-hahn-banach).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The resolvent is holomorphic on $\rho(a) = \mathbb{C}$, so the scalar function is entire. For $|\lambda| > 2\|a\|$, $\|(\lambda -
a)^{-1}\| \leq \sum\|a\|^n|\lambda|^{-n - 1} \leq 2/|\lambda| \to 0$. By Liouville the function is $0$ for every $\varphi$, so
$(\lambda - a)^{-1} = 0$ by Hahn-Banach, which is impossible for an invertible element.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Polynomials map spectra to spectra, which is the algebraic half of the functional calculus. The second exercise proves the spectral
mapping for polynomials @landsman1998 [Lemma 2.2.8].

::: {#exr-fan-spectral-mapping-polynomial}
#### Spectral mapping for polynomials

For a polynomial $p$ and $\mu \in \mathbb{C}$, factor $p(z) - \mu = c\prod_j(z - z_j)$ and show $p(a) - \mu = c\prod_j(a - z_j)$. Using
@exr-fan-commuting-inverse, conclude that $\mu \in \sigma(p(a))$ iff some $z_j \in \sigma(a)$, that is $\sigma(p(a)) = p(\sigma(a))$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The factorisation in $\mathcal{A}$ holds because the factors commute. If every $a - z_j$ is invertible, so is the product; if the
product is invertible, each factor is, by @exr-fan-commuting-inverse applied to commuting factors. So $\mu \in \sigma(p(a))$ iff $z_j
\in \sigma(a)$ for some root $z_j$ of $p - \mu$, iff $\mu = p(z)$ for some $z \in \sigma(a)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A Banach algebra in which every non-zero element is invertible is just the complex numbers, by the non-emptiness of the spectrum. The
third exercise proves this theorem of Gelfand and Mazur @landsman1998 [Cor. 2.2.6].

::: {#exr-fan-gelfand-mazur}
#### Gelfand-Mazur

Let $\mathcal{A}$ be a unital Banach algebra in which every $a \neq 0$ is invertible. For $a \in \mathcal{A}$ pick $\lambda \in
\sigma(a)$ and show $a = \lambda 1$. Why does this fail for real Banach algebras such as the quaternions?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\lambda - a$ is not invertible, hence zero, so $a = \lambda1$ and $\mathcal{A} = \mathbb{C}1$. The argument needs a point in the
spectrum, which comes from Liouville's theorem over $\mathbb{C}$; over $\mathbb{R}$ the quaternion $i$ has no real $\lambda$ with $\lambda -
i$ non-invertible, and the quaternions are a real division algebra of dimension $4$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

The size of the spectrum is measured by the norms of powers, a formula that refines the bound $r(a) \leq \|a\|$. The theorem below
states it; it is the principle behind the power iteration of numerical linear algebra.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-spectral-radius-formula}
#### Spectral radius formula

For every element $a$ of a unital Banach algebra, $r(a) = \lim_{n \to \infty}\|a^n\|^{1/n} = \inf_n\|a^n\|^{1/n}$ (**Gelfand**)
@arcozzi2025 [Thm. 6.7]; @landsman1998 [Prop. 2.2.7]. In particular $r(a) \leq \|a\|$, with equality when $\|a^n\| = \|a\|^n$ for all
$n$, and the Neumann series $\sum_n\lambda^{-n - 1}a^n$ of $(\lambda - a)^{-1}$ converges exactly for $|\lambda| > r(a)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A nilpotent matrix has norm one and spectral radius zero, the extreme case of the formula. The first example computes it, together
with the non-normal matrix of the figure.

::: {#exm-fan-nilpotent-radius}
#### Nilpotent and non-normal matrices

$N = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}$ has $\|N\| = 1$ and $N^2 = 0$, so $r(N) = 0 = \lim\|N^n\|^{1/n}$ and $\sigma(N) =
\{0\}$. For $A = \tfrac12 + 4N$, $\|A^n\| \approx 8n2^{-n}$ for large $n$, so $\|A^n\|^{1/n} \to \tfrac12 = r(A)$, slowly, as the
figure shows.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Volterra operator is the infinite-dimensional analogue of a nilpotent matrix. The second example reads off its spectral
radius from the norms of its powers.

::: {#exm-fan-volterra-radius}
#### The Volterra operator

$\|V^n\|_{C \to C} = 1/n!$ (@exr-fan-volterra-powers), and $(n!)^{-1/n} \sim e/n \to 0$, so $r(V) = 0$ and $\sigma(V) = \{0\}$
(@exm-fan-volterra-spectrum). $V$ is **quasinilpotent**: no power vanishes, but the powers decay faster than any geometric sequence,
so the Volterra equation $u - \mu Vu = f$ is solvable for every $\mu$ by its Neumann series.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

For the matrix of @izaac2018computational [Problem P7.6] the spectral radius is shared by two eigenvalues of opposite signs, which
defeats the power iteration. The third example explains this.

::: {#exm-fan-izaac-matrix}
#### Two dominant eigenvalues

$B = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 9 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 2\end{pmatrix}$ has characteristic polynomial $(\lambda - 2)(\lambda^2 - 9)$, so
$\sigma(B) = \{3, -3, 2\}$ and $r(B) = 3 = \lim\|B^n\|^{1/n}$. The power iteration $x_{n + 1} = Bx_n/\|Bx_n\|$, whose convergence
rests on a single dominant eigenvalue @izaac2018computational [Sec. 7.2, eqs. 7.20-7.21], oscillates here between two vectors,
because the components along the eigenvalues $\pm3$ keep their ratio up to sign.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The shift has norm one and powers of norm one, so its spectral radius is one, and the spectrum is the whole disc. The fourth example
combines the formula with @exm-sp-shift.

::: {#exm-fan-shift-radius}
#### The shift

$\|S^n\| = 1$ for all $n$, so $r(S) = 1$, and $\sigma(S) = \{|\lambda| \leq 1\}$ (@exm-sp-shift). The Neumann series $\sum\lambda^{-n -
1}S^n$ converges for $|\lambda| > 1$ and diverges on the circle, where $\lambda - S$ is not invertible.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
